jangang bli bli di sini, ini su malam\\
neg.imp rdp buy at l.prox d.prox already night\\

‘(you) shouldn’t buy (your sweets at the kiosk) here at all (because) it is already night’ [080917-008-NP.0061]
summary: Reduplicated verbs commonly signal intensity: reduplicated dynamic verbs mean something like “base intensely,” while reduplicated stative verbs mean “very base.” When such verbs are negated with *tra* ‘not’ or *jangang* ‘don’t’, the result is an intensified negative meaning, “not base at all.”

text:
Reduplicated verbs can indicate immediacy in the sense of ``as soon as base ''. This is illustrated with the reduplicated dynamic verbs in the elicited examples in ( Example_4.39 ) and ( Example_4.40 ).

pulang pulang dari kantor pace de tidor\\
rdp go.home from office man 3sg sleep\\

‘ as soon as (he) came home from the office, the man slept’ [Elicited BR120813.007]

mace ni datang datang trus de makang\\
woman d.prox rdp come next 3sg eat\\

‘ as soon as this woman arrived, she ate’ [Elicited BR120813.008]
summary: Reduplicated dynamic verbs can express immediacy, meaning “as soon as” the base event happens. The examples show that forms like *pulang pulang* ‘came home’ and *datang datang* ‘arrived’ introduce a following event that occurs immediately afterward, such as sleeping or eating.

text:
Quite often, reduplication adds the connotation of aimlessness or casualness. That is, the reduplicated verb may signal that an activity is done repeatedly without a specific goal, as in ( Example_4.41 ) and ( Example_4.42 ).

sa itu sa pegang sagu sa makang jalang jalang\\
1sg d.dist 1sg hold sago 1sg eat rdp walk\\

‘as for me, I was holding (some) sago, I ate (it) while strolling around’ [081025-009a-Cv.0073]

malam kitong duduk duduk kitong menyanyi menyanyi\\
night 1pl rdp sit 1pl rdp sing\\

‘in the evening we were sitting around, we were singing casually’ [081025-009a-Cv.0001]
summary: Reduplication often adds a sense of aimlessness or casualness, indicating that an activity is repeated without a specific goal. In the examples, the reduplicated verbs describe actions done casually or while wandering around, such as eating while strolling and sitting and singing in an unplanned way.

text:
Depending on the context, reduplicated stative verbs may signal attenuation in the sense of ``rather base '', as demonstrated in ( Example_4.43 ) and ( Example_4.44 ).

biking macang kam pu Jayapura pu sayur\\
make variety 2pl poss Jayapura poss vegetable\\
gnemo yang pahit pahit itu\\
melinjo rel rdp be.bitter d.dist \\

‘[then she asked, ‘you don’t fear the bitter (taste of melinjos)?, then mama Pawla said,] ``do you think this (melinjo) is like your Jayapura melinjo vegetable which is somewhat bitter?''' [080923-004-Cv.0016]

badang kurus kurus, rambut ini tebal, de pu\\
body rdp be.thin hair d.prox be.thick 3sg poss \\
kuku ini panjang panjang, kaki kurus kurus\\
digit.nail d.prox rdp be.long foot rdp be.thin\\

‘(his) body was somewhat thin, (his) hair was thick, his fingernails were rather long, (and his) legs were rather thin’ [081006-035-CvEx.0077]
summary: Depending on the context, reduplicated stative verbs can express attenuation, meaning “somewhat” or “rather.” The examples show this with adjectives like *pahit* ‘bitter,’ *kurus* ‘thin,’ and *panjang* ‘long,’ where reduplication weakens the intensity of the property.

text:
Reduplicated verbs may also mark imitation in the sense of ``something is an imitation of X'' or ``something is similar to X''. This is illustrated with the dynamic verbs in ( Example_4.45 ) and ( Example_4.46 ), and the stative verbs in the elicited examples in ( Example_4.47 ) and ( Example_4.48 ).

sa tendang dia di kaki sampe de lari lari babi\\
1sg kick 3sg at leg until 3sg rdp run pig\\

‘I kicked him against (his) lower leg with the result that he staggered’ (Lit. ‘he ran ran (like) a pig (which has been shot)’) [Elicited BR120813.004]

dia mati mati ayam\\
3sg rdp die chicken\\

‘he had an epileptic seizure’ (Lit. ‘he died died (like) a chicken’; that is, he was shaking like a chicken with its head cut off) [Elicited BR120813.006]

pace ni de su tua tua kladi tapi suka\\
man d.prox 3sg already rdp be.old taro.root but enjoy\\
cari prempuang muda\\
search woman be.young\\

‘this guy, he’s already very old but (he) likes to have young women’ (Lit. ‘he’s old old (like) a taro root)’ [Elicited BR120813.038]

prempuang itu de pu kulit hitam hitam panta blanga\\
woman d.dist 3sg poss skin rdp be.black buttock cooking.pot\\

‘that woman, her skin is black (like) the bottom of a frying pan’ (Lit. ‘her skin is black black (like) the bottom ’) [Elicited BR120813.046]
summary: Reduplicated verbs can mark imitation or resemblance, meaning “something is an imitation of X” or “something is similar to X.” The examples show this with both dynamic verbs, where the reduplicated form describes acting like something else, and stative verbs, where it describes a property such as being old or black “like” a comparative object.

text:
Reduplicated verbs can also undergo an interpretational shift. Such a shift can result in a nominal reading of reduplicated verbs, as in the elicited examples in ( Example_4.49 ) and ( Example_4.50 ), or an adverbial reading, as in ( Example_4.51 ) to ( Example_4.53 ).

Reduplicated verbs with a nominal reading typically denote the instrument of the action specified by the verbal base, such as garo garo ‘rake’ (literally ‘ rdp scratch’) in ( Example_4.49 ) or gait gait ‘pole’ (literally ‘ rdp hook’) in ( Example_4.50 ).

styleExampleTitle
Reduplicated verbs: Nominal reading
styleExampleTitle

tadi de pake garo garo buat garo rumput\\
earlier 3sg use rdp scratch for scratch grass\\

‘earlier he took a rake to rake the grass’ [Elicited BR120813.010]

sa gait mangga deng gait gait\\
1sg hook mango with rdp hook\\

‘I plucked mangoes with a pole’ [Elicited BR120813.033]

Reduplicated verbs can also receive an adverbial reading, as in ( Example_4.51 ) to ( Example_4.53 ). Certain reduplicated dynamic verbs may take on the function as modal adverbs, such as taw taw ‘suddenly’ (literally ‘ rdp know’) in ( Example_4.51 ). Some reduplicated stative verbs are used as temporal adverbs such as lama lama ‘gradually’ (literally ‘ rdp be.long (of.duration)’) in ( Example_4.52 ), while others are used as manner adverbs, such as cepat cepat ‘quickly’ (literally ‘ rdp be.fast’) in ( Example_4.53 ).

styleExampleTitle
Reduplicated verbs: Adverbial reading
styleExampleTitle

taw taw orang itu tida keliatang\\
rdp know person d.dist neg be.visible\\

‘ suddenly, that person wasn’t visible (any longer)’ [080922-002-Cv.0123]

lama lama de padat itu macang aspal\\
rdp be.long 3sg be.solid d.dist variety asphalt\\

‘ gradually, it (the lime stone) becomes solid like asphalt’ [081011-001-Cv.0304]

yo, pak Hendrik ini de bilang, mandi cepat cepat\\
yes father Hendrik d.prox 3sg say bathe rdp be.fast\\

‘yes, Mr. Hendrik here, he said, ``bathe quickly''' [080917-008-NP.0133]
summary: Reduplicated verbs can undergo an interpretational shift that gives them either a nominal or an adverbial reading. With a nominal reading, they typically refer to the instrument used in the action of the verbal base, while with an adverbial reading they may function as modal, temporal, or manner adverbs, depending on the verb.

text:
Reduplication of adverbs typically signals intensity, similar to the reduplication of verbs, discussed in § Para_4.2.2 (concerning the similarities between adverbs and verbs, see also § Para_5.4 ). This is illustrated with the grading ad verb paling ‘most’, the temporal ad verb skarang ‘now’, and the frequency ad verb sring ‘often’ in the three elicited examples in ( Example_4.54 ) to ( Example_4.56 ).

de bilang de mo kerja tapi paling paling de tidor\\
3sg say 3sg want work but rdp most 3sg sleep\\

‘he says, he wants to work but most likely he’ll sleep’ [Elicited BR120813.015]

skarang skarang de ada di polisi\\
rdp now 3sg exist at police\\

‘ right now he/she is at the police (station)’ [Elicited BR131231.002]

sa pu kaka sring sring ke Jayapura\\
1sg poss oSb rdp often to Jayapura\\

‘my older sibling (travels) to Jayapura very often’ [Elicited BR131231.001]
summary: Reduplication of adverbs typically marks intensification, paralleling the reduplication of verbs. This is shown with examples of the adverbs paling ‘most’, skarang ‘now’, and sring ‘often’, where reduplication yields meanings like ‘most likely,’ ‘right now,’ and ‘very often.’

text:
Across languages, reduplication of numerals “has been found to express various categories including collectives, distributives, multiplicatives, and limitatives”. In Papuan Malay, reduplicated numerals typically express collectivity or distributiveness, while quantifiers signal distributiveness.

Reduplicated numerals have two meaning aspects. They may express collectivity in the sense of ``all base ' as in ( Example_4.57 ) and the elicited example in ( Example_4.58 ), or signal distributiveness in the sense of `` base by base '' as in ( Example_4.59 ) and ( Example_4.60 ).

styleExampleTitle
Reduplication of numerals: Collectivity and distributiveness
styleExampleTitle

yo, kas tinggal dua dua\\
yes give stay rdp two\\

‘yes, let both of them stay’ [080919-006-CvNP.0018]\\

karna pesta tu de su kasi mati tiga tiga\\
because party d.dist 3sg already give die rdp three\\

‘[he/she has three pigs (but)] because of that festivity he/she already killed all three of them’ [Elicited BR120813.043]\\

jadi lega ada lepas lepas satu satu\\
so be.relieved exist rdp free rdp one\\

‘[fortunately, (the people) over there have already received Jesus,] so (you can feel) relieved, they were freed one-by-one’ [081025-007-Cv.0017]\\

sa minum lima lima mangkok \\
1sg drink rdp five cup\\
\\
[About the lack of water during a retreat:] ‘I drank five cups ( every morning)’ (Lit. ‘ five-by-five cups’) [081025-009a-Cv.0070] \\

Reduplicated quantifiers signal distributiveness, as in ( Example_4.61 ) and ( Example_4.62 ).

styleExampleTitle
Reduplication of quantifiers: Distributiveness
styleExampleTitle

kariawang dong banyak banyak dong baru turung ini\\
employee 3pl rdp many 3pl recently descend d.prox \\

[Waiting for other boat passengers:] ‘the employees came recently down(stream) in groups of numerous people’ (Lit. ‘ many-by-many’) [080922-001a-CvPh.0812]

dong blum isi, selaing dong isi sedikit sedikit to?\\
3pl not.yet fill besides 3pl fill rdp few right?\\

[About how best to distribute food during a retreat:] ‘they haven’t yet filled (their plates), moreover each one of them (should) fill (their plates with) little (food), right?’ (Lit. ‘ little by little’) [081025-009a-Cv.0081]
summary: In Papuan Malay, reduplicated numerals typically express either collectivity or distributiveness, while quantifiers are used to mark distributiveness. Reduplicated numerals can mean “all of the base” or “one by one,” as shown by examples like “two two,” “three three,” and “one one,” whereas reduplicated quantifiers such as “many many” and “few few” indicate distributive meanings.

text: Reduplication of function words occurs considerably less often than that of content words. This section describes reduplication of the following function words: personal pronouns (§ Para_4.2.5.1 ), demonstratives and locatives (§ Para_4.2.5.2 ), interrogatives (§ Para_4.2.5.3 ), and the causative verb kasi ‘give’ and the reciprocity marker baku ‘ recp ’ (§ Para_4.2.5.4 ).
summary: Reduplication of function words is much less common than reduplication of content words. The passage introduces reduplication patterns for personal pronouns, demonstratives and locatives, interrogatives, and also the causative verb *kasi* ‘give’ and the reciprocity marker *baku* ‘recp’.

text:
Personal pronouns can be reduplicated when used pronominally (for details on their different uses, see § Para_5.5 and § Para_6.1 ). Reduplicated personal pronouns have three meaning aspects. Depending on the context, they signal collectivity, disparagement, or imitation, As mentioned in § Para_4.2.2.7, the term `` imitation'' includes meanings such as ``something is an imitation of X'' or ``something is similar to X''. as in ( Example_4.63 ) and in the elicited examples in ( Example_4.64 ) and ( Example_4.65 ), respectively.

kamu kamu ini bangung bangung bangung bangung\\
rdp 2pl d.prox wake.up wake.up wake.up wake.up\\

‘ all of you here wake-up, wake-up, wake-up, wake-up’ [081115-001a-Cv.0329]

knapa saya saya saja yang bapa kasi tugas\\
why rdp 1sg just rel father give duty\\

‘why is it (always) poor me whom father gives chores’ [Elicited BR120813.025]

dorang dorang tra perna kasi bersi halamang\\
rdp 3pl neg ever give be.clean yard\\

‘ people like them never clean (their) yard’ [Elicited BR120813.024]
summary: Personal pronouns can be reduplicated when used pronominally, and this reduplication has three main meanings: collectivity, disparagement, and imitation. In the examples, reduplication expresses meanings such as “all of you,” “poor me,” and “people like them,” showing how context determines the interpretation.

text:
Demonstratives and locatives can also be reduplicated when used pronominally (for details on their different uses, see § Para_5.6 and § Para_5.7, respectively). Reduplicated demonstratives express diversity as in ( Example_4.66 ) and ( Example_4.67 ). Demonstrative sequences such as itu tu ‘ d.dist d.dist ’ also convey intensity or emphasis, as discussed in detail in § Para_7.1.2.3. Given its phonological properties, however, juxtaposed itu tu ‘ d.dist d.dist ’ is not taken as an instance of partial reduplication. As discussed in § Para_4.1.2, partial reduplication of the stem itu ‘ d.dist ’ should result in the reduplicated form it itu ‘ d.dist d.dist ’. Therefore, itu tu ‘ d.dist d.dist ’ is taken as an instance of demonstrative stacking (see § Para_5.6.4 ). Depending on the context, reduplicated locatives may signal diversity as in ( Example_4.68 ), or emphasize the core meaning of the respective locative, as in ( Example_4.69 ).

setela itu nanti buat ini ini\\
after d.dist very.soon make rdp d.prox \\

‘soon after that (they) did these various (things)’ [080923-013-CvEx.0030]

yang laing itu itu honorer smua itu\\
rel be.different rdp d.dist be.honorary all d.dist \\

‘[there are no school teachers, only him and Markus,] (as for) the others, those various (teachers) are all honorary (teachers)’ [081011-024-Cv.0054]

jadi de bapa ke Jayapura tinggal situ situ\\
so 3sg father to Jayapura stay rdp l.med \\

‘so her father (went) to Jayapura and lived there in a number of different places’ [081011-023-Cv.0163]

di sini ada air, mari sini sini\\
at l.prox exist water hither rdp l.prox \\

‘[(you) may fish from up here,] here is water, (come) here, right here’ [081025-003-Cv.0093]
summary: Demonstratives and locatives can be reduplicated when used pronominally. Reduplicated demonstratives may express diversity, while sequences like *itu tu* can also mark intensity or emphasis and are analyzed as demonstrative stacking rather than partial reduplication; reduplicated locatives likewise can indicate diversity or emphasize the locative’s core meaning depending on context.

text:
Likewise, interrogatives can be reduplicated when used pronominally (for details on their different uses, see § Para_5.8 ). Reduplicated interrogatives signal indefiniteness by referring to an unspecified group member, in the sense of ``any'' or ``Wh-ever''. This is illustrated with the examples in ( Example_4.70 ) to ( Example_4.73 ); the example in ( Example_4.73 ) is elicited.

yo, tida bole kas taw siapa siapa\\
yes neg may give know rdp who\\

‘yes, (you) must not tell anybody’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0288]

saya tida biking apa apa karna babi suda mati\\
1sg neg make rdp what because pig already die\\

[About hunting a wild pig:] ‘I didn’t do anything because the pig was already dead’ [080919-004-NP.0023]

nanti kapang kapang ka ko jalang jalang ke mari\\
very.soon rdp when or 2sg rdp walk to hither\\

‘later whenever (you have time) you come here’ [Elicited BR120813.029]

di mana mana smua pake ini, tajam besi ini\\
at rdp where all use d.prox be.sharp metal d.prox \\

[About sagu production:] ‘ wherever everybody uses it, this sharp metal’ [081014-006-CvPr.0059]

Alternatively, speakers may use the bare interrogative followed by the focus ad verb saja ‘just’ to encode an indefinite referent, as discussed in § Para_5.8.8.
summary: Interrogatives can be reduplicated when used pronominally, and this reduplication marks indefiniteness, referring to an unspecified member of a set in the sense of “any” or “wh-ever.” The examples show forms like *siapa siapa*, *apa apa*, *kapang kapang*, and *di mana mana* used with this indefinite meaning. Speakers may also express an indefinite referent with a bare interrogative followed by the focus adverb *saja* ‘just’.

subsubsection: Causative verb kasi ‘give’ and reciprocity marker baku ‘ recp ’
text:
Reduplication of the causative verb kasi ‘give’ and reciprocity marker baku ‘ recp ’, as in ( Example_4.74 ) and ( Example_4.75 ) respectively, signals repetition or continuation. (For more details on causative and reciprocal constructions, see § Para_11.2 and § Para_11.3, respectively.)

knapa kam kas kas bangung dia, de masi mo tidor\\
why 2pl rdp give wake.up 3sg 3sg still want sleep\\

‘why do you keep waking him up?, he still wants to sleep’ (Lit. ‘ give give to wake up’) [080918-001-CvNP.0039]

itu sampe tong baku baku tawar ini deng doseng\\
d.dist until 1pl rdp recp bargain d.prox with lecturer\\

‘it got to the point that we and the lecturer were arguing constantly with each other’ [080917-010-CvEx.0177]
summary: Reduplication of the causative verb *kasi* ‘give’ and the reciprocity marker *baku* ‘recp’ indicates repetition or continuation. In the examples, *kasi* reduplication expresses repeated waking, and *baku* reduplication shows that an argument continued repeatedly between the speaker’s group and the lecturer.

text:
Reduplication in Papuan Malay conveys a number of different meaning aspects ranging from continuation and diversity to disparagement and imitation. This variety in meaning raises two questions: first, does reduplication have a general meaning or gesamtbedeutung, and second, is there a specific relation between the meaning and the syntactic class of the base word.

Table_4.6 lists the Papuan Malay word classes which attract reduplication and the meaning aspects they convey.

Some of the meaning aspects which reduplication in Papuan Malay conveys include, what cross-linguistically refers to as “contradictory senses”. The aspect `` immediacy'', for instance, represents an increase in intensity, while the aspect `` aimlessness'' refers to a decrease in intensity. This phenomenon that reduplication brings together a variety of meanings, some of which are opposite, is quite common cross-linguistically (see, for instance,;;; ).

Examining the “crosslinguistically recurrent semantic properties of reduplication”, comes to the conclusion that

quote
reduplication may be viewed as a marking device to indicate that the word is to be understood in an out-of-the-ordinary sense: the meaning deviates from the normal sense of the base either by being “more” or by being “less”.
quote

These contradictory meaning aspects of augmentation and diminution have also been noted for Malayo-Polynesian languages. In her study on reduplication in 30 of these languages, considers these two meanings of reduplication to be

quote
two manifestations of the same semantic principle of ‘a er degree of ’, which is projected in the opposite directions. Then one can postulate that the prototypical meanings of reduplication represent the semantic principle ‘ a higher / lower degree of ’
quote

The overview presented in Table_4.6 indicates that this semantic principle of “a er degree of ” in terms of augmentation or diminution also accounts for the different meaning aspects of reduplication in Papuan Malay.

In Papuan Malay, the notion of ``higher degree of '' involves augmentation in terms of quantity or intensity. Cross-linguistically, specifies that in the context of reduplication quantity can refer to the “participants of [an] event or the events themselves”, while intensity refers to the amount of “energy investment or size of effect”. In Papuan Malay, the augmentation of quantity includes meaning aspects such as collectivity or repetition, while the increase in intensity includes the meaning aspects of intensity and immediacy, as listed in Table_4.6.

The notion of ``lesser degree of '' involves, generally speaking, diminution which typically “adds the meaning of smallness to the stem meaning”. As points out, however, the diminutive exhibits a variety of “metaphorical extensions” which involve “meaning shifts from the physical world to the social domain, and from the physical world to the conceptual or category domain”. Such semantic extensions of the diminutive are also found in Papuan Malay, in that the semantic effect of diminution brings together the meaning aspects of disparagement, indefiniteness, aimlessness, attenuation, and imitation.

The ``disparagement'' sense is linked to the notion of diminution metaphorically in that it has to do with social importance or power. The `` indefiniteness'' sense is also a metaphorical extension in that it conveys toned-down reference. Likewise, the `` aimlessness'' sense is linked to the notion of diminution in that it denotes actions which are done with less intensity. The `` attenuation'' sense is a metaphorical extension of the core sense ``size'' in that it denotes properties which are weaker, or activities which are carried out less intensely. The `` imitation'' sense refers to objects or activities which copy or imitate what the base denotes. This sense is linked to the core sense of diminution in that the objects and activities are not identical with their models but merely resemble them a little bit. (See;; V. Mattes p.c. 2013;.)

In summarizing the above and in applying Kiyomi’s Kiyomi.2009 terminology, it is concluded that in Papuan Malay, the gesamtbedeutung of reduplication is ``a higher / lower degree of ''. Table_4.7 gives examples for the two dimensions of augmentation and diminution conveyed by reduplication.

With respect to the relation between the meaning and the syntactic class of the base word, two major observations are made. First, across word classes, reduplicated lexemes differ in terms of the meaning aspects which they convey. Second, meaning aspects differ as regards the range of word classes they attract for reduplication. (See Table_4.6.)

First, concerning the reduplicated lexemes and the meaning aspects they convey, the gathered data indicates that within certain word classes reduplication tends to convey more than one specific meaning. Reduplication in certain verbs, for example, can express immediacy while in other verbs it signals continuation or repetition. It is notably content words which carry this variety of different meanings, that is, nouns, verbs, and numerals. In addition, reduplication within two classes of function words also conveys more than one meaning aspect, namely in the classes of personal pronouns and locatives. Reduplication within the other three classes of function words, by contrast, tends to carry specific meanings: reduplicated demonstratives express diversity, interrogatives indicate indefiniteness, and the causative and reciprocity markers signal continuation or repetition. In relating the word classes which attract reduplication to certain meaning aspects it is noted, however, that the meaning of a given reduplicated form is more than the meaning of its constituents. The fact that the entire reduplicated form and not its individual constituents carry this meaning, indicates, what calls, a “holistic” or constructional meaning of the reduplicated forms.
summary:
Papuan Malay reduplication expresses a wide range of meanings, but these can be unified under the general semantic principle of “a higher/lower degree of,” covering both augmentation and diminution. Augmentation includes quantity and intensity, while diminution extends metaphorically to disparagement, indefiniteness, aimlessness, attenuation, and imitation.

The passage also notes that reduplication’s meaning varies by syntactic class: some word classes, especially content words, can show several different meanings, while others tend to be associated with more specific ones. Overall, the meaning of a reduplicated form is described as holistic or constructional, not simply the sum of the meanings of its parts.

text: Second, regarding the meaning aspects and the range of word classes they attract for reduplication, three meaning aspects bring together the largest number of different word classes, namely four each. The continuation/ repetition/habit meaning aspect brings together nouns, verbs, and the causative and reciprocity markers. The collectivity meaning aspect brings together nouns, verbs, numerals, and personal pronouns. And the diversity meaning aspect brings together nouns, verbs, demonstratives, and locatives. Another pertinent meaning aspect is intensity, which attracts three different word classes for reduplication, namely verbs, adverbs, and locatives. Three more meaning aspects, which attract two word classes each for reduplication, are distributiveness, indefiniteness, and imitation. The remaining meaning aspects attract only one word class each for reduplication, that is, verbs for immediacy, aimlessness, and attenuation, and personal pronouns for disparagement. These observations suggest that there is not a specific, one-to-one relation between the meaning and the syntactic class of the base word.
summary: The passage explains that different semantic functions of reduplication attract varying ranges of word classes, with continuation/repetition/habit, collectivity, and diversity each involving four classes, and intensity involving three. Other meanings attract only two or even one class, leading to the conclusion that there is no fixed one-to-one relationship between a reduplication’s meaning and the syntactic class of its base word.

text: Reduplication is also very common in other eastern Malay varieties, such as Ambon Malay (AM), Banda Malay (BM), Kupang Malay (KM), Larantuka Malay (LM), Manado Malay (MM), and Ternate Malay (TM). This section compares reduplication across these Malay varieties in terms of lexeme formation (§ Para_4.3.1 ), lexeme interpretation (§ Para_4.3.2 ), and interpretational shift (§ Para_4.3.3 ), as far as mentioned in the literature. For comparison, reduplication in Papuan Malay (PM) is also included. Also included for comparison is Standard Indonesian (SI) ( ).
summary: Reduplication is common in several eastern Malay varieties, including Ambon, Banda, Kupang, Larantuka, Manado, and Ternate Malay. The section compares how these varieties, plus Papuan Malay and Standard Indonesian, handle reduplication in lexeme formation, lexeme interpretation, and interpretational shift, based on the literature.

text:
Similar to Papuan Malay, the above-mentioned six Malay varieties also employ full reduplication, as shown in Table_4.8. Typically, reduplication affects content words, while reduplication of function words is rarer. Manado and Ternate Malay also employ reduplication of bound morphemes. The data in Table_4.8 also shows which varieties use a combination of reduplication and affixation, and in which varieties reduplicated forms without corresponding base words are found. Besides Papuan Malay, only two of the six other eastern Malay varieties use partial and imitative reduplication, namely Ambon and Larantuka Malay.

The data given in Table_4.8 shows that reduplication in Ambon Malay is about as pervasive as in Papuan Malay, with both varieties sharing many features. This applies to the attested reduplication types (full, partial, and imitative), as well as to the attested morpheme types which can be reduplicated. For the five other eastern Malay varieties and Standard Indonesian, reduplication seems to play a much lesser role, as shown by the gaps in Table_4.8. For the eastern Malay varieties, this applies especially to the reduplication of function words; furthermore, these varieties appear not to have reduplicated forms which lack a corresponding unreduplicated base.

Two explanations present themselves for these observations. One explanation is that the commonalities between Papuan Malay and Ambon Malay, together with the lack of overlap with the five other eastern Malay varieties, are due to the distinct history of Papuan Malay, argued for in § Para_1.8. An alternative explanation is that the differences among the eastern Malay varieties are due to differing degrees of depth with which the different authors describe reduplication in the Malay varieties presented in Table_4.8. This grammar on Papuan Malay, as well as that of Ambon Malay, and also those of Standard Indonesian, describe reduplication as a word-formation process rather thoroughly, while the descriptions of the five other eastern Malay varieties mention only the most salient features of reduplication in these varieties; hence, the rather large number of gaps in Table_4.8.
summary:
The passage reports that all six eastern Malay varieties, like Papuan Malay, use full reduplication, but reduplication is generally more limited in the other varieties, especially for function words; only Ambon and Larantuka Malay also show partial and imitative reduplication, and Manado and Ternate Malay reduplicate bound morphemes. Ambon Malay is described as closest to Papuan Malay in the range and productivity of reduplication, while the other varieties and Standard Indonesian show many gaps and less extensive use.

The differences may reflect either the distinct historical development of Papuan Malay or simply uneven depth of description in the sources, since some grammars treat reduplication much more thoroughly than others.

text:
As in Papuan Malay, the gesamtbedeutung of reduplication in the six other eastern Malay varieties is ``a higher / lower degree of ''. Table_4.9 gives examples for this gesamtbedeutung across the seven Malay varieties.

Table_4.10 demonstrates in more detail which word classes attract reduplication and which meaning aspects they convey in all seven Malay varieties.

First, the data in Table_4.10 shows that across the seven Malay varieties, reduplication of content words tends to convey more than one meaning aspect, while reduplicated function words tend to carry specific meaning aspects, such as indefiniteness for interrogatives. The exception is Manado Malay, where reduplication of content words tends to carry a specific meaning, such as plurality for nouns.

Second, the data in Table_4.10 illustrates that in the other eastern Malay varieties some meaning aspects also attract a wider range of word classes for reduplication than other meaning aspects. This applies to the plurality/diversity, the intensity, the continuation/ repetition/habit, and the indefiniteness meaning aspects.

Of all the eastern Malay varieties, the different meaning aspects attested in Papuan Malay attract the widest range of different word classes. For Ambon Malay, the range of attracted word classes is also rather large. In the other eastern Malay varieties, however, the attracted range of word classes is much smaller. At this point, it remains unclear, though, whether these smaller ranges are due to inherent properties of these varieties or due to an incomplete documentation in the respective literature.

Overall, there is not a specific, one-to-one relation between the meaning aspects of the reduplicated lexemes and the syntactic class of the corresponding base words in any of the Malay varieties discussed here.
summary:
Across the eastern Malay varieties, reduplication generally expresses a higher or lower degree of a meaning, and content words often show multiple meaning aspects while function words tend to express more specific ones, such as indefiniteness with interrogatives. Manado Malay is an exception, since reduplicated content words there usually have a specific meaning, such as plurality for nouns.  

The passage also notes that some meaning aspects attract reduplication across a wider range of word classes than others, with Papuan Malay showing the widest range and Ambon Malay also relatively broad. Overall, there is no one-to-one correspondence between the semantic function of reduplication and the syntactic class of the base word in these varieties.

text:
Interpretational shift of reduplicated lexemes, as described for Papuan Malay (see § Para_4.2.1.4 and § Para_4.2.2.8 ), is also attested for Ambon Malay, Larantuka Malay, Manado Malay, and Ternate Malay.

With respect to the patterns of interpretational shift, two observations are made which are summarized in Table_4.11. First, in each of the varieties for which interpretational shift is mentioned, it is content words that may undergo such a shift. Second, the Malay varieties differ in terms of the syntactic categories of the base and the readings which the reduplicated forms can receive. In Papuan and Ambon Malay, nouns and verbs can undergo interpretational shift, while in Manado Malay only nouns and in Larantuka and Ternate Malay only verbs are affected. Most often, such a shift results in the reduplicated form receiving an adverbial reading. Such is the case in Papuan, Ambon, Larantuka, and Ternate Malay; the exception is Manado Malay. Considerably less often the shift results in a nominal reading (Papuan and Ambon Malay) or a verbal reading (Papuan Malay) of reduplicated lexemes.

The ability of reduplicated lexemes to undergo interpretational shift seems to be best explained in terms of a slot filling-function of reduplication. Cross-linguistically, temporal noun phrases, for instance, are prone to fill adverbial slots; an example is the English sentence ``she came home late at night''.

Hence, in this grammar of Papuan Malay, the interpretational shifts described in § Para_4.2.1.4 and § Para_4.2.2.8 are taken to result from a slot filling-function of reduplication. That is, reduplication enables base words to fill different syntactic slots, such as an adverbial or a nominal slot.

In Ternate Malay, interpretational shifts also seem to be the results of a slot-filling function of reduplication, with noting that “both reduplicated quality words and activity words may serve to express manner when they immediately follow an activity”. For Ambon Malay, by contrast, considers the observed interpretational shifts as “transpositions” which result from “derivational” processes. For Manado Malay, notes that when kinship terms or similar words are reduplicated “then the reduplicated form is an adjective referring to a certain age group”. This statement suggests that considers interpretational shifts to result from a category-changing function of reduplication. For Larantuka Malay, does not discuss the attested interpretational shifts.
summary:
Interpretational shift of reduplicated lexemes is reported not only for Papuan Malay but also for Ambon, Larantuka, Manado, and Ternate Malay. Across these varieties, only content words undergo such shifts, but the relevant base categories and resulting readings differ: nouns and verbs are affected in Papuan and Ambon Malay, only nouns in Manado Malay, and only verbs in Larantuka and Ternate Malay, with adverbial readings being the most common outcome.

The passage argues that these shifts are best explained by a slot-filling function of reduplication, allowing base words to occupy different syntactic positions such as adverbial or nominal slots. It also notes that different descriptions are given for some varieties: Ternate Malay is said to show slot-filling reduplication, Ambon Malay is analyzed in terms of derivational transpositions, and Manado Malay is treated as involving category change, while Larantuka Malay is not discussed in this

text:
Reduplication in Papuan Malay is a very productive morphological device for deriving new words. In terms of lexeme formation, three different types of reduplication are attested: full, partial, and imitative reduplication. The most common type is full reduplication, which involves the repetition of an entire root, stem, or word; bound morphemes are not reduplicated. Full reduplication usually applies to content words, although some function words can also be reduplicated. Partial and imitative reduplication are rare. The gesamtbedeutung of reduplication is ``a higher / lower degree of '' in the sense of augmentation and diminution, applying Kiyomi.2009 terminology. There is, however, no specific, one-to-one relation between the meaning aspects of the reduplicated lexemes and the syntactic class of the corresponding base words.

A comparison of reduplication in Papuan Malay and six other eastern Malay varieties shows that Papuan Malay shares many features with Ambon Malay. In both varieties, reduplication plays an important role. In Banda, Kupang, Manado, Larantuka, and Ternate Malay, by contrast, reduplication seems to be much less pervasive. These commonalities and differences may well point to the particular history of Papuan Malay, argued for in § Para_1.8. The observed differences could, however, also result from gaps in the descriptions of Banda, Kupang, Manado, Larantuka, and Ternate Malay.
summary:
Reduplication is a highly productive morphological process in Papuan Malay, with three attested types: full, partial, and imitative reduplication. Full reduplication is by far the most common, usually affecting content words, and the general semantic effect is augmentation or diminution, though there is no fixed relation between the meaning of a reduplicated form and the syntactic class of its base.

A comparison with six other eastern Malay varieties shows that Papuan Malay is especially similar to Ambon Malay in the importance of reduplication, while the other varieties appear to use it less extensively. The passage notes that these differences may reflect Papuan Malay’s history, but they could also be due to incomplete descriptions of the other varieties.

text:
This chapter discusses the Papuan Malay word classes, or parts of speech. Some of the word classes are examined in more detail in separate chapters.

The notion of “word class” is defined as a class of “words that share morphological or syntactic properties”. In general, pertinent criteria for establishing class membership are a “word’s distribution, its range of syntactic functions, and the morphological or syntactic categories for which it is specifiable”. In Papuan Malay, morphological criteria do not play a major role in distinguishing different word classes, given the lack of inflectional morphology and the rather limited productivity of derivational patterns (see § Para_3.1 ). Instead the main criteria for defining distinct word classes are their syntactic properties.

Based on their syntactic properties, three open and several closed lexical classes are distinguished. It is acknowledged, however, that Papuan Malay has membership overlap between a number of categories (see § Para_5.14 ). Most of this variation involves verbs, including overlap between verbs and nouns, which is typical of Malay varieties and other western Austronesian languages. In discussing lexical and syntactic categories in western Austronesian languages, More specifically, refers to western Austronesian “symmetrical voice languages”, that is languages that have “at least two voice alternations marked on the verb, neither of which is clearly the basic form”.
points out, that “the syntactic distinction between nouns and verbs is often somewhat less clearly delineated in that word-forms which semantically appear to be verbs easily and without further morphological modification occur in nominal functions and vice versa”. This applies especially to languages with “multifunctional lexical bases'', that is, “lexical bases which occur without further affixation in a variety of syntactic functions”.

As for the analytical consequences of such overlap, notes that most authors “assume underlying syntactic differences based on the semantics of the forms”, analyzing such instances of variation “as involving zero conversion”. As far as the description of regional Malay varieties is concerned, this approach is accepted, for example, by in his grammar of Ambon Malay, in his description of Manado Malay, and in his discussion of regional Malay varieties such as Banda Malay, Kupang Malay, or Larantuka Malay. Some authors, however, “argue for a basic lack of a morphosyntactic noun/ verb distinction”, as points out. Examples for this alternative approach are Gil’s ( Gil.2013) description of Riau Indonesian (see also ), Himmelmann’s ( Himmelmann.2008) analysis of Tagalog (see also ), and Litamahuputty’s ( Litamahuputty.2012) grammar of Ternate Malay.

In discussing Papuan Malay lexical and syntactic categories in this grammar, nouns and verbs are analyzed as belonging to distinct word classes, in spite of the attested variation in membership, discussed in § Para_5.14. This approach is chosen because of the distinct syntactic properties of the categories under discussion, as shown in more detail throughout this chapter. In cases of variation, the category membership of a given lexeme can usually be deduced from the context in which an utterance occurs. Rather than proposing additional special word classes for lexical items with dual distribution, the lexemes in question are analyzed as having dual class membership and the variation as involving zero conversion.

In the next two sections, the two major open lexical classes of nouns and verbs are discussed. The class of nouns, described in § Para_5.2, includes common nouns, proper nouns, location, and direction nouns. Verbs, discussed in § Para_5.3, are divided into trivalent, bivalent, and monovalent verbs, with the class of monovalent verbs including dynamic and stative verbs. Adverbs, discussed in § Para_5.4, constitute the third open word class. The closed word classes are then described, that is, personal pronouns in § Para_5.5, demonstratives in § Para_5.6, locatives in § Para_5.7, interrogatives in § Para_5.8, numerals in § Para_5.9, quantifiers in § Para_5.10, prepositions in § Para_5.11, and conjunctions in § Para_5.12. Tags, placeholder and hesitation makers, interjections, and ideophones are presented in § Para_5.13. The categories with variation in word class membership are discussed (§ Para_5.14 ).The main points of this chapter are summarized in (§ Para_5.15 ).
summary:
The chapter introduces Papuan Malay word classes and defines them mainly by syntactic rather than morphological criteria, since Papuan Malay has little inflectional morphology and limited derivation. It distinguishes three open lexical classes and several closed classes, while noting overlap in membership—especially between nouns and verbs—and treats such cases as dual class membership with zero conversion.

Although some analyses of related Malay varieties argue that noun/verb distinctions may be weak or absent, this grammar maintains that Papuan Malay nouns and verbs are distinct because they show different syntactic properties. The chapter then outlines the major open classes, the closed classes, and categories with variable word-class membership.

text:
Papuan Malay has a large open class of nouns which refer to persons, things, and places, as well as abstract concepts and ideas. Typically, nouns have head-function in noun phrases and argument function in verbal clauses.

Based on their syntactic properties, the nouns are divided into common nouns (§ Para_5.2.1 ), proper nouns (§ Para_5.2.2 ), location nouns (§ Para_5.2.3 ), and direction nouns (§ Para_5.2.4 ). Their defining syntactic and functional properties are discussed in more detail in the respective sections.

Morphological properties do not play a major role in defining nouns as a distinct word class. This is due to the lack of inflectional morphology and the limited role of derivational processes. The latter include reduplication, and, to a limited extent, affixation with suffix - ang or prefix pe(n)- (for details see § Para_3.1.3 and § Para_3.1.4, respectively).

Nouns are distinct from other word classes such as verbs (§ Para_5.3 ), adverbs (§ Para_5.4 ), personal pronouns (§ Para_5.5 ), and demonstratives (§ Para_5.6 ) in terms of the following distributional properties. Some of these properties, however, do not apply to all four noun types. The exceptions are mentioned below and discussed in more detail in the respective sections on the different noun types.

enumerate

Nouns are distinct from verbs (a) in terms of their predominant functions as heads in noun phrases and as arguments in verbal clauses, (b) in that they can be quantified with numerals and quantifiers (this only applies to common and proper nouns), and (c) in that they are only negated with bukang ‘ neg ’.

Unlike adverbs, nouns (a) have predicative uses, and (b) can modify other nouns.

Nouns are distinct from personal pronouns, in that nouns (a) can be modified with personal pronouns, while personal pronouns are not modified with nouns, (b) can be modified with numerals/quantifiers in pre- or posthead position, while personal pronouns are only modified with numerals or quantifiers in posthead position, and (c) can express the possessum in adnominal possessive constructions, while personal pronouns do not take this slot. (Most of these properties only apply to common and (to a lesser extent to) proper nouns but not to location and direction nouns.)

Nouns can be modified with demonstratives, whereas demonstratives cannot be modified with nouns.

enumerate

The following sections describe the four noun types in more detail: common nouns are discussed in § Para_5.2.1, proper nouns in § Para_5.2.2, location nouns in § Para_5.2.3, and direction nouns in § Para_5.2.4. Also included are brief descriptions of time-denoting nouns in § Para_5.2.5, classifying nouns in § Para_5.2.6, and kinship terms in § Para_5.2.7.
summary: Papuan Malay has a large open class of nouns referring to persons, things, places, and abstract concepts, and these nouns typically function as heads of noun phrases and as arguments in verbal clauses. They are classified syntactically into common, proper, location, and direction nouns, while morphology plays only a minor role because the language lacks inflection and has limited derivation. Nouns are distinguished from verbs, adverbs, personal pronouns, and demonstratives by their distributional behavior, including their ability to be quantified, negated with bukang, used predicatively, and modified in ways that vary somewhat by noun type.

text:
Common nouns have general reference, in that they “do not refer to individual entities (‘tokens’) but only connote classes (‘types') of entities”. They have the following defining syntactic and functional properties:

enumerate

Head function in noun phrases is predominant ( Para_8); in addition, they also have predicative function in nonverbal clauses ( Para_12).

Argument function (subject or object) in verbal clauses is predominant ( Para_11). As points out, it is technically speaking “not the noun but rather the noun phrase that assumes the various grammatical roles [ ] However, within the noun phrase, a noun is typically the syntactic and semantic head, defining the type of entity involved. All other elements in the noun phrase are modifiers of that head noun”.

Quantification (with numerals and quantifiers) and modification with adnominal constituents (including other nouns, verbs, personal pronouns, demonstratives, locatives, interrogatives, noun phrases, prepositional phras\-es, and/or relative clauses) ( Para_8).

Negation only with bukang ‘ neg ’ (§ Para_13.1.2 ).

In adnominal possessive constructions, common nouns can express the possessor and/or the possessum ( Para_9).

enumerate

Cross-linguistically, two types of common nouns can be distinguished, count nouns and mass nouns. While a count noun designates “a separate, one of a number of such entities which can be counted”, a mass noun “denotes a quantity or mass of unindividuated material”. Examples of Papuan Malay count and mass nouns, both concrete and abstract, are presented in Table_5.1.

Count nouns can be modified with numerals as in ( Example_5.1 ) and ( Example_5.2 ), or with quantifiers as in ( Example_5.3 ) to ( Example_5.6 ). The numerals and quantifiers can occur in prehead position, as in ( Example_5.1 ), ( Example_5.3 ), or ( Example_5.5 ), or in posthead position as in ( Example_5.2 ), ( Example_5.4 ), or ( Example_5.6 ). (Concerning the position of adnominal numerals vis-à-vis their head nominal and their semantics, see § Para_5.9 and § Para_8.3.1.)

Common nouns are described as referring to general types rather than individual entities, and they typically serve as the syntactic and semantic head of noun phrases, can function predicatively, and can appear as subjects or objects in verbal clauses. They may be quantified and modified by a wide range of adnominal elements, negate only with *bukang*, and occur in possessive constructions as either possessor or possessum.

Cross-linguistically, common nouns divide into count and mass nouns: count nouns can combine with numerals and quantifiers in either prehead or posthead position, while mass nouns allow only posthead quantifiers and cannot co-occur with numerals.

text:
Proper nouns have specific reference in that they “refer to individual entities (or specific groups)”. Hence, proper nouns are distinct from common nouns, which have general reference. More specifically, proper nouns express the names of specific people and geographical places. In Papuan Malay proper nouns are distinct from common nouns in terms of the following properties:

enumerate

Proper nouns can be modified with the following constituents: monovalent stative verbs, personal pronouns, demonstratives, locatives, interrogatives, numerals, quantifiers, and/or relative clauses ( Para_8). Unlike common nouns, they are not readily modified with other nouns, noun phrases, or prepositional phrases.

Proper nouns always occur as bare nouns; reduplicated proper nouns are unattested (§ Para_4.1.1.1 ).

Proper nouns typically express the possessor but not the possessum in adnominal possessive constructions ( Para_9).

enumerate

Some examples of person and place names attested in the corpus are presented in Table_5.2. Original Papuan Malay names, however, do not exist as such. The person names are very commonly taken from the Bible or originate from European languages. Family or clan names and place names originate from local languages, such as the Papuan language Isirawa (see also § Para_1.4 ). The examples in Table_5.2 also illustrate that person names with more than two syllables are most commonly shortened to two-syllable names.

Modification of proper nouns with monovalent stative verbs, personal pronouns, de\-monstratives, locatives, interrogatives, numerals, quantifiers, and relative clauses is illustrated in ( Example_5.13 ) to ( Example_5.20 ), respectively. summary: Proper nouns in Papuan Malay have specific reference and are distinct from common nouns, especially because they name particular people and places. They can be modified by stative verbs, pronouns, demonstratives, locatives, interrogatives, numerals, quantifiers, and relative clauses, but not typically by other nouns, noun phrases, or prepositional phrases; they also occur only as bare nouns and are not reduplicated. The passage also notes that person names are often borrowed from Biblical or European sources, place and clan names from local languages, and that names with more than two syllables are often shortened.

text:
Location nouns, or locative nouns, designate locations rather than physical objects. The Papuan Malay location nouns are given in Table_5.4, together with their token frequencies in the corpus.

Location nouns are distinct from common nouns (§ Para_5.2.1 ) in terms of the following properties:

enumerate

In their nominal uses, location nouns (a) only occur in prepositional phrases, (b) can be modified with nouns, demonstratives, or locatives, but with no other constituents, and (c) do not take the possessor or possessum slots in adnominal possessive constructions. The exception is blakang ‘backside’. It also has the body part meaning ‘back’. As such it can denote the possessum in an adnominal possessive construction such as sa pu blakang ‘ 1sg poss backside’ ‘my back’ [081015-005-NP.0032].

In their adnominal uses, location nouns are juxtaposed to common nouns only; that is, unlike common nouns, they cannot be stacked.

enumerate

Location nouns are distinct from direction nouns (§ Para_5.2.4 ) in that they can be modified with juxtaposed adnominal nouns, while direction nouns cannot be modified in this way.

The nominal uses of the location nouns are discussed in § Para_5.2.3.1 and their adnominal uses in § Para_5.2.3.2.
summary: Location nouns in Papuan Malay designate places rather than physical objects and are distinct from common nouns in several ways. In nominal use, they occur only in prepositional phrases, may be modified only by nouns, demonstratives, or locatives, and normally do not function in possessive constructions, except for blakang ‘backside/back.’ In adnominal use, they can only be juxtaposed with common nouns and, unlike direction nouns, may be modified by juxtaposed adnominal nouns.

text:
In their nominal uses, the nouns always occur inside prepositional phras\-es and are typically modified with a juxtaposed adnominal noun such that `` prep n.loc n ''. Semantically, n.loc n noun phrases are characterized by the subordination of the adnominal noun in N2 position under the head nominal location noun in N1 position (see also § Para_8.2.2 ).

Generally speaking, the main function of location nouns is to specify the spatial relationship between a figure and the ground, with the ground being encoded by the juxtaposed adnominal noun. The same applies to the Papuan Malay location nouns, in that they more fully specify the spatial relationship between figure and ground than is achieved by a bare preposition that introduces the ground. This is illustrated with the contrastive examples in ( Example_5.21 ) to ( Example_5.23 ) and in ( Example_5.24 ) and ( Example_5.25 ).

The examples in ( Example_5.39 ) and ( Example_5.40 ) also illustrate that an independently used location noun can be modified with a demonstrative or a locative, respectively.

As shown so far, location nouns more fully specify the spatial relationship between a figure and the ground than is achieved by a bare preposition that introduces the ground. If the specific spatial relationship can be deduced from the context, though, the location noun can be omitted as illustrated with elided atas ‘top’ in ( Example_5.41 ) and dalam ‘inside’ in ( Example_5.42 ).

styleExampleTitle
Omitted location nouns
styleExampleTitle

de kas turung mama Petrus dari atas kursi to?\\
3sg give descend mother Petrus from top chair right?\\

‘he (the evil spirit) threw mother Petrus from (the top of her) chair, right?’ [081025-008-Cv.0158]

dong mandi di dalam kamar mandi sana\\

‘they were bathing in(side of) the bathroom over there’ [081109-001-Cv.0081]
summary: Location nouns in Papuan Malay typically occur in prepositional phrases as nominal expressions of the form “prep + location noun + noun,” where the adnominal noun in N2 names the ground and is subordinated to the location noun in N1. They specify spatial relations more precisely than a bare preposition, but the ground noun can be omitted when it is recoverable from context, allowing the location noun to function independently. Likewise, the location noun itself may be omitted when the spatial relation is clear enough from context.

text:
In their adnominal uses, the location nouns are juxtaposed to common nouns or, although much less frequently, to common nouns with juxtaposed adnominal personal pronouns, such that `` n ( pro ) n.loc ''. In their adnominal uses, they signal locational relations. Overall, though, the adnominal uses of location nouns are marginal: of a total of 981 tokens, only 35 (4%) have adnominal uses, whereas 946 have nominal uses (96%).

In designating locational relations, the location nouns have restrictive function. That is, they signal that the referent encoded by the head nominal is precisely the one situated in the spatial location designated by the location noun. Thereby, the location noun aids the hearer in the identification of the referent, as in jalang atas ‘upper road’ in ( Example_5.43 ), rem blakang ‘rear brakes’ in ( Example_5.44 ), or tetangga dong sebla ‘the neighbors next door’ in ( Example_5.49 ). The locational relation can also be figurative as in generasi bawa ‘next generation’ in ( Example_5.51 ), or in dunia luar ‘outside world’ in ( Example_5.46 ), or temporal as in bulang depang ‘next month’ in ( Example_5.52 ). Adnominal uses for sekitar ‘vicinity’ are unattested in the corpus.

summary:
Location nouns can be used adnominally by juxtaposing them to common nouns, where they signal locational relations in an n (pro) n.loc structure. However, such uses are rare in the corpus: only 35 of 981 tokens (4%) are adnominal, while the vast majority are nominal.

In adnominal use, the location noun has a restrictive function, identifying the referent as the one located in the spatial position named by the noun. These relations may be spatial, figurative, or temporal, as in examples like *jalang atas* ‘upper road,’ *dunia luar* ‘outside world,’ and *bulang depang* ‘next month’; adnominal uses of *sekitar* ‘vicinity’ are not attested.

text:
Direction nouns express cardinal directions and relative directions. The former designate the four principal compass points, while the latter express left-right orientation. The Papuan Malay direction nouns are presented in Table_5.5, together with their token frequencies in the corpus (given their low token frequencies, most examples in this section are elicited).

Direction nouns have the following distributional properties:

enumerate

Direction nouns occur in prepositional phrases as independent heads of the noun phrase within the prepositional phrase; they are unattested as head nominals in unembedded noun phrases.

Direction nouns have adnominal uses; that is, they occur in noun phrases with a preceding noun as nominal head.

Direction nouns can be modified with adnominally used demonstratives or locatives.
enumerate

Direction nouns are distinct from common nouns (§ Para_5.2.1 ) and location nouns (§ Para_5.2.3 ) in terms of the following properties:

enumerate

Contrasting with common nouns, direction nouns (a) are unattested as heads of unembedded noun phrases, (b) are only modified with demonstratives and locatives, and (c) are unattested in adnominal possessive constructions, neither as the possessor nor as the possessum.

Contrasting with location nouns, direction nouns with juxtaposed adnominal nouns are unattested when employed as nominals in prepositional phrases.

enumerate

Direction nouns typically occur as complements in prepositional phrases, as shown with the four cardinal directions in ( Example_5.53 ) to ( Example_5.56 ) and the two relative directions in ( Example_5.57 ) and ( Example_5.58 ). Direction nouns can be modified with demonstratives as in utara ini ‘this north’ in ( Example_5.53 ) or kiri ini ‘this left’ in ( Example_5.57 ), or with locatives as in slatang sana ‘south over there’ in ( Example_5.54 ) or kanang sana ‘right over there’ in ( Example_5.58 ).

In ( Example_5.57 ) and ( Example_5.58 ) the preposition is obligatory. With motion verbs that also express direction, however, the allative preposition ke ‘to’ may also be omitted. This is illustrated in ( Example_5.59 ) with the motion verb belok ‘turn’. (For details on the elision of prepositions encoding location, see § Para_10.1.5.)

Semantically, these noun phrases designate ``subtype-of'' relations as in bagiang barat ‘western part’ and bagiang timur ‘eastern part’ in ( Example_5.60 ), or they denote locational relations as in sebla kiri ‘left side’ in ( Example_5.61 ), or in tangang kanang ‘right hand/arm’ in ( Example_5.62 ).

They differ from common nouns in that they are not used as heads of unembedded noun phrases and do not occur in adnominal possessive constructions, and they differ from location nouns in that they do not appear as nominals with juxtaposed adnominal nouns in prepositional phrases. In adnominal use, direction nouns are juxtaposed to a head noun and express subtype or locational relations, such as “western part” or “left side.”

text: The label ``time-denoting nouns'' refers to nouns which denote time units (§ Para_5.2.5.1 ), the periods of the day (§ Para_5.2.5.2 ), the days of the week and months of the year (§ Para_5.2.5.3 ), and relative time (§ Para_5.2.5.4 ). Time-denoting nouns have the same syntactic properties as common nouns (for details see § Para_5.2.1.)
summary: Time-denoting nouns are nouns that express time units, periods of the day, days of the week and months of the year, and relative time. They have the same syntactic properties as common nouns.

text:
Table_5.6 lists the different time-denoting nouns that divide a year into smaller units.

The time units listed in Table_5.6 are count nouns that can be modified with numerals or quantifiers, as illustrated in ( Example_5.63 ) and ( Example_5.64 ). In addition to designating a time unit, minggu ‘week’ also denotes a day of the week, namely ‘Sunday’ (see Table_5.8 ).

bapa bilang begini, tunggu lima blas minit to?\\
father say like.this wait five teens minute right?\\

‘father said like this, ``wait fifteen minutes, right?!''' [081025-006-Cv.0173]

brapa bulang dorang skola ka mace, lima bulang ka?\\
several month 3.pl go.to.school or woman five month or\\

‘for how many months have they been going to school, Madam, for five months, right?’ [081025-003-Cv.0207]
summary: Table 5.6 shows that the nouns used to denote smaller units of time within a year are count nouns, since they can be modified by numerals or quantifiers. The noun minggu ‘week’ has an additional meaning, referring not only to a time unit but also to the day ‘Sunday’.

text:
Table_5.7 presents the time-denoting nouns for the four periods of the day. More specifically, pagi ‘morning’ designates the period from just after midnight until about eleven o’clock, while siang ‘midday’ refers to the time from about eleven o’clock until about fourteen hours. The next period, sore ‘afternoon’, lasts until about eighteen hours when darkness sets in, while malam ‘night’ denotes nighttime.

The four periods-of-the-day expressions are count nouns that can be modified with numerals or quantifiers, as shown in ( Example_5.66 ) and ( Example_5.67 ). In addition, these expressions are also used as modifiers within noun phrases, as in ( Example_5.68 ) to ( Example_5.70 ).

Within the clause, the four expressions typically occur at clause boundaries. Most often, they occur in clause-initial position where they set the temporal stage for the entire clause. Alternatively, although less often, the temporal expressions occur in clause-final position, where they are less prominent. This is illustrated in ( Example_5.71 ) to ( Example_5.74 ) with near contrastive examples. The time expression pagi ‘morning’ occurs in clause-initial position in ( Example_5.71 ) and in clause-final position in ( Example_5.72 ). Likewise, malam ‘night’ occurs in clause-initial position in ( Example_5.73 ) and in clause-final position in ( Example_5.74 ).

These expressions can be modified by numerals or quantifiers, used as noun phrase modifiers, and occur mainly at clause boundaries—most often clause-initially to set the temporal frame, though sometimes clause-finally. They are also used in greetings such as ‘good morning’ and ‘good evening.’

subsubsection: Days of the week and months of the year
text:
The seven days of the week and the twelve months of the year are listed in Table_5.8.

Typically, the days of the week and the months of the year occur in n1n2 noun phrases, headed by the common nouns hari ‘day’ and bulang ‘month’, respectively (see Table_5.6; see also § Para_8.2.2 ). Examples for the days of the week are given in ( Example_5.79 ) and ( Example_5.80 ) and for the months of the year in ( Example_5.81 ). Occasionally, however, speakers omit hari ‘day’ or bulang ‘month’ as with rabu ‘Wednesday’ in ( Example_5.80 ) and with oktober ‘October’ and januari ‘January’ in ( Example_5.82 ), respectively.

yo bapa, hari minggu sa datang\\

‘yes father, on Sunday I’ll come’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0344]

hari slasa itu de pu ana prempuang meninggal\\
day Tuesday d.dist 3sg poss child woman die\\
jadi tong tinggal di ruma sampe rabu\\

‘that Monday his daughter died, so we stayed at home until Wednesday’ [080925-003-Cv.0001]

‘you have lots of (unexcused) absences in October’ [081023-004-Cv.0015]

o nanti oktober e januari baru kitong antar\\
oh! very.soon October uh January and.then 1pl bring\\

[About wedding customs:] ‘oh later in October uh January, and then we’ll bring (our daughter to your house)’ [081110-005-CvPr.0049]
summary: The days of the week and months of the year are usually expressed in n1n2 noun phrases headed by the common nouns *hari* ‘day’ and *bulang* ‘month,’ respectively. However, speakers sometimes omit these head nouns, using forms like *rabu* ‘Wednesday,’ *oktober* ‘October,’ and *januari* ‘January’ on their own.

text:
Relative time is expressed with the three time-denoting nouns and two phrasal expressions presented in Table_5.9.

Within the clause, the relative-time denoting expressions typically occur in clause-initial position. Here they set the temporal stage for the entire clause, similar to the nouns denoting periods of the day, discussed in § Para_5.2.5.2. This is illustrated with the examples in ( Example_5.83 ) to ( Example_5.85 ). Alternatively, but less often, the relative-time expressions directly precede the predicate where they are less prominent, as shown in ( Example_5.86 ). The contrast in meaning conveyed by the different positions within the clause is illustrated with besok ‘tomorrow’ in the near contrastive examples in ( Example_5.85 ) and ( Example_5.86 ). By fronting besok ‘tomorrow’ in ( Example_5.85 ), the speaker accentuates the temporal setting of the entire clause. This is not the case in ( Example_5.86 ), where besok ‘tomorrow’ directly precedes the predicate, where it is less salient.

The examples in ( Example_5.83 ) and ( Example_5.85 ) also illustrate that the temporal scope of kemaring ‘yesterday’ and besok ‘tomorrow’ is larger than the preceding or following 24-hour period, respectively. Generally speaking kemaring ‘yesterday’ denotes a past point in time such as kemaring ‘some time ago’ in ( Example_5.83 ). Along similar lines, besok ‘tomorrow’ refers to a future point in time which in ( Example_5.85 ) is besok ‘next year’.

In addition, the corpus includes a small number of utterances in which the nouns designating relative-time occur as subjects in nonverbal clauses. This is illustrated with besok ‘tomorrow’ and lusa ‘the day after tomorrow’ in ( Example_5.87 ).

Like other nouns, relative-time denoting nouns also have adnominal uses as shown in ( Example_5.88 ) and ( Example_5.89 ). In their adnominal uses, they occur in posthead position and have restrictive function. That is, they specify whether the period or point in time encoded by the head nominal is situated in the future or in the past, as in hari minggu besok ‘next Sunday’ in ( Example_5.88 ) or taung kemaring ‘a few years back’ in ( Example_5.89 ).

Relative-time expressions also occur as complements in prepositional phrases as, for instance, in sampe besok ‘until the next day’ (literally ‘until tomorrow’) in ( Example_5.90 ). This example also illustrates that besok ‘tomorrow’ denotes relative time. As the events described here happened in the past, besok ‘tomorrow’ refers to a future point in time relative to the narrated events. Hence, besok translates as ‘the next day’. (Prepositions encoding time are discussed in more detail in § Para_10.1.)

Relative-time expressions are formed with three time-denoting nouns and two phrasal expressions, and they usually appear clause-initially to set the temporal frame for the whole clause. Less often they occur directly before the predicate, where they are less prominent; the passage also notes that words like kemaring ‘yesterday’ and besok ‘tomorrow’ can refer to broader past or future points in time, not just the preceding or following 24 hours.

These nouns can also function as subjects in nonverbal clauses, appear adnominally after a head noun with a restrictive meaning, and occur as complements in prepositional phrases such as sampe besok ‘until the next day.’

text:
Papuan Malay has a very reduced inventory of classifying nouns. Attested is only one, namely the common noun ekor ‘tail’ which is used to count animals. In this function, it always follows a posthead numeral, as shown in ( Example_5.91 ).

styleExampleTitle
Enumeration of animals
styleExampleTitle

dong dua dapat ikang ini tiga ekor\\
3pl two get fish d.prox three tail\\
dapat ikang tiga ekor dong dua \\
get fish three tail 3pl two \\

‘the two of them get these fish, three (of them), having gotten three fish, the two of them ’ (Lit. ‘ three tails’) [081109-011-JR.0003]

As a classifying noun, ekor ‘tail’ does not refer to the entities themselves being counted but rather to their form, as is rather common in Malay and other Austronesian varieties; see for instance Ambon Malay, Ternate Malay, Tetun, or Standard Malay.

Enumeration of people and objects, by contrast, is done without a classifier as illustrated in ( Example_5.92 ) and ( Example_5.93 ), respectively.

styleExampleTitle
Enumeration of people and objects
styleExampleTitle

jadi saya empat ana\\
so 1sg four child\\

‘so I (have) four children’ [081006-024-CvEx.0002]

orang Sarmi harus siap untuk orang Sorong\\
