ten cloth d.dist cloth tradition d.dist \\

[About bride-prices:] ‘a Sarmi person has to provide a Sorong person with those ten cloths, those traditional cloths’ [081006-029-CvEx.0012]
summary: Papuan Malay has only one attested classifying noun, ekor ‘tail,’ which is used to count animals and follows the numeral. In this classifier use, ekor refers to the form of the counted entities rather than to the entities themselves, as is common in other Malay and Austronesian varieties. By contrast, people and objects are counted without a classifier.

text:
This section presents the most common Papuan Malay terms for consanguineal and affinal kin. An initial investigation of the kinship system indicates that Papuan Malay uses a combination of Iroquois and Hawaiian terminologies and makes a relative age discrimination.

Before presenting the Papuan Malay kinship terms, Table_5.10 lists the standard symbols used to abbreviate basic terms.

More complex kinship terms are expressed by chains of these abbreviations, such as FZ for ‘father’s sister’ or MF for ‘mother’s father’.
summary: The passage says that Papuan Malay kinship vocabulary includes the most common terms for consanguineal and affinal relatives, and that its kinship system appears to combine Iroquois and Hawaiian terminology while also distinguishing relative age. It also notes that kinship terms can be represented by standard abbreviations, which are combined into chains to express more complex relations such as FZ ‘father’s sister’ and MF ‘mother’s father’.

text:
The kinship system is Iroquois, in that Papuan Malay makes a distinction in the first ascending generation between same-sex and cross-sex parents’ siblings in a bifurcate merging pattern, as demonstrated in Table_5.11. Contrasting with typical Iroquois systems, however, the cross-parallel distinction only applies to parents’ younger siblings. That is, only parents’ same-sexed younger siblings are considered as consanguines: bapa-ade ‘uncle’ (literally ‘younger father’) and mama-ade ‘aunt’ (literally ‘younger mother’). Parents’ opposite-sexed younger siblings are called om ‘uncle’ and tanta ‘aunt’; both terms are loanwords from Dutch. By contrast, Papuan Malay does not distinguish between parents’ older siblings of opposite sex. That is, all parents’ older siblings are considered as consanguines regardless of their sex: bapa-tua ‘uncle’ (literally ‘old father’) and mama-tua ‘aunt’ (literally ‘old mother’). The six consanguineal terms also extend to affinal kin, as discussed in § Para_5.2.7.2.

With respect to other generations, the kinship system is Hawaiian, in that it extends bilaterally, without making distinctions between lineal and collateral consanguines, or between cross and parallel consanguines. Consequently, Papuan Malay does not distinguish between siblings and cousins, as shown in Table_5.11. That is, children of parents’ siblings are also classified as siblings. In addition, the system makes a relative age discrimination. Older siblings and children of parents’ older siblings are called kaka ‘older sibling’ while younger siblings and children of parents’ younger siblings are called ade ‘younger sibling’. The same relative age discrimination applies to cousins in the second degree of collaterality: their relative ages are determined by the ages of the linking grandparents. With the exception of the reference term orang-tua ‘parent’, speakers use the consanguineal terms, listed in Table_5.11, both for reference and for address.

To signal the gender of a sibling or child, the kinship terms kaka ‘older sibling’, ade ‘younger sibling’, and ana ‘child’ are modified with the common nouns laki laki ‘man’ or prempuang ‘woman’, giving kaka laki laki ‘older brother’, ade prempuang ‘younger sister’, or ana laki laki ‘son’.
summary:
Papuan Malay has an Iroquois kinship system in the first ascending generation, distinguishing same-sex from cross-sex parents’ siblings, but only for parents’ younger siblings: same-sex younger siblings are treated as consanguines, while opposite-sex younger siblings receive Dutch loan terms. For parents’ older siblings, however, sex is not distinguished, and all are treated as consanguines; the six consanguineal terms also extend to affinal kin.

In other generations, the system is Hawaiian, with no distinction between lineal and collateral or between cross and parallel kin, so siblings and cousins are not separated. It also marks relative age, using kaka for older and ade for younger relatives, and gender can be added to sibling and child terms with laki laki ‘man’ or prempuang ‘woman’.

text:
The Papuan Malay affinal terms, listed in Table_5.12, include two terms for spouse, that is, paytua ‘husband’ and maytua ‘wife’, and two terms for in-laws, namely mantu ‘(parent/child) in-law’ and ipar ‘sibling in-law’. Speakers employ these terms for both reference and address.

Papuan Malay distinguishes between in-laws belonging to different generations and those belonging to the same generation, as illustrated in Table_5.12.

The expression for in-laws belonging to the first ascending or descending generation is the self-recipro\-cal term mantu ‘(parent/child) in-law’. This term, however, is unattested on its own. It is always modified with the common nouns bapa ‘father’, mama ‘mother’, or ana ‘child’ to specify the affinal relationship, giving bapa mantu ‘father in-law’, mama mantu ‘mother in-law’, or ana mantu ‘child in-law’.

The term for same-generation in-laws is ipar ‘sibling in-law’. This self-reciproc\-al term extends to spouses’ siblings and those siblings’ spouses, as well as to children’s spouses’ parents (co-parents-in-law). Again, a relative age discrimination is made similar to that for siblings: kaka ipar ‘older sibling in-law’ and ade ipar ‘younger sibling in-law’.

The six consanguineal terms that distinguish between same-sex and cross-sex parents’ siblings in the first ascending generation, mentioned in § Para_5.2.7.1, also extend to affinal kin, as shown in Table_5.13.
summary: Papuan Malay has affinal terms for spouses, in-laws, and sibling-in-laws: paytua ‘husband,’ maytua ‘wife,’ mantu ‘(parent/child) in-law,’ and ipar ‘sibling in-law,’ and these terms are used both for reference and address. It distinguishes in-laws by generation, with mantu used for first ascending/descending generation in-laws only in combination with bapa ‘father,’ mama ‘mother,’ or ana ‘child,’ while ipar covers same-generation in-laws and can also be marked for relative age as kaka ipar ‘older sibling in-law’ and ade ipar ‘younger sibling in-law.’

text:
Papuan Malay has a large open class of verbs which express actions, events, and processes, as well as states or more time-stable properties. They have the following defining syntactic and functional properties:

enumerate

Valency: each verb takes a specific number of arguments (§ Para_5.3.1 ).

Predicative function is predominant; besides, verbs also have attributive uses in noun phrases (§ Para_5.3.2 ).

Modification with adverbs, including intensification and grading (§ Para_5.3.4 and § Para_5.3.5 ).

Negation only with tida ‘ neg ’ or tra ‘ neg ’ (§ Para_5.3.6 ). As for the occurrence of bukang ‘ neg ’ in verbal clauses, see Footnote Footnote_5.155 in § Para_5.3.6 (p. Footnote_5.155).

Occurrence in causative and in reciprocal constructions (§ Para_5.3.7 and § Para_5.3.8 ).
enumerate

Morphological properties play only a minor role in defining verbs as a distinct word class, due to the lack of inflectional morphology and the limited role of derivational processes. The latter include reduplication (for details see § Para_4.2.2 ), and, to a limited extent, affixation with prefix ter- or suffix - ang (§ Para_5.3.9; see also § Para_3.1 ).

Verbs are divided into three classes on the basis of their valency and their tendency to function predicatively, namely trivalent, bivalent, and monovalent verbs. In turn, monovalent verbs are further divided into dynamic and stative verbs. That is, Papuan Malay does not have a distinct class of adjectives. Instead, monovalent stative verbs encode, what calls “the four core semantic types” of dimension, age, value, and color which are “typically associated with the word class adjective”. The two criteria of valency and prevalent predicative function also account for the other properties of verbs, listed above and discussed in more detail in the following sections.

Verbs are distinct from nouns (§ Para_5.2 ) and adverbs (§ Para_5.4 ) in terms of the following distributional properties:

enumerate

Contrasting with nouns, verbs (a) have valency, It is acknowledged that some authors maintain that nouns have valency., for instance, discuss the “layered structure of adpositional and noun phrases” ( vanValin.1997) and the “semantic representation of nouns and noun phrases” ( vanValin.1997), and examines “[t]ypes of dependencies”. See also Croft’s ( Croft.1991) discussion on “structural markedness and the semantic prototypes”, as well as,, and. and (b) are negated with tida/ tra ‘ neg ’. In addition (c) verbs, except for monovalent stative ones, occur as predicates in reciprocal constructions, and (d) monovalent stative and bivalent verbs occur as predicates in comparative constructions.

Unlike adverbs, verbs (a) are used predicatively, and (b) can modify nouns.

enumerate

The following sections explore the characteristics and properties of verbs in more detail. As for their syntactic properties the following topics are discussed: valency in § Para_5.3.1, predicative and attributive functions in § Para_5.3.2, adverbial modification in § Para_5.3.3, intensification in § Para_5.3.4, grading in § Para_5.3.5, negation in § Para_5.3.6, occurrences in causative constructions in § Para_5.3.7, and uses in reciprocal constructions in § Para_5.3.8. Finally, the morphological properties of verbs are briefly examined in § Para_5.3.9. In each section, dynamic verbs are discussed first, and stative verbs second. Dynamic verbs, in turn, are described in order from those with three arguments to those with one argument. Each section also discusses the type and token frequencies in the corpus for the respective properties and summarizes these frequencies in a table. These tables form the basis for the summary in § Para_5.4.11.
summary:
Papuan Malay has a large open class of verbs that denote actions, events, processes, and also states or stable properties. Verbs are defined mainly by syntactic and functional criteria: they have valency, are primarily predicative, can be modified by adverbs, are negated only with *tida* or *tra*, and occur in causative and reciprocal constructions; morphology plays only a minor role because inflection is lacking and derivation is limited.

Verbs are classified by valency into trivalent, bivalent, and monovalent verbs, with monovalent verbs further divided into dynamic and stative types. Papuan Malay has no separate adjective class; instead, monovalent stative verbs express meanings typically associated with adjectives, such as dimension, age, value, and color.

text:
Valency is defined as a “weighting or quantification of verbs in terms of the number of dependents (or arguments or valents) they take”. Papuan Malay verbs are classified into three classes on the basis of their valency, namely verbs with one, two, or three core arguments. Examples are given in Table_5.14 and Table_5.14a: verbs that have two or three arguments are listed first, followed by verbs with one argument. Monovalent verbs are further distinguished according to their semantics into dynamic and stative verbs, and other properties, discussed in the following sections.

Trivalent verbs have three core arguments, that is, a subject and two grammatical objects. This is illustrated with kasi ‘give’ in ( Example_5.94 ). It is important to note, however, that the attested trivalent verbs allow but do not require three syntactic arguments. (For details, see § Para_11.1.3.)

styleExampleTitle
Trivalent verbs with three core arguments
styleExampleTitle

dia kasi kitong daging\\
3sg give 1pl meat\\

‘he gave us (fish) meat’ [080919-004-NP.0061]

Bivalent verbs have two core arguments, a subject and one grammatical object. This is shown with pukul ‘hit’ in ( Example_5.95 ) and mara ‘feel angry (about)’ in ( Example_5.96 ). Bivalent verbs also allow, but do not require two syntactic arguments. (For details see § Para_11.1.2.)

styleExampleTitle
Bivalent verbs with two core arguments
styleExampleTitle

bapa de pukul sa deng pisow\\
father 3sg hit 1sg with knife\\

‘(my) husband hit me with a knife’ [081011-023-Cv.0167]

jadi sa mara dia\\
so 1sg feel.angry(.about) 3sg \\

‘[he doesn’t report to me in a good way,] so I feel angry about him’ [081011-020-Cv.0107]

Monovalent verbs have only one core argument. They are further divided into dynamic and stative verbs. Dynamic verbs such as lari ‘run’ in ( Example_5.97 ) denote actions involving one participant, while stative verbs, such as besar ‘be big’ or kecil ‘be small’ in ( Example_5.98 ), express states or more time-stable properties.

styleExampleTitle
Monovalent verbs with one core argument
styleExampleTitle

Nofita de lari dari saya\\
Nofita 3sg run from 1sg \\

‘Nofita ran (away) from me’ [081025-006-Cv.0322]

kepala ni besar baru badang ni kecil\\
head d.prox be.big and.then body d.prox be.small\\

‘(his) head here is big but (his) body here is small’ [081025-006-Cv.0278]

In the corpus, the class of trivalent verbs is the smallest one with seven, as shown in Table_5.15. A small majority of attested verbs are bivalent with 535 entries (52%), while 490 verbs are monovalent (48%). Most of the monovalent verbs are stative (351/490 – 72%), while 139 verbs are dynamic (28%).

In addition, the corpus contains 43 derived monovalent verbs prefixed with ter- that denote accidental or unintentional actions or events (167 tokens). These lexemes are examined in detail in § Para_3.1.2, and briefly reviewed in § Para_5.3.9; therefore, they are not further discussed in this section.
summary: Papuan Malay verbs are classified by valency into trivalent, bivalent, and monovalent verbs, based on whether they take three, two, or one core argument(s). Trivalent verbs are rarest in the corpus (seven types), bivalent verbs are slightly more frequent than monovalent verbs (535 vs. 490), and most monovalent verbs are stative rather than dynamic. The passage also notes that attested trivalent and bivalent verbs may allow, but do not require, all of their possible syntactic arguments, and that there are 43 derived monovalent ter- verbs expressing accidental or unintentional events.

text:
Verbs can function predicatively as well as attributively. The identified verb classes display clear distributional preferences, however. Dynamic verbs usually function predicatively, and less frequently attributively. Monovalent stative verbs, by contrast, typically occur as adnominal modifiers in noun phrases, although they also have predicative function.

In their predicative uses, verbs act “as ‘comment’ on a given noun as ‘topic’”, using Dixon’s ( Dixon.1994) terminology. This typical function of dynamic verbs is demonstrated with bivalent bunu ‘kill’ in ( Example_5.99 ). The predicative use of monovalent stative verbs is illustrated with tinggi ‘be high’ in ( Example_5.100 ). In the corpus, all dynamic verbs have predicative function, while only 40% of the stative verbs (139/351) are used predicatively.

styleExampleTitle
Predicative uses
styleExampleTitle

bapa Iskia dong bunu babi\\
father Iskia 3pl kill pig\\

‘father Iskia and his companions killed a pig’ [080917-008-NP.0120]

glombang itu tinggi\\
wave d.dist be.high\\

‘that wave was high’ [080923-015-CvEx.0016]

In their attributive function within noun phrases, the modifying verbs serve to specify or restrict “the reference of the noun”, in Dixon’s ( Dixon.1994) terminology. Cross-linguistically, this is achieved in one of two ways, as points out. One option is verb-via- juxtaposition modification; that is, the modifying verb is directly juxtaposed to a noun in a noun phrase. The second option is “verb-via-relative-clause modification”; that is, modification is achieved by means of a relative clause. Papuan Malay also makes use of these two options, as illustrated in ( Example_5.101 ) to ( Example_5.105 )

The first option of verb-via- juxtaposition modification is illustrated in ( Example_5.101 ). The examples show that all verb types can occur in noun phrases as adnominal modifiers in posthead position, both with agentive and non-agentive head nominals (the examples in ( Example_5.101a ) and ( Example_5.101b ) are elicited).

styleExampleTitle

sifat kasi\\

‘disposition of giving’\\

‘one who likes to buy’\\

‘drunkard’\\

bua mera \\

‘red fruit’ \\

The second option of modifying nouns within a noun phrase is by placing the verb within a relative clause, as illustrated in ( Example_5.102 ) to ( Example_5.105 ). This verb-via-relative-clause modification typically applies to dynamic verbs, such as (monotransitively used) trivalent bawa ‘bring’ in the elicited example in ( Example_5.102 ), bivalent kawing ‘marry unofficially’ in ( Example_5.103 ), or monovalent dynamic tinggal ‘stay’ in ( Example_5.104 ).

styleExampleTitle
Attributive uses: Verb-via-relative-clause modification
styleExampleTitle

ojek yang bawa tete tu su pulang\\
motorbike.taxi rel bring grandfather d.dist already go.home\\

‘that motorbike taxi driver who brought grandfather has already returned home’ [Elicited MY131119.001]

orang Papua yang kawing orang pendatang de tinggal \\
person Papua rel marry.inofficially person stranger 3sg stay \\

‘a Papuan person who married a stranger, he/she’ll stay (in Papua)’ [081029-005-Cv.0046]

buat sodara sodara yang tinggal di kampung\\
for rdp sibling rel stay at village\\

‘[we cut (the pig meat) up that day, we divided (it) for us who cut (it) up that day, (and) then] for the relatives and friends who live in the village’ [080919-003-NP.0014]

de ada potong ikang yang besar di pante\\
3sg exist cut fish rel be.big at coast\\

‘at the beach he was cutting up a fish that was big’ [080919-004-NP.0061]

All verb types can be used attributively. However, when comparing the attested attributively used verb tokens across the two types of noun phrase modification, a clear pattern emerges, shown in Table_5.16. The vast majority of attributively used monovalent stative verbs occur in noun phrases involving verb-via-juxtapos\-ition modification, although stative verbs also occur in verb-via-relative-clause modification, such as besar ‘be big’ in ( Example_5.105 ). The vast majority of attributively used dynamic verbs, by contrast, occur in noun phrases involving verb-via-relative-clause modification. Cross-linguistically these preferences are rather common.

So far 612 noun phrases have been identified which involve verb-via-juxtapos\-ition modification, and 834 noun phrases with verb-via-relative-clause modification. This total of 1,446 noun phrases involves 36 noun phrases (2.5%) which are formed with seven distinct trivalent verbs, 432 noun phrases (29.9%) formed with 146 distinct bivalent verbs, 170 noun phrases (11.8%) formed with 37 distinct monovalent dynamic verbs, and 808 noun phrases (55.9%) formed with 146 distinct monovalent stative verbs. About two thirds of the attested 808 attributively used monovalent stative verb tokens occur in noun phrases with verb-via-juxtapos\-ition modification (520/808 – 64%), while only about one third occurs in noun phrases with verb-via-relative-clause modification (288/808 – 36%). The opposite holds for dynamic verbs. The vast majority of attributively used dynamic verb tokens occur in noun phrases with verb-via-relative-clause modification: 35/36 trivalent verb tokens (97%), 371/432 bivalent verb tokens (86%), and 140/170 monovalent dynamic verb tokens (82%). By contrast, only few dynamic verbs are used in noun phrases with verb-via- juxtaposition modification: 1/36 trivalent verb tokens (3%), 61/432 bivalent verb tokens (14%), and 30/170 monovalent dynamic verb tokens (18%).
summary: Verbs in Papuan Malay can be used both predicatively and attributively, but they show clear preferences: dynamic verbs are usually predicative, while monovalent stative verbs more often function as adnominal modifiers in noun phrases. All verb types can modify nouns either by direct juxtaposition or inside a relative clause, but stative verbs strongly favor juxtaposition whereas dynamic verbs overwhelmingly occur in relative-clause modification.

text:
In their predicative uses, tri-, bi-, and monovalent verbs can be modified with adverbs, as shown in ( Example_5.106 ) to ( Example_5.113 ). In ( Example_5.106 ) to ( Example_5.109 ), the temporal ad verb langsung ‘immediately’ modifies trivalent kasi ‘give’, bivalent tanya ‘ask’, monovalent dynamic pulang ‘go home’, and stative basa ‘be wet’, respectively; the example in ( Example_5.106 ) is elicited.

styleExampleTitle
Adverbial modification with temporal ad verb langsung ‘immediately’
styleExampleTitle

pace dong langsung kasi dia senter\\
man 3pl immediately give 3sg flashlight\\

‘the men immediately gave him a flashlight’ [Elicited BR130221.013]

sa langsung tanya dorang\\
1sg immediately ask 3pl \\

`I immediately asked them’ [080919-007-CvNP.0045]

sa langsung pulang\\
1sg immediately go.home\\

‘I went home immediately’ [081014-008-CvNP.0018]

bapa langsung diam\\
father immediately be.quiet\\

‘the gentleman was immediately quiet’ [080917-010-CvEx.0213]

Along similar lines, frequency ad verb lagi ‘again, also’ modifies the verbs in ( Example_5.110 ) to ( Example_5.113 ); the example in ( Example_5.110 ) is elicited. (For more details on adverbs see § Para_5.4.)

styleExampleTitle
Adverbial modification with frequency ad verb lagi ‘again, also’
styleExampleTitle

Dodo ambil Agus air lagi\\
Dodo fetch Agus water again\\

‘Dodo fetched water for Agus again’ [Elicited BR130409.001]

sa tampeleng dia lagi\\
1sg slap.on.face/ears 3sg again\\

‘I slapped him across the face again’ [081013-002-Cv.0007]

nanti Lodia dong datang lagi\\

‘very soon Lodia and her companions will also come’ [081006-016-Cv.0010]

sampe mungking dua taung baru rame lagi\\

‘[it goes on like that] for maybe two years before (the situation gets) lively again’ [081025-004-Cv.0102]
summary: The passage states that in predicative uses, tri-, bi-, and monovalent verbs can all be modified by adverbs. It illustrates this with the temporal adverb langsung “immediately” and the frequency adverb lagi “again, also,” each of which can modify verbs of different valency, including trivalent, bivalent, monovalent dynamic, and stative verbs.

text:
In their predicative uses, monovalent stative and bivalent verbs can be intensified with the degree adverbs skali ‘very’ or terlalu ‘too’, as shown in ( Example_5.114 ) to ( Example_5.117 ). While skali ‘very’ follows the verb as in ( Example_5.114 ) and ( Example_5.115 ), terlalu ‘too’ precedes it as in ( Example_5.116 ) and ( Example_5.117 ). Intensification of predicatively used monovalent dynamic and trivalent verbs is unattested in the corpus. Furthermore, intensification of attributively used verbs is unattested. (For details on degree adverbs see § Para_5.4.7.)

styleExampleTitle
Intensification
styleExampleTitle

sa snang skali dong pu cara masak\\
1sg feel.happy(.about) very 3pl poss manner cook\\

‘I very (much) enjoy their way of cooking’ [081014-017-CvPr.0029]

Aris tinggi skali\\
Aris be.high very\\

‘Aris is very tall’ [080922-001b-CvPh.0026]

ade kecil terlalu menangis kitorang\\
ySb be.small too cry 1pl \\

‘[Hana’s husband didn’t come along,] the small younger sibling cried too much (for) us’ [080921-002-Cv.0008]

sa liat mama terlalu baik\\
1sg see mother exceedingly be.good\\

‘I see you (‘mother’) are too good’ [081115-001a-Cv.0324]

As mentioned, intensification of monovalent dynamic verbs is unattested in the corpus. According to one consultant, though, it is possible to intensify them with the expressions terlalu banyak ‘too much’ or terlalu sedikit ‘too little’, as in the elicited examples in ( Example_5.118 ) and ( Example_5.119 ).

styleExampleTitle
Grading of monovalent dynamic verbs with terlalu banyak/ sedikit ‘too much\-/little’
styleExampleTitle

Dodo de terlalu banyak tidor\\
Dodo 3sg too many sleep\\

‘Dodo sleeps too much’ [Elicited BR130410.005]

Dodo de terlalu sedikit lari\\
Dodo 3sg too few run\\

‘Dodo runs too little’ [Elicited BR130410.008]

In addition, one of the consultants came up with the two examples in ( Example_5.120 ) and ( Example_5.121 ), respectively, in which dynamic lari ‘run’ and tunduk ‘bow’ are directly modified with terlalu ‘too’. In ( Example_5.120 ), however, lari means ‘deviate’ rather than ‘run’, and tunduk ‘bow’ in ( Example_5.121 ) receives the stative reading ‘be obedient’.

styleExampleTitle
Grading of monovalent dynamic verbs with terlalu ‘too’
styleExampleTitle

prahu ini pu ukurang terlalu lari dari ukurang\\
boat d.prox poss measurement too run from measurement\\
yang ko kasi\\
rel 2sg give\\

‘the size of this boat deviates too much from the size that you gave’ [Elicited BR130410.017]

Agus de terlalu tunduk\\
Agus 3sg too bow\\

‘Agus is too obedient’ [Elicited BR130410.004]

When examining the attested intensified monovalent stative and bivalent verb tokens as to whether they are intensified with skali ‘very’ or with terlalu ‘too’, the data shows clear distributional preferences, presented in Table_5.17. The corpus contains 155 verb phrases, made up of 80 different verbs, in which skali ‘very’ intensifies a verb. Most of these verbs are stative ones (81%), accounting for 80% of the skali- intensification tokens. The corpus also contains 33 verb phrases, formed with 27 different verbs, in which terlalu ‘too’ intensifies a verb. Again, most of the intensified verbs are stative ones (74%) accounting for 73% of the terlalu- intensification tokens.
summary:
The passage states that in predicative use, monovalent stative verbs and bivalent verbs can be intensified by the degree adverbs *skali* ‘very’ and *terlalu* ‘too’, with *skali* following the verb and *terlalu* preceding it. Intensification of predicative monovalent dynamic verbs and trivalent verbs, as well as attributively used verbs, is unattested in the corpus, though some elicited examples suggest limited possibilities for dynamic verbs.  

The corpus data further show that most intensified verb phrases involve stative verbs: 155 cases with *skali* and 33 with *terlalu*, and stative verbs make up the large majority of both sets.

text:
In their predicative uses, monovalent stative and bivalent verbs can occur with grading adverbs, as shown in ( Example_5.122 ) to ( Example_5.125 ), whereas grading of monovalent dynamic and trivalent verbs is unattested. The comparative degree is marked with the grading ad verb lebi ‘more’ and the superlative degree with paling ‘most’; both adverbs precede the verb. (For details on degree adverbs see § Para_5.4.7; for details on comparative clauses see § Para_11.5.)

styleExampleTitle
Grading of bivalent verbs
styleExampleTitle

a, dong mala lebi sayang saya\\
ah! 3pl in.fact more love 1sg \\

‘ah, they actually loved me more’ [Elicited BR130221.034] The elicited example in ( Example_5.122 ) is the corrected version of the original recording dong mana lebi sayang saya ‘they actually[ spm ] loved me more’ [081110-008-NPHt.0021]. That is, the speaker mispronounced mala ‘in.fact’, realizing it as mana.

tempat itu sa paling takut\\
place d.dist 1sg most feel.afraid(.of)\\

‘that place I feel most afraid of’ [081025-006-Cv.0285]

styleExampleTitle
Grading of monovalent stative verbs
styleExampleTitle

yo kaka, itu yang lebi baik untuk saya\\
yes oSb d.dist rel more be.good for 1sg \\

[Talking about her husband:] ‘yes older sibling, that (is the one) who is better for me’ [081110-008-CvNP.0178]

puri tu paling besar\\
anchovy-like.fish d.dist most be.big\\

‘that anchovy-like fish is the biggest’ [080927-003-Cv.0002]

Again, monovalent dynamic verbs differ from monovalent stative and bivalent verbs in that they are not directly modified with a grading ad verb. Instead they are modified with lebi banyak ‘(do s.th.) more’ to indicate comparative degree, as in the elicited example in ( Example_5.126 ), or with paling banyak ‘(do s.th.) most’ to indicate superlative degree, as in the elicited example in ( Example_5.127 ).

‘that anchovy-like fish is the biggest’
styleExampleTitle
Grading of monovalent dynamic verbs
styleExampleTitle

Dodo lebi banyak bertriak dari Agus\\
Dodo more many scream with Agus\\

‘Dodo screams more than Agus’ [Elicited BR130221.025]

Dodo paling banyak tertawa\\
Dodo most many scream\\

‘Dodo laughs most’ [Elicited BR130221.030]

With respect to the frequencies of the monovalent stative and bivalent verbs in comparative constructions, the data indicates a clear pattern, presented in Table_5.18. The vast majority of graded verbs are monovalent stative ones. The corpus contains 54 lebi-comparative constructions, formed with 22 different verbs. Of these, 77% are monovalent stative, accounting for 89% of the attested comparative constructions. In addition, the corpus contains 46 paling-superlative constructions, formed with 30 different verbs. Again, most of these verbs are monovalent stative (80%) which account for 83% of the superlative constructions. Cross-linguistically, this distributional pattern corresponds to the “prototypical comparative scheme” in which the parameter of comparison “is typically expressed by an adjective, in a language with a large open class of adjectives; or else by a stative verb (with an adjective-like meaning)”.
summary:
In predicative uses, monovalent stative and bivalent verbs can be graded with the adverbs lebi ‘more’ and paling ‘most’, which precede the verb, but monovalent dynamic and trivalent verbs are not directly graded this way. Instead, monovalent dynamic verbs take lebi banyak and paling banyak to express comparative and superlative degree.  

The corpus data show that graded verbs are overwhelmingly monovalent stative: they make up most lebi and paling constructions, and this distribution matches the cross-linguistic “prototypical comparative scheme,” where comparison is typically expressed by adjectives or stative verbs.

text:
Verbs are negated with tida ‘ neg ’ or tra ‘ neg ’. The negator bukang ‘ neg ’ also occurs in verbal clauses. However, it does not negate the verb as tida/tra ‘ neg ’ does. Instead, bukang ‘ neg ’ has scope over the entire proposition and expresses contrastive negation of that proposition as a whole (for details see § Para_13.1.2 ). This is demonstrated with trivalent kasi ‘give’ in ( Example_5.128 ), bivalent pake ‘use’ in ( Example_5.129 ), monovalent dynamic datang ‘come’ in ( Example_5.130 ), and monovalent stative baik ‘be good’ in ( Example_5.131 ). These examples also illustrate that both negators are used interchangeably (for more details on negation see § Para_13.1 ).

kaka su bilang de begitu, sa tra kasi ko jempol\\
oSb already say 3sg like.that 1sg neg give 2sg thumb\\

‘I (‘older sibling’) already told him like that, ``I won’t give you a thumbs up''' [081115-001a-Cv.0042]

The negator bukang also appears in verbal clauses, but unlike tida/tra it does not negate the verb itself; instead, it has scope over the whole proposition and expresses contrastive negation of that proposition.

text:
Papuan Malay syntactic causatives are monoclausal V 1V 2 constructions. A caus\-ative verb V 1, encodes the notion of cause, while the V 2 denotes the notion of effect. Two full verbs both of which are still used synchronically function as causative verbs, namely trivalent kasi ‘give’, with its short form kas, and bivalent biking ‘make’. Syntactic causatives have monovalent or bivalent bases, while causative constructions with trivalent verbs are unattested.

In kasi-causatives the V 2 can be bivalent or monovalent, while in biking-causatives the V 2 is always monovalent. (See § Para_11.2 for a detailed discussion of causative constructions.)

Causative constructions with kasi ‘give’ are presented in ( Example_5.132 ) to ( Example_5.134 ). The V 2 is bivalent masuk ‘enter’ in ( Example_5.132 ), monovalent dynamic bangung ‘wake up’ in ( Example_5.133 ), and stative sembu ‘be healed’ in ( Example_5.134 ). (For more details on kasi-causatives, see § Para_11.2.1.2.)

In causatives with biking ‘make’, the V 2 is always monovalent. Most often, the monovalent verb is stative, such as pusing ‘be dizzy, be confused’ in ( Example_5.135 ). However, biking-causatives can also be formed with non-agentive dynamic bases, such as tenggelam ‘sink’ in the elicited example in ( Example_5.136 ). If the causee is inanimate, or animate but helpless, the base can also be agentive dynamic, such as hidup ‘live’ in the elicited example in ( Example_5.137 ). (For more details on biking-causatives, see § Para_11.2.1.3; see also examples ( Example_11.55 ) and ( Example_11.57 ) in § Para_11.2.1.2, p. Example_11.55.)

Concerning the frequencies of mono- and bivalent verbs in causative constructions, the following pattern emerges. Most of the attested verb tokens in kasi- causative constructions are bivalent or monovalent dynamic ones, whereas the attested verbs in biking-causatives are always monovalent stative ones, as shown in Table_5.19. The corpus contains 478 kasi- causative constructions, formed with 81 different verbs. Most verbs in kasi-constructions are dynamic one (78%), including 48% bivalent and 22% monovalent dynamic verbs. Together the attested dynamic verbs account for 92% of the kasi-causatives. By contrast, biking-causatives are always formed with monovalent stative verbs. In all, the corpus contains 25 biking-causatives, formed with 16 different verbs.
summary:
Papuan Malay syntactic causatives are monoclausal V1V2 constructions in which a causative verb expresses cause and a second verb expresses effect. Two causative verbs are used synchronically: trivalent **kasi** ‘give’ (and its short form **kas**) and bivalent **biking** ‘make’; causative constructions with trivalent verbs are unattested.

In **kasi**-causatives, the V2 can be either bivalent or monovalent, while in **biking**-causatives V2 is always monovalent, usually stative. The corpus shows 478 **kasi**-causatives with 81 verbs, mostly dynamic, whereas **biking**-causatives are less frequent (25 tokens, 16 verbs) and always involve monovalent stative verbs.

Reciprocal constructions are formed by placing the reciprocity marker baku ‘recp’ before the verb, and they are attested with trivalent ceritra ‘tell’, bivalent gendong ‘hold’, and monovalent dynamic saing ‘compete’. Reciprocal constructions with monovalent stative verbs are not found.

The corpus shows 101 reciprocal constructions with 42 different verbs, and most of the verbs involved are bivalent (88%), which account for 94% of the reciprocal constructions.

text:
Papuan Malay has only two somewhat productive affixes, as discussed in Para_3, prefix ter- ‘ acl ’ and suffix - ang ‘ nmlz ’. Mono- and bivalent verbs can be prefixed with ter- ‘ acl ’ to derive verbs which denote accidental or unintentional actions or events. Examples are given in Table_5.21, such as bivalent angkat ‘lift’ and lempar ‘throw’, monovalent dynamic jatu ‘fall’, and stative lambat ‘be slow’ and sala ‘be wrong’. Likewise, mono- and bivalent verbs can be suffixed with- ang ‘ nmlz ’ to derive nouns, such as bivalent jual ‘sell’ and pake ‘use’, monovalent dynamic jalang ‘walk’ and libur ‘take vacation’, and stative pica ‘be broken’ and sial ‘be unfortunate’. Some lexemes suffixed with- ang ‘ nmlz ’ also function as verbs, such as jualang ‘merchandise, to sell’. Affixation of trivalent verbs is unattested. (For details on affixation with ter- ‘ acl ’ and- ang ‘ nmlz ’ see § Para_3.1.2 and § Para_3.1.3, respectively).

In the corpus, affixation of bivalent bases occurs much more often than that of monovalent bases, as shown in Table_5.22. Regarding prefix ter- ‘ acl ’, the corpus includes 43 lexemes derived from verbal bases with a total of 166 tokens. Most of them are bivalent verbs (88%), accounting for 92% of all ter-tokens. As for suffix- ang ‘ nmlz ’, the corpus contains 69 lexemes with verbal bases, with a total of 403 tokens. Again, most of the verbal bases are bivalent (90%), accounting for 89% of all- ang-tokens.
summary:
Papuan Malay has only two somewhat productive affixes: the prefix **ter-** and the suffix **-ang**. **ter-** attaches to mono- and bivalent verbs to form verbs expressing accidental or unintentional actions, while **-ang** attaches to mono- and bivalent verbs to form nouns, though some **-ang** forms can also function as verbs; affixation of trivalent verbs is unattested.  

In the corpus, affixation occurs much more often with bivalent than monovalent bases. For **ter-**, 43 lexemes and 166 tokens are found, with bivalent verbs making up most cases; for **-ang**, there are 69 lexemes and 403 tokens, again mostly from bivalent verbal bases.

text:
Tri-, bi-, and monovalent verbs have partially distinct and partially overlapping properties, which are summarized in Table_5.23 (in this table bi- and trivalent verbs are listed summarily in the column ``Valency of 2 or 3''). They are distinct from each other in terms of two main criteria, namely their valency and their function, which is mainly predicative. Related to the criterion on valency is the ability of verbs to occur in causative and reciprocal expressions and to be affixed. Therefore, Table_5.23 lists these characteristic under the label ``Valency''. The criterion of function has to do with the predicative ( pred ) and attributive ( attr ) uses of the verbs, their negation, and adverbial modification. Hence, Table_5.23 lists these characteristics under the label ``Function''.

In terms of valency, Papuan Malay has three verb classes, mono-, bi- and trivalent verbs. Related to the valency criterion is the ability of verbs to be used in causative constructions. All three verb types occur in causatives formed with kasi ‘give’. Most often, however, kasi-causatives are formed with bi- or trivalent verbs. By contrast, causative constructions with biking ‘make’ are typically formed with stative verbs; dynamic verbs are unattested in biking-causatives. Also related to the valency criterion is the ability of bi- and trivalent verbs to occur in reciprocal expressions. Monovalent dynamic verbs, by contrast, occur only rarely in such expressions, while reciprocal constructions with stative verbs are unattested. Finally, with respect to affixation, it is typically bivalent verbs that form the bases for lexemes prefixed with ter- or suffixed with -ang.

With respect to their function, all verbs are used predicatively, dynamic verbs much more often though, than stative verbs. In their predicate uses, all three verb types can be modified adverbially and all verbs are negated with tida/ tra ‘ neg ’. Less often, verbs have attributive function in noun phrases. Verb-via- juxtaposition modification most commonly applies to stative verbs, while modification with dynamic verbs typically involves verb-via-relative-clause modification. Related to their attributive uses is the intensification and grading of verbs. Typically, this applies to monovalent stative verbs, while intensification and grading of bivalent verbs occurs much less often. Monovalent dynamic and trivalent verbs are neither intensified nor graded.
summary:
Papuan Malay verbs show both shared and distinct properties across mono-, bi-, and trivalent classes, especially in terms of valency and function. Valency is reflected in their use in causative and reciprocal constructions and in affixation: all three verb types occur in kasi ‘give’ causatives, but bi- and trivalent verbs are most common, biking ‘make’ causatives are typically stative, and bi- and trivalent verbs are the main bases for certain affixed forms.  

Functionally, all verbs can be used predicatively, modified adverbially, and negated with tida/tra, though dynamic verbs are more common in predicative use. Attributive uses are less frequent and differ by verb type: stative verbs are more often modified by juxtaposition and are the main verbs that undergo intensification and grading, whereas dynamic monovalent and trivalent verbs do not.

text:
Papuan Malay has a large open class of adverbs, which modify constituents other than nouns. Their main function is to indicate aspect, frequency, affirmation and negation, modality, time, focus, and degree. Within the clause, the adverbs most commonly occur in prepredicate position. Unlike the other two open lexical classes of nouns and verbs, Papuan Malay adverbs are not used predicatively.

Cross-linguistically, note that in terms of their semantics and morphology, “adverbs are most closely related to adjectives, from which they are often derived”. With the restriction that Papuan Malay has a class of monovalent stative verbs instead of adjectives (see § Para_5.3.1 ), this observation also seems to apply to the Papuan Malay adverbs. First, a number of adverbs are related to monovalent stative verbs, such as the temporal ad verb dulu ‘first, in the past’ which is related to stative dulu ‘be prior’ (see § Para_5.4.5 ), or the focus ad verb pas ‘precisely’ which is related to stative pas ‘be exact’ (see § Para_5.4.6; see also § Para_5.14 ). Second, manner is expressed through stative verbs (see § Para_5.4.8 ). Third, reduplicated verbs can receive an adverbial reading due to an interpretational shift. Examples are taw taw ‘just now’ with its base taw ‘know’ (see § Para_5.4.5; see also § Para_4.2.2.8 ). In Papuan Malay this link with verbs extends to dynamic verbs, in that reduplicated dynamic verbs can also receive an adverbial reading. Examples are the modal adverbs kira kira ‘probably’ and taw taw ‘suddenly’ which are related to the respective dynamic verbs kira ‘think’ and taw ‘know’ (see § Para_5.4.4; see also § Para_5.14 ).

In addition to this prominent link with verbs, Papuan Malay adverbs are also related to nouns, although this link appears to be less prominent. First, a number of modal adverbs are historically derived from nouns by unproductive affixation with - nya ‘ 3possr ’. Examples are artinya ‘that means’ (literally ‘the meaning of’), katanya ‘it is being said’ (literally ‘the word of’), or maksutnya ‘that is to say’ (literally ‘the purpose of’). Second, reduplicated nouns can receive an adverbial reading due to an interpretational shift (see § Para_4.2.1.4 ).

The adverbs occur in different positions within the clause. They can take a prepredicate or postpredicate position, with the prepredicate position being the most common. There are also a fair number of adverbs which can occur in both positions. For the prepredicate adverbs two positions are possible, directly preceding the predicate and preceding the subject. Likewise, two positions are possible for the postpredicate adverbs, directly following the predicate and, in clauses with peripheral adjuncts, following the adjunct. Depending on their positions within the clause, the adverbs differ in terms of their semantic effect. Generally speaking, prepredicate adverbs which precede the subject have scope over the entire proposition. The semantic effect of prepredicate adverbs which directly precede the predicate and of postpredicate adverbs is more limited. On the whole, however, these distinctions are subtle, as shown with the temporal ad verb langsung ‘immediately’ in § Para_5.4.5.

The following sections describe the adverbs in terms of their positions within the clause and their overall semantic functions. Aspect adverbs are discussed in § Para_5.4.1, frequency adverbs in § Para_5.4.2, affirmation and negation adverbs in § Para_5.4.3, modal adverbs in § Para_5.4.4, temporal adverbs in § Para_5.4.5, focus adverbs in § Para_5.4.6, and degree adverbs in § Para_5.4.7. Papuan Malay does not have manner adverbs; instead, manner is expressed through stative verbs which always follow the main verb, as briefly discussed in § Para_5.4.8. Each of these sections includes a table which lists the different adverbs and indicates whether they take a prepredicate ( pre-pred ) and/or postpredicate ( post-pred ) position within the clause (empty cells signal unattested constituent combinations). The different positions are also illustrated with (near) contrastive examples. An investigation of the semantic effects encoded by these positions, however, is left for future research. Also left for future research is the question of which adverbs can co-occur and in which positions.

Following the description of the different types of adverbs, § Para_5.4.9 summarizes the main points of this section, especially with respect to the interplay between syntactic properties and functions of the adverbs.
summary:
Papuan Malay has a large class of adverbs that modify non-nominal constituents and mainly express aspect, frequency, affirmation/negation, modality, time, focus, and degree. They occur most often before the predicate, are not used predicatively, and can appear in prepredicate or postpredicate positions with subtle differences in scope.

The passage also notes that Papuan Malay adverbs are closely linked to verbs, especially monovalent stative verbs and reduplicated verbs, and less prominently to nouns through historical derivation and reduplication. Manner is not expressed by adverbs but by stative verbs that follow the main verb.

text:
Aspectual adverbs provide temporal information about the event or state denoted by the verb in terms of their “duration or completion”. Thereby they differ from the temporal adverbs which designate temporal points. The Papuan Malay aspectual adverbs are presented in Table_5.24.

Aspectual blum ‘not yet’ and masi ‘still’ have prospective meanings; that is, they point “forward to possible transitions in the future”, using Smessaert and ter Meulen’s ( Smessaert.2004) terminology. More specifically, blum ‘not yet’ indicates that the event or state denoted by the verb is not yet completed or has not yet occurred, while masi ‘still’ signals that the event or state is still continuing. Aspectual suda ‘already’, by contrast, has a retrospective meaning; that is, it marks “a realized transition in the past”, again employing Smessaert and ter Meulen’s ( Smessaert.2004) terminology ( suda ‘already’ is very often shortened to su). Besides, suda ‘already’ can signal imperative mood, in which case it occurs in clause-final position, as discussed in § Para_13.3. Progressive aspect is not encoded by an ad verb but with the existential verb ada ‘exist’; for expository reasons, however, the progressive marking function of ada ‘exist’ is discussed here (existential clauses are discussed in § Para_11.4 ).

The three adverbs always occur in prepredicate position, as shown in Table_5.24. This applies to their uses in verbal clauses, as in ( Example_5.141 ) and ( Example_5.142 ), and in nonverbal clauses, as in ( Example_5.145 ) to ( Example_5.147 ). Likewise, adverbially used ada ‘exist’ precedes the predicate, as shown in ( Example_5.143 ), ( Example_5.144 ), and ( Example_5.148 ).

In verbal predicate clauses, the aspectual adverbs and adverbially used ada ‘exist’ modify dynamic verbs, as in ( Example_5.141 ) and ( Example_5.143 ), or stative verbs as in ( Example_5.142 ) and ( Example_5.144 ).

The main adverbs are blum ‘not yet’ and masi ‘still’, which have prospective meanings, and suda ‘already’ (often shortened to su), which has a retrospective meaning and can also mark imperative mood in clause-final position. Progressive aspect is not expressed by an adverb but by the existential verb ada ‘exist’; all these forms occur in prepredicate position and can modify both verbal and nonverbal predicates.

text:
Frequency adverbs “typically indicate the number of times something happened” during a given time interval. The Papuan Malay frequency adverbs are listed in Table_5.25; they always occur in prepredicate position. In the corpus only biasanya ‘usually’ and perna ‘ever’ are attested in the clause-initial position; for the remaining frequency adverbs, their uses in this position were established by means of elicitation.

The prepredicate position of the frequency adverbs is illustrated in ( Example_5.149 ) to ( Example_5.152 ). The adverbs can directly precede the predicate, such as kadang kadang ‘sometimes’ in ( Example_5.149 ) or perna ‘ever’ in ( Example_5.151 ), or they can precede the subject, such as kadang( kadang) ‘sometimes’ in ( Example_5.150 ) or perna ‘ever’ in ( Example_5.152 ). These examples also show that frequency adverbs not only modify verbal predicates as in ( Example_5.149 ) to ( Example_5.151 ), but also nonverbal predicates as in ( Example_5.152 ). The semantics conveyed by the different positions have to do with scope.

styleExampleTitle

styleExampleTitle

yo, de kadang kadang terlalu, ini, egois\\

‘yes, she’s sometimes too, what’s-its-name, egoistic’ [081115-001a-Cv.0218/0220]

In the corpus, only **biasanya** ‘usually’ and **perna** ‘ever’ occur clause-initially, while other clause-initial uses were established through elicitation. These adverbs can appear before the predicate or before the subject, and they modify both verbal and nonverbal predicates, with the different positions affecting scope.

text:
The affirmation and negation adverbs listed in Table_5.26 indicate general affirmation, negation, or prohibition, and provide responses to polar questions (see also Para_13).

The four adverbs always take a prepredicate position. Affirmative yo ‘yes’ is always fronted, while the negative and prohibitive adverbs directly precede the predicate. Affirmative yo ‘yes’ is often realized as ya, and negative jangang ‘ neg.imp ’ is quite commonly shortened to jang. Examples are provided in ( Example_5.153 ) to ( Example_5.156 ): affirmation with yo ‘yes’ in ( Example_5.153 ), negation with interchangeably used tra ‘ neg ’ and tida ‘ neg ’ in ( Example_5.154 ), and with bukang ‘ neg ’ ( Example_5.155 ), and prohibition with jangang ‘ neg.imp ’ in ( Example_5.156 ). Negation and prohibition are discussed in more detail in § Para_13.1 and § Para_13.3.3, respectively.

All four occur before the predicate: affirmative **yo** ‘yes’ is fronted, while negative and prohibitive forms directly precede the predicate; **yo** is often realized as **ya**, and **jangang** ‘don’t’ is commonly shortened to **jang**.

text:
Modal adverbs “express the subjective evaluation of the speaker toward a state of affairs”. This includes “epistemic” adverbs which “denote the speaker’s attitude toward the truth, certainty or probability of the state or event” and “evaluative” adverbs which express “the speaker’s evaluative attitudes, i.e. judgments of preference for or desirability of a state or event”.

The Papuan Malay modal adverbs are presented in Table_5.27.

Most of them are historically derived by (unproductive) affixation (for details on affixation see § Para_3.1 ). All Papuan Malay modal adverbs take a pre-pred\-icate position. Besides the adverbs listed in Table_5.27, degree ad verb paling ‘most’ also has an epistemic function when it precedes the subject, as discussed in § Para_5.4.7.

The prepredicate position of the modal adverbs is demonstrated in ( Example_5.157 ) to ( Example_5.160 ). Typically, they precede the subject. This is illustrated with epistemic memang ‘indeed’ in ( Example_5.157 ) and pasti ‘definitely’ in ( Example_5.158 ), and with evaluative akirnya ‘finally’ in ( Example_5.159 ) and taw taw ‘suddenly’ in ( Example_5.160 ). Functioning at clause level, the epistemic adverbs introduce propositions which offer explanations and clarifications for the events depicted in the preceding discourse, while the evaluative adverbs provide an evaluation of the events described in the preceding discourse.

styleExampleTitle
Modal adverbs in prepredicate position preceding the subject
styleExampleTitle

kas tinggal, memang de nakal\\
give stay indeed 3sg be.mischievous\\

‘let it be, indeed, he is mischievous’ [081015-001-Cv.0027]

pasti de pulang\\
definitely 3sg go.home\\

‘ certainly, she’ll come home’ [081006-019-Cv.0010]

akirnya asap asap naik, langsung api menyala\\
finally rdp smoke ascend immediately fire flame\\

‘ finally smoke ascended, immediately the fire flared up’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0079]

taw taw orang itu tida keliatang\\
rdp know person d.dist neg be.visible\\

‘ suddenly that person wasn’t visible (any longer)’ [080922-002-Cv.0123]

While evaluative modal adverbs always precede the subject, most epistemic adverbs can take two prepredicate positions. Besides preceding the subject, as in ( Example_5.157 ) and ( Example_5.158 ), they can also directly precede the predicate. The exceptions are artinya ‘that means’ and maksutnya ‘that is to say’, both of which always precede the subject. This position directly preceding the predicate is illustrated with memang ‘indeed’ in ( Example_5.161 ) and with pasti ‘definitely’ in ( Example_5.162 ) (compare both examples with the examples in ( Example_5.157 ) and ( Example_5.158 ), respectively). Both examples also show that modal adverbs not only occur in verbal clauses as in ( Example_5.162 ), but also in nonverbal clauses, as in ( Example_5.161 ).

styleExampleTitle
Modal adverbs in prepredicate position preceding the predicate
styleExampleTitle

jangang ko singgung, tapi ini memang bukti\\
neg.imp 2sg offend but this indeed proof\\

[About problems with the local elections:] ‘don’t feel offended but this is indeed the proof’ [081011-024-Cv.0150]

tapi de pasti kasi swara\\
but 3sg definitely give voice\\

[About meeting strangers in remote areas:] ‘[most likely, he/she won’t know your name yet,] but he/she’ll definitely call (you)’ [080919-004-NP.0078]
summary: Modal adverbs in Papuan Malay express the speaker’s subjective evaluation of a state of affairs, including epistemic meanings such as certainty or probability and evaluative meanings such as preference or desirability. Most are historically derived by unproductive affixation and all occur in pre-predicate position; evaluative adverbs always precede the subject, while most epistemic adverbs can either precede the subject or directly precede the predicate, with *artinya* ‘that means’ and *maksudnya* ‘that is to say’ always preceding the subject. These adverbs can occur in both verbal and nonverbal clauses, and epistemic adverbs often introduce explanations or clarifications of previous discourse, whereas evaluative adverbs assess the events described.

text:
Temporal adverbs designate temporal points. Thereby they differ from aspectual adverbs which provide temporal information about the event or state denoted by the verb in terms of their completion or duration. The Papuan Malay temporal adverbs are listed in Table_5.28. Within the clause, almost all of them occur in prepredicate or in postpredicate position. The exceptions are baru ‘recently’ and baru baru ‘just now’ which only occur in prepredicate position. Three of the adverbs listed in Table_5.28 have dual word class membership with monovalent stative verbs: baru ‘recently’, dulu ‘be prior’, and skarang ‘now’ ( variation in word class membership is discussed in § Para_5.14 ).

Examples for the prepredicate position are given in ( Example_5.163 ) to ( Example_5.166 ), and for the postpredicate position in ( Example_5.167 ) to ( Example_5.170 ). The different meaning aspects conveyed by both positions are discussed in connection with the examples in ( Example_5.172 ) to ( Example_5.174 ).

In prepredicate position, the adverbs can directly precede the predicate, such as langsung ‘immediately’ in ( Example_5.163 ) and nanti ‘very soon’ in ( Example_5.165 ), or precede the subject, such as langsung ‘immediately’ in ( Example_5.164 ) and nanti ‘very soon’ in ( Example_5.166 ).

styleExampleTitle
Temporal adverbs in prepredicate position
styleExampleTitle

de langsung ke asrama polisi cari bapa\\
3sg immediately to dormitory police search father\\

‘he (went) immediately to the police dormitory to look for father’ [081011-022-Cv.0242]

wa, ko datang, langsung ko lapar?\\
wow! 2sg come immediately 2sg be.hungry\\

‘wow!, you come (here, and) immediately you’re hungry?’ [081110-002-Cv.0049]

dang ko nanti kena picaang\\
and 2sg very.soon hit splinter\\

‘[don’t (go down to the beach, (it’s) dirty,] and later you’ll run into broken glass and cans’ [080917-004-CvHt.0002]

nanti bapa mo brangkat, nanti bapa kas taw\\
very.soon father want leave very.soon father give know\\
sama bapa-ade pendeta\\
with uncle pastor\\

‘ very soon I (‘father’) will leave (and) then I (‘father’) will inform uncle pastor’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0339]

The postpredicate position is illustrated in ( Example_5.167 ) to ( Example_5.170 ). In clauses with peripheral adjuncts, the ad verb follows the predicate and precedes the adjunct, such as nanti ‘very soon’ in the elicited example in ( Example_5.167 ) and langsung ‘immediately’ in ( Example_5.169 ). Clauses, in which the temporal ad verb follows the peripheral adjunct are either ungrammatical, such as nanti ‘very soon’ in the elicited examples in ( Example_5.168 ), or only marginally grammatical such as langsung ‘immediately’ in the elicited contrastive examples in ( Example_5.170 ).

styleExampleTitle
Temporal adverbs in postpredicate position
styleExampleTitle

tong pergi nanti ke Sarmi\\
1pl go very.soon to Sarmi\\

‘we’ll go very soon’ to Sarmi’ [Elicited MY131113.001]

* tong pergi ke Sarmi nanti\\
1pl come to Sarmi very.soon\\

Intended reading: ‘we’ll go to Sarmi very soon’ [Elicited MY131113.002]

tak!, masuk langsung di bawa meja sana\\

bang! enter at bottom table l.dist immediately\\

Intended reading: ‘whump!, (the kid) went under the table over there immediately’ [Elicited MY131113.003]

The meaning aspects conveyed by the different positions of the temporal adverbs have to do with scope. This is demonstrated with langsung ‘immediately’ in three (near) contrastive examples: the prepredicate position following the subject is shown in ( Example_5.171 ), the prepredicate position preceding the subject in ( Example_5.172 ), and the postpredicate position in ( Example_5.173 ).

styleExampleTitle
Positions and scope of temporal adverbs
styleExampleTitle

bapa langsung diam\\
father immediately be.quiet\\

‘the gentleman was immediately quiet’ [080917-010-CvEx.0186]

langsung dong diam\\
immediately 3pl be.quiet\\

‘ immediately they were quiet’ [080922-003-Cv.0085]

bapa de diam langsung\\
father 3sg be.quiet immediately\\

‘the gentleman was quiet immediately’ [080917-010-CvEx.0191]

Only one temporal ad verb has clear distinct meanings depending on its positions, namely dulu ‘first, in the past’. Prepredicate dulu translates with ‘in the past’, whereas postpredicate dulu translates with ‘first’, as shown in ( Example_5.174 ).

styleExampleTitle
Temporal dulu ‘first, in the past’ in clause-initial and postpredicate positions
styleExampleTitle

dulu kitong pu orang-tua itu tida bisa\\
first 1pl poss parent d.dist neg be.able\\
berhubungang dulu\\
have.sexual.intercourse first\\

‘ in the past our parents couldn’t have sex first (before getting married)’ [081110-006-CvEx.0012]

Temporal baru ‘recently’ and baru baru ‘just now’ only occur in prepredic\-ate position, as in ( Example_5.175 ) and ( Example_5.176 ). While baru ‘recently’ directly precedes the predicate, baru baru ‘just now’ precedes the subject.

styleExampleTitle
Temporal baru ‘recently’ and baru baru ‘just now’ in prepredicate position only
styleExampleTitle

kariawang dong baru lewat\\
employee 3pl recently pass.by\\

‘the employees recently walked by’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0830]

baru baru de masuk ruma-sakit\\
