‘ just now, he got into hospital’ [081115-001a-Cv.0070]
summary: Temporal adverbs in Papuan Malay mark temporal points and differ from aspectual adverbs, which describe completion or duration. Most can occur either before or after the predicate, but *baru* ‘recently’ and *baru baru* ‘just now’ are restricted to prepredicate position, and *dulu* changes meaning by position: prepredicate *dulu* means ‘in the past,’ while postpredicate *dulu* means ‘first.’ The passage also notes that position affects scope, especially for *langsung* ‘immediately,’ which can occur before the subject, directly before the predicate, or after the predicate.

text:
Focus adverbs indicate “an accentual peak or stress which is used to contrast or compare [ an] item either explicitly or implicitly with a set of alternatives”. That is, focus adverbs highlight information and signal some kind of restriction, thereby adding emphasis to an utterance. Hence, they are also known as “emphatic” adverbs. In Papuan Malay, almost all focus adverbs take a prepredicate position, as shown in Table_5.29. The exceptions are juga ‘also’, lagi ‘again, also’, and saja ‘just’ which take a postpredicate position. While the latter two only occur in postpredicate position, juga ‘also’ also takes a prepredicate position.

The prepredicate position of the focus adverbs is illustrated in ( Example_5.177 ) to ( Example_5.181 ). Focus adverbs typically precede the subject. This is shown with cuma ‘just’ in ( Example_5.177 ) and hanya ‘only’ in ( Example_5.179 ). Most of them can also take a prepredicate position directly preceding the predicate; the exceptions are apalagi ‘moreover’, kecuali ‘except’ and kususnya ‘especially’ which always precede the subject. The position directly preceding the predicate is shown with cuma ‘just’ in ( Example_5.178 ) and hanya ‘only’ in ( Example_5.180 ), respectively. Another exception is prepredicate juga ‘also’, which always directly precedes the predicate, as in ( Example_5.181 ); for its postpredi\-cate uses see ( Example_5.182 ). These examples also illustrate that focus adverbs not only modify verbal predicates, as in ( Example_5.177 ), and ( Example_5.179 ) to ( Example_5.181 ), but also nonverbal predicates, such as the numeral predicate dua ‘two’ in ( Example_5.178 ).

styleExampleTitle
Focus adverbs in clause-initial and prepredicate positions
styleExampleTitle

baru baru de su turung, cuma de su pulang\\
rdp recently 3sg already descend just 3sg already go.home\\

[Reply to an interlocutor who is looking for someone:] ‘just now he already came by, (it’s) just (that) he already went home’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0554]

tapi [sa pu alpa] cuma dua\\
but 1sg poss be.absent just two\\

[About unexcused school absences:] ‘[I was absent many times,] but I had just two (official) absences’ (Lit. ‘my being absent was just two’) [081023-004-Cv.0014]

jadi kalo nika di kantor itu begitu, hanya dong bilang\\
so if marry at office d.dist like.that only 3pl say\\
nika sipil\\
marry be.civil\\

[About marrying civically:] ‘so if (one) marries at the office it’s like that, only (that) they call (it) ``marrying civically''' [081110-007-CvPr.0030]

prempuang hanya duduk makang pinang saja\\
woman only sit eat betel.nut just\\

‘the girls just sit (around) and eat betel nut’ [081014-007-CvEx.0045]

Ise dong juga duduk di sana\\
Ise 3pl also sit at l.dist \\

‘Ise and the others are also sitting over there’ [081025-009b-Cv.0075]

Three focus adverbs take a postpredicate position, namely juga ‘also’, lagi ‘again, also’, and saja ‘just’. This is demonstrated with the examples in ( Example_5.182 ) to ( Example_5.184 ). (As shown in ( Example_5.181 ), juga ‘also’ can also take a prepredicate position.) In clauses with peripheral adjuncts, the three adverbs can directly follow the predicate, such as the first juga ‘also’ token in ( Example_5.182 ) and lagi ‘again, also’ in ( Example_5.183 ). Alternatively, they can follow the adjunct, such as the second juga ‘also’ token in ( Example_5.182 ) and lagi ‘again, also’ in ( Example_5.184 ). Focus ad verb saja ‘just’ has the same distributional properties as lagi ‘again, also’. The semantics expressed with the different positions again have to do with scope.

styleExampleTitle
Focus adverbs in postpredicate position
styleExampleTitle

dari sini deng Papua-Lima, kembali juga deng Papua-Lima\\
from l.prox with Papua-Lima return also with Papua-Lima\\
ke sana deng Papua-Lima kembali deng Papua-Lima juga\\
to l.dist with Papua-Lima return with Papua-Lima also\\

‘(I’ll leave) from here with the Papua-Lima (ship) and return also with the Papua-Lima (ship) (I’ll get) over there with the Papua-Lima (ship and) return with the Papua-Lima (ship) also’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0483/0493]

de kembali lagi ke Papua\\
3sg return again to Papua\\

‘he came back again to Papua’ [081025-004-Cv.0008]

sa pulang ke Waim lagi\\
1sg go.home to Waim again\\

‘I went home to Waim again’ [081015-005-NP.0051]
summary: Focus adverbs in Papuan Malay signal emphasis by highlighting an item against alternatives, and they usually occur in prepredicate position, often before the subject or directly before the predicate. The main exceptions are *juga* ‘also’, *lagi* ‘again, also’, and *saja* ‘just’, which occur postpredicatively; *juga* can also appear prepredicatively, while *apalagi* ‘moreover’, *kecuali* ‘except’, and *kususnya* ‘especially’ always precede the subject. These adverbs can modify both verbal and nonverbal predicates, and their position affects scope.

text:
Degree adverbs “describe the extent of a characteristic”, that is, they “emphasize that a characteristic is either greater or less than some typical level”. Amplifiers or intensifiers “increase intensity”, while diminishers or downtoners “decrease the effect of the modified item” ( Biber.2002).

The Papuan Malay degree adverbs are presented in Table_5.30. The table includes four amplifiers/intensifiers and two diminishers/downtoners. Most of the adverbs occur in prepredicate position. The exception is skali ‘very’, which takes a postpredicate position. Two of the amplifiers modify gradable verbs, namely lebi ‘more’ and paling ‘most’. The former signals comparative degree while the latter marks superlative degree.

The four amplifiers modify monovalent stative and bivalent verbs, as discussed in § Para_5.3.4 and § Para_5.3.5 (comparative constructions are discussed in § Para_11.5 ). The amplifiers occur in prepredicate position, following the subject, such as paling ‘most’ in ( Example_5.185 ). Furthermore, paling ‘most’ can precede the subject, although not very often. In this clause-initial position it functions as an epistemic modal ad verb which has scope over the entire proposition, as in ( Example_5.186 ) (modal adverbs are discussed in § Para_5.4.4 ).

styleExampleTitle
Amplifier degree adverbs
styleExampleTitle

ana ini paling bodo\\
child d.prox most be.stupid\\

‘this child is most stupid’ [081011-005-Cv.0035]

waktu saya bilang sa mo biking acara, paling sa tra\\
time 1sg say 1sg want make ceremony most 1sg neg \\
kerja, sa sebagey kepala acara\\
work 1sg as head ceremony\\

‘when I say, I want to hold a festivity, most likely I won’t (have to) work, I’ll be the head of the festivity’ [080919-004-NP.0068]

The intensifier terlalu ‘too’ also occurs in prepredicate position, as in ( Example_5.187 ). By contrast, skali ‘very’ takes a postpredicate position, as illustrated in ( Example_5.188 ) to ( Example_5.190 ). In clauses with peripheral adjuncts, as in ( Example_5.189 ), skali ‘very’ follows the predicate, such as enak ‘be pleasant’ in ( Example_5.189 ). Clauses in which skali ‘very’ follows the peripheral adjunct, as in the elicited example in ( Example_5.190 ), are ungrammatical.

styleExampleTitle
Intensifier degree adverbs
styleExampleTitle

a, ko terlalu bodo\\
ah! 2sg too be.stupid\\

‘ah, you are too stupid’ [080917-003a-CvEx.0009]

ade bongso jadi ko sayang dia skali e?\\
ySb youngest.offspring so 2sg love 3sg very eh\\

‘(your) youngest sibling, so you love her very much, eh?’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0302]

kamu orang-tua enak skali di sana\\
2pl parent be.pleasant very at l.dist \\

‘you, the parents, (have) very pleasant (lives) over there’ (Lit. ‘you are very pleasant’) [081115-001a-Cv.0106]

* kamu orang-tua enak di sana skali\\
2pl parent pleasant at l.dist very\\

Intended reading: ‘you, the parents, (have) very pleasant (lives) over there’ [Elicited MY131113.004]

The diminishers agak ‘rather’ and hampir ‘almost’ also occur in prepredicate position, as illustrated in ( Example_5.191 ) to ( Example_5.194 ). Always directly preceding the verb, agak ‘rather’ modifies stative verbs, as in ( Example_5.191 ). Clauses in which agak ‘rather’ precedes the subject, as in the elicited example in ( Example_5.192 ), are ungrammatical. Diminisher hampir ‘almost’ typically modifies dynamic verbs, as in ( Example_5.193 ) and ( Example_5.194 ). According to one consultant, some Papuan Malay speakers also use hampir ‘almost’ to modify stative verbs. Much more often though they employ a construction with su mulay ‘already start to’ as in ( Footnote_Example_5.1 ) below:
-5pt

baru kita pergi skola, suda mulay sembu\\
and.then 1pl go school already start be.healed \\
[After an accident:] ‘and then we went (back) to school, (our wounds) were almost healed’ (Lit. ‘ already started to be healed’) [081014-012-NP.0005]\\

The ad verb can directly precede the predicate, as in the elicited example in ( Example_5.193 ), or precede the subject, as in ( Example_5.194 ). In the corpus, hampir ‘almost’ always occurs in the latter position, where the ad verb has scope over the entire proposition.

styleExampleTitle
Diminisher/downtoner degree adverbs
styleExampleTitle

sa su agak besar\\
1sg already rather be.big\\

[About the speaker’s childhood:] ‘I was already rather big’ [080922-008-CvNP.0025]

* agak sa su besar\\
rather 1sg already be.big\\

Intended reading: ‘I was already rather big’ [Elicited MY131113.006]

dong hampir bunu bapa\\
3pl almost kill father\\

‘they almost killed (my) father’ [Elicited MY131113.005]

hampir dong bunu bapa\\
almost 3pl kill father\\

‘(it) almost (happened that) they killed (my) father’ [081011-022-Cv.0210]
summary: Papuan Malay has four amplifier/intensifier degree adverbs and two diminishers/downtoners. Most occur in prepredicate position, but *skali* ‘very’ is postpredicate; *lebi* ‘more’ marks comparative degree and *paling* ‘most’ marks superlative degree, though *paling* can also occur clause-initially as an epistemic modal adverb. The diminishers *agak* ‘rather’ and *hampir* ‘almost’ normally precede the verb, with *agak* modifying stative verbs and *hampir* typically modifying dynamic verbs, sometimes with clause-initial placement giving scope over the whole proposition.

text:
Papuan Malay does not have manner adverbs. Instead, manner is expressed through stative verbs, as shown in ( Example_5.195 ) to ( Example_5.200 ). The modifying stative verbs always take a postpredicate position. In ( Example_5.195 ), for instance, postpredicate stative kras ‘be harsh’ modifies stative sakit ‘be sick’, and in ( Example_5.198 ) trus ‘be continuous’ modifies tatap dia ‘observe him’. In verbal clauses with peripheral adjuncts, the modifying stative verb can directly follow the predicate as in ( Example_5.199 ), or follow the adjunct, as in ( Example_5.200 ).

baru satu kali sa sakit kras\\
and.then one time 1sg be.sick be.harsh\\

‘but then one time I was badly sick’ [080922-008-CvNP.0009]

e, kam mandi cepat suda!\\
hey! 2pl bathe be.fast already\\

‘hey, you bathe quickly!’ [080917-008-NP.0128]

dong dua lari trus\\
3pl two run be.continuous\\

[About a motorbike trip:] ‘the two of them drove continuously’ [081015-005-NP.0011]

langsung sa tatap dia trus\\
immediately 1sg gaze.at 3sg be.continuous\\

‘immediately I gazed at him continuously’ [081006-035-CvEx.0071]

de buka trus siang malam\\
3sg open be.continuous day night\\

[About opening hours of an office] ‘it is open continuously day and night’ [081005-001-Cv.0003]

terendam di air trus\\
be.soaked at water be.continuous\\

[About a motorbike that got stuck in a river:] ‘[(the motorbike) is still there,] (it) is immersed in water continuously’ [081008-003-Cv.0026]
summary: Papuan Malay does not use manner adverbs; instead, manner is expressed by stative verbs. These modifying stative verbs always occur after the predicate, and in clauses with peripheral adjuncts they may follow the predicate directly or come after the adjunct.

text:
The Papuan Malay adverbs take different positions within the clause, that is, they can occur in prepredicate or in postpredicate position. The most common position, however, is the prepredicate one. There are also a fair number of adverbs which can occur in both positions.

For the prepredicate adverbs two positions are attested, one directly preceding the predicate and one preceding the subject. A fair number of prepredicate adverbs can occur in both positions. Likewise, for the postpredicate adverbs two positions are attested, one directly following the predicate and, in clauses with peripheral adjuncts, one following the adjunct. Most postpredicate adverbs can occur in both positions. In terms of their functions, the adverbs designate aspect, frequency, affirmation and negation, modality, time, focus, and degree; manner is expressed through stative verbs in postpredicate position.

Listed according to their semantic functions, the adverbs have the following distributional preferences.

enumerate

Aspect adverbs

styleIiI
They only occur in prepredicate position, directly preceding the predicate.
styleIiI

Frequency adverbs

styleIiI
They only occur in prepredicate position where they directly precede the predicate or the subject.
styleIiI

Affirmation and negation adverbs

styleIiI
They always occur in a predicate position. The affirmation ad verb always precedes the subject, while the three negation adverbs directly precede the predicate.
styleIiI

Modal adverbs

styleIiI
All epistemic and evaluative adverbs take a prepredicate position, preceding the subject. Besides, most of the epistemic adverbs can also directly precede the predicate; the exceptions are artinya ‘that means’ and maksutnya ‘that is to say’ which always precede the subject.
styleIiI

Temporal adverbs

styleIiI
All but two can occur in pre- or in postpredicate position. In prepredicate position, the adverbs can directly precede the predicate or the subject. In postpredicate position, they always follow the predicate and, in clauses with peripheral adjuncts, precede the adjunct. Two adverbs only occur in prepredicate position, namely baru ‘recently’ and baru baru ‘just now’.
styleIiI

Focus adverbs

styleIiI
All but three only occur in prepredicate position where they can directly precede the predicate or the subject. The exceptions are juga ‘also’, lagi ‘again, also’, and saja ‘just’, which take a postpredicate position. While lagi ‘again, also’, and saja ‘just’ only occur in postpredicate position, juga ‘also’ also takes a prepredicate position. In postpredicate position, the three adverbs can either directly follow the predicate or, in clauses with peripheral adjuncts, follow the adjunct.
styleIiI

Degree adverbs

styleIiI
All but one only take a prepredicate position, where most of them directly precede the predicate. The exception is hampir ‘almost’ which can also precede the subject. The one degree ad verb which is unattested in prepredicate position is skali ‘very’. It only occurs in postpredicate position, directly following the predicate.
styleIiI
enumerate

These distributional preferences are summarized in Table_5.31.

As for those adverbs which can take more than one position within the clause, the semantic distinctions conveyed by the different positions have to do with scope. Overall, however, these distinctions are subtle and require further investigation.

Papuan Malay does not have manner adverbs. Instead, manner is expressed with monovalent stative verbs which always take a postpredicate position.
summary:
Papuan Malay adverbs may occur either before or after the predicate, with prepredicate placement being most common. Their position depends partly on semantic class: aspect, frequency, most modality and degree adverbs are mainly prepredicate, while affirmation/negation are predicate-adjacent, and some temporal and focus adverbs can appear in both positions.

For adverbs that allow more than one position, the differences in meaning are mainly matters of scope and are subtle. The language does not have manner adverbs; instead, manner is expressed by monovalent stative verbs in postpredicate position.

text:
The Papuan Malay personal pronoun system distinguishes singular and plural numbers and three persons; the personal pronouns do not mark case, clusivity, gender, or politeness. Referring to animate and inanimate entities, they allow the unambiguous identification of their referents. They do so by signaling not only the person-number values of their referents, but also their definiteness.

The Papuan Malay personal pronouns are presented in Table_5.32.

Each personal pronoun, except for 2sg, has at least one long and one short form. The use of the long and short pronoun forms does not mark grammatical distinctions but represents speaker preferences. These distributional preferences are discussed in detail in § Para_6.1.1.

The Papuan Malay personal pronouns have the following distributional properties:

enumerate

Substitution for noun phrases (pronominal uses) (§ Para_6.1 ).

Modification with demonstratives, locatives, numerals, quantifiers, prepositional phrases, and/or relative clauses (pronominal uses) (§ Para_6.1 ).

Co-occurrence with noun phrases (adnominal uses): n/np pro (§ Para_6.2 ).

enumerate

Personal pronouns are distinct from other word classes such as nouns (§ Para_5.2 ) and demonstratives (§ Para_5.6 ) in terms of the following distributional properties:

enumerate

Personal pronouns are distinct from nouns in that personal pronouns (a) very commonly modify nouns, while nouns do not modify personal pronouns, (b) are modified with numerals or quantifiers in posthead position, while with nouns the modifying numerals/quantifiers can also occur in prehead position, and (c) only designate the possessor in adnominal possessive constructions, while nouns can also express the possessum.

Unlike demonstratives, personal pronouns (a) express person and number, (b) signal definiteness, while demonstratives indicate specificity, According to, definiteness indicates that “an np has [...] a referent uniquely identifiable to the hearer”. Hence, the hearer is expected to be in a position to identify the referent. Specificity, by contrast, signals that “the speaker is referring to a particular instance of an entity as opposed to any instance of it”. That is, the identifiability of the referent is not presupposed. Instead, the speaker makes the entity under discussion identifiable to the hearer by pointing out “a particular instance of an entity” among other possible referents ( Andrews.2007). (See also.) and (c) cannot be stacked.

enumerate

The personal pronouns have pronominal and adnominal uses. This is illustrated with two examples. The utterance in ( Example_5.201 ) demonstrates the pronominal uses of short sa ‘ 1sg ’ and long dia ‘ 3sg ’, while the example in ( Example_5.202 ) shows the adnominal uses of short dong ‘ 3pl ’. The personal pronouns are discussed in detail in Para_6.

ana itu sa paling sayang dia tu ana itu\\
child d.dist 1sg most love 3sg d.dist child d.dist \\

‘that child, I love her ( emph ) most, that child’ [081011-023-Cv.0097]

Natanael dong menang\\
Natanael 3pl win\\

[About a volleyball game:] ‘ Natanael and his friends won’ [081109-001-Cv.0002]
summary:
Papuan Malay personal pronouns distinguish singular vs. plural and three persons, but they do not mark case, clusivity, gender, or politeness. They identify referents by person-number and definiteness, and most pronouns have both long and short forms whose use reflects speaker preference rather than grammatical meaning.

The pronouns can be used pronominally, modified by various elements, or adnominally with noun phrases. They differ from nouns and demonstratives in their distribution: they commonly modify nouns, only express the possessor in possessive constructions, encode definiteness rather than specificity, and cannot be stacked.

text:
Papuan Malay has a two-term demonstrative system: proximal ini ‘ d.prox ’ and distal itu ‘ d.dist ’, together with their reduced fast-speech forms ni ‘ d.prox ’ and tu ‘ d.dist ’. As deictic expressions they orient the hearers and signal specificity. That is, they draw the hearers’ attention to particular occurrences of an entity in the surrounding situation or in the discourse. While ini ‘ d.prox ’ indicates proximity of this entity, itu ‘ d.dist ’ signals its distance – in spatial and in nonspatial terms.

Papuan Malay demonstratives have the following distributional properties:

enumerate

Co-occurrence with noun phrases (adnominal uses): n / np dem (§ Para_5.6.1 ).

Substitution for noun phrases (pronominal uses) (§ Para_5.6.2 ).

Modification with relative clauses (pronominal uses (§ Para_5.6.2 ).

Co-occurrence with verbs or adverbs (adverbial uses) (§ Para_5.6.3 ).

Stacking of demonstratives: dem dem and n dem dem (§ Para_5.6.4 ).

enumerate

Demonstratives are distinct from other word classes such as personal pronouns (§ Para_5.5 ) and locatives (§ Para_5.7 ) in terms of the following syntactic properties:

enumerate

Demonstratives are distinct from personal pronouns, in that demonstratives (a) have adverbial uses, (b) can be stacked, (c) can take the possessum slot in adnominal possessive constructions, and (d) signal specificity, while personal pronouns express definiteness. Concerning the semantic distinctions between the notion of definiteness and the notion of specificity see Footnote Footnote_5.17 in § Para_5.5 (p. Footnote_5.17).

Contrasting with locatives, demonstratives (a) are employed as independent nominals in unembedded noun phrases, (b) occur in adnominal possessive constructions either as the possessor or the possessum, and (c) can be stacked.

enumerate

The adnominal uses of the demonstratives are discussed in § Para_5.6.1, their pronominal uses in § Para_5.6.2, their adverbial uses in § Para_5.6.3, and stacking of demonstratives in § Para_5.6.4. A full discussion of the Papuan Malay demonstratives is presented in § Para_7.1.
summary:
Papuan Malay has a two-term demonstrative system, with proximal **ini/ni** and distal **itu/tu**, which function deictically to direct attention to specific entities in the situation or discourse. **Ini** marks proximity and **itu** marks distance in both spatial and nonspatial terms.

These demonstratives can occur as noun modifiers, stand alone as pronouns, modify relative clauses, co-occur with verbs or adverbs, and be stacked. They are distinguished from personal pronouns and locatives by properties such as adverbial use, stacking, participation in possessive constructions, and their role in signaling specificity rather than definiteness.

text:
Adnominally used demonstratives occur in posthead position at the right periphery of the noun phrase. That is, all noun phrase constituents occur to the left of the demonstrative, with the demonstrative having scope over the entire noun phrase as illustrated in ( Example_5.203 ) to ( Example_5.205 ). Constituents occurring to the right of the demonstratives such as liar ‘be wild’ in ( Example_5.206 ) are not part of the noun phrase: liar ‘be wild’ is a clausal predicate. The examples in ( Example_5.203 ) and ( Example_5.204 ) show that the demonstratives signal specificity (and not definiteness). The noun phrase tanta dia itu ‘that aunt’ (literally ‘that she aunt’) designates a specific and definite referent with distal itu ‘ d.dist ’ indicating specificity while adnominally used dia ‘ 3sg ’ signals definiteness (§ Para_5.5 ). By contrast, the noun phrase ana kecil satu ini ‘this particular small child’ in ( Example_5.204 ) denotes a specific but indefinite referent with proximal ini ‘ d.prox ’ again indicating specificity while posthead satu ‘one’ signals indefiniteness (see also § Para_5.9.4 ).

styleExampleTitle

styleExampleTitle

Wili ko jangang gara gara tanta dia itu!\\

and.then child be.small one d.prox 3sg neg draw\\

‘ because this pig is wild’ [080919-004-NP.0019]

Demonstratives can also modify constituents other than nouns, namely personal pronouns as in ( Example_5.207 ), interrogatives as in ( Example_5.208 ), or locatives as in ( Example_5.209 ).

styleExampleTitle
Posthead demonstratives: Modifying personal pronouns, interrogatives, or locatives
styleExampleTitle

ko itu manusia yang tra taw bicara temang\\

‘ you ( emph ) are a human being who doesn’t know how to talk (badly about) friends’ [081115-001a-Cv.0245]

ana laki laki ini de mo ke mana ni\\

‘this boy, where ( emph ) does he want to (go)?’ [080922-004-Cv.0017]

summary: Adnominal demonstratives in this language occur after the noun phrase, at the right edge, where they take scope over the whole noun phrase; anything to their right is not part of the noun phrase but a clausal predicate. The examples show that these demonstratives mark specificity rather than definiteness: distal forms can indicate specific definite referents, while proximal forms can mark specific but indefinite referents. Demonstratives can also modify personal pronouns, interrogatives, and locatives.

text:
In their pronominal uses, the demonstratives stand for noun phrases, as illustrated in ( Example_5.210 ) to ( Example_5.215 ). They occur in all syntactic positions within the clause. In ( Example_5.210 ), a demonstrative takes the subject slot, in ( Example_5.211 ) the direct object slot, and in ( Example_5.212 ) the oblique object slot.

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses in argument position
styleExampleTitle

yo, itu mo putus\\
yes d.dist want break\\

[About redirecting a river for a street building project:] ‘yes, it (the river) is going to get dispersed’ [081006-033-Cv.0064]

ko suka makang ini?\\
2sg like eat d.prox \\

[About fried bananas:] ‘do you like to eat these?’ [081006-023-CvEx.0071-0072]

dong percaya sama itu\\
3pl trust to d.dist \\

[About believing in evil spirits:] ‘they believe in those’ [081006-023-CvEx.0001]

In their pronominal uses, the demonstratives can be modified with relative clauses, as in the elicited example in ( Example_5.213 ).

styleExampleTitle
Modification of pronominally used demonstratives with relative clauses
styleExampleTitle

sa pili ini yang mera, ade pili itu yang\\
1sg choose d.prox rel be.red ySb choose d.dist rel \\
warna puti\\
color be.white\\

[About buying new shirts:] ‘I chose this (one) which is red, (my) younger sibling chose that (one) which is (of) white color’ [Elicited MY131119.004]

Pronominally used demonstratives also occur in adnominal possessive constructions (see Para_9). They can designate the possessor as in ( Example_5.214 ) or the possessum as in ( Example_5.215 ).

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses in adnominal possessive constructions
styleExampleTitle

bapa masi kenal ini pu muka?\\

‘do you (‘father’) still know this (one)’s face?’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1123]

They may also be modified by relative clauses and occur in adnominal possessive constructions, where they can refer either to the possessor or to the possessum.

text:
In their adverbial uses, the demonstratives co-occur with verbs as in pikir ni ‘think ( emph )’ in ( Example_5.216 ) or with adverbs as in pasti tu ‘exactly ( emph )’ in ( Example_5.217 ).

de pikir ni, dong ribut apa ka\\
3sg think d.prox 3pl trouble what or\\

‘he thought ( emph ), ``what are they troubled about?''' [081014-005-Cv.0036]

yo, brita pasti tu yang sa bilang\\
yes new definitely d.dist rel 1sg say\\

‘yes, the news are exactly ( emph ) as I told (you)’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0767]
summary: The passage notes that demonstratives can be used adverbially and may co-occur with verbs, as in *pikir ni* ‘think (emph)’, or with adverbs, as in *pasti tu* ‘exactly (emph)’. The examples show these demonstratives functioning as emphatic elements in the clause.

text:
Papuan Malay also allows the stacking of demonstratives. Typically, only identical demonstratives are stacked, as in ( Example_5.218 ) and ( Example_5.219 ). To some degree, however, non-identical demonstratives can also be stacked, as shown in ( Example_5.220 ) and ( Example_5.221 ). Juxtaposed ini ni ‘ d.prox d.prox ’ and itu tu ‘ d.dist d.dist ’ are not taken as instances of partial reduplication. As discussed in § Para_4.1.2, partial reduplication of the stems ini ‘ d.prox ’ and itu ‘ d.dist ’ should result in the reduplicated forms in ini ‘ d.prox d.prox’ and it itu ‘ d.dist d.dist ’, respectively. Therefore, ini ni ‘ d.prox d.prox ’ and itu tu ‘ d.dist d.dist ’ are taken as instances of demonstrative stacking. Reduplication of demonstratives does occur, however, as discussed in § Para_4.2.5.2.

In ( Example_5.218 ), short proximal ni ‘ d.prox ’ modifies the pronominally used long proximal demonstrative, such that `` dem dem ''. In ( Example_5.219 ), short distal tu ‘ d.dist ’ modifies a nested noun phrase with the adnominally used long distal demonstrative, such that ``[[ n dem ] dem ]''.

ada segala macang tulang dia buang [ ini ni]\\
exist all variety bone 3sg throw(.away) d.prox d.prox \\

‘there were all kinds of bones, he threw away these very (ones)’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0101]

waktu kitorang masuk di [[ ruma itu] tu] \\
when 1pl go.in at house d.dist d.dist \\

‘when we moved into that very house, ’ [081006-022-CvEx.0167]

While unattested in the corpus, speakers do allow one combination of non-identical demonstrative stacking in elicitation. Acceptable is the order of proximal ini ‘ d.prox ’ followed by short distal itu ‘ d.dist ’, as shown in the elicited example in ( Example_5.220 ). The reverse order is not permitted by speakers even in elicitation, as illustrated in ( Example_5.221 ). At this point in the research on Papuan Malay, however, the semantics of `` n ini tu'' constructions as compared to `` n ini ni''' and `` n itu tu'' constructions remain uncertain.

styleExampleTitle
Non-identical stacked demonstratives The elicited examples are based on the example in ( Example_7.23 ) in § Para_7.1.2.3 (p. Example_7.23).
styleExampleTitle

orang ini tu percaya sama Tuhang Yesus\\
person d.prox d.dist trust to God Jesus\\

‘ that person here believes in God Jesus’ [Elicited BR111017.009]

* orang itu ni percaya sama Tuhang Yesus\\
person d.dist d.prox trust to God Jesus\\

Intended reading: ‘ this person there believes in God Jesus’ [Elicited BR111017.010]
summary: Papuan Malay allows demonstrative stacking, most often with identical demonstratives such as ini ni ‘d.prox d.prox’ and itu tu ‘d.dist d.dist’, which are analyzed as stacking rather than partial reduplication. Non-identical stacking is only marginally accepted: speakers allow proximal ini followed by distal itu, but not the reverse order. The semantics of these non-identical stacked demonstratives remain uncertain.

text:
Papuan Malay has a distance oriented three-term locative system: proximal sini ‘ l.prox ’, medial situ ‘ l.med ’, and distal sana ‘ l.dist ’. The locatives provide orientation to the hearer in the outside world and in the speech situation by signaling distance, both spatial and nonspatial. Hence, they are similar to the demonstratives. The demonstratives, however, draw the hearer’s attention to specific entities in the discourse or surrounding situation. The locatives, by contrast, focus the hearer’s attention to the specific location of these entities and the relative distance of this location to the deictic center.

The distributional properties of the locatives are as follows:

enumerate

Substitution for noun phrases embedded in prepositional phrases (pronominal uses) (§ Para_5.7.1 ).

Modification with demonstratives or relative clauses (pronominal uses) (§ Para_5.7.1 ).

Co-occurrence with noun phrases (adnominal uses): n / np loc (§ Para_5.7.2 ).

enumerate

Locatives are distinct from other word classes such as personal pronouns (§ Para_5.5 ) or demonstratives (§ Para_5.6 ) in terms of the following syntactic properties:

enumerate

Locatives only occur in prepositional phrases; that is, they are unattested as nominal heads in unembedded noun phrases.

Locatives can be modified with adnominally used demonstratives and relatives clauses, but with no other adnominal modifier; hence, locatives cannot be stacked.

Locatives are unattested in adnominal possessive constructions as possessor or as possessum.

enumerate

The pronominal uses of the locatives are discussed in § Para_5.7.1 and their adnominal uses in § Para_5.7.2. Generally speaking, the pronominally used locatives provide additional information about the location of an entity, information nonessential for its identification. Adnominally used locatives, by contrast, limit the referential scope of their head nominals and thereby assist in the identification of their referents. A full discussion of the Papuan Malay locatives is found in § Para_7.2.
summary:
Papuan Malay has a three-term, distance-based locative system: proximal sini, medial situ, and distal sana. These locatives orient the hearer to the location of entities by indicating spatial or nonspatial distance from the deictic center, and unlike demonstratives, which identify discourse entities, locatives highlight the entities’ locations.

Syntactically, locatives occur only in prepositional phrases and do not function as nominal heads in unembedded noun phrases. They can be used pronominally, where they add nonessential location information, or adnominally with noun phrases, where they restrict reference and help identify the referent.

text:
In their pronominal uses the locatives substitute or stand for noun phrases, as illustrated with the four elicited contrastive examples in ( Example_5.222 ). Distal sana ‘ l.dist ’ in ( Example_5.222b ) substitutes for the noun phrase ruma yang paling di bawa itu ‘that house that’s the furthest down’ in ( Example_5.222a ). The ungrammatical construction in ( Example_5.222c ) shows that the locative replaces the entire noun phrase and not only its nominal head ruma ‘house’.

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses: Substitution for noun phrases
styleExampleTitle

sa tinggal di ruma yang paling di bawa itu\\
1sg stay at house rel most at bottom d.dist \\
‘I live in the house that’s the furthest down there’ [Elicited FS120314-001.007]\\
5pt

sa tinggal di sana\\
1sg stay at l.dist \\
‘I live over there’ [Elicited FS120314-001.008]\\
5pt

* sa tinggal di sana yang paling di bawa itu\\
1sg stay at l.dist rel most at bottom d.dist \\
Intended reading: ‘I live over there that’s the furthest down’ [Elicited FS120314-001.010]\\

Locatives are always embedded in prepositional phrases. The prepositional phrase can be a peripheral adjunct, as in the first clause in ( Example_5.223 ) or in ( Example_5.225 ), a prepositional predicate, as in the second clause in ( Example_5.223 ), or an adnominal prepositional phrase, as in ( Example_5.224 ). Usually, the locatives are introduced with an overt preposition as in ( Example_5.223 ) or ( Example_5.224 ). The preposition may, however, also be elided as in ( Example_5.225 ): the omitted preposition is allative ke ‘to’ (the elision of prepositions is discussed in § Para_10.1.5 ).

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses in prepositional phrases
styleExampleTitle

ko datang ke sini, nanti bapa ke situ \\
2sg come to l.prox very.soon father to l.med \\

‘you come here, later I (‘father’) (go) there ’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0462]

orang dari sana itu dorang itu kerja sendiri\\
person from l.dist d.dist 3pl d.dist work be.alone\\
‘ those people from over there,. they work by themselves’ [081014-007-CvEx.0050]

kam datang Ø sini, kam biking kaco saja\\
2pl come l.prox 2pl make be.confused just\\
‘you come here, you’re just stirring up trouble’ [081025-007-Cv.0013]

The pronominally used locatives can be modified with demonstratives or relative clauses. Modification with the demonstratives typically involves short distal tu ‘ d.dist ’ as in ( Example_5.226 ), while modification with long distal itu ‘ d.dist ’ is only attested for the non-proximal locatives, as in sana itu ‘over there ( emph )’ in ( Example_5.227 ). These distributional patterns still require further investigation. Modification with proximal ini ‘ d.prox ’ is unattested but possible, as shown in the elicited example in ( Example_5.228 ). Modification with relative clauses is also possible, as illustrated for proximal sini ‘ l.prox ’ in ( Example_5.229 ) and medial situ ‘ l.med ’ in ( Example_5.230 ). In the corpus, however, such modification is rare and unattested for distal sana ‘ l.dist ’.

styleExampleTitle
Modification of pronominally used locatives
styleExampleTitle

sampe di sini tu dia langsung sakit karna \\
reach at l.prox d.dist 3sg immediately be.sick because \\

‘having arrived here ( emph ), he was sick immediately because (he hadn’t eaten)’ [081025-008-Cv.0050]

dong lobe ke sana itu\\
3pl walk.searchingly.with.lamp to l.dist d.dist \\

‘they walk searchingly with lights to over there ( emph )’ [081108-001-JR.0002]

di sini ni orang tida taw makang pinang\\
at l.prox d.prox person neg know eat betel.nut\\

‘ here ( emph ) people don’t habitually eat betel nuts’ [Elicited BR111017.001]

di sini yang tra banyak\\
at l.prox rel neg many\\

[About logistic problems:] ‘(it’s) here where there weren’t many (passengers)’ [081025-008-Cv.0140]

sa mandi di situ, di situ yang mungking nangka\\
1sg bathe at l.med at l.med rel maybe jackfruit\\

‘[I saw (the poles),] I bathed there, there where (there are) maybe jackfruits’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0298]
summary:
Pronominally used locatives can substitute for whole noun phrases, not just noun heads, as shown by *sana* replacing an entire noun phrase and the ungrammaticality of adding a relative clause to it. They also occur inside prepositional phrases as adjuncts, predicates, or adnominal modifiers, and the preposition may be overt or elided.  

These locatives can be modified by demonstratives or relative clauses, though such modification is distributionally limited and relatively rare in the corpus, especially for distal *sana*.

text:
Adnominally used locatives always occur in posthead position. Most commonly, they occur in noun phrases embedded in prepositional phrases, as illustrated in ( Example_5.231 ). In ( Example_5.231a ), proximal sini ‘ l.prox ’ modifies the locational noun sebla ‘side’; the noun phrase is introduced with allative ke ‘to’. In ( Example_5.231b ), distal sana ‘ l.dist ’ modifies the noun laut ‘sea’; the preposition is locative di ‘at, in’.

styleExampleTitle
Adnominal uses in embedded noun phrases
styleExampleTitle

ke sebla sini\\
to side l.prox \\
‘to the side here’ [081011-001-Cv.0148] \\
5pt

di laut sana\\
at sea l.dist \\
‘in the sea over there’ [080917-006-CvHt.0004]\\

Adnominally used locatives also occur in unembedded noun phrases as in ( Example_5.232 ), although considerably less frequently. In ( Example_5.232a ), proximal sini ‘ l.prox ’ modifies the personal pronoun dong ‘ 3pl ’, while in ( Example_5.232a ) medial situ ‘ l.med ’ modifies the noun phrase orang kantor ‘office employees’.

styleExampleTitle
Adnominal uses in unembedded noun phrases
styleExampleTitle

dong sini\\
3pl l.prox \\
‘they here’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0556]\\
5pt

orang kantor situ\\
person office l.med \\
‘the office employees there’ [081005-001-Cv.0018]
summary:
Adnominally used locatives always follow the noun they modify, most commonly inside noun phrases embedded in prepositional phrases. Examples include sini modifying sebla in *ke sebla sini* ‘to the side here’ and sana modifying laut in *di laut sana* ‘in the sea over there’.  

They can also occur in unembedded noun phrases, though less often, as in *dong sini* ‘they here’ and *orang kantor situ* ‘the office employees there’.

text:
Papuan Malay has six interrogatives which serve to form content questions. That is, marking a clause as a question, they signal to the hearer which piece of information is being asked for.

The Papuan Malay interrogatives and their functions within the clause are presented in Table_5.33. All of them are used pronominally. Most of them also have predicative uses; the exception is kapang ‘when’. Besides, the majority of interrogatives also have adnominal uses, except for bagemana ‘how’, kapang ‘when’, and knapa ‘why’ which are unattested. Furthermore, three interrogatives are used as placeholders. In their pronominal and adnominal uses, the interrogatives typically remain in-situ, that is, in the position of the constituents they replace.

Besides, the mid-range quantifier brapa ‘several’ (§ Para_5.10 ) also functions as an interrogative, which questions quantities in the sense of ‘how many’. For expository reasons, this interrogative function of quantifier brapa ‘several, how many’ is discussed here.

In their predicative uses, most of the five interrogatives can take two positions, as shown in Table_5.34; the same applies to quantifier brapa ‘several, how many’. That is, all of them can remain in-situ, in the unmarked clause-final position, following the clausal subject. Besides, most of them can also be fronted to the marked clause-initial position, preceding the subject; the exception is knapa ‘why’. In its interrogative uses, quantifier brapa ‘several, how many’ can also take two positions. That is, it can remain in-situ, in the clause-final position, or be fronted to the marked clause-initial position. These positions and the semantics they convey are discussed in detail in the following sections.

In the following, the interrogatives are described in turn, siapa ‘who’ in § Para_5.8.1, apa ‘what’ in § Para_5.8.2, mana ‘where, which’ in § Para_5.8.3, bagemana ‘how’ in § Para_5.8.4, kapang ‘when’ in § Para_5.8.5, and knapa ‘why’ in § Para_5.8.6, and quantifier brapa ‘several, how many’ in § Para_5.8.7. Some of the interrogatives also express non- interrogative indefinite meanings; this function is summarily discussed in § Para_5.8.8.
summary: Papuan Malay has six interrogatives used to form content questions, each indicating the information being sought, and these are generally used pronominally while many also have predicative and adnominal uses. Most interrogatives stay in situ in pronominal and adnominal contexts, but in predicative uses most can either remain clause-final or be fronted clause-initially, with *knapa* ‘why’ unable to be fronted; the quantifier *brapa* also functions as an interrogative meaning ‘how many’ and shows the same positional options. The passage also notes that some interrogatives can serve as placeholders and that some have non-interrogative indefinite meanings.

text:
The interrogative siapa ‘who’ questions the identity of human referents. Its pronominal uses are illustrated in ( Example_5.233 ) to ( Example_5.240 ), its adnominal uses in ( Example_5.241 ) and ( Example_5.242 ), and its predicative uses in ( Example_5.243 ) and ( Example_5.244 ). In addition, siapa ‘who’ serves as a placeholder as shown in ( Example_5.245 ). Furthermore, the interrogative is also used in one-word utterances.

In its pronominal uses, siapa ‘who’ occurs in all syntactic positions, as shown ( Example_5.233 ) to ( Example_5.240 ), typically remaining in-situ. In the verbal clause in ( Example_5.233 ), siapa ‘who’ takes the subject slot. In the corpus, however, verbal clauses with siapa ‘who’ in the subject slot are rare. Typically, speakers use equative nominal clauses when they want to question the identity of the clausal subject. In such nonverbal clauses, siapa ‘who’ takes the subject slot while a headless relative clause takes the predicate slot. This is shown with the elicited contrastive example in ( Example_5.234 ). In this equative clause, siapa ‘who’ is the subject, while the headless relative clause yang suru ‘(the one) who ordered ’ is the predicate. Likewise in ( Example_5.235 ), the interrogative takes the subject slot while the headless relative clause yang datang ‘(the one) who came ’ takes the predicate slot. Alternatively, as one anonymous reviewer points out, one could argue that in ( Example_5.234 ) and ( Example_5.235 ) the typical subject-predicate word order is inverted and that siapa ‘who’ does not take the subject but the predicate slot, whereas the relative clause introduced with yang ‘ rel ’ takes the subject slot.
(For details on relative clauses see § Para_14.3.2.)

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses of siapa ‘who’: Subject slot
styleExampleTitle

e, siapa suru kam minum minum di sini?\\
hey who order 2pl rdp drink at l.prox \\

‘hey, who told you to keep drinking here’ [081014-005-Cv.0006]

e, siapa yang suru kam minum minum di sini?\\
hey who rel order 2pl rdp drink at l.prox \\

‘hey, who (is the one) who told you to keep drinking here’ [Elicited MY131112.004]

siapa yang datang jemput saya?\\
who rel come pick.up 1sg \\

‘ who (is the one) who came (and) picked me up?’ [080918-001-CvNP.0001]

Interrogative siapa ‘who’ also takes non-subject slots. In ( Example_5.236 ), siapa ‘who’ takes the direct object slot in a mono transitive clause, in ( Example_5.237 ) a direct object slot in a double-object construction, in ( Example_5.238 ) the oblique object slot, and in ( Example_5.239 ) the peripheral adjunct slot. Alternatively, one could argue that in ( Example_5.238 ) siapa ‘who’ does not take an oblique object but an adjunct slot. In addition, siapa ‘who’ questions the possessor’s identity in adnominal possessive constructions, as in ( Example_5.240 ).

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses of siapa ‘who’: Non-subject slots
styleExampleTitle

dong cari siapa?\\
3pl search who\\

‘for whom are they looking?’ [080921-010-Cv.0010]

kwe mo pi kasi siapa di sana?\\
cake want go give who at l.dist \\

‘as for the cake, to whom do (you) want to go and give (it) over there?’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0670]

ke mana?, ke kampung?, deng siapa?\\
to where to village with who\\

[Talking to her young son:] ‘[do you want to leave today?,] where to?, to the village?, with whom?’ [080917-003a-CvEx.0048-0044]

baru nanti minggu keduanya sembayang di siapa?\\
and.then very.soon week second: 3possr worship at who\\

‘then later in the second week (of this month), (we’ll) worship at whose (place)?’ (Lit. ‘at who’) [081011-005-Cv.0037]

siapa pu mata yang buta?\\
who poss eye rel be.blind\\

‘ whose eyes are blind?’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0142]

As a nominal modifier, siapa ‘who’ takes the position of a modifying noun which it replaces. This illustrated with the interrogative clauses ( Example_5.241 ) and ( Example_5.242.

styleExampleTitle
Adnominal uses of siapa ‘who’
styleExampleTitle

[ prempuang siapa] biking sa jadi bingung?\\
woman who make 1sg become be.confused\\

‘ which woman made me become confused?’ [080922-004-Cv.0028]

skarang sa tanya, [ orang siapa] yang benar?\\
now 1sg ask person who rel be.true\\

‘now I asked, `` which person (is the one) who is right?''' [080917-010-CvEx.0197]

In its predicative uses, siapa ‘who’ occurs in equative nominal predicate clauses where it questions the identity of the clausal subject, as shown in ( Example_5.243 ) and ( Example_5.244 ) (for more details on nominal clauses see § Para_12.2 ). The interrogative can remain in-situ, in the clause-final position, following the subject as in ( Example_5.243 ), or it can be fronted to the marked clause-initial position, preceding the subject, as in ( Example_5.244 ). In the corpus, the token frequencies for both positions are about the same. When speakers want to accentuate the subject, such as ini ‘ d.prox ’ in ( Example_5.243 ), the interrogative remains in-situ, where it is less prominent. When, by contrast, speakers want to stress the questioning of the subject’s identity, they front siapa ‘who’ to the clause-initial position, as in ( Example_5.244 ). Besides their different functions, the contrastive examples in ( Example_5.243 ) and ( Example_5.244 ) also have distinct intonation contours. When siapa ‘who’ remains in-situ, as in ( Example_5.243 ), the clause has a rising intonation, typical of interrogatives. When it is fronted, the clause has a falling intonation, typical of declaratives. In both cases, siapa ‘who’ is marked with a slight increase in pitch of its stressed penultimate syllable (“ \' ”).

styleExampleTitle
Predicative uses of siapa ‘who’
styleExampleTitle

-- -- 7mm — — 7mm -- -- 7mm — — \\
ini siápa? ini siápa?\\
d.prox who d.prox who\\

‘ who is this? who is this?’ [080916-001-CvNP.0006]

-- -- 7mm -- \\
siápa ini?\\
who d.prox \\

‘ who is this?’ [081011-023-Cv.0104]

In addition, siapa ‘who’ functions as a placeholder when speakers do not recall a referent’s name, as in ( Example_5.245 ).

styleExampleTitle
Placeholder uses of siapa ‘who’
styleExampleTitle

Sarles antar siapa, Bolikarfus\\
Sarles bring who Bolikarfus\\

‘Sarles gave a ride to, who-is-it, Bolikarfus’ [081002-001-CvNP.0031]
summary:
The interrogative **siapa** ‘who’ asks for the identity of human referents and is used pronominally, adnominally, predicatively, and as a placeholder, as well as in one-word utterances. As a pronominal form, it can occur in all syntactic positions but usually remains in situ; verbal clauses with **siapa** in subject position are rare, and speakers often prefer equative nominal clauses for asking about a clausal subject.  

In non-subject positions, **siapa** can question direct objects, oblique objects, adjuncts, and possessors. In predicative equative clauses, it may stay clause-final or be fronted clause-initially, with the two orders differing in prominence and intonation.

text: Rather commonly, speakers also employ the interrogative in one-word utterances, when they question the identity of a referent, in the sense of ‘who (do you mean)?’
summary: Speakers often use the interrogative as a one-word utterance to ask about the identity of a referent. In this use, it means something like “who do you mean?”

text:
The interrogative apa ‘what’ questions the identity of nonhuman referents, name\-ly entities and events; in addition, it can question reason. The pronominal uses of apa ‘what’ are illustrated in ( Example_5.246 ) to ( Example_5.251 ), its adnominal uses in ( Example_5.252 ) and ( Example_5.253 ), and its predicative uses in ( Example_5.254 ) and ( Example_5.255 ). The interrogative is also used as a placeholder as shown in ( Example_5.256 ). Besides, apa ‘what’ is also used in one-word utterances.

In its pronominal uses, apa ‘what’ occurs in all syntactic positions, as demonstrated in ( Example_5.246 ) to ( Example_5.251 ), always remaining in-situ. In the elicited verbal clause in ( Example_5.246 ), apa ‘what’ takes the subject slot. While this construction is grammatically correct and acceptable, verbal clauses with apa ‘what’ in the subject slot are unattested in the corpus. Instead, speakers always use equative clauses when they want to question the identity of the clausal subject, similar to the questions formed with siapa ‘who’ in ( Example_5.234 ) and ( Example_5.235 ) (§ Para_5.8.1 ). This is demonstrated with the contrastive equative clause in ( Example_5.247 ). In this example, apa ‘what’ takes the subject slot, while the headless relative clause yang su gigit ‘(the one) who has already bitten ’ takes the predicate slot. Similar to the comment in Footnote Footnote_5.168 in § Para_5.8.1 (p. Footnote_5.168), one could argue that in ( Example_5.246 ) the subject-predicate word order is inverted and that apa ‘what’ fills the predicate rather than the subject slot, while the relative clause introduced with yang ‘ rel ’ takes the subject slot. (For details on relative clauses see § Para_14.3.2.)

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses of apa ‘what’: Subject slot
styleExampleTitle

apa su gigit sa pu lutut\\
what already bite 1sg poss knee\\

‘ what has bitten my knee?’ [Elicited MY131112.005]

apa yang su gigit sa pu lutut?\\
what rel already bite 1sg poss knee\\

‘ what (is it) that has bitten my knee?’ [080916-001-CvNP.0004]

Interrogative apa ‘what’ also takes non-subject slots. In ( Example_5.248 ), apa ‘what’ takes the direct object slot, in ( Example_5.249 ) the oblique object slot, and in ( Example_5.250 ) the peripheral adjunct slot. Alternatively, one could argue that in ( Example_5.249 ) apa ‘what’ does not take an oblique object but an adjunct slot. Besides, speakers use apa ‘what’ to question reasons or motives, as in ( Example_5.251 ).

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses of apa ‘what’: Non-subject slots
styleExampleTitle

kam cari apa?\\
2pl search what\\

‘ what are you looking for?’ [080917-006-CvHt.0001]

tokok sagu tu deng apa ini?\\
tap sago d.dist with what d.prox \\

‘ what are you pounding that sagu with?’ [081014-006-CvPr.0014]

sa tra taw tugu ini dari apa?\\
1sg neg know monument d.prox from what\\

‘I don’t’ know from where this monument comes?’ (Lit. ‘from what (place)’) [080917-008-NP.0003]

de bilang, ko tidor apa?\\
3sg say 2sg sleep what\\

‘he said, `` why are you sleeping?''' [081006-034-CvEx.0022]

In its adnominal uses, apa ‘what’ takes the position of a nominal modifier which it replaces, such as the name of a weekday in ( Example_5.252 ), or the name of a clan in ( Example_5.253 ).

styleExampleTitle
Adnominal uses of apa ‘what’
styleExampleTitle

[ hari apa] baru sa minta ijing?\\
day what and.then 1sg request permission\\

[A school boy asking his mother:] ‘on which day will I ask for permission (to be absent)?’ [080917-003a-CvEx.0003]

dia tanya saya, ko [ marga apa]?\\
3sg ask 1sg 2sg clan what\\

‘he asked me, `` which clan do you (belong to)?''' (Lit. ‘you are what clan’) [080922-010a-CvNF.0281]

In its predicative uses, apa ‘what’ questions the identity or pertinent characteristics of the clausal subject (for more details on nominal predicate clauses see § Para_12.2 ). Like siapa ‘who’ (§ Para_5.8.1 ), apa ‘what’ can remain in the unmarked clause-final position, as in ( Example_5.254 ). Alternatively, it can be fronted to the marked clause-initial position, as in ( Example_5.255 ), where it stresses the questioning of the subject’s identity or characteristics. The contrastive clauses in ( Example_5.254 ) and ( Example_5.255 ) have the same distinct intonation contours as the corresponding questions with siapa ‘who’ in ( Example_5.243 ) and ( Example_5.244 ) (§ Para_5.8.1 ). Clauses with in-situ apa ‘what’, as in ( Example_5.254 ), have the typical rising interrogative intonation. Clauses with fronted apa ‘what’ have the typical falling declarative intonation. Like siapa ‘who’, apa ‘what’ is marked with a slight increase in pitch of its stressed penultimate syllable (“ \' ”).

styleExampleTitle
Predicative uses of apa ‘what’
styleExampleTitle

-- 3pt-- 5mm — — \\
ini ápa?\\
d.prox what\\

‘ what is this?’ [081109-001-Cv.0012]

-- 5mm -- 3pt-- 5mm -- \\
adu, ápa ini?\\
oh.no! what d.prox \\

‘oh no!, what is this?’ [081109-001-Cv.0012]

In addition, apa ‘what’ functions as a placeholder, when speakers do not recall the name of a lexical item, as in ( Example_5.256 ).

styleExampleTitle
Placeholder uses of apa ‘what’
styleExampleTitle

de bisa bantu deng apa, ijasa\\
3sg be.able help with what diploma\\

‘he can help (us) with, what-is-it, the diploma’ [081011-023-Cv.0107]

Speakers also employ apa ‘what’ in one-word utterances to question the overall situation in the sense of ‘what (is wrong)?’, or to signal lack of understanding, in the sense of ‘what?’, for example during phone conversations with a bad connection.
summary:
The interrogative **apa** ‘what’ asks about nonhuman referents, including entities and events, and can also ask about reasons. It is used pronominally in subject and non-subject positions, adnominally as a nominal modifier, and predicatively to question the identity or characteristics of a clause subject; it can also appear as a placeholder or in one-word utterances.

In pronominal uses, **apa** remains in-situ in all syntactic positions, though subject questions in verbal clauses are unattested in the corpus and are instead expressed with equative clauses. Predicative **apa** may be left in clause-final position or fronted clause-initially, with different intonational patterns.

text:
The interrogative mana ‘where, which’ questions locations and single items. Its pronominal uses are illustrated in ( Example_5.257 ) and ( Example_5.258 ), its adnominal uses in ( Example_5.259 ) and ( Example_5.260 ), and its predicative uses in ( Example_5.261 ) to ( Example_5.263 ). The interrogative is also used in one-word utterances, as shown in ( Example_5.264 ).

In its pronominal uses as the head of a noun phrase, mana ‘where, which’ questions locations, as in ( Example_5.257 ) and ( Example_5.258 ). More specifically, it functions as the complement in a prepositional phrase which is headed by a preposition encoding location (details on prepositional phrases are provided in Para_10).

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses of mana ‘where, which’
styleExampleTitle

ko tinggal di mana?\\
2sg stay at where\\

‘ where do you live?’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0237]

ko datang dari mana?\\
2sg come from where\\

‘ from where do you come?’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0236]

In its adnominal uses, mana ‘where, which’ questions single entities among larger numbers of identical or similar entities expressed by its referents, as in ( Example_5.259 ) and ( Example_5.260 ).

styleExampleTitle
Adnominal uses of mana ‘where, which’
styleExampleTitle

kalo [ ana mana] yang sa duduk ceritra deng dia,\\
if child where rel 1sg sit tell with 3sg \\
itu ana itu, de hormat torang\\
d.dist child d.dist 3sg respect 1pl \\

[Conversation about a certain teenager:] ‘as for which kid with whom I sit and talk with, that is that kid, she respects us’ [081115-001a-Cv.0282]

dong bilang, [ badang mana] yang sakit?\\
3pl say body where rel be.sick\\

‘they said, `` which (part of your) body (is the one) that is hurting?''' [081015-005-NP.0031]

In its predicative uses, mana ‘where, which’ occurs in prepositional predicates which question the subject’s location (for details on prepositional predicates see § Para_12.4 ). Like predicate clauses with siapa ‘who’ (§ Para_5.8.1 ) and apa ‘what’ (§ Para_5.8.2 ), prepositional predicates with mana ‘where, which’ can take two positions. They can remain in-situ, following the clausal subject, as in ( Example_5.261 ). Alternatively, they can be fronted to the marked clause-initial position, where they stress the questioning of the subject’s location, as in the elicited example in ( Example_5.262 ). In the corpus, though, the preposition is always omitted from fronted prepositional predicates, as in ( Example_5.263 ).

styleExampleTitle
Predicative uses of mana ‘where, which’
styleExampleTitle

sabung mandi di mana?\\
soap bathe at where\\

‘ where is (our) soap?’ [081025-006-Cv.0026]

di mana sabung mandi?\\
at where soap bathe\\

‘ where is (our) soap?’ [Elicited MY131112.006]

Nofi, Ø mana kitong pu ikang ikang?\\
Nofi where 1pl poss rdp fish\\

‘Nofi, where are our fish?’ [080917-006-CvHt.0002]

Quite commonly, the interrogative is used to form one-word utterances in which case it questions an entire proposition, as in ( Example_5.264 ).

styleExampleTitle
One-word utterances with mana ‘where, which’
styleExampleTitle

Speaker-2: di mana?\\
at where\\

[Speaker-1: ‘(I used to) stay with my aunt Marta’]\\
Speaker-2: ‘ where?’ [080922-002-Cv.0029-0030]
summary: The interrogative *mana* ‘where, which’ is used to ask about locations and single items. It appears as a pronominal head of a noun phrase for location questions, as an adnominal interrogative selecting one entity from a set, and as a predicative form in prepositional predicates that question a subject’s location. It can also occur as a one-word utterance that questions an entire proposition.

text:
The interrogative bagemana ‘how’ questions manner or circumstance in the sense of ‘how, what (is it) like’. The interrogative has pronominal uses, as illustrated in ( Example_5.265 ) and ( Example_5.267 ), and predicative uses, as shown in ( Example_5.268 ) to ( Example_5.271 ). In addition, bagemana ‘how’ has placeholder uses as in ( Example_5.272 ). It also occurs in one-word utterances, as in ( Example_5.273 ) and ( Example_5.274 ).

In its pronominal uses, bagemana ‘how’ can remain in-situ, in the unmarked clause-final position, or can occur in the marked clause-initial position. In the clause-final position, the interrogative questions the specific manner of an event or activity such as the best way of transporting a pig in ( Example_5.265 ). In the clause-initial position, the scope of bagemana ‘how’ is larger. Here it questions an entire proposition, as in ( Example_5.266 ) and ( Example_5.267 ), and not only a specific manner, as in ( Example_5.265 ). The example in ( Example_5.267 ) also shows that, depending on the context, fronted bagemana ‘how’ also question reasons.

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses of bagemana ‘how’
styleExampleTitle

adu, babi ni sa harus angkat bagemana?\\
oh.no! pig d.prox 1sg have.to lift how\\

‘[the pig was very big, I alone could not transport it, I thought,] ``oh no!, this pig, how am I going to transport it?''' [080919-003-NP.0008]

bagemana kitong mo dapat uang?\\
how 1pl want get money\\

‘ how are we going to get money?’ [080927-006-CvNP.0041]

de tanya juga, bagemana ko bisa kasi ana ini?\\
3sg ask also how 2sg be.able give child d.prox \\

[About bride-price children:] ‘she also asked (me), `` how can you give this child (of yours away)?''' [081006-026-CvEx.0003]

When used predicatively, bagemana ‘how’ can remain in-situ, as in ( Example_5.268 ) and ( Example_5.270 ), or can be fronted, as in ( Example_5.269 ) and ( Example_5.271 ). Similar to the predicative uses of the interrogatives discussed in the previous sections, the clause-final in-situ position is the unmarked one where the interrogative is less prominent in comparison to the clause-initial subject, as shown in ( Example_5.268 ). When placed in the marked clause-initial position, by contrast, bagemana ‘how’ accentuates the questioning of the subject’s circumstance, as in ( Example_5.269 ). In addition, predicatively used bagemana ‘how’ inquires about the well-being of one’s interlocutor(s) as in ( Example_5.270 ) and ( Example_5.271 ).

styleExampleTitle
Predicative uses of bagemana ‘how’
styleExampleTitle

dong tida taw itu, Yesus itu, injil itu bagemana?\\
3pl neg know d.dist Jesus d.dist Gospel d.dist how\\
‘they don’t know, what’s-his-name, Jesus, (they don’t know) what the Gospel (is like)’ (Lit. ‘the gospel is how?’) [081006-023-CvEx.0005]

susa liat setang itu, bagemana rupa setang\\
be.difficult see evil.spirit d.dist how form evil.spirit\\
[About evil spirits:] ‘[but for us who already believe in Jesus, we can’t,] (for us) it is difficult to see that evil spirit, what the evil spirit’s face (is like)’ (Lit. ‘ how (is) the evil spirit’s form?’) [081006-022-CvEx.0069]\\

yo, ko Herman bagemana?\\
yes 2sg Herman how\\
[Greeting a visitor:] ‘yes, how are you, Herman?’ [081014-011-CvEx.0072]\\

eh, bagemana ipar?, sore, dari Jayapura?\\
hey! how sibling-in-law afternoon from Jayapura\\
[Greeting a visitor:] ‘hey, how (is it going) brother-in-law?, (good) afternoon! (did you just get here) from Jayapura?’ [081110-002-Cv.0003]\\

Another use of bagemana ‘how’ is that of a placeholder, as shown in ( Example_5.272 ).

styleExampleTitle
Placeholder uses of bagemana ‘how’
styleExampleTitle

sa macang, sa macang bagemana, e, rasa sa \\
1sg variety 1sg variety how uh feel 1sg \\

‘[so when I (went) to Biak there, I felt very strange] I kind of, I kind of, what-is-it, uh, felt (that) I ’ [081011-013-Cv.0009]

In one-word utterances, bagemana ‘how’ questions the circumstances of an event or state, as in ( Example_5.273 ), or signals lack of understanding as in ( Example_5.274 ).

styleExampleTitle
One-word utterances with bagemana ‘how’
styleExampleTitle

saya tanya saya punya bapa, bagemana?\\
1sg ask 1sg poss father how\\

‘I asked my father, `` how (did this happen)?''' [080921-011-Cv.0012]

bagemana? bagemana?\\
how how\\

[During a phone conversation with a bad connection:] ‘ what?, what?’ [080922-001b-CvPh.0027]
summary: The interrogative **bagemana** ‘how’ asks about manner or circumstance, and it is used both pronominally and predicatively. In pronominal uses it may stay clause-final, where it asks about a specific manner, or move clause-initial, where it has broader scope over the whole proposition and can even ask about reasons; in predicative uses it can also be in-situ or fronted, with the fronted position emphasizing the subject’s circumstance. It also appears as a placeholder and in one-word utterances, where it can question an event’s circumstances or express lack of understanding.

text:
The interrogative kapang ‘when’ questions time. Always used pronominally, kapang ‘when’ usually occurs in clause-initial position, as shown with its first and third occurrences in ( Example_5.275 ). Here, kapang ‘when’ questions the temporal setting of the events or states expressed by the entire clause. When the temporal setting is less important, kapang ‘when’ occurs in clause-final position, as shown with the second kapang ‘when’ token in ( Example_5.275 ). Hence, the different positions of kapang ‘when’ within the clause have functions which parallel those of the time-denoting nouns which the interrogative replaces (see § Para_5.2.5 ). Alternatively, but rarely, the interrogative occurs between the subject and the predicate, as in ( Example_5.276 ). According to one consultant, this position of kapang ‘when’ is acceptable, although the semantics conveyed by this position are still ill understood.

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses of kapang ‘when’
styleExampleTitle

kapang kita mo antar?, kitong antar kapang? \\
when 1pl want deliver 1pl deliver when \\
kapang kitong antar dia?\\
when 1pl bring 3sg \\

[Discussing when the bride’s parents will bring their daughter to the groom’s parents:] ‘[they (the bride’s parents) start asking, ``,] when should we bring her? we bring her when?, when do we bring her?''' [081110-005-CvPr.0043-0044]

kasiang, sa kapang mandi deng dorang lagi e?\\
pity 1sg when bathe with 3pl again eh\\

[About a sick boy:] ‘what a pity, when will I bathe with them (my friends) again, eh?’ [081025-009b-Cv.0044]
summary:
The interrogative **kapang** ‘when’ asks about time and is always used pronominally. It usually appears clause-initially to question the temporal setting of the whole clause, but it can also occur clause-finally when the time setting is less important, and this positional contrast parallels the use of time-denoting nouns that it replaces.

Rarely, **kapang** may appear between the subject and predicate, a position one consultant accepted, though its meaning in that position is not well understood.

text:
The interrogative knapa ‘why’ questions reasons and motives. Its pronominal uses are illustrated in ( Example_5.277 ) to ( Example_5.279 ), its predicative uses in ( Example_5.280 ), and its uses in one-word utterances in ( Example_5.281 ).

Typically, knapa ‘why’ is used pronominally. Most often it occurs in clause-initial position, as in ( Example_5.277 ). In clauses marked with an initial conjunction, knapa ‘why’ follows the conjunction as in ( Example_5.278 ). Alternatively, but rarely, knapa ‘why’ occurs between the subject and the predicate, as in ( Example_5.279 ). According to one consultant, this position of knapa ‘why’ is acceptable; the semantics of this position still need to be investigated, though.

styleExampleTitle
Pronominal uses of knapa ‘why’
styleExampleTitle

e, knapa kam kas kas bangung dia?\\
hey! why 2pl rdp give wake.up 3sg \\

‘hey, why do you keep waking him up?’ [080918-001-CvNP.0039]

tapi knapa ana ini sakit?\\
but why child d.prox be.sick\\

‘but why is this child sick’ [080917-010-CvEx.0133]

Matius itu dia knapa maju begitu?\\
Matius d.dist 3sg why advance like.that\\

‘[as for Matius, I’m very surprised,] Matius there, how come he could advance like that?’ [081006-032-Cv.0025]

Interrogative knapa ‘what’ can also be used predicatively. In this case, knapa ‘what’ remains in-situ, in the clause-final position, following the subject, as in ( Example_5.280 ).

styleExampleTitle
Predicative uses of knapa ‘why’
styleExampleTitle

bapa ko knapa?\\
father 2sg why\\

[After an accident]: ‘Sir, what happened?’ (Lit. ‘you father (are) why?’) [081108-001-JR.0005]

The interrogative can also form one-word utterances in which case it questions an entire proposition, as in ( Example_5.281 ).

styleExampleTitle
One-word utterances with knapa ‘why’
styleExampleTitle

Speaker-2: e, knapa?\\
hey! why\\

[About the birth of twins] [Speaker-1: ‘ as for the girl, they say it’s an evil spirit, so they kill (her)’]\\
Speaker-2: ‘hey, why?’ [081011-022-Cv.0147-0151]
summary:
The interrogative **knapa** ‘why’ is used to ask about reasons and motives, and it appears mainly in **pronominal** uses. It usually occurs clause-initially, follows an initial conjunction if there is one, and more rarely appears between the subject and predicate, though the semantics of this latter position are still unclear.  

Knapa can also be used **predicatively**, in which case it remains clause-final after the subject, and it can form **one-word utterances** that question an entire proposition.

subsection: Interrogative uses of mid-range quantifier brapa ‘several’
text:
In its interrogative uses, the mid-range quantifier brapa ‘several’ receives the reading ‘how many’. It questions quantities of countable entities and, in combination with the mid-range quantifier banyak ‘many’, of non-countable entities. Its adnominal uses are shown in ( Example_5.282 ) to ( Example_5.284 ), and its predicative uses in ( Example_5.286 ) and ( Example_5.289 ).

Most often, brapa ‘several, how many’ functions as a nominal modifier which takes the position of the numeral or quantifier it replaces. Corresponding to the syntax of adnominally used numerals and quantifiers, it precedes or follows its head nominal, as in ( Example_5.282 ) to ( Example_5.284 ). In prehead position of countable referents, brapa ‘several, how many’ questions the absolute numbers of items denoted by the head nominals, as in ( Example_5.282 ). In posthead position of countable referents, it questions unique positions within series, as in ( Example_5.283 ). When following mass nouns, the interrogative questions the nonnumeric amounts of its referents, as in the elicited example in ( Example_5.284 ). Like other quantifiers, brapa ‘several, how many’ is unattested in prehead position of mass nouns. If the referent’s identity is known from the context, the head nominal can be omitted, as with numerals and other quantifiers. This is illustrated in ( Example_5.285 ), where the omitted head is rupia ‘rupiah’. (Details on numerals and quantifiers are given in § Para_5.9 and § Para_5.10, respectively.)

styleExampleTitle
Adnominal uses of brapa ‘how many’
styleExampleTitle

brapa bulang dorang skola ka?\\
several month 3pl go.to.school or\\

‘(for) how many months will they go to school?’ [081025-003-Cv.0207]

jadi mama, mama pulang jam brapa?\\
so mother mother go.home hour several\\

‘so mama, what time will you (‘mother’) come home?’ (Lit. ‘ how manyeth hour’) [080924-002-Pr.0002]

ko minta minyak brapa banyak?\\
2pl request oil several many\\

‘ how much oil do you request’ [Elicited BR120520.001]

kemaring dapat brapa Ø?\\
yesterday get several \\

[Collecting money for a project:] ‘ how many (rupiah) did (you) get yesterday?’ [080925-003-Cv.0090]

The predicative uses of brapa ‘several, how many’ are shown in ( Example_5.286 ) to ( Example_5.289 ). Like siapa ‘who’ (§ Para_5.8.1 ), apa ‘what’ (§ Para_5.8.2 ), and mana ‘where, which’ (§ Para_5.8.3 ), brapa ‘several, how many’ can remain in the unmarked clause-final position, as in ( Example_5.286 ) and Example_5.288 ), or it can be fronted to the marked clause-initial position, as in the elicited example in ( Example_5.287 ) and Example_5.289 ). Again, the fronting of the interrogative serves to emphasize the questioning, namely of numeric quantities in ( Example_5.287 ), and of nonnumeric quantities in ( Example_5.289 ). These two examples are elicited, though, as interrogatives with fronted brapa ‘several, how many’ are unattested in the corpus. (See also § Para_12.3 for details on numeral and quantifier predicate clauses.)

styleExampleTitle
Predicative uses of brapa ‘how many’
styleExampleTitle

bapa pu ana ana brapa?\\
father poss rdp child several\\

‘ how many children do you (‘father’) have?’ (Lit. ‘father’s children are how many?’) [080923-009-Cv.0010]

brapa bapa pu ana ana?\\
several father poss rdp child\\

‘ how many children do you (‘father’) have?’ [Elicited MY131112.007]

tong pu uang brapa?\\
1pl poss money several\\

‘ how much money do we have?’ (Lit. ‘our money is how many?’) [081006-017-Cv.0015]

brapa tong pu uang?\\
several 1pl poss money\\

‘ how much money do we have?’ [Elicited MY131112.008]
summary: The quantifier **brapa** ‘several, how many’ is used interrogatively to ask about quantities: with countable nouns it means ‘how many,’ and with **banyak** ‘many’ it can also ask about non-countable quantities. As an adnominal modifier, it usually occupies the position of the numeral or quantifier it replaces, appearing before or after the head noun depending on the construction, while in predicative clauses it may remain clause-final or be fronted clause-initially for emphasis, though fronted examples are only elicited and not found in the corpus.

text:
Cross-linguistically, interrogatives may also function as “general indefinites” by referring “to a general population, of unknown size”. In this case, the interrogatives translate with ‘whoever’, ‘whatever’, ‘wherever’, etc.

In Papuan Malay, the indefinite reading is achieved by juxtaposing the focus ad verb saja ‘just’ to the interrogative, as illustrated in ( Example_5.290 ) to ( Example_5.295 ). In the corpus, this function of the interrogatives is only attested for siapa ‘who’, apa ‘what’, and mana ‘where, which’, as shown in ( Example_5.290 ) to ( Example_5.293 ). The elicited respective examples in ( Example_5.293 ) to ( Example_5.295 ) illustrate, however, that bagemana ‘how’, kapang ‘when’, and knapa ‘why’ can also have this function.

kalo ko liat ko pu sodara siapa saja, kalo dia \\
if 2sg see 2sg poss sibling who just if 3sg \\

‘when you see your relatives whoever (they are), when he/she ’ [080919-004-NP.0078]

bicara apa saja, bicara saja\\
speak what just speak just\\

‘speak (to me about) whatever, just speak (to me)’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1174]

di mana saja bapa bisa tinggal, di tempat mana saja\\
at where just father be.able stay at place where just\\

‘I (‘father’) can live wherever, (I can) live in whatever place’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1116]

sa tra mo taw!, bagemana saja ko harus pigi skola!\\
1sg neg want know how just 2sg have.to go school\\

[Addressing a child who does not want to go to school for various reasons:] ‘I don’t want to know!, you have to go to school, no matter what!’ (Lit. ‘ however’) [Elicited MY131112.001]

kapang saja ko bisa datang\\

‘you can come whenever’ [Elicited MY131112.002]

knapa saja sa pu kaka de mo pulang Jayapura\\
