text:
The demonstratives have identificational uses when they appear in the subject slot of a nominal predicate clause (§ Para_12.2 ). In this context, the demonstratives aid in the identification of a definite or identifiable referent encoded by the predicate. For instance, ini ‘ d.prox ’ takes the subject slot in ( Example_7.32 ) and itu ‘ d.dist ’ in ( Example_7.33 ). In this domain of use only the long demonstratives are attested.

ini daging yang saya bawa antar buat sodara dorang\\
d.prox meat rel 1sg bring deliver for sibling 3pl \\

‘ this is the (wild pig) meat that I brought (and) delivered for (my) relatives’ [080919-003-NP.0021]

itu kali Biri\\
d.dist river Biri\\

‘ that is the Biri river’ [081025-008-Cv.0006]
summary: Demonstratives can be used identificationally when they occur in the subject position of a nominal predicate clause, where they help identify a definite or otherwise identifiable referent expressed by the predicate. In this use, only the long forms are attested, as in *ini* ‘this’ and *itu* ‘that’ introducing identifiable referents such as meat or a river.

text:
In their textual uses, the demonstratives provide discourse orientation. Across languages, two major discourse uses of demonstratives can be distinguished, according to: “anaphoric” and “discourse deictic” uses. In their anaphoric uses, the demonstratives “are coreferential with a prior np ” and thereby “keep track of discourse participants” ( Diessel.1999). In their discourse deictic uses, the demonstratives are not coreferent with the referent of a previously established noun phrase. Instead, they are coreferential with a preceding or following proposition. That is, they “establish an overt link between two propositions: the one in which they are embedded and the one to which they refer” ( Diessel.1999).

Both discourse functions also apply to the Papuan Malay demonstratives.

Anaphoric uses

The anaphoric uses of the Papuan Malay demonstratives are demonstrated in ( Example_7.34 ) to ( Example_7.39 ). Being coreferential with a preceding np, they keep track of different discourse participants. In this use the demonstratives may be employed adnominally as in ( Example_7.34 ) and ( Example_7.35 ), pronominally as in ( Example_7.36 ) and ( Example_7.37 ), or adverbially as in ( Example_7.38 ) and ( Example_7.39 ). The exact semantic distinctions between ini ‘ d.prox ’ and itu ‘ d.dist ’ as participant tracking devices, however, are yet to be investigated in more detail.

The examples in ( Example_7.34 ) and ( Example_7.35 ) demonstrate the adnominal anaphoric uses of the demonstratives. The utterance in ( Example_7.34 ) is part of a joke about a school student who does not know to draw. The teacher orders the students to gambar monyet ‘draw a monkey’. When the monyet ‘monkey’ is mentioned the next time, it is marked with ini ‘ d.prox ’ thereby indicating coreference with this specific monkey. The example in ( Example_7.35 ) is part of a narrative that describes how the speaker’s ancestor first came down to the coast where he finds a bua mera ‘red fruit’. At its next mention, the noun phrase bua mera ‘red fruit’ is marked with itu ‘ d.dist ’ to signal coreference with that specific fruit.

It states that both functions occur in Papuan Malay, and gives examples of anaphoric uses in adnominal, pronominal, and adverbial positions. The exact semantic difference between ini ‘proximal’ and itu ‘distal’ in participant tracking is noted as still needing further investigation.

Alternatively, however, one might argue that in ( Example_7.38 ) and ( Example_7.39 ) the demonstratives do not function as participant tracking devices, but rather signal emotional involvement.

Discourse deictic uses

The discourse deictic uses of the Papuan Malay de\-mon\-stratives are demonstrated in ( Example_7.40 ) to ( Example_7.44 ). In this use, they are coreferential with a preceding or following proposition. As shown in ( Example_7.40 ) to ( Example_7.44 ), though, only the pronominally used demonstratives have discourse deictic uses.

Proximal ini ‘ d.prox ’ may refer to a preceding statement as in ( Example_7.40 ) or to a following statement as in ( Example_7.41 ). The example in ( Example_7.40 ) is part of a conversation about difficult children. Maintaining that children should be disciplined, the speaker makes a number of suggestions how to do so. Employing short ini ‘ d.prox ’, the speaker summarizes her previous statements. Thereby she creates a link to her closing statement that her interlocutor should decide for herself what to make of these suggestions. In ( Example_7.41 ), ini ‘ d.prox ’ creates a link to the following direct quote.

Distal itu ‘ d.dist ’ is used only to create a link to a preceding statement, as in ( Example_7.42 ). This example is part of joke about an uneducated person who notes that di kalender dua blas ‘in the calendar are twelve (moons)’ while di langit ini cuma satu ‘in this sky is only one’. Distal itu ‘ d.dist ’ summarizes these remarks, creating an overt link to the speaker’s conclusion that this state of affairs is tipu skali ‘very deceptive’.

The discourse deictic uses of itu ‘ d.dist ’ are very commonly extended to that of a “sentence connective” that signals “a causal link between two propositions”, employing Diessel.1999 terminology. This is illustrated in ( Example_7.43 ) and ( Example_7.44 ). Standing alone, itu ‘ d.dist ’ introduces a reason relation as in ( Example_7.43 ). When co-occurring with the relativizer yang ‘ rel ’, itu ‘ d.dist ’ marks a result relation as in ( Example_7.44 ).

In ( Example_7.40 ), the speaker recounts a conversation with a local doctor after a motorbike accident. In using itu ‘ d.dist ’ the doctor summarizes the speaker’s comments concerning her health and creates an overt link to his explanation why she is in pain. In this context itu ‘ d.dist ’ functions as a causal link that marks a reason relation.

Recounting some details about the journey, the speaker relates that her husband had returned home hungry. summary: Papuan Malay demonstratives can be used discourse-deictically, where they refer to a preceding or following proposition rather than to a participant, but this use is found only with the pronominal demonstratives. Proximal **ini** can refer backward or forward in discourse, while distal **itu** refers only backward and often functions as a sentence connective marking a causal relation. With **itu yang**, the construction can signal a result relation.

text:
Demonstratives are also rather commonly employed pronominally as “placeholders” in the context of “word-formulation trouble”, as show in their cross-linguistic study. In this function, they serve “as temporary substitutes for specific lexical items that have eluded the speaker” ( Hayashi.2006). Besides, demonstratives are also used as “interjective hesitators” that signal “the speaker’s hesitation in utterance production” ( Hayashi.2006).

The placeholder and hesitator uses also apply to the Papuan Malay demonstratives, as shown in ( Example_7.45 ) to ( Example_7.47 ) and in ( Example_7.48 ), respectively. In this function, however, only the long demonstrative forms are attested, while the short forms are unattested.

As placeholders, the demonstratives can substitute for any lexical item, such as nouns as in ( Example_7.45 ), personal pronouns as in ( Example_7.46 ), or verbs as in ( Example_7.47 ). More investigation is needed, though, to account for the alternation of ini ‘ d.prox ’ and itu ‘ d.dist ’ in this context. In most cases, as in ( Example_7.46 ) and ( Example_7.47 ), the demonstrative is set off from the subsequently produced target word by a comma intonation (`` ''). Often, however, there is no audible pause between the placeholder and the target word as in ( Example_7.45 ).

‘(at that particular time) I remembered, what’s-her-name, Ise’ [080917-008-NP.0102]

styleExampleTitle

‘wow!, what’s-their-name, we drove yesterday all the way to ’ [081006-033-Cv.0007]

styleExampleTitle

‘now I (already), what’s-its-name, set aside one hundred thousand (rupiah)’ [081110-002-Cv.0039]

While in ( Example_7.45 ) to ( Example_7.47 ), the demonstratives are used referentially to substitute for a lexical item, this is not the case in ( Example_7.48 ). In this example, itu ‘ d.dist ’ is used as a nonreferential interjective hesitator. This is evidenced by the fact that itu ‘ d.dist ’ does not agree with adnominally used ini ‘ d.prox ’, which modifies the head nominal pace ‘man’. Overall, however, the hesitator uses of the demonstratives are rare; most commonly, Papuan Malay speakers use the hesitator e(m) ‘uh’ (see § Para_5.13.2 ).

Interjective hesitator
styleExampleTitle

‘oh, umh, umh, this man, he recently took ’ [081011-009-Cv.0007]

Further investigation is required, to explore whether and in which ways Papuan Malay makes a distinction between the placeholder and nonreferential hesitator uses of its demonstratives and whether it may in fact be using the right-displacement attested in ( Example_7.48 ) as a deliberate construction for emphasis in some contexts.
summary: Demonstratives in cross-linguistic and Papuan Malay use can function as pronominal placeholders during word-finding trouble, temporarily substituting for lexical items such as nouns, pronouns, or verbs, and they can also serve as interjective hesitators that signal speaker hesitation. In Papuan Malay, only the long demonstrative forms occur in these functions; placeholder uses appear referential, while the hesitator use in the cited example is nonreferential, though such uses are rare compared with the more common hesitator *e(m)* “uh.”

text: In the following sections, the syntactic properties and forms of the Papuan Malay locatives are reviewed and discussed (§ Para_7.2.1 ), followed by an in-depth discussion of their different functions and domains of use (§ Para_7.2.2 ).
summary: The passage says that the next sections will first review and discuss the syntactic properties and forms of Papuan Malay locatives. It will then provide a more detailed discussion of their different functions and domains of use.

text: The distributional properties of the locatives are briefly reviewed in § Para_7.2.1.1. This review is followed in § Para_7.2.1.2 by a discussion of the distribution and frequencies of the pronominally versus the adnominally used locatives.

text:
The Papuan Malay locatives have the following distributional properties (for more details see § Para_5.7 ):

enumerate

Substitution for noun phrases that occur in prepositional phrases (pronominal uses) (§ Para_5.7.1 )

Modification with demonstratives or relative clauses (pronominal uses) (§ Para_5.7.1 )

Co-occurrence with noun phrases(adnominal uses): n / np loc (§ Para_5.7.2 )

enumerate
summary: Papuan Malay locatives have several distributional properties. They can substitute for noun phrases in prepositional phrases, be modified by demonstratives or relative clauses in pronominal uses, and co-occur with noun phrases in adnominal uses as n/np loc.

subsubsection: Distribution of the pronominally versus the adnominally used locatives
text:
This section describes the distribution and frequencies of the pronominally versus the adnominally used locatives (their semantic distinctions are discussed in § Para_7.2.2 ).

The corpus includes a total of 1,366 locative tokens: 494 sini ‘ l.prox ’ (36%), 411 situ ‘ l.med ’ (30%), and 461 sana ‘ l.dist ’ (34%) tokens. Most commonly the locatives are employed pronominally (1,106/1,366 tokens – 91%), while their adnominal uses are considerably less common (260/1,366 tokens – 19%), as shown in Table_7.7.

The distribution of the pronominally used locatives is presented in Table_7.8. In their pronominal uses, as mentioned in § Para_5.7.1, the locatives always occur in prepositional phrases. Most often they are introduced with an overt preposition: 384/416 sini ‘ l.prox ’ (92%), 302/345 situ ‘ l.med ’ (87%), and 311/345 sana ‘ l.dist ’ (90%) tokens. When the context allows the disambiguation of the semantic role or relationship of the locative, however, the preposition can also be deleted (the elision of prepositions is discussed in § Para_10.1.5 ): 32/416 sini ‘ l.prox ’ (8%), 45/345 situ ‘ l.med ’ (13%), and 34/345 sana ‘ l.dist ’ (10%) tokens. Overall, however, pronominally used locatives with zero- preposition are rather rare (109/1,106 tokens – 10%), as shown in Table_7.8.

The distribution of the adnominally used locatives is presented in Table_7.9. In their adnominal uses, as mentioned in § Para_5.7.2, the locatives most commonly co-occur with noun phrases that occur in prepositional phrases (225/260 tokens – 87%). Like the pronominally used locatives, the vast majority of adnominally used locatives occur in prepositional phrases with an overt preposition: 46/78 sini ‘ l.prox ’ (59%), 55/66 situ ‘ l.med ’ (84%), and 86/116 sana ‘ l.dist ’ (74%) tokens. Far fewer locative tokens occur in prepositional phrases with zero preposition: 16/78 sini ‘ l.prox ’ (21%), 6/66 situ ‘ l.med ’ (9%), and 16/116 sana ‘ l.dist ’ (14%) tokens. The number of locative tokens occurring in unembedded noun phrases is equally low or still lower: 16/78 sini ‘ l.prox ’ (21%), 5/66 situ ‘ l.med ’ (7%), and 14/116 sana ‘ l.dist ’ (12%) tokens.
summary: The corpus contains 1,366 locative tokens, with sini, situ, and sana occurring in fairly similar proportions, and locatives are used much more often pronominally than adnominally. Pronominal locatives almost always appear in prepositional phrases, usually with an overt preposition, while zero-preposition uses are uncommon. Adnominal locatives likewise most often co-occur with noun phrases in prepositional phrases, and both zero-preposition and unembedded noun phrase uses are comparatively rare.

text: The locatives have a number of different functions and uses which are discussed in more detail in the following sections: spatial uses in § Para_7.2.2.1, figurative locational uses in § Para_7.2.2.2, temporal uses in § Para_7.2.2.3, psychological uses in § Para_7.2.2.4, and textual uses in § Para_7.2.2.5.
summary: The locatives are used in several different ways, including spatial, figurative locational, temporal, psychological, and textual functions. These uses are treated in more detail in later sections, each devoted to one of these categories.

text:
In their spatial uses, the Papuan Malay locatives designate the location of an entity relative to that of the speaker and focus the hearer’s attention to the specific location of these entities. In the following, two issues are explored in more detail: the semantic distinctions between the three locatives, and the semantic distinctions between the pronominally and adnominally used locatives.

Semantic distinctions between the three locatives

Generally speaking, proximal sini ‘ l.prox ’ signals proximity to a deictic center, while distal sana ‘ l.dist ’ expresses distance from this center. Medial situ ‘ l.med ’ indicates mid distance; that is, the referent is more remote from the speaker than the referent of sini ‘ l.prox ’ but not as far as the referent of sana ‘ l.dist ’. The actual distances signaled with the locatives are relative, however, and depend on the speakers’ perceptions. The data also shows that the locatives are very commonly used independently of the parameter of visibility. Although sini ‘ l.prox ’ most commonly denotes visible locations, it can also refer to invisible ones; likewise, the non-proximal locatives can refer to visible or invisible locations.

The spatial uses of sini ‘ l.prox ’ are illustrated in ( Example_7.49 ) and ( Example_7.50 ). The semantic distinctions between sini ‘ l.prox ’ and sana ‘ l.dist ’ are shown in ( Example_7.51 ). The spatial uses of situ ‘ l.med ’ and its semantic distinctions from sini ‘ l.prox ’ and sana ‘ l.dist ’ are illustrated in ( Example_7.52 ) and ( Example_7.53 ).

The examples in ( Example_7.49 ) and ( Example_7.50 ) illustrate the spatial uses of sini ‘ l.prox ’. In both cases, adnominally used sini ‘ l.prox ’ indicates the location of an entity close to the speaker: ember sini ‘the bucket here’ in ( Example_7.49 ) and Sawar sini ‘Sawar here’ in ( Example_7.50 ). The actual distances signaled with sini ‘ l.prox ’ differ, however, depending on the speakers’ perceptions. In ( Example_7.49 ), ember sini ‘the bucket here’ is standing right next to the speaker. By contrast in ( Example_7.50 ), Sawar sini ‘Sawar here’ denotes a location that is situated about ten kilometers away from the speaker’s location. The speaker, however, perceives Sawar as being close to his own location given that Apawer is situated still further away. The examples in ( Example_7.49 ) and ( Example_7.50 ) also illustrate that sini ‘ l.prox ’ is used independently of the parameter of visibility: the locative is used for a visible location in ( Example_7.49 ) and for an invisible one in ( Example_7.50 ).

The example in ( Example_7.51 ) illustrates the semantic distinctions between sini ‘ l.prox ’ and sana ‘ l.dist ’. The utterance occurred during a conversation outside at night. Noting that their neighbors are also sitting outside, the speaker employs the distal locative to refer to the neighbors’ location sana ‘over there’ and the proximal locative to refer to their own location sini ‘here’.

The examples in ( Example_7.52 ) and ( Example_7.53 ) show the spatial uses of situ ‘ l.med ’ and its semantic distinctions from sini ‘ l.prox ’ and sana ‘ l.dist ’.

The exchange in ( Example_7.52 ) took place at night in front of the house while a meeting took place inside in the living room where the teenagers usually sleep. The young people were waiting for the guests to leave so that they could go to sleep. Employing situ ‘ l.med ’, the first teenager wonders what the adults are doing situ ‘there’ in the living room. summary: Papuan Malay spatial locatives mark the location of an entity relative to the speaker and direct the hearer’s attention to that location. The three forms contrast as proximal sini ‘here,’ distal sana ‘there/over there,’ and medial situ ‘mid-distance there,’ though the distances are relative to speaker perception and not tied strictly to visibility. The passage also shows that these locatives can be used both for visible and invisible locations.

text:
The examples in ( Example_7.51 ) and ( Example_7.53 ) again show that distances signaled with the non-prox\-i\-mal locatives are relative. In ( Example_7.51 ) sana ‘ l.dist ’ refers to the neighbor’s house, situated about fifty meters away from where the speakers are sitting. By contrast, situ ‘ l.med ’ in ( Example_7.53 ) denotes the village of Warmer which is located several kilometers away from the speaker’s location, while sana ‘ l.dist ’ refers to the area beyond Warmer. Besides, these examples show that the non-proximal locatives are also used independently of the parameter of visibility. Distal sana ‘ l.dist ’ is used for a visible location in ( Example_7.51 ) and an invisible one in ( Example_7.53 ). Medial situ ‘ l.med ’ refers to a visible location in ( Example_7.52 ) and an invisible one in ( Example_7.53 ).

Semantic distinctions between the pronominally and adnominally used locatives

In designating the location of a referent relative to that of the speaker, Papuan Malay makes a distinction between the pronominally and the adnominally used locatives.

Pronominally used locatives provide additional information about the location of an entity or referent without restricting its referential scope. Adnominally used locatives, by contrast, have a restrictive function, thereby assisting the hearer in the identification of the referent. That is, by directing the hearer’s attention to the referent’s location, adnominal locatives indicate that the referent is precisely the one situated in the location designated by the locative. This distinction is illustrated with the (near) contrastive examples in ( Example_7.54 ) and ( Example_7.55 ).

The prepositional phrases with pronominally used sini ‘ l.prox ’ in ( Example_7.54a ) and ( Example_7.55a ) provide additional information about the location of the referents, information that is nonessential for their identification: orang di sini ‘the people here’ in ( Example_7.54a ) and dorang di sini ‘them here’ in ( Example_7.55a ). By contrast, in ( Example_7.54b ) and ( Example_7.55b ) the respective head nominals orang ‘person’ and dorang ‘ 3pl ’ are modified with sini ‘ l.prox ’. In both cases, the locatives indicate that the referents of orang ‘person’ and dorang ‘ 3pl ’ are precisely the ones located sini ‘here’ as opposed to other locations: orang sini ‘the people that are here’ in Example_7.54b ) and dorang sini ‘they that are here’ in ( Example_7.55b ).

summary:
The passage shows that Papuan Malay non-proximal locatives are relative in distance: *sana* ‘distal’ and *situ* ‘medial’ can refer to locations at different ranges depending on the context. It also notes that these locatives are not determined by visibility, since both visible and invisible locations can be described with either form.  

It further distinguishes between pronominal and adnominal uses of locatives. Pronominal locatives add nonessential information about location, while adnominal locatives restrict the noun’s reference by identifying the referent as the one located there.

text:
The spatial uses of the locatives can be expanded to figurative locational uses in narratives. Employing a locative preceded by sampe di ‘reach at’, the narrators bring their stories to a figurative locational endpoint. Such uses are attested for sini ‘ l.prox ’ as in ( Example_7.56 ) and situ ‘ l.med ’ as in ( Example_7.57 ), but not for sana ‘ l.dist ’.

sa su sembu, trima-kasi sampe di sini\\
1sg already be.healed thank.you reach at l.prox \\

‘[after this accident] I already recovered, thank you! this is all’ (Lit. ‘reach here’) [081015-005-NP.0051]

sa pikir mungking sampe di situ dulu\\
1sg think maybe reach at l.med first\\

‘I think maybe that’s all for now’ (Lit. ‘reach there’) [080919-004-NP.0083]
summary: The locatives can extend from spatial to figurative narrative uses, where a locative introduced by *sampe di* ‘reach at’ marks a story’s figurative endpoint. This use is attested with *sini* ‘proximal’ and *situ* ‘medial’, but not with *sana* ‘distal’.

text:
The locative situ ‘ l.med ’ also has temporal uses. Preceded by the preposition dari ‘from’, situ ‘ l.med ’ signals the temporal setting of the event talked about with respect to some temporal reference point in the past, as illustrated in ( Example_7.58 ). Overall, however, this domain of use is not very common, with the corpus containing only two such occurrences. The proximal and distal locatives are not attested to have temporal uses.

dari situ sa punya mama tida maw jualang pagi lagi\\
from l.med 1sg poss mother neg want merchandise/sell morning again\\
‘ from that moment on my mother didn’t want to do any more vending in the morning’ (Lit. ‘ from there’) [081014-014-NP.0006]
summary: The locative situ ‘l.med’ can also be used temporally when preceded by dari ‘from’, where it marks the temporal point from which an event is viewed in relation to a past reference point. This usage is rare, with only two examples in the corpus, and the proximal and distal locatives are not reported to have temporal uses.

text:
The locatives also have limited psychological uses to signal the speakers’ emotional involvement and attitudes. The corpus contains a fair number of utterances in which the speakers switch from sana ‘ l.dist ’ to situ ‘ l.med ’ to refer to the same location. With this switch the speakers indicate that the location has become vivid to their minds and psychologically closer than sana ‘ l.dist ’ would signal, as illustrated in ( Example_7.59 ) and ( Example_7.60 ).

In ( Example_7.59 ), a father relates that he will bring his two oldest children to the provincial capital Jayapura for further schooling once the younger one has finished high school. Anaphorically used sana ‘ l.dist ’ signals that Jayapura is at considerable distance from the speaker’s current location (ca. 300 km). The subsequent use of situ ‘ l.med ’ indicates that with his two children going to live there, distant Jayapura has become psychologically much closer.

styleExampleTitle
Psychological uses: Example #1
styleExampleTitle

kalo Ise ni selesay saya mo bawa dong dua\\
if Ise d.prox finish 1sg want bring 3pl two\\
ke sana tinggal di situ\\
to l.dist stay at l.med \\

‘when Ise here has finished (her schooling) I want to bring the two of them to (Jayapura) over there to live there’ [081025-003-Cv.0135]

Likewise in ( Example_7.60 ), the speaker switches from sana ‘ l.dist ’ to situ ‘ l.med ’ to refer to the Mambramo area sana ‘over there’, situated about 100 km to the west. The switch occurs at the moment when the speaker considers his own involvement with the Mambramo area, namely that he has never been situ ‘there’. Again, this switch indicates that the location talked about has become more vivid and psychologically closer to the speaker’s mind.

In the corpus, speakers sometimes switch from sana ‘l.dist’ to situ ‘l.med’ for the same place to show that it has become vivid in their mind and psychologically closer than ordinary distance would suggest.

text:
In their textual uses, locatives are used anaphorically; that is, they are coreferen\-tial with a discourse antecedent that denotes a location. In ( Example_7.61 ) sini ‘ l.prox ’ corefers with the place where the speaker was standing, namely where there were daung klapa itu ‘those coconut leaves’. Medial situ ‘ l.med ’ in ( Example_7.62 ) corefers with laut ‘sea’, and sana ‘ l.dist ’ in ( Example_7.63 ) with sa pu temang ‘my friend’. The three examples also show that in their anaphoric uses the locatives may be employed pronominally as in ( Example_7.61 ) and ( Example_7.62 ), or adnominally as in ( Example_7.63 ).

baru daung klapa itu daung klapa yang saya ada\\
and.then leaf coconut d.dist leaf coconut rel 1sg exist\\
berdiri itu sa bilang dari sini sa kutuk dia\\
stand d.dist 1sg say from l.prox 1sg curse 3sg \\

‘and then those coconut leaves, those coconut leaves where I was standing I said, `` from here I curse him (the evil spirit)''' [080917-008-NP.0101/0103]

ey, kam dua pi mandi di laut suda!, trus kam\\
hey! 2pl two go bathe at sea already next 2pl \\
dua cuci celana di situ\\
two wash trouser at l.med \\

[A mother addressing her young sons:] ‘hey, you two go bathe in the sea already!, then you two wash (your) trousers there!’ [080917-006-CvHt.0007]

tong dari sa pu temang pinjam trening untuk besok\\
1pl from 1sg poss friend borrow tracksuit for tomorrow\\
tu yang tadi sa ke temang sana\\
d.dist rel earlier 1sg to friend l.dist \\

‘we (are back) from my friend (from whom we) borrowed a tracksuit for tomorrow that’s why a short while ago I (went) to (my) friend (who is) over there’ [081011-020-Cv.0052/0056]
summary: In textual uses, locatives are used anaphorically, meaning they refer back to a previously mentioned location in the discourse. The examples show that *sini* ‘proximal’, *situ* ‘medial’, and *sana* ‘distal’ can corefer with locations such as where the speaker was standing, the sea, or a friend’s place. In these anaphoric uses, locatives may function either pronominally or adnominally.

text:
Demonstratives and locatives can be combined with an adnominally used demonstrative modifying a pronominally used locative as in ( Example_7.64 ) and ( Example_7.65 ), or an adnominally used locative as in ( Example_7.66 ). In these constructions, the demonstrative serves to intensify the locative, resulting in an emphatic reading that conveys vividness.

Short distal itu ‘ d.dist ’ modifies proximal sini ‘ l.prox ’ in ( Example_7.64 ) and medial situ ‘ l.med ’ in ( Example_7.65 ). In ( Example_7.66 ) long distal itu ‘ d.dist ’ modifies distal sana ‘ l.dist ’.

dorang tida bisa dekat sama dorang di sini tu\\
3pl neg be.able near with 3pl at l.prox d.dist \\
ada orang swanggi satu de bertobat \\
exist person nocturnal.evil.spirit one 3sg repent \\

‘they (the evil spirits) can’t be close to them (God’s children) here ( emph ) is one evil sorcerer, he has become a Christian’ [081006-022-CvEx.0146/0150]

tida bisa kamu tinggal di situ, di situ tu\\
neg be.able 2pl stay at l.med at l.med d.dist \\
ruma tu ada setang banyak\\
house d.dist exist evil.spirit many\\

‘you can’t live there, there ( emph ), (in) that house are many evil spirits’ [081006-022-CvEx.0164]

sana, te ada di sana itu\\
l.dist tea exist at l.dist d.dist \\

‘there, the tea (is) over there ( emph )’ [081014-011-CvEx.0010]

In all attested combinations, it is the distal demonstrative that modifies a locative. Modification of a locative with proximal ini ‘ d.prox ’ is also possible although unattested, as discussed in § Para_5.7.1 ).
summary: Demonstratives and locatives can combine so that a demonstrative modifies a locative used either pronominally or adnominally, and this use intensifies the locative to create an emphatic, vivid reading. In the attested examples, the distal demonstrative itu modifies locatives of different distances (sini, situ, sana), and the text notes that proximal ini could also modify a locative, though this is not attested here.

text:
The Papuan Malay demonstratives and locatives are deictic expressions. They provide orientation to the hearer in the outside world and in the speech situation, in spatial as well as in nonspatial domains. Both deictic systems are distance oriented, in that they signal the relative distance of an entity vis-à-vis a deictic center. At the same time, the two systems differ in a number of respects. They are distinct both in terms of their syntactic characteristics and forms and in terms of their functions.

The differences between the demonstratives and the locatives with respect to their syntactic characteristics and forms are summarized in Table_7.10.

The main distinctions between the demonstratives and the locatives in terms of their various functions are summarized in Table_7.11.

In summary, with respect to their syntactic properties, the demonstratives have a wider range of uses (adnominal, pronominal, and adverbial uses) than the locatives. Likewise, in terms of their functions, the demonstratives have a wider range of uses than the locatives. The locative system, by contrast, allows finer semantic distinctions to be made than the demonstrative system, given that the former expresses a three-way deictic contrast, whereas the latter expresses a two-way deictic contrast.
summary: Papuan Malay demonstratives and locatives are deictic expressions that orient the hearer in spatial and nonspatial domains by indicating the relative distance of an entity from a deictic center. Although both systems are distance-oriented, they differ in form, syntax, and function: demonstratives have a wider range of syntactic uses and functions, while locatives make finer semantic distinctions because they express a three-way deictic contrast, compared with the demonstratives’ two-way contrast.

text:
This chapter describes the Papuan Malay noun phrase with its different types of structures. Also included is a description of noun phrase apposition; noun phrase coordination is not discussed here but in Para_14.

An overview of the possible constituents of the Papuan Malay noun phrase is given in Table_8.1
(the parenthesis in the table header signal that the modifiers are optional). Modifying elements listed in the same column represent choices; constituents in the same row do not necessarily co-occur.

In the following, examples are presented for the different types of constituents that can function as the head of a noun phrase. In giving examples, brackets are used to indicate the constituent structure within the noun phrase, where deemed necessary. In ( Example_8.1 ) the head is a noun, in ( Example_8.2 ) it is a personal pronoun, in ( Example_8.3 ) a demonstrative, in ( Example_8.4 ) a locative, and in ( Example_8.5 ) an interrogative. Head nouns allow the widest range of modifiers, while personal pronouns, demonstrative, locatives, and interrogatives allow only a subset of modifiers, as shown throughout this chapter.

styleExampleTitle
Types of constituents functioning as heads in noun phrases
styleExampleTitle

kitong cari ana kecil itu\\
1pl search child be.small d.dist \\

‘we were looking for that small kid’ [080921-004a-CvNP.0070]

dong dua tu ikut\\
3pl two d.dist follow\\

[About an upcoming event:] ‘both of them ( emph ) are going to participate’ [081115-001a-Cv.0115]

itu tu rahasia mo mo biking apa ka, mo \\
d.dist d.dist secret want want make what or want \\

[About raising children:] ‘ that ( emph ) is the secret (when we) want want to do something or want to ’ [080917-010-CvEx.0160]

e, sa tinggal di situ tu\\
uh 1sg stay at l.med d.dist \\

‘uh, I lived there ( emph )’ [080922-002-Cv.0112]

ana laki laki ini de mo ke mana ni?\\
child rdp husband d.prox 3sg want to where d.prox \\

‘this boy, where ( emph ) does he want to (go)?’ [080922-004-Cv.0017]

The minimal noun phrase consists of a bare head nominal. Modifiers are optional and occur in pre- and/or posthead position. Attested in the corpus is the co-occurrence of up to three posthead constituents. Modifiers listed in the same pre- or posthead slots in Table_8.1
are unattested. This observation also applies to adnominal possessive relations where a numeral or quantifier precedes a possessor. Such pre-possessor numerals or quantifiers are not analyzed as “co-occurring” with the possessor noun phrase. Instead they are analyzed as prehead modifiers of the possessor noun phrase. This is shown in the elicited example in ( Footnote_Example_8.1 ): the prehead modifier smua ‘all’ modifies the head nominal of the possessor phrase, ana ‘child’. (For details on adnominal possession see § Para_8.4 and Para_9.)
-5pt

smua ana ini pu tugas su selesay\\
[[all] child [ d.prox ]] poss duty already finish\\
‘the duties of all these children are already taken care of’ [Elicited ME151120.002]

There is one exception, however, namely the quantifier brapa ‘several’, as shown in in ( Example_8.9 ).

Prehead modifiers can be numerals such as empat ‘four’ in ( Example_8.6 ), quantifiers such as smua ‘all’ in ( Example_8.7 ), or possessor noun phrases in adnominal possessive constructions such orang orang besar ‘big people’ in ( Example_8.8 ). The co-occurrence of prehead modifers is unattested, with one exception. The mid-range quantifier brapa ‘several’ co-occurs with certain numerals, such as ratus ‘hundred’, or ribu ‘thousand’, as in brapa ratus orang ‘several hundred people’ in ( Example_8.9 ).

styleExampleTitle
mod – head
styleExampleTitle

jadi saya empat ana\\
so 1sg four child\\

num – head: ‘so, I (have) four children’ [081006-024-CvEx.0002]

smua buku bisa basa\\
all book be.able be.wet\\

qt – head: ‘ all books could get wet’ [080917-008-NP.0189]

bukang orang orang besar pu ana \\
neg [rdp person big] poss child \\

‘(she’s the child of farmers) not the child of big people ’ [081110-005-Pr.0094]

tentara itu ada brapa ratus orang\\
soldier d.dist exist several hundred person\\

qt – num – head: ‘[one time, I brought the military (into the forest),] those soldiers were several hundred people’ [081029-005-Cv.0131]

The posthead modifier slots attract a wider range of constituents: verbs, nouns, prepositional phrases, and relative clauses occur in slot Post-1, personal pronouns in slot Post-2, and demonstratives, locatives, interrogatives, numerals, and quantifiers in slot Post-3. In addition, the demonstratives also occur in slot Post-4. The modifiers occurring in slot Post-1 have attributive function, while those in slot Post-2 to Post-4 have determining function.

Co-occurrences of modifiers listed in the same slot are unattested, whereas those listed in different slots are attested to co-occur, as demonstrated in ( Example_8.10 ) to ( Example_8.16 ). In tangang pendek satu tu ‘that one short-handed (one)’ in ( Example_8.10 ), an adnominally used stative verb co-occurs with a numeral and a demonstrative. In babi puti ko ‘you white pig’ in ( Example_8.11 ), an adnominally used verb co-occurs with a personal pronoun. In pisang Sorong sana tu ‘those bananas (from) Sorong over there’ in ( Example_8.12 ), an adnominally used noun co-occurs with a locative and a demonstrative. In pace dorang dua ini ‘the two men here’ in ( Example_8.13 ), an adnominally used personal pronoun co-occurs with a numeral and a demonstrative. In kaka dari Mambramo satu ‘a certain older brother from (the) Mambramo (area)’ in ( Example_8.14 ), an adnominally used prepositional phrase co-occurs with a numeral. In dong di Papua tu ‘they in Papua there’ in ( Example_8.15 ), an adnominally used prepositional phrase co-occurs with a demonstrative. Finally, in kata itu tu ‘those very words’ in ( Example_8.16 ) two adnominally used demonstratives co-occur.

summary:
The chapter outlines the structure of the Papuan Malay noun phrase, including noun phrase apposition, and shows that noun phrases may have a bare head or an optional combination of prehead and posthead modifiers. Head constituents can be nouns, personal pronouns, demonstratives, locatives, or interrogatives, but head nouns allow the widest range of modifiers, while the other head types take only a subset.

Prehead modifiers include numerals, quantifiers, and possessor noun phrases, though co-occurrence among prehead modifiers is generally unattested except for the quantifier brapa ‘several’ with some numerals. Posthead modifiers are organized into slots: Post-1 takes verbs, nouns, prepositional phrases, and relative clauses; Post-2 takes personal pronouns; Post-3 takes demonstratives, locatives, interrogatives, numerals, and quantifiers; and Post-4 also contains demonstratives.

text:
pisang Sorong sana tu, iii, besar besar manis\\

head – n – loc – dem: ‘ those bananas (from) Sorong over there, oooh, (they) are all big (and) sweet’ [081011-003-Cv.0017]

head – pp – dem: ‘ they in Papua there, they eat sagu porridge’ [081109-009-JR.0001]

kata itu tu yang biking sa bertahang\\
word d.dist d.dist rel make 1sg hold.(out/back)\\

head – dem – dem ‘(it was) those very words that made me hold out’ [081115-001a-Cv.0235]

This brief overview shows that Papuan Malay employs two distinct types of noun phrase structures: (1) a head – modifier or `` n-mod '' structure, and (2) a modifier – head or `` mod-n '' structure. The particular structure of a noun phrase depends on the syntactic properties of its adnominal constituents:

itemize

n-mod structure with adnominally used verbs, nouns, personal pronouns, demonstratives, locatives, interrogatives, prepositional phrases, and relative clauses.

n-mod or mod-n structure with adnominally used numerals and quantifiers (the constituent order depends on the semantics of the phrasal structure).

mod-n structure in adnominal possessive constructions.

itemize

Noun phrases with an n-mod structure are examined in § Para_8.2 and those with an n-mod or mod-n structure in § Para_8.3. Adnominal possessive constructions with a mod-n structure are briefly mentioned in § Para_8.4, and fully discussed in Para_9. In addition, apposition is discussed in § Para_8.5. The main points of this chapter are summarized in § Para_8.6.
summary: The passage shows that Papuan Malay noun phrases can be built either as head–modifier (n-mod) or modifier–head (mod-n) structures. Which order is used depends on the type of adnominal element: verbs, nouns, pronouns, demonstratives, locatives, interrogatives, prepositional phrases, and relative clauses occur in n-mod order, while numerals and quantifiers may appear in either order depending on meaning, and possessive constructions use mod-n order.

text: In noun phrases with an n-mod structure, the head occurs in initial position followed by the modifying elements. The following modifiers are discussed: verbs (§ Para_8.2.1 ), nouns (§ Para_8.2.2 ), personal pronouns (§ Para_8.2.3 ), demonstratives (§ Para_8.2.4 ), locatives (§ Para_8.2.5 ), interrogatives (§ Para_8.2.6 ), prepositional phrases (§ Para_8.2.7 ), and relative clauses (§ Para_8.2.8 ).
summary: In noun phrases with an n-mod structure, the head noun appears first, followed by modifying elements. The passage lists the types of modifiers discussed in this structure: verbs, nouns, personal pronouns, demonstratives, locatives, interrogatives, prepositional phrases, and relative clauses.

text:
Adnominally used verbs always follow their head nominals such that `` n v '', as shown in ( Example_8.17 ) to ( Example_8.26 ). Most often, the adnominal modifier is a stative verb, as in ( Example_8.17 ) to ( Example_8.20 ), although noun phrases with adnominally used dynamic verbs also occur, as in ( Example_8.21 ) to ( Example_8.24 ). (The distributional preferences of attributively used stative and dynamic verbs are discussed in § Para_5.3.2 ).

In noun phrases with adnominally used stative verbs, as in ( Example_8.17 ) to ( Example_8.20 ), the head nominal is typically a bare noun as in ( Example_8.17 ), or a reduplicated noun as in ( Example_8.18 ). The adnominal modifier is usually a bare stative verb, such as besar ‘be big’ in ( Example_8.17 ) or panjang ‘be long’ in ( Example_8.18 ). However, the modifier can also be a multi-word phrase with an overt coordinator as in puti dengang hitam ‘white and black’ in ( Example_8.19 ), or with juxtaposed constituents as in the elicited near contrastive example in ( Example_8.20 ). Overall, though, multi-word modifier phrases are rare and limited to phrases with two adnominally used verbs.

‘immediately (his) long claws came out’ [081115-001a-Cv.0077]

‘my father buried my grandfather’s white and black cloth’ [081014-014-NP.0047]

sa pu bapa kubur sa pu tete pu\\
1sg poss father bury 1sg poss grandfather poss \\

‘my father buried my grandfather’s white (and) black cloth’ [Elicited BR130221.036] According to one consultant, Papuan Malay speakers prefer hitam puti ‘black (and) white’ over puti hitam ‘white (and) black’, although both constructions are acceptable.

Adnominally used dynamic verbs denote activities, associated with the head nominal, as in ( Example_8.21 ) to ( Example_8.24 ). The head nominal can denote an agent who carries out the activity encoded by the verb, as with monovalent jalang ‘walk’ in ( Example_8.21 ), or a patient who undergoes this activity, as with bivalent bakar ‘burn’ in ( Example_8.22 ). The head can also express a spatial or temporal location where the activity occurs as with monovalent mandi ‘bathe’ in ( Example_8.23 ) and bangung ‘get up’ in ( Example_8.24 ), respectively.

styleExampleTitle

Noun phrases with adnominally used verbs can further be modified with numerals. In the corpus, the adnominally used numeral is always the numeral satu ‘one’, as in ( Example_8.25 ) and ( Example_8.26 ) (the non-enumerating function of satu ‘one’ as a marker of ``specific indefiniteness'', as in ( Example_8.26 ), is discussed in § Para_5.9.4 ).

Noun phrases with adnominal verbs and numerals
styleExampleTitle

[About an acquaintance:] ‘ that one short-handed (one) ((laughter))’ [081006-016-Cv.0036]

[[ kampung tua] satu] yang perna om Wili \\

summary: Adnominally used verbs in these noun phrases always follow the head nominal. Stative verbs are the most common modifiers, typically appearing as bare verbs after a bare or reduplicated noun, though occasional multi-word modifiers with coordination or juxtaposition occur and are rare. Dynamic verbs also appear adnominally, where they describe an activity associated with the head nominal, which may be interpreted as an agent, patient, or a spatial/temporal location; such noun phrases can also be modified by the numeral satu ‘one’.

text:
In noun phrases with adnominally used nouns, a posthead noun n2 modifies the head nominal n1, such that `` n1n2 ''. Such constructions are characterized by the semantic subordination of the n2 modifier under the head nominal n1.

In Papuan Malay, the distinction between a noun phrase with an adnominally used noun, hereafter n1n2-np, and a compound with juxtaposed nominal constituents is not clear-cut, however. Word combinations or collocations range from two word expressions with compositional transparent semantics such as air sagu ‘liquid of the sago palm tree’, to less compositional two-word expressions, such as kampung-tana ‘home village’ (literally ‘village-ground’). This section focuses on n1n2-np s; the demarcation of such phrasal expression from compounds, and compounding in general, are discussed in § Para_3.2.1.

n1n2-np s denote important features for subclassification of the superordinate head nominal. Typically, the head of an n1n2-np is a noun, as shown in ( Example_8.27 ) to ( Example_8.40 ). Less often, the head is a deverbal constituent as in ( Example_8.41 ) and ( Example_8.42 ). Semantically, n1n2-np s denote a wide range of associative relations between the n1 and the n2, as shown in ( Example_8.27 ) to ( Example_8.42 ): part-whole, property-of, affiliated-with, name-of, subtype-of, composed-of, and purpose-for relations, as well as locational, temporal, and event relations. n1n2-np s encode inalienable and alienable concepts.

Inalienable ``part-whole'' relations of body parts and plants are given in ( Example_8.27 ) and ( Example_8.28 ), respectively, while ( Example_8.29 ) illustrates an alienable ``part-whole'' relation. (More types of ``part-whole'' relations are found in Table Table_8.2 and Table Table_8.2a.)

summary:
Papuan Malay noun phrases with adnominally used nouns consist of a head nominal followed by a modifier noun, but the boundary between these phrases and compounds is not always clear. Such n1n2 noun phrases are semantically subordinate constructions used to specify important features of the head nominal, and they express a wide range of associative relations, including part-whole, property-of, affiliated-with, name-of, subtype-of, composed-of, purpose-for, locational, temporal, and event relations.

The head is usually a noun, though it can also be deverbal, and these constructions can encode both inalienable and alienable meanings. The passage emphasizes that Papuan Malay n1n2 phrases are diverse in form and meaning, with some examples being highly transparent and others more lexicalized.

text:
Papuan Malay noun phrases are often modified with personal pronouns in posthead position, such that `` n pro '', as illustrated in ( Example_8.43 ) to ( Example_8.45 ). Signaling the definiteness, person, and number of their referents, the adnominally used personal pronouns allow the unambiguous identification of their referents. They are available for all person-number values, except for first person singular saya/ sa ‘ 1sg ’ which is unattested; the long and short pronoun forms are used interchangeably. (Personal pronouns and their adnominal uses are discussed in detail in Para_6; see also § Para_5.5 ).

Adnominal singular personal pronouns indicate the singularity of their referents, as shown with ko ‘ 2sg ’ and dia ‘ 3sg ’ in ( Example_8.43 ). In addition, they have pertinent discourse functions, discussed in detail in § Para_6.2.1. Noun phrases with adnominally used plural personal pronouns have two readings. With an indefinite referent, such as laki laki ‘man’ in ( Example_8.44 ), the noun phrase receives an additive plural reading. With a definite referent such as Roni in ( Example_8.45 ), the noun phrase receives an associative inclusory plural reading. Both readings are discussed in detail in § Para_6.2.2.

These adnominal pronouns occur for all person-number combinations except first person singular, and singular forms simply indicate singular reference. Plural forms have two interpretations: with indefinite nouns they give an additive plural reading, while with definite nouns they express an associative inclusory plural reading.

text:
Within the noun phrase, adnominally used demonstratives are placed at the right periphery, where they have scope over the entire noun phrase, such that `` n dem '': proximal ini ‘ d.prox ’ or distal itu ‘ d.dist ’, or their respective reduced forms ni ‘ d.prox ’ and tu ‘ d.dist ’. Like adnominally used personal pronouns (§ Para_8.2.3 ), the adnominal demonstratives function as determiners. Unlike the personal pronouns, however, they signal specificity rather than definiteness. Concerning the semantic distinctions between the notion of definiteness and the notion of specificity, see Footnote Footnote_5.164 in § Para_5.5 (p. Footnote_5.164).

The head nominal can be a noun such as ana ‘child’ in ( Example_8.46 ), a personal pronoun such as dia ‘ 3sg ’ in ( Example_8.46 ), a locative such as sana ‘ l.dist ’ in ( Example_8.47 ), or another demonstrative such as itu ‘ d.dist ’ in ( Example_8.48 ). (Demonstratives and their adnominal uses are discussed in detail in § Para_7.1; see also § Para_5.6 ).

‘ that child, I love her ( emph ) most’ [081011-023-Cv.0097]

‘there, the tea is over there ( emph )’ [081014-011-CvEx.0010]

itu tu kata kata dasar yang harusnya kamu taw\\

summary:
Adnominal demonstratives in the noun phrase occur at the right edge and scope over the whole noun phrase; they may appear in full or reduced forms, such as proximal *ini/ni* and distal *itu/tu*. Like adnominal personal pronouns, they function as determiners, but unlike those pronouns they mark specificity rather than definiteness.

The head nominal may be a noun, a personal pronoun, a locative, or even another demonstrative. Examples show demonstratives combining with different head nominals to indicate referential specificity.

Adnominally used locatives occur in posthead position, such that `` n loc ''. text:
In their adnominal uses, the interrogatives occur in posthead position, such that `` n int ''. Syntactically, the interrogatives remain in-situ; that is, noun phrases with adnominally used interrogatives correspond to their non- interrogative expressions. This is illustrated with siapa ‘who’ in ( Example_8.51 ), apa ‘what’ in ( Example_8.52 ), and mana ‘where, which’ in ( Example_8.53 ).

The interrogatives always occur in noun phrases with a nominal head such as the common noun kaka ‘older sibling’ in ( Example_8.51 ). Modification of personal pronouns or other constituents is unattested. (More details on the interrogatives and their adnominal uses are found in § Para_5.8 ).

summary: In adnominal uses, the interrogatives appear after the noun and remain in situ, so noun phrases with these interrogatives correspond to their non-interrogative counterparts. They occur only within noun phrases headed by a nominal, such as a common noun, and are not attested modifying personal pronouns or other constituents.

text:
Noun phrases can be modified with prepositional phrases, such that `` n pp ''. Overall, however, such noun phrases are uncommon. In the corpus, four prepositions occur in adnominally used prepositional phrases, namely locative di ‘at, in’ as in ( Example_8.15 ), repeated as ( Example_8.54 ), elative dari ‘from’ as in ( Example_8.55 ), benefactive untuk ‘for’ as in ( Example_8.56 ), and similative sperti ‘like’ as in ( Example_8.57 ). (For a detailed discussion on prepositions and prepositional phrases see Para_10; see also § Para_5.11 ).

text: Noun phrases with adnominally used numerals or quantifiers can have an n-mod or a mod-n structure, depending on the semantics of the phrasal structure. When preposed, adnominal numerals and quantifiers signal individuality, while postposed numerals and quantifiers express exhaustivity or positions within series. Posthead numerals and quantifiers have scope over their head nominal including its verbal and/or nominal modifiers, while they, in turn, are within the scope of the demonstratives. Adnominally used numerals are discussed in § Para_8.3.1, and adnominal quantifiers in § Para_8.3.2.
summary: Noun phrases with adnominal numerals or quantifiers may be structured either as n-mod or mod-n, depending on the meaning of the phrase. Preposed numerals and quantifiers indicate individuality, whereas postposed ones express exhaustivity or a position in a series. Posthead numerals and quantifiers take scope over the head nominal and its modifiers, but remain under the scope of demonstratives.

text:
Two types of noun phrases with adnominally used numerals can be distinguished: (1) noun phrases with prehead numerals, such that `` n um n '', are presented in ( Example_8.63 ) to ( Example_8.66 ), and (2) noun phrases with posthead numerals, such that `` n n um'', are illustrated in ( Example_8.67 ) to ( Example_8.70 ). (For a discussion of numerals as a word class see § Para_5.9.)

Noun phrases with preposed numerals (`` n um n-np '') express a sense of individuality by signaling the composite nature of their referents. This is achieved in that n um n-np s denote absolute numbers of items expressed by their head nominals, including quantities as in ( Example_8.63 ) or periods of time as in ( Example_8.64 ).

If the exact absolute number of items is unknown, two numerals can be juxtaposed to indicate approximate quantities, as in ( Example_8.65 ) and ( Example_8.66 ). The approximated quantities are usually rather small, such as satu dua ‘one or two’ in ( Example_8.65 ) or tiga empat ‘three or four’ as in ( Example_8.66 ).

Noun phrases with posthead numerals (`` nn um -np'') signal exhaustivity of definite referents, as in ( Example_8.67 ) and ( Example_8.68 ), or mark unique positions within series or sequences as in ( Example_8.69 ) and ( Example_8.70 ).

With head nominals undifferentiated in terms of their ranking, nn um -nps indicate exhaustivity of definite referents. The head can be a noun, as in the elicited example in ( Example_8.67 ), or a personal pronoun as in ( Example_8.68 ). The elicited example in ( Example_8.67 ) is based on the example in ( Example_8.14 ) in § Para_8.1 (p. Example_8.14).

In ( Example_8.71 ) to ( Example_8.73 ), the opposition between the pre- and posthead positions is illustrated with (near) contrastive examples. In ( Example_8.71 ) prehead dua ‘two’ designates the absolute number of items expressed by its head. In ( Example_8.72 ) posthead dua ‘two’ modifies a head nominal undifferentiated in terms of its ranking, whereby it signals the exhaustivity of its referent. The data in ( Example_8.63 ) to ( Example_8.73 ) suggests that the nn um order is favored in more specific and definite constructions, namely to signal exhaustivity of definite referents or unique positions within series or sequences. The n um n order, by contrast, is associated with less specific or less definite constructions which express the absolute number of items denoted by the head nominal. These patterns contrast with Greenberg.1978b cross-linguistic findings concerning the word order in noun phrases with adnominal numerals:

quote
44. The order noun- numeral is favored in indefinite and approximative constructions.
quote

does note, however, that this statement is a generalization rather than a universal, given cross-linguistic variations in quantifier- noun [Q-N] order. Noting that “in some languages either QN or NQ may occur with any numeral” and that this “contrast of order may then have semantic or syntactic function”, presents a number of languages that, like Papuan Malay, employ nn um order in definite constructions rather than in indefinite ones.
summary:
The passage distinguishes two noun-phrase patterns with adnominal numerals: prehead numerals (n um n) and posthead numerals (n n um). Prehead numerals express the absolute number of items and are associated with less specific or approximate quantities, while posthead numerals mark exhaustivity of definite referents or a unique position in a series or time sequence.  

The data suggest that the posthead order is favored in more definite and specific constructions, whereas the prehead order is used for quantity expressions; this differs from Greenberg’s general cross-linguistic tendency for noun-numeral order to occur in indefinite or approximative contexts, though the passage notes that languages vary in this respect.

text: Following, the Papuan Malay nn um order in definite constructions is a variation of a much more common n um n order for these constructions. In his critique of Greenberg.1978b generalization #44, demonstrates, however, that the nn um order in definite constructions is not a mere “ variation” found in “some languages”. Rather, “there is a strong tendency for postnominal numerals to be interpreted in highly specific, highly definite ways” ( Donohue.2005). The data presented here suggests that the Papuan Malay word order in noun phrases with adnominally used numerals follows this same “strong tendency”.
summary: The passage says that Papuan Malay’s **n n um** order in definite constructions is a less common variant of the more usual **n um n** order. It argues, following Donohue, that postnominal numerals are not just a rare variation but are strongly associated with highly specific, highly definite interpretations, and that Papuan Malay noun phrases with adnominal numerals fit this tendency.

text:
Noun phrases with adnominally used quantifiers have syntactic properties similar to those with adnominally used numerals. Noun phrases with prehead quantifiers (`` q t n-np '') express nonnumeric amounts or quantities of the items indicated by their head nominals; they only modify countable referents. Noun phrases with posthead quantifier (`` nq t -np''), by contrast, either denote exhaustivity of indefinite referents or signal unknown positions within series or sequences; they modify countable as well as uncountable referents. (For a discussion of quantifiers as a word class see § Para_5.10 ).

The following adnominal quantifiers are attested: universal masing-masing ‘each’, segala ‘all’, sembarang ‘any (kind of)’, (se)tiap ‘every’, and smua ‘all’, and mid-range banyak ‘many’, brapa ‘several’, sedikit ‘few’, and stenga ‘half’.

Five quantifiers can occur in pre- or posthead position, namely banyak ‘many’, brapa ‘several’, masing-masing ‘each’, sedikit ‘few’, and smua ‘all’, as shown in ( Example_8.78 ) to ( Example_8.92 ). The other four quantifiers, that is, segala ‘all’, sembarang ‘any (kind of)’, (se)tiap ‘every’, and stenga ‘half’, only occur in prehead position where they signal nonnumeric quantities of countable referents, as illustrated in ( Example_8.74 ) to ( Example_8.77 ). While sembarang ‘any (kind of)’ is only used with animate referents as in ( Example_8.75 ), (se)tiap ‘every’ and stenga ‘half’ are only used with inanimate referents as in ( Example_8.76 ) and ( Example_8.77 ), respectively. To express the notion of ``every person'', speakers prefer quantification with masing-masing ‘each’. Quantifier segala ‘all’ is always combined with the noun macang ‘variety’ with segala macang expressing the notion of ``all kinds, whatever kind'' as in ( Example_8.74 ).

The quantifiers banyak ‘many’, brapa ‘several’, masing-masing ‘each’, sedikit ‘few’, and smua ‘all’ can precede or follow their head nominals, as demonstrated in ( Example_8.78 ) to ( Example_8.92 ). Both phrasal structures serve distinct semantic functions similar to those of adnominal numerals, discussed in § Para_8.3.1, although the contrast is more subtle. The examples presented in this section also illustrate that the quantifiers can be used with animate or inanimate referents.

q t n-np s with prehead banyak ‘many’, brapa ‘several’, masing-masing ‘each’, sedi\-kit ‘few’, and smua ‘all’ denote the nonnumeric quantities of countable referents. Thereby, q t n-np s express the composite nature of their referents which conveys a sense of individuality, such that `` q t amount of n '' as in ( Example_8.78 ) to ( Example_8.82 ). The corpus includes only few noun phrases with adnominally used sedikit ‘few’ all of which have sedikit ‘few’ in posthead position. According to one of the consultants, however, adnominal modification with prehead sedikit ‘few’ is natural and common, as illustrated with the elicited example in ( Example_8.81 ).

Most often, nq t -nps signal a contrastive sense of exhaustivity: n banyak translates with ``many (and not just a few) n '' as in ( Example_8.83 ), n masing-masing with ``several (and not just a few) n '' as in ( Example_8.84 ), n masing-masing with ``each n (with nobody missing)'' as in the elicited example in ( Example_8.85 ), n sedikit with ``few (and not many) n '' as in ( Example_8.86 ), and n smua with ``the entire collection of n (with nobody/nothing missing)'' as in ( Example_8.88 ). summary:
Adnominal quantifiers pattern syntactically much like adnominal numerals. Prehead quantifiers express nonnumeric quantities of countable referents and are used with countable nouns only, while posthead quantifiers can mark exhaustivity or unknown positions in a series and may occur with both countable and uncountable referents.

The language attests universal quantifiers such as masing-masing, segala, sembarang, (se)tiap, and smua, as well as mid-range quantifiers like banyak, brapa, sedikit, and stenga. Of these, banyak, brapa, masing-masing, sedikit, and smua can appear before or after the noun, whereas segala, sembarang, (se)tiap, and stenga occur only prehead; some have additional restrictions on referent type, such as sembarang with animates and (se)tiap and stenga with inanimates.

text:
In Papuan Malay, adnominal possessive relations between two noun phrases are marked with the possessive ligature punya; alternative realization of the ligature are reduced pu, clitic =p, or a zero morpheme.

Such possessive constructions have a mod-n constituent order which is opposite to the canonical n-mod structure. That is, the head nominal encoding the possessum ( possm ) takes the n2 slot, following the possessive ligature ( lig ), whereas the modifier expressing the possessor ( possr ) takes the n1 slot, such that `` possr - np – lig – possm - np ''. This is shown with the adnominal possessive construction in ( Example_8.95 ).

45pt possr 10pt lig 10pt possm \\
nanti Hendro punya ade prempuang kawing \\
very.soon Hendro poss ySb woman marry.inofficially \\

‘eventually Hendro’s younger sister would marry ’ [081006-028-CvEx.0007]

Syntactically, a variety of constituents can encode the possessor and the possessum, as shown in ( Example_8.96 ). The possessor slot can be taken by a lexical noun as in ( Example_8.96a, Example_8.96b,) a personal pronoun as in ( Example_8.96c, Example_8.96d ), a demonstrative as in ( Example_8.96e ), the interrogative siapa ‘who’ as in ( Example_8.96f ), or a noun phrase as in ( Example_8.96g ). The possessum can be encoded by a lexical noun as in ( Example_8.96c, Example_8.96e, Example_8.96f ), a demonstrative as in ( Example_8.96a, Example_8.96b ), the interrogative siapa ‘who’ as in ( Example_8.96d ), or a noun phrase as in ( Example_8.96g ). Possessive noun phrases with a personal pronoun possessum are unattested.

summary:
In Papuan Malay, adnominal possessive relations between two noun phrases are marked by the possessive ligature *punya*, with reduced forms *pu*, clitic *=p*, or even zero marking. The construction has a noncanonical modifier-head order (*possessor–ligature–possessum*), and the possessor and possessum can each be expressed by several constituent types, including lexical nouns, pronouns, demonstratives, interrogatives, and noun phrases, though possessum pronouns are unattested.

These adnominal possessive constructions are used to express possession of a definite possessum. Indefinite possession is instead expressed by a two-argument existential clause or a nominal clause.

text:
In an apposition two “or more noun phrases” have “the same referent” and stand “in the same syntactical relation to the rest of the sentence”. Papuan Malay employs two types of appositional constructions, namely apposition of a noun with another noun or noun phrase, such that `` n np '', and apposition of a personal pronoun with a noun or noun phrase, such that `` pro np ''. This section describes `` n np '' appositions, while `` pro np '' appositions are discussed in § Para_6.1.6.

Papuan Malay `` n np '' appositions are restrictive. That is, the apposited or juxtaposed noun phrase is needed for the appropriate identification of the referent encoded by the initial noun. There are no formal distinctions, though, between the `` n np '' appositions discussed here and noun phrases with adnominally used nouns ( n1n2-np ), discussed in § Para_8.2.2; the distinction is based on semantics.

In the corpus, `` n np '' appositions are rare, and in each case the initial noun encodes a kinship term, as in ( Example_8.97 ) and ( Example_8.98 ). The juxtaposed noun phrase ibu pendeta ‘Ms. Pastor’ in ( Example_8.97 ) is appositional to the first noun kaka ‘older sibling’. It provides information necessary for the identification of the referent. In ( Example_8.98 ), the appositional noun phrase ketua klasis ‘church district chairperson’ serves as an identifying explanation for the reference of the initial noun bapa ‘father’.

bapa-ade ini, kaka, [ kaka] [ ibu pendeta] dengang ini\\
uncle d.prox oSb oSb woman pastor with d.prox \\
mama-tua, nene ini dong tertawa\\
aunt grandmother d.prox 3pl laugh\\

‘uncle here (and) older sibling, older sibling, Ms. Pastor, and, what’s-her-name, aunt, grandmother here, they were laughing’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0824]

bapa di dalam, [ bapa] [ ketua klasis]\\
father at inside father chairperson church.district\\

‘[that’s what I’ve never told older sibling, what’s-his-name,] father (who’s) inside, father, the church district chairperson’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0104]
summary: Papuan Malay has two appositional construction types: noun-with-noun/noun phrase (`n np`) and personal pronoun with noun/noun phrase (`pro np`), with this section focusing on `n np` appositions. These appositions are restrictive, meaning the second noun phrase is needed to identify the referent of the first noun, and in the corpus they are rare and occur only when the first noun is a kinship term. There is no formal difference between these appositions and noun phrases with adnominally used nouns; the distinction is semantic.

text:
The head of a noun phrase is typically a noun or personal pronoun. Further, although less common, demonstratives, locatives, or interrogatives can also function as heads. The canonical word order within the noun phrase is head-modifier. Depending on the syntactic properties of the adnominal constituents, though, a modifierhead order is also common. Attested in the corpus is the co-occurr\-ence of up to three posthead modi\-fiers. The possible constituents of the maximally extended noun phrase and the order of these constituents is summarized in the template in Table_8.3 (the items in parenthesis are optional).

The template in Table_8.3 shows that noun phrases with adnominally used verbs, nouns, personal pronouns, demonstratives, locatives,
prepositional phrases,
interrogatives,
and relative clauses have an n-mod structure. Adnominal possessive constructions, by contrast, have a mod-n structure with the modifying possessor phrase occurring in prehead position. Noun phrases with adnominally used numerals and quantifiers have an n-mod or mod-n structure depending on the semantics of the phrasal structure. Adnominally used demonstratives can occur in two slots. They can take the same slot as adnominally used locatives, interrogatives, numerals, or quantifiers, and in addition they can occur at the right periphery of the noun phrase where they have scope over the entire noun phrase.

Papuan Malay uses two types of appositional constructions: those consisting of a noun followed by another noun or noun phrase, and those consisting of a personal pronoun followed by a noun or noun phrase, the latter being discussed in § Para_6.1.6. Appositions with juxtaposed nouns or noun phrases are restrictive.
summary: The passage describes noun phrase structure in Papuan Malay: the head is usually a noun or personal pronoun, though demonstratives, locatives, and interrogatives can also serve as heads, and the basic order is head–modifier with up to three posthead modifiers. It also notes several subtype-specific patterns, including n-mod structure for many adnominal constituents, mod-n for possessive constructions, and variable order for numerals and quantifiers; demonstratives may occur in a shared slot or at the right edge of the noun phrase with scope over the whole phrase. Finally, it states that Papuan Malay has two appositional constructions, and that appositions made of juxtaposed nouns or noun phrases are restrictive.

text:
In Papuan Malay, adnominal possessive relations between two noun phrases are encoded with the possessive ligature punya ‘ poss ’. The noun phrase preceding the ligature ( lig ) designates the possessor ( possr ), while the noun phrase following it expresses the possessum ( possm ), such that `` possr - np – punya ‘ poss ’ – possm - np ''.

The main function of adnominal possessive constructions is to denote possession of a definite possessum. In addition, punya ‘ poss ’ serves other functions in `` possr - np – punya ‘ poss ’ – possm - np '' constructions. It is employed to mark and emphasize locational, temporal, or associative relations, to indicate beneficiary relations, or to signal speaker attitudes and evaluations. Besides, the ligature is also used in reflexive expressions. (Possession of an indefinite possessum is not expressed with an adnominal possessive construction, but with a two-argument existential clause or a nominal clause; details are presented in § Para_11.4.2 and § Para_12.2, respectively.)

The three constituents of an adnominal possessive construction have different realizations, as illustrated in Table_9.1. The possessive marker can be realized with unreduced punya, reduced pu, clitic =p, or a zero morpheme. The noun phrases expressing the possessor and possessum can belong to different syntactic categories. The most common constituents are lexical nouns and noun phrases. Demonstratives can also take either slot. Also very common are personal pronoun possessors. In noncanonical possessive constructions, the possessor and possessum slots can also be filled by verbs. In addition, mid-range quantifiers, temporal adverbs and prepositional phrases can take the possessum slot. In both canonical and noncanonical possessive constructions, the possessum can be omitted.

Semantically, the possessor and the possessum can designate human, nonhuman animate, or inanimate referents. Overall, adnominal possessive constructions do not make a distinction between alienable and inalienable possession, with one exception. Possessive constructions with the elided possessive marker signal inalienable possession of body parts or kinship relations (see § Para_9.1.3 ).

In the following sections, adnominal possessive constructions are discussed in more detail. The possessive marker punya ‘ poss ’ with its different realizations is examined in § Para_9.1. The different realizations of the possessor and possessum noun phrases are described in § Para_9.2. Noncanonical possessive constructions are discussed in § Para_9.3. The main points of this chapter are summarized in § Para_9.4. (For the uses of adnominal possessive constructions in two-argument existential clauses, see § Para_11.4.1.)
summary:
In Papuan Malay, adnominal possessive constructions use the ligature punya ‘poss’, with the possessor before it and the possessum after it, and they mainly express possession of a definite possessum. The same construction also marks or emphasizes locational, temporal, associative, beneficiary, and evaluative relations, and is used in reflexive expressions; possession of an indefinite possessum is expressed instead by existential or nominal clauses.

The possessive marker has several realizations, including unreduced punya, reduced pu, clitic =p, or zero, and both possessor and possessum can be realized by a range of categories such as nouns, pronouns, demonstratives, verbs, quantifiers, adverbs, or prepositional phrases, with the possessum sometimes omitted. These constructions generally do not distinguish alienable from inalienable possession, except that zero-marked constructions indicate inalienable body-part or kinship possession.

text:
The possessive marker punya ‘ poss ’ is related to the full bivalent verb punya ‘have’ which is still used synchronically in two-argument clauses to predicate possession of an indefinite possessum. In such clauses, the possessor is encoded by the grammatical subject ( s ) while the indefinite possessum is the direct object ( o ) of the verb ( v ) punya ‘have’. This is illustrated in ( Example_9.1 ): the possessor sa ‘1 sg ’ is the grammatical subject while the possessum rencana ‘thought’ is the direct object of punya ‘have’. Overall, however, verbal clauses with punya ‘have’ are rather rare. Instead, speakers typically express possession of an indefinite possessum with a two-argument existential clause with ada ‘exist’. This is demonstrated in ( Example_9.2 ): the possessor sa ‘ 1sg ’ is the subject while the indefinite possessum ana ‘child’ is the direct object of existential ada ‘exist’. (This type of two-argument existential clause is discussed in detail in § Para_11.4.2.)

The most common function of Papuan Malay punya ‘ poss ’ is that of a ligature in adnominal referential possessive constructions, that is, possessive constructions with definite referents. Such constructions have the syntactic structure `` possr-np punya possm-np ''. As shown in ( Example_9.3 ), this type of possessive construction contrasts with the verbal constructions in ( Example_9.1 ) and ( Example_9.2 ): the possessive relation is not encoded by a two-argument clause but in a single construction which consists of two noun phrases, which in turn functions as an argument in a clause. Hence, Yosina in ( Example_9.3 ) is not a grammatical subject but the possessor. Likewise, swara ‘voice’ is not the direct object of a verbal clause, but a definite possessum. The entire possessive construction in ( Example_9.3 ) functions as the direct object of the bivalent verb dengar ‘hear’. The contrastive examples in ( Example_9.2 ) and ( Example_9.3 ) also illustrate the distinctions between possession of an indefinite and a definite possessum, respectively.

In adnominal possessive constructions, the ligature punya ‘ poss ’ has four different realizations which are discussed in the following sections: long punya ‘ poss ’ and its reduced form pu in § Para_9.1.1, the clitic =p ‘ poss ’ in § Para_9.1.2, and elision in § Para_9.1.3. In § Para_9.1.4, a possible grammaticalization of the possessive marker is examined.
summary: Papuan Malay punya is historically related to the full verb punya ‘have’, which can still be used in rare two-argument clauses expressing possession of an indefinite possessum, with the possessor as subject and the possessum as direct object. More commonly, possession is expressed either by an existential clause with ada ‘exist’ for indefinite possessums, or by adnominal possessive constructions with definite referents, where punya links two noun phrases and the whole construction functions as an argument in the clause. Some punya constructions are ambiguous between predicative and adnominal readings, and the marker has several realizations in adnominal possessives, including pu, =p, and zero marking.

text:
In adnominal possessive constructions, the possessive marker is most commonly realized with the long form punya ‘ poss ’ or the reduced monosyllabic form pu ‘ poss ’. This reduction is independent of the syntactic or semantic properties of the possessor or possessum, as illustrated in ( Example_9.5 ).

Both ligature forms occur with possessors encoded by lexical nouns as in ( Example_9.5a - Example_9.5g, by personal pronouns as in ( Example_9.5h, Example_9.5i ), or by noun phrases as in ( Example_9.5j - Example_9.5l ). With either ligature form, the possessor can denote a human referent as in ( Example_9.5a - Example_9.5d, Example_9.5i - Example_9.5k ), a nonhuman animate referent as in ( Example_9.5e, Example_9.5f, Example_9.5h ), or an inanimate referent as in ( Example_9.5g, Example_9.5l ). Likewise, the reduction is independent of the possessum’s properties. Both markers occur with possessa encoded by nouns as in ( Example_9.5b, Example_9.5e, Example_9.5f, Example_9.5l ), by demonstratives as in ( Example_9.5c, Example_9.5d ), or by noun phrases as in ( Example_9.5a, Example_9.5g, Example_9.5i - Example_9.5k ). With either marker, the possessum can express an inalienably possessed referent as in ( Example_9.5a, Example_9.5b, Example_9.5h, Example_9.5k ) or an alienably possessed referent as in ( Example_9.5c - Example_9.5g, Example_9.5i, Example_9.5j, Example_9.5l ).

With respect to the possessive marking of personal pronouns, there are no prosodic restrictions on the use of the two possessive marker forms: either can occur with the long and the short pronoun forms, as illustrated in Table Table_9.2 and Table Table_9.2a. In the corpus there are only two unattested combinations, namely the marking with short pu ‘ poss ’ of long third person plural dorang ‘ 3pl ’ and of short first person plural torang ‘ 1pl ’. The elicited examples in ( Footnote_Example_9.1 ) show, however, that possessive constructions with torang/ dorang pu ‘our/their’ are possible:
-5pt
