1pl / 3pl poss house exist at l.med \\
‘ our/their house is over there’ [Elicited BR111020-001.002-003]

(The pronoun ko ‘2sg’ does not have a short form.) (Pronouns are discussed in detail in Para_6.)

These examples show that the reduction of the disyllabic form punya ‘ poss ’ to monosyllabic pu ‘ poss ’ does not interact with the long versus reduced shape of the personal pronouns. These findings contrast with those of who found that the long pronoun forms may not co-occur with the reduced possessive marker pu ‘ poss ’ (for more details see ).

Very occasionally, the reduced ligature takes on the form / pum/, / pun/, or / puŋ/ ‘ poss ’. This variation is usually due to assimilation to the word-initial segment of the following possessum, as illustrated in Table_9.3. That is, speakers realize short pu ‘ poss ’ with a word-final nasal which receives its place features from the onset segment of the following prosodic word; when the following word has a vowel as onset, the nasal is typically realized as velar [ ŋ]. (For more details on nasal place assimilation see § Para_2.2.1.)

In a few cases, however, the reduced ligature takes on the form / puŋ/ regardless of the form of the following segment, as illustrated in ( Example_9.6 ) to ( Example_9.8 ).

ada sa / puŋ/ dusung\\
exist 1 sg poss garden\\

‘(over there) is my garden’ [081110-008-CvNP.0009]

dong / puŋ/ peserta juga macang tra \\
3pl poss participant also variety neg \\

‘ their participants also, like (they) didn’t ’ [081025-009a-Cv.0132]

tong / puŋ/ cara makang babi juga\\
1pl poss manner eat pig also\\

‘[our way of eating is just like the Toraja one,] our way of eating pigs also’ [081014-017-CvPr.0053]
summary:
Adnominal possessive constructions use either the full marker punya ‘poss’ or the reduced form pu ‘poss’, and this reduction does not depend on the syntactic or semantic type of the possessor or possessum. Both forms occur with lexical nouns, pronouns, and noun phrases, and with possessors and possessa referring to human, nonhuman animate, or inanimate entities, as well as to alienably or inalienably possessed items.  

For personal pronouns, there are no prosodic restrictions on which possessive marker form can appear, though the corpus lacks two combinations that are nonetheless shown to be possible in elicited examples. The reduced marker may also appear as pum, pun, or puŋ through nasal assimilation to the following word, though in a few cases puŋ occurs regardless of the following segment.

text:
The possessive marker can be reduced further to =p ‘ poss ’, if the possessor noun phrase ends in a vowel, as in ( Example_9.9 ) to ( Example_9.11 ). In this case, the marker is cliticized to the possessor. In this type of reduced possessive construction, the possessor is almost always a singular personal pronoun, such as short first person sa ‘ 1sg ’, second person ko ‘ 2sg ’ in ( Example_9.9 ), or short third person de ‘ 3sg ’ as in ( Example_9.10 ). The possessor may, however, also be expressed by a noun as in ( Example_9.11 ), although in the corpus this example is the only one attested. Again, the same construction is used for alienable and inalienable possession.

sa bilang, i, sa=p kaka, de bilang ko=p kaka?\\
1sg say ugh! 1sg=poss oSb 3sg say 2sg=poss oSb\\

‘I said, ``ugh!, (that’s) my older sister'', she said, `` your older sister?''' [080919-006-CvNP.0026]

de timbul de=p cucu tanya dia, tete knapa\\
3sg emerge 3sg=poss grandchild ask 3sg grandfather why\\

‘(when) he (grandfather) emerged, his grandchild asked him, ``grandfather, what happened?''' [081109-005-JR.0009]

Fredi de pu ade=p motor \\
Fredi 3sg poss ySb =poss motorbike \\

‘Fredi’s younger brother’s motorbike ’ [081002-001-CvNP.0058]
summary: The possessive marker can be reduced to =p when the possessor noun phrase ends in a vowel, in which case it cliticizes to the possessor. This reduced construction is used mostly with short singular personal pronouns, though it can also occur with a noun possessor, and it applies to both alienable and inalienable possession.

text:
The possessive marker can also be elided, as illustrated in ( Example_9.12 ) to ( Example_9.16 ). The elision is limited, however, to certain semantic kinds of possession. Attested are inalienable possession of body parts, as in ( Example_9.12 ) and ( Example_9.13 ), and kinship relations, as in ( Example_9.14 ) and ( Example_9.15 ). Most commonly, the possessor is human as in ( Example_9.12 ) to ( Example_9.15 ), but it may also be animate nonhuman as in ( Example_9.16 ).

In possr-possm constructions, the possessor is usually encoded by a short personal pronoun form, as in ( Example_9.14 ) to ( Example_9.16 ). Much less often, the possessor is expressed with a lexical noun, such as bapa ‘father’ in ( Example_9.12 ). Also rather infrequently, the possessor is expressed by a noun phrase such as pace de ‘the man’ in ( Example_9.13 ), where adnominally used de ‘ 3sg ’ modifies pace ‘man’ (for details on the adnominal uses of the personal pronouns, see § Para_6.2 ).

adu, bapa Ø mulut jahat skali\\
oh.no! father mouth be.bad very\\

‘oh no!, father’s language is very bad’ (Lit. ‘ father’s mouth’) [080923-008-Cv.0019]

pace de Ø tangang kluar ke samping\\
man 3sg hand go.out to side\\

[About an accident:] ‘ the man’s arm stuck out sideways’ [081108-001-JR.0003]

de Ø mama ini ke atas\\
3sg see 3sg poss wife\\

‘ his mother here (went) up (there)’ [080923-001-CvNP.0019]

dia liat dia pu maytua ah, sa Ø maytua cantik\\
3sg see 3sg poss wife ah! 1sg wife be.beautiful\\

‘he saw his wife ``ah!, my wife is beautiful''' [080922-010a-CvNF.0020]

langsung potong dia buang tali-prutnya\\
immediately cut 3sg throw(.away) intestines: 3possr \\
de Ø tali-prut buang, tinggal isi saja\\
3sg intestines throw(.away) stay contents just\\

[About killing dogs:] ‘cut him up at once (and) throw away the intestines, (after having) thrown away his intestines, just the meat remains’ [081106-001-CvPr.0005]

Contrary to the possessive constructions presented in § Para_9.1.1 and § Para_9.1.2, the data presented in ( Example_9.12 ) to ( Example_9.16 ) shows that Papuan Malay also has the option to signal inalienable possession by omitting the possessive marker.

This alienable versus inalienable distinction is also found in other Austronesian languages of the Papuan contact zone, whereas it is not found in Western Malayo-Poly\-ne\-sian languages. As in other Austronesian and Papuan languages of this contact zone, it is body parts and kinship terms that can be inalienably possessed. note that this “innovation must have occurred prior to the population of Oceania”, a conclusion that is based on Ross.2001 hypothesis that it “is also probable that the formal distinction between alienable and inalienable possession entered Proto- Oceanic or an immediate precursor through Papuan contact”.
summary: Papuan Malay allows the possessive marker to be omitted, but only with certain kinds of inalienable possession, especially body parts and kinship relations. In these constructions, the possessor is usually a short personal pronoun, though it can less often be a lexical noun or noun phrase, and the text notes that this alienable/inalienable distinction is shared with other Austronesian languages in the Papuan contact zone but not with Western Malayo-Polynesian languages.

text:
In § Para_9.1.1 to § Para_9.1.3, the reduction of possessive marker punya ‘ poss ’ to its monosyllabic variants pu or =p ‘ poss ’ and its omission in possr-possm constructions was described.

One explanation for this reduction would be to consider it as the result of a grammaticalization process. As observes, the phonetic reduction of high-frequency words “can lead to the establishment of a new construction with its own categories” and “the grammaticization of the new construction”. One could argue that Bybee.2006 observation also applies to the high-frequency morpheme punya with its variable status between a full verb ‘have’, a clitic possessive marker, and a zero morpheme. That is, the variable status could be taken as an as-yet incomplete grammaticalization from the independent lexical item punya ‘have’ via the possessive marker punya ‘ poss ’ into a clitic =p ‘ poss ’ or a new possessive construction without overt marker. One reason why punya constructions are so frequent in Papuan Malay and other eastern Malay varieties, is that unlike the western Malay varieties, the eastern Malay varieties do not use suffix -nya ‘ 3poss ’ as a marker of possessive relations, as for instance in western Malay tangang\-nya ‘his/her hand’ (H. Hammarström p.c. 2013).

In the corpus, reductions of the possessive marker to the clitic =p ‘ poss ’ or a zero morpheme occur with about the same frequency. Typically, the two constructions occur when the possessor is expressed with a short singular personal pronoun. It remains to be seen whether and to what extent over time (1) one of the constructions is going to become dominant, and (2) one or both constructions are going to occur with possessors encoded by the plural personal pronouns or common nouns. Such developments could be taken as an indication of a grammaticalization process of the possessive marker.
summary: The passage argues that the reduction of possessive marker *punya* to *pu* or *=p*, and sometimes its omission, may reflect an ongoing grammaticalization process from a full lexical verb ‘have’ to a clitic possessive marker or even a zero-marked possessive construction. It notes that this variability is especially frequent in Papuan Malay and other eastern Malay varieties, possibly because these varieties do not use the western Malay suffix *-nya* for possession. In the corpus, the clitic and zero-marked constructions occur about equally often, usually with short singular pronoun possessors, and future change may show whether one construction becomes dominant or expands to other possessor types.

text: This section discusses the different realizations of the possessor and possessum noun phrases in adnominal possessive constructions. The syntactic categories that can take the possessor or possessum slots, together with their semantic properties are discussed in § Para_9.2.1.1. Elision of the possessum noun phrase is described in § Para_9.2.1.2, followed by a brief discussion of recursive possessive constructions in § Para_9.2.1.3.
summary: The section examines how possessor and possessum noun phrases are realized in adnominal possessive constructions. It also notes that §9.2.1.1 covers the syntactic categories and semantic properties of the possessor and possessum slots, §9.2.1.2 discusses possessum elision, and §9.2.1.3 briefly addresses recursive possessive constructions.

text:
In adnominal possessive constructions, the possessor and/or possessum can be expressed by lexical nouns as in ( Example_9.17 ) and ( Example_9.18 ), by demonstratives as in ( Example_9.19 ) and ( Example_9.20 ), or by noun phrases as in ( Example_9.21 ) to ( Example_9.26 ). Further, the possessor can be encoded by a personal pronoun as in ( Example_9.23 ) to ( Example_9.26 ). Semantically, the possessor and the possessum can be human as in ( Example_9.17 ), nonhuman animate as in ( Example_9.18 ), or inanimate as in ( Example_9.27 ), respectively.

In ( Example_9.17 ) and ( Example_9.18 ), the possessor and the possessum are expressed by lexical nouns.

styleExampleTitle
Lexical nouns expressing the possessor / possessum
styleExampleTitle

sa masi ingat bapa pu muka\\
1sg still remember father poss front\\

‘I still remember father’s face’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1307]

pake setang punya kwasa\\
use evil.spirit poss power\\

[About the power of evil spirits:] ‘[the sleeping person can’t wake up because the sorcerers are] using the evil spirit’s power’ [081006-022-CvEx.0084]

In ( Example_9.19 ) the proximal demonstrative ini ‘ d.prox ’ takes the possessor slot and in ( Example_9.20 ) distal itu ‘ d.dist ’ takes the possessum slot.

styleExampleTitle
Demonstratives expressing the possessor / possessum
styleExampleTitle

bapa masi kenal kaka Siduas pu, masi kenal\\
father still know oSb Siduas poss still know\\
ini pu muka\\
d.prox poss front\\

‘do you (‘father’) still know Siduas’, still know this (one)’s face?’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1123]

ko ambil dulu ade pu itu\\
2sg fetch first ySb poss d.dist \\

‘you pick (it) up first, that (fish) of (your) younger sister’ (Lit. ‘ younger sibling’s that’) [081006-019-Cv.0002]

In ( Example_9.21 ) to ( Example_9.26 ), noun phrases take the possessor or the possessum slot (the scope of the noun phrases is indicated with brackets). In ( Example_9.21 ) the possessor is encoded by a noun phrase with a verbal modifier plus an adnominal demonstrative, while in ( Example_9.22 ) the possessor is expressed by a coordinate noun phrase.

styleExampleTitle
Noun phrases expressing the possessor
styleExampleTitle

sebut [[[ orang mati] tu] pu [ nama]] karna \\
name person die d.dist poss name because \\

‘(he has) to mention that dead person’s name because ’ [080923-013-CvEx.0019]

itu ko pu [[ ko deng Mateus] pu [ tugas]]\\
d.dist 2sg poss 2sg with Mateus poss duty\\

‘that is your, your and Mateus’ duty’ [081005-001-Cv.0035]

In ( Example_9.23 ), the possessum is encoded by a noun phrase with an adnominally used stative verb plus an adnominal demonstrative. In ( Example_9.24 ), a noun phrase with nominal modifier plus an adnominal demonstrative takes the possessum slot. In ( Example_9.25 ) the possessum is expressed by a coordinate noun phrase. In ( Example_9.8 ), repeated as ( Example_9.26 ), a noun phrase with a modifying non-finite clause takes the possessum slot. The examples in ( Example_9.23 ) to ( Example_9.26 ) also illustrate that a personal pronoun can take the possessor slot; personal pronouns do not take the possessum slot.

[[ de] pu [[ cucu kecil] itu]] tiap hari de\\
3sg poss grandchild be.small d.dist every day 3sg \\
menangis trus\\

‘ that small grandchild of his, every day he/she cries continuously’ [081011-009-Cv.0055]

sa tida maw [[ sa] punya [[ sodara prempuang] itu]] mendrita\\

‘I don’t want that sister of mine to suffer’ [081006-024-CvEx.0108]

nanti [[ de] punya [ bapa dengang mama]] langsung pergi \\

‘very soon her father and mother will go ’ [081110-005-CvPr.0079]

[[ tong] pu [ cara [ makang babi]]] juga\\

In ( Example_9.17 ) to ( Example_9.26 ) the possessor is always animate and/or human. It can, however, also be inanimate as shown in ( Example_9.27 ).

Inanimate possessor
styleExampleTitle

LNG pu terpol itu tinggal\\

summary: The passage describes adnominal possessive constructions in which either the possessor or possessum may be expressed by lexical nouns, demonstratives, noun phrases, or, for the possessor only, personal pronouns. It also shows that these possessive relations can involve human, nonhuman animate, or inanimate referents, though the examples from (9.17) to (9.26) mostly have animate or human possessors, with an inanimate possessor illustrated in (9.27).

subsection: Elision of the possessum noun phrase
text:
It is also possible to omit the possessum when its identity was established earlier; this applies to inalienably as well as alienably possessed referents, as illustrated in ( Example_9.28 ) to ( Example_9.31 ). Such ‘ possessor punya’ constructions are typically used in contexts where the possessor identity is under discussion.

In ` possessor punya’ constructions, speakers most commonly employ long punya ‘ poss ’, but as shown in ( Example_9.30 ) and ( Example_9.31 ), constructions with reduced pu ‘ poss ’ are also possible. In their analysis of similar possessive constructions in Classical Malay, conclude that Classical Malay (em)punya constructions with omitted possessum denote “pronominal possessive constructions”. More specifically, maintains that “in such constructions (em)punya identifies a possessee in relation to its possessor (the genitive function), while at the same time alluding to the morphologically unrealized possessee as well (the pronominal function). Consequently, possessive pronominal (em)punya allows us to focus on the possessor, while still referring to the possessee”. It seems that this analysis is also applicable to Papuan Malay. Elision of the possessor is unattested. Instead speakers employ a demonstrative, as in ( Example_9.19 ), when the identity of the possessor has already been established.

Nofi tu itu bukang bapa Lukas punya Ø mama Nofita punya Ø\\
Nofi d.dist d.dist neg father Lukas poss mother Nofita poss \\

‘Nofi here, that’s not father Lukas’ (son nor) mother Nofita’s (son)’ [081006-024-CvEx.0011]

itu de punya Ø\\
d.dist 3sg poss \\

‘those are his (banana plants)’ [081110-008-CvNP.0121]

sedangkang Pawlus ini itu jing pu Ø\\
whereas Pawlus d.prox d.dist genie poss \\

‘whereas Pawlus here, that’s the genie’s (child)’ [081025-006-Cv.0276]

ko liat Luisa pu Ø bagus, suda kembang banyak\\
2sg see Luisa poss be.good already f lowering many\\

‘you see Luisa’s (flowers) are good, (they are) already f lowering a lot’ [081006-021-CvHt.0002]
summary:
The passage says that in Papuan Malay, the possessum can be omitted when it has already been established, for both alienably and inalienably possessed referents, especially in contexts where the possessor is the focus of discussion. These “possessor punya” constructions usually use long *punya*, though reduced *pu* also occurs, and they are analyzed as pronominal possessive constructions that refer to an unexpressed possessee while highlighting the possessor.

It also notes that possessor omission is not attested; instead, when the possessor has already been established, speakers use a demonstrative.

text:
Adnominal possessive constructions can be stacked to form recursive possessive constructions, as illustrated in ( Example_9.32 ) to ( Example_9.34 ). Double possessive constructions, as in ( Example_9.32 ) and ( Example_9.33 ) are quite common, especially to express kinship and social relations, as in ( Example_9.32 ). Triple possessive constructions are also possible but extremely rare: the corpus contains only one such construction, which is presented in ( Example_9.34 ) in slightly modified form.

kalo memang ko punya maytua punya waktu pas di kapal \\
if indeed 2 sg poss wife poss time precisely at ship \\

‘if indeed your wife’s time (to give birth) is right then (when you’re) on the ship ’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0010]

ini kaka Natanael pu laki pu mobil\\
d.prox oSb Natanael poss husband poss car\\

‘this is sister Natanael’s husband’s car’ [081006-015-Cv.0001]

de i pu ana kawing de i pu laki punya\\
3sg poss child marry.inofficially 3sg poss husband poss \\
kaka prempuang pu ana\\
oSb woman poss child\\

‘her i child (wants to) marry the son of her i husband’s older sister’ [Elicited BR111020.026] The elicited utterance in ( Example_9.34 ) is based on an original triple possessive construction which contains the demonstrative ini ‘ d.prox ’: de pu laki, ini, punya kaka prempuang pu ana. In this context, ini ‘ d.prox ’ functions as a placeholder and therefore is not part of the noun phrase de pu laki ‘her husband’ (see § Para_7.1.2.6 for a discussion of the placeholder uses of demonstratives).\\
The subscript letters indicate which personal pronouns have which referents.

As discussed in § Para_9.1.1, the long ligature form punya ‘ poss ’ and short pu ‘ poss ’ are freely used in adnominal possessive constructions without any syntactic or semantic restrictions. This also applies to recursive possessive constructions, as illustrated in ( Example_9.32 ) to ( Example_9.34 ). In terms of the attested frequencies in such constructions, however, short pu ‘ poss ’ is employed more often than long punya ‘ poss ’.
summary:
Adnominal possessive constructions can be recursively stacked to form double and even triple possessive constructions. Double possessives are common, especially for kinship and social relations, while triple possessives are possible but extremely rare, with only one attested corpus example.  

Both the long form punya and the short form pu can be used freely in these possessive constructions without syntactic or semantic restriction, including recursive ones, though pu is more frequent than punya.

text:
In addition to encoding adnominal possession, punya ‘ poss ’ (including its reduced forms) also serves other functions in possessive constructions, namely as (1) an emphatic marker that signals locational relations or association (§ Para_9.3.1 ), (2) a marker of beneficiary relations (§ Para_9.3.2 ), or (3) an attitudinal intensifier or stance (§ Para_9.3.3 ). And (4), the possessive ligature is also used in reflexive construction (§ Para_9.3.4 ).

Syntactically, not only nouns, personal pronouns, demonstratives, or noun phrases can take the possessor or possessum slots. In addition, these slots can be filled by verbs. Further, the possessum slot can be taken by mid-range quantifiers, temporal adverbs, or prepositional phrases. Finally, the possessum can be omitted.
summary: The passage explains that **punya** not only marks adnominal possession but also functions as an emphatic marker for location or association, a marker of beneficiary relations, an attitudinal intensifier or stance marker, and a ligature in reflexive constructions. It also notes that possessive constructions are syntactically flexible: the possessor and possessum slots may be filled by nouns, pronouns, demonstratives, noun phrases, or even verbs, while the possessum slot can also contain quantifiers, temporal adverbs, or prepositional phrases, and may sometimes be omitted.

text:
Cross-linguistically, one noncanonical function of possessive constructions is to signal that the possessum is “perceived to be closely related” to the possessor. In Papuan Malay, this includes locational relations, both spatial and temporal, and relations that express an association, as illustrated in ( Example_9.35 ) to ( Example_9.41 ). With this function of punya ‘ poss ’, the possessive construction receives an emphatic reading; in the following examples the English translation attempts to convey this emphatic reading with the additional italicized information.

The possessive marker can signal locational relations, or, employing Dixon.2010 terminology, relations of “orientation or location”. The locational relations can be spatial, as in ( Example_9.35 ) and ( Example_9.36 ), or temporal, as in ( Example_9.37 ) to ( Example_9.39 ). Dixon.2010 term “orientation/location” refers to spatial relations; temporal relations are not mentioned.

In ( Example_9.35 ) and ( Example_9.36 ), pu ‘ poss ’ marks spatial relations between the possessor and the possessum, with the possessive construction receiving an emphatic reading. In ( Example_9.36 ), a spatial referent, encoded with the proper noun Jayapura, takes the possessor slot. It denotes the location or source for the referent expressed by the possessum, dua blas orang ‘twelve people’. In ( Example_9.35 ), the spatial referent, encoded in the prepositional phrase di dalam itu ‘in that inside’, takes the possessum slot. The locative preposition di ‘at, in’ can also be deleted (see § Para_10.1.5 ) resulting in de pu dalam itu ‘that inside (part) of it’. It designates the location for the referent expressed by the pronominal possessor de ‘ 3sg ’.

styleExampleTitle
Spatial locational relations
styleExampleTitle

Jayapura pu dua blas orang yang lulus ka?\\
Jayapura poss two teens person rel pass(.a.test) or\\

‘aren’t there twelve people from Jayapura who graduated ( as opposed to other cities with fewer graduates)?’ (Lit. ‘ Jayapura’s twelve people’) [081025-003-Cv.0311]

baru ambil bayi tu, bayi yang de pu\\
and.then fetch palm.stem d.dist palm.stem rel 3sg poss \\
di dalam itu kang kaya kapas to?\\
at inside d.dist you.know like cotton right?\\

‘and then (he) took that palm stem, that inside (part) of it ( as opposed to other parts), you know, is like cotton, right?’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0073]

In the elicited examples in ( Example_9.37 ) to ( Example_9.39 ), the possessive marker signals temporal locational relations. In these examples, the third person singular pronoun de ‘ 3sg ’ takes the possessor slot. It designates the temporal reference point for the event under discussion. The possessum slot is taken by a temporal expression such as besok ‘tomorrow’ in ( Example_9.37 ), pagi ‘morning’ in ( Example_9.38 ), and malam ‘night’ in ( Example_9.39 ). This temporal expression denotes a specific point in time relative to the temporal reference point expressed by the possessor.

styleExampleTitle
Temporal locational relations
styleExampleTitle

trus sa tinggal di sana, trus de pu besok\\
next 1sg stay at l.dist next 3sg poss tomorrow\\
baru sa kembali \\
and.then 1sg return \\

‘[two days ago I went to Abepura,] and then I stayed there, and then the ( very) next day only then did I return ’ (Lit. ‘ its tomorrow’) [Elicited BR111020.008]

dong kerja ruma dari pagi sampe malam de pu pagi,\\
3pl work house from morning until night 3sg poss morning\\
baru dong kasi selesay smua\\
and.then 3pl give finish all\\

‘they worked on the house from morning until evening, the ( very) next morning only then did they finish everything’ (Lit. ‘ its morning’) [Elicited BR111020.009]

Petrus deng Tinus dong pi mandi di pante tadi pagi,\\
Petrus with Tinus 3pl go bathe at coast earlier morning\\
de pu malam dong pi ke Jayapura\\
3sg poss night 3pl go to Jayapura\\

‘Petrus and Tinus went bathing at the beach this morning (and) this ( very) evening they went to Jayapura’ (Lit. ‘ its night’) [Elicited BR111020.009]

Another cross-linguistically rather common function of the possessive marker it to indicate an “association” between the possessum and the possessor. This also applies to Papuan Malay, as shown in ( Example_9.40 ) and ( Example_9.41 ). In ( Example_9.40 ), punya ‘ poss ’ signals that the possessum tu ‘ d.dist ’ is associated with the possessor lima juta ‘five million’, giving the emphatic reading ``a minimum of five-million ( as opposed to lower prices)''. Alternatively, one might classify the possessive construction in ( Example_9.40 ) as an “‘appositive genitive’, where the two noun phrases are equated denotatively”, adopting the terminology used by. Along similar lines, in ( Example_9.41 ), the ligature indicates an association between the possessum tu ‘ d.dist ’ and the possessor tingkat propinsi ‘provincial level’, resulting in the emphatic reading ``(a meeting at) the provincial level ( and not at the regency level)''.

styleExampleTitle
Association
styleExampleTitle

yang mahal yang di atas satu jut\\
rel be.expensive rel at top one tru -million\\
lima juta punya tu\\
five million poss d.dist \\

‘(traditional cloths from Sorong) which are expensive, which (cost) more than one million[ tru ], a minimum of five million ( as opposed to lower prices)’ (Lit. ‘ that (price) of five million’) [081006-029-CvEx.0009]

kitong ikut ini tingkat propinsi punya tu\\
1pl follow d.prox floor province poss d.dist \\

‘we attended (a meeting at), what’s-its-name, the provincial level ( and not at the regency level)’ (Lit. ‘ that (meeting) of the provincial level’) [081010-001-Cv.0043]
summary:
The passage explains that Papuan Malay possessive constructions can have noncanonical meanings beyond ownership, especially marking a close relationship between possessor and possessum. Specifically, punya/pu can express spatial or temporal location and an association between two entities, and these uses often create an emphatic interpretation.

In spatial cases, the possessive relation can indicate where something is located or its source, while in temporal cases it can link a reference point to times like “tomorrow,” “morning,” or “night.” In association cases, the construction highlights a close connection such as “at least five million” or “at the provincial level,” contrasting the marked interpretation with alternatives.

text:
The possessive marker punya ‘ poss ’ is also used to signal beneficiary relations. Speakers employ this construction when they want to signal that the recipient is the beneficiary of a definite theme, as discussed in § Para_11.1.3.3. This is illustrated in ( Example_9.42 ) and ( Example_9.43 ). In the respective examples, the possessors mama ‘mother’ and de ‘ 3sg ’ express the recipients/beneficiaries of the events expressed by the verbs simpang ‘store’ and bli ‘buy’, while the possessa makang ‘food’ and alat alat ‘utensils’ denote the anticipated objects of possession or themes.

mama, kitong suda simpang mama punya makang\\
mother 1pl already store mother poss food\\

‘mother, we already put food for you aside’ (Lit. ‘ mama’s food’) [080924-002-Pr.0005]

dong su bli de punya alat alat ini\\
3pl already buy 3sg poss rdp equipment d.prox \\

‘they already bought these utensils for him’ (Lit. ‘ his utensils’) [080922-001a-CvPh.0558]
summary: The possessive marker **punya** can also mark **beneficiary relations**, especially when the recipient is understood as the beneficiary of a definite theme. In these cases, the possessor noun or pronoun expresses the recipient/beneficiary of the event, while the possessed noun refers to the item being stored or bought, as in “mother’s food” meaning food set aside for mother and “his utensils” meaning utensils bought for him.

text: Another noncanonical function of possessive punya ‘ poss ’ is that of an intensifier or stance that signals speaker attitudes or evaluations. The attested data suggests three different constructions in which Papuan Malay speakers use punya ‘ poss ’ in such a way: constructions with (1) a nominal possessor and a quantifier possessum (§ Para_9.3.3.1 ), (2) a nominal possessor and a verbal possessum (§ Para_9.3.3.2 ), and (3) a verbal possessor and a verbal possessum (§ Para_9.3.3.3 ).
summary: Possessive **punya** can also function as an intensifier or stance marker that conveys speaker attitudes or evaluations. The data show three constructions where this use occurs: with a nominal possessor and quantifier possessum, with a nominal possessor and verbal possessum, and with both a verbal possessor and verbal possessum.

text:
In the possessive constructions in ( Example_9.44 ) to ( Example_9.47 ), a nominal constituent takes the possessor slot while a quantifier takes the possessum slot.

Attested in the corpus is only the one example in ( Example_9.44 ) in which the mid-range quantifier banyak ‘many’ takes the possessum slot. A second, elicited example is presented in ( Example_9.45 ). Possessive constructions with the mid-range quantifier sedikit ‘few’ are also possible, as illustrated with the elicited examples in ( Example_9.46 ) and ( Example_9.47 ). In these examples punya ‘ poss ’ functions as an attitudinal intensifier, expressing speaker evaluations, such as feelings of annoyance in ( Example_9.44 ), of surprise in ( Example_9.45 ) and ( Example_9.46 ), or of alarm in ( Example_9.47 ).

baru, mama, setang pu banyak di situ\\
and.then mother evil.spirit poss many at l.med \\

‘and then, mother, (there) are really many evil spirits over there’ (Lit. ‘ many of’) [081025-006-Cv.0062]

natal tu ana ana dong maing kembang-api pu banyak\\
Christmas d.dist rdp child 3pl play fire-cracker poss many\\

‘(during) Christmas (time) the children play with really many fire-crackers’ (Lit. ‘ many of’) [Elicited BR111020.005]

di gunung itu pohong pu sedikit\\
at mountain d.dist tree poss few\\

‘on that mountain, there are very few trees’ (Lit. ‘ few of’) [Elicited BR111020.006]

tete de minum air pu sedikit\\
grandfather 3sg drink water poss few\\

‘grandfather drinks very little water’ (Lit. ‘ few of’) [Elicited BR111020.007]

Possessive constructions with other quantifiers or with numerals taking the possessum slot are ungrammatical.
summary: In these possessive constructions, a nominal constituent occupies the possessor slot while a quantifier occupies the possessum slot. The corpus contains only one attested example with banyak ‘many,’ while elicited examples show that sedikit ‘few’ is also possible; in these cases, punya functions as an attitudinal intensifier expressing speaker reactions such as annoyance, surprise, or alarm. Possessive constructions with other quantifiers or with numerals in the possessum slot are ungrammatical.

text:
In the possessive constructions in ( Example_9.48 ) to ( Example_9.52 ), a nominal constituent takes the possessor slot while a mono- or bivalent verb takes the possessum slot. In these constructions, speakers typically use short pu ‘ poss ’ rather than long punya ‘ poss ’; more investigation is needed however, to further explore these speaker preferences.

In the examples in ( Example_9.48 ) to ( Example_9.52 ), a monovalent verb takes the possessum slot. Again, the ligature functions as an attitudinal intensifier. In ( Example_9.48 ) pu ‘ poss ’ adds emphasis to stative malas ‘be listless’. In ( Example_9.49 ), pu ‘ poss ’ precedes stative brat ‘be heavy’, and thereby signals feelings of annoyance. Finally, in ( Example_9.50 ), the possessive marker precedes dynamic mendrita ‘suffer’, thereby indicating negative feelings of disbelief.

styleExampleTitle
Intensifying function of punya ‘ poss ’: Preceding monovalent verbs
styleExampleTitle

dong tida taw umpang, smua tra taw toser,\\
3pl neg know pass.ball all neg know pass.ball\\
adu, sa pu malas\\
oh.no! 1sg poss be.listless\\

[About playing volleyball:] ‘none of them knows (how) to pass a ball, none of them knows (how) to pass a ball, oh no!, I’m so very listless (to play with them)’ (Lit. ‘ the being listless of’) [081109-001-Cv.0127]

damay, de pu brat\\
peace 3sg poss be.heavy\\

‘my goodness!, he was so heavy’ (Lit. ‘ the being heavy of’) [081025-009b-Cv.0041]

adu, dong dua pu mendrita\\
oh.no! 3pl two poss suffer\\

‘oh no!, the two of them were suffering so much’ (Lit. ‘ the suffering of’) [081025-006-Cv.0059]

In ( Example_9.51 ) to ( Example_9.52 ), the possessum slot is taken by a bivalent verb. Again, the possessive marker has intensifying, asserting and/or evaluative function.

styleExampleTitle
Intensifying function of punya ‘ poss ’: Preceding bivalent verbs
styleExampleTitle

ka Sarles juga de pu maing pisow\\
oSb Sarles also 3sg poss play knife\\

‘older brother Sarles also, he has a fast and smart way of playing’ (Lit. ‘ the knife playing of’) [081023-001-Cv.0009]

baru nanti tong pu lawang deng siapa\\
and.then very.soon 1pl poss oppose with who\\

‘and then later who will be our opponent?’ (Lit. ‘ the opposing of’) [081109-001-Cv.0136]
summary: In these possessive constructions, a nominal constituent fills the possessor position while a mono- or bivalent verb fills the possessum position, and speakers usually prefer the short form pu rather than the longer punya, though this preference needs further study. Here, pu functions as an attitudinal intensifier: with monovalent verbs it adds emphasis or signals negative feelings such as annoyance or disbelief, and with bivalent verbs it has an intensifying, asserting, and/or evaluative effect.

text:
In noncanonical possessive constructions, both the possessor and the possessum slot can be taken by verbs, as illustrated in ( Example_9.53 ) to ( Example_9.56 ). More specifically, a dynamic verb takes the possessor slot, while a stative verb takes the possessum slot. The only example attested in the corpus is ( Example_9.53 ), while the examples in ( Example_9.54 ) to ( Example_9.56 ) are elicited.

With its intensifying function, punya ‘ poss ’ signals an emphatic reading of both the verbal possessor and the verbal possessum, as illustrated in ( Example_9.53 ): mandi punya ‘really bathing’ and punya jaw ‘very far away (of)’.

dong mandi di kali Biri, mm-mm, mandi punya jaw itu\\
3pl bathe at river Biri mhm bathe poss be.far d.dist \\

[About a run-away boy:] ‘they were bathing in the Biri river, mhm, (they were) really bathing very far away’ (Lit. ‘ the being far away of the bathing’) [081025-008-Cv.0032-0033]

de kerja punya cepat\\
3sg work poss be.fast\\

‘he really worked very fast’ (Lit. ‘ the being fast of the working’) [Elicited BR111020.022]

mama de masak punya enak\\
mother 3sg cook poss be.pleasant\\

‘mother really cooks very tastily’ (Lit. ‘ the being tasty of the cooking’) [Elicited BR111020.023]

Marice deng Matius dong dua bicara punya kras\\
Marice with Matius 3pl two speak poss be.harsh\\

‘the two of them Marice and Matius really spoke very loudly (with each other)’ (Lit. ‘ the being loud of the speaking’) [Elicited BR111020.024]
summary:
In noncanonical possessive constructions, verbs can fill both the possessor and possessum positions: a dynamic verb occurs in the possessor slot, and a stative verb in the possessum slot. The only corpus-attested example is the one with *mandi punya jaw*, while the other examples were elicited.  

With its intensifying function, *punya* marks an emphatic reading of both verbs, yielding meanings such as “really bathing very far away,” “he really worked very fast,” and similar emphatic interpretations.

text:
The possessive marker punya ‘ poss ’ is also used to create reflexive expressions. Generally speaking, reflexives designate constructions “where subject and object refer to the same entity, explicitly [ ] or implicitly”. Typically, explicit reflexive expressions are formed with a reflexive pronoun “which refers to the same person or thing as the subject of the verb”. As Papuan Malay does not have reflexive pronouns, an alternative strategy is used. Reflexive relations are expressed with an adnominal possessive construction where a personal pronoun in the possessor slot and the reflexive noun diri ‘self’ in the possessum slot express the reflexive relationship between both, as illustrated with sa pu diri ‘myself’ in ( Example_9.57 ) and kita punya diri ‘ourselves’ in ( Example_9.58 ).

bukang sa rasa bahwa sa ini sa banggakang\\
neg 1sg feel that 1sg d.prox 1sg praise\\
sa pu diri tapi itu yang terjadi\\
1sg poss self but d.dist rel happen\\

‘it’s not that I feel that I ( emph ), (that) I praise myself, but that’s what happened’ (Lit. ‘ the self of me’) [081110-008-CvNP.0152]

kita rencana, manusia yang mengatur kita punya diri\\
1pl plan human.being rel arrange 1pl poss self\\

‘we make plans, (it’s us) human beings who manage our own lives’ (Lit. ‘ the self of us’) [080918-001-CvNP.0032]
summary: Papuan Malay does not use reflexive pronouns; instead, reflexive meaning is expressed with an adnominal possessive construction consisting of a personal pronoun in the possessor slot and diri ‘self’ in the possessum slot. Forms like sa pu diri ‘myself’ and kita punya diri ‘ourselves’ show how the possessive marker punya can be used to create reflexive expressions.

text:
In Papuan Malay, adnominal possessive constructions consist of two noun phrases linked with the possessive marker punya ‘ poss ’, such that `` possessor punya possessum ''. In addition to signaling adnominal possessive relations between two noun phrases, punya ‘ poss ’ has a number of derived, noncanonical functions, namely as (1) an emphatic marker of locational relations or relations of association, (2) a marker of beneficiary relations, (3) an attitudinal intensifier or stance, and (4) a ligature in reflexive constructions.

Such noncanonical functions of the possessive ligature have also been noted in other eastern Malay varieties. Examples are its functions as a marker of beneficiary relations in Ambon Malay, as a marker of locational or temporal relations in Ternate Malay, and as an attitudinal intensifier in Manado Malay.

Two explanations have been suggested for the extended uses of the possessive marker in Malay speech varieties.

One is to propose a substratum influence of Chinese languages. Some of the noncanonical functions of the possessive marker have long been noted for Bazaar Malay and have been linked to the substratum influence of Chinese speech varieties, namely the function of punya ‘ poss ’ to link a locative or temporal modifier or a modifying adjective in the possessor slot preceding the ligature with its head in the possessum slot (See;; Winstedt.1938;; ). argues that under the influence of southern Chinese speech varieties, the colloquial Malay possessive marker developed into an “attitudinal intensifier” or “stance” that transforms statements into evaluative “assertions that are often laced with strong feelings, including feelings of awe, [ ] or feelings of incredulity or even annoyance”. For the different synchronic functions of (em)punya in classical and colloquial Malay, propose the following development or grammaticalization path: “lexical verb genitive pronominal stance development”.

A second explanation proposes a grammaticalization process of the possessive marker without any substratum influence from Chinese varieties. argues that the influence of Chinese languages does not “account for the presence of the punya construction” in Malay varieties which have “little obvious contact with Chinese languages”, such as Riau Indonesian or Papuan Malay; neither does this influence “account for the choice of the specific marker punya”. Instead, Gil submits that the interpretation of the punya construction underwent a semantic change from predicative possessive to adnominal possessive to noncanonical possessive, such that: “thing associated with X’s having” “thing associated with X” “property associated with X” (1999: 6, 8).

Possessive constructions with punya ‘ poss ’ have a number of different realizations. The possessive marker can be represented with unreduced punya, reduced pu, clitic =p, or a zero morpheme. There are no syntactic or semantic restrictions on the uses of the long and reduced possessive marker forms. By contrast, omission of punya only occurs when the possessive construction expresses inalienable possession of body parts or kinship relations. The possessor and the possessum can be expressed with different kinds of syntactic constituents, such as lexical nouns, noun phrases, or demonstratives. In addition, personal pronouns can also express the possessor. In noncanonical possessive constructions, verbs can also take the possessor and/or possessum slots. Further, mid-range quantifiers, temporal adverbs, and prepositional phrases can take the possessum slot. In canonical possessive constructions, the possessum can also be omitted. Semantically, the possessor and the possessum can denote human, nonhuman animate, or inanimate referents.
summary:
Papuan Malay adnominal possession is expressed by linking two noun phrases with the possessive marker punya ‘poss’ in the order “possessor punya possessum,” but punya also appears in several noncanonical roles, including marking location/association, beneficiary relations, stance or intensification, and reflexive linkage. Similar extended functions are found in other eastern Malay varieties, and scholars have explained them either through Chinese substratum influence or through an internal grammaticalization path from predicative possession to adnominal and then noncanonical possessive uses.

The marker has several surface forms, including unreduced punya, reduced pu, clitic =p, and zero; omission is limited to inalienable possession such as body parts and kinship. Possessors and possessums may be expressed by nouns, noun phrases, demonstratives, pronouns, and in noncanonical constructions even verbs, quantifiers, temporal adverbs, or prepositional phrases.

text:
This chapter describes prepositional phrases in Papuan Malay, that is, constructions which consist of a preposition followed by a noun phrase, such that `` prep np ''.

Papuan Malay employs eleven prepositions that can be grouped semantically into (1) prepositions encoding location in space and time, (2) prepositions encoding accompaniment/instruments, goals, and benefaction, and (3) prepositions encoding comparisons. The defining characteristics of prepositions are discussed in § Para_5.11.

Prepositional phrases have the following defining characteristics:

enumerate

All prepositional phrases function as peripheral adjuncts; as such they do not have a grammatically restricted position within the clause but can be moved to different positions.
Most prepositional phrases also function as nonverbal predicates and/\-or oblique arguments (see § Para_12.4 and § Para_11.1.3.2, respectively).

Some prepositional phrases also function as modifiers within noun phrases (§ Para_8.2.7 )

Prepositional phrases that function as nonverbal predicates can be modified by aspectual adverbs (§ Para_5.4.1 ), while such modification is unattested for prepositional phrases having other functions.

enumerate

In the following, Papuan Malay prepositional phrases are discussed according to the semantics of their prepositional head: location in space and time in § Para_10.1, accompaniment/instruments, goals, and benefaction in § Para_10.2, and comparisons in § Para_10.3. The main points of this chapter are summarized in § Para_10.4.
summary: Papuan Malay has eleven prepositions, grouped into those expressing location in space and time, accompaniment/instruments, goals and benefaction, and comparison. Prepositional phrases are defined as a preposition plus noun phrase and function mainly as peripheral adjuncts, though they may also serve as nonverbal predicates, oblique arguments, or noun-phrase modifiers. Only prepositional phrases used as nonverbal predicates can be modified by aspectual adverbs.

section: Prepositions encoding location in space and time
text: Papuan Malay employs four prepositions that express location in space and time: locative di ‘at, in’ designates static location (§ Para_10.1.1 ), allative ke ‘to’ denotes direction toward a location (§ Para_10.1.2 ), elative dari ‘from’ expresses direction away from or out of a location (§ Para_10.1.3 ), and lative sampe ‘until’ designates direction up to a nonspatial temporal location (§ Para_10.1.4 ).
summary: Papuan Malay uses four prepositions to express spatial and temporal relations. **Di** marks static location, **ke** indicates movement toward a place, **dari** indicates movement away from or out of a place, and **sampe** expresses direction up to a nonspatial temporal endpoint.

section: Prepositions encoding location in space and time
text:
Prepositional phrases introduced with locative di ‘at, in’ indicate static location in spatial and nonspatial figurative terms. Most often the preposition denotes location ‘at’ or ‘in’ a referent; depending on its context, though, it is also translatable as ‘on’.

Very commonly, di ‘at, in’ introduces a peripheral location as in di kampung ‘in the village’ in ( Example_10.1 ), or di dia ‘at hers’ in ( Example_10.2 ). When following placement verbs such as taru ‘put’ in ( Example_10.3 ), di ‘at, in’ introduces oblique locative arguments that indicate the location of the referent, as in di sini ‘here’. Frequently, di ‘at, in’ also introduces nonverbal predicates, as in ( Example_10.4 ) (see § Para_12.4 ). Only rarely, di ‘at, in’ introduces locations encoded by adnominal prepositional phrases, as in pasar di bawa tu ‘the market down there’ in ( Example_10.5 ). The examples in ( Example_10.1 ) to ( Example_10.5 ) also show that di ‘at, in’ introduces animate and inanimate, as well as nominal and pronominal referents. In the corpus only the following pronominal complements of di ‘at, in’ are attested: 2sg, 1pl, and 3pl.

waktu saya dengang bapa tinggal di kampung saya kerja\\
time 1sg with father stay at village 1sg work\\
sperti laki laki\\
similar.to rdp husband\\

‘when I and (my) husband (‘father’) were living in the village, I worked like a man’ [081014-007-CvEx.0048]

jadi saya besar di Ida dengang de punya laki tu\\
so 1sg be.big at Ida with 3sg poss husband d.dist \\
besar di dia\\
be.big at 3sg \\

‘so I grew up with Ida and that husband of hers, (I) grew up at hers’ [080927-007-CvNP.0017/0019]

skarang kamu kasi terpol terpol, taru di sini\\
now 2pl give rdp jerry.can put at l.prox \\

‘now you give (me) the jerry cans, put (them) here’ [081110-002-Cv.0065]

sa di IPS satu\\
1sg at social.sciences one\\

[About course tracks in high school:] ‘I (am) in Social Sciences I’ [081023-004-Cv.0020]

pasar di bawa tu raaame\\
market at bottom d.dist be.bustling\\

‘ the market down there is very bustling’ [081109-005-JR.0008]
summary: The locative preposition **di** ‘at, in’ marks static location in both spatial and figurative uses, and is most commonly translated as **‘at’** or **‘in’**, though it can sometimes mean **‘on’** depending on context. It commonly introduces peripheral locations, oblique locative arguments after placement verbs, and nonverbal predicates, and only rarely appears in adnominal prepositional phrases. The examples show that **di** can take animate or inanimate, nominal or pronominal complements, with only a few pronominal forms attested in the corpus.

section: Prepositions encoding location in space and time
text:
Prepositional phrases introduced with allative ke ‘to’ denote direction toward a referent. Following motion verbs such as lari ‘run’ in ( Example_10.6 ) or datang ‘come’ in ( Example_10.7 ), ke ‘to’ introduces oblique locative arguments which indicate the goal of the motion, as in ke pante ‘to the beach’ or ke kitong ‘to us’, respectively. Allative ke ‘to’ also very often introduces nonverbal predicates as in ( Example_10.8 ). The three examples also show that ke ‘to’ introduces animate and inanimate, as well as nominal and pronominal referents. In the corpus only the following pronominal complements of ke ‘to’ are attested: 1sg, 3sg, 2pl.

dong lari ke pante\\
3pl run to coast\\

‘they ran to the beach’ [081115-001a-Cv.0008]

dia punya aroa datang ke kitong kasi tanda\\
3sg poss departed.spirit come to 1pl give sign\\

‘[so when there is another person (who) dies in a different village,] (then) his/her departed spirit comes to us (and) gives (us) a sign’ [081014-014-NP.0048]

sa ke ruma-sakit\\
1sg to hospital\\

‘I (went) to the hospital’ [081015-005-NP.0047]
summary: The allative preposition **ke** ‘to’ marks direction toward a referent and, after motion verbs like **lari** ‘run’ and **datang** ‘come,’ introduces oblique locative arguments indicating the goal of motion, such as ‘to the beach’ or ‘to us.’ It is also frequently used with nonverbal predicates and can take both animate and inanimate, nominal and pronominal complements, though only 1sg, 3sg, and 2pl pronominal complements are attested in the corpus.

section: Prepositions encoding location in space and time
text:
Prepositional phrases introduced with elative dari ‘from’ designate direction away from or out of a source location; depending on its context, though, dari also translates with ‘of’. Most commonly, the source location is spatial. In addition, dari ‘from’ expresses nonspatial figurative sources, temporal starting points, and the notions of superiority and dis similarity in comparison constructions.

Elative dari ‘from’ forms peripheral adjuncts, as in dari blakang ‘from the back’ in ( Example_10.9 ). When following motion verbs such as kluar ‘go out’, it expresses the source of the motion in an oblique argument, as in ( Example_10.10 ). Besides, elative dari ‘from’ expresses spatial source locations in nonverbal predicates, as in ( Example_10.11 ). Much less often, dari ‘from’ introduces sources encoded by adnominal prepositional phrases, as in ( Example_10.12 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing spatial source locations
styleExampleTitle

de tutup itu spit itu dari blakang \\
3sg close d.dist speedboat d.dist from backside \\

‘(this wave,) it totally covered, what’s-its-name, that speedboat from the back [to the front]’ [080923-015-CvEx.0021]

sa harus kluar dari kam pu kluarga\\
1sg have.to go.out from 2pl poss family\\

‘[I hadn’t thought that] I would have to depart from your family’ [080919-006-CvNP.0012]

tong smua dari kampung\\
1pl all from village\\

‘we all are from the village’ [081010-001-Cv.0084]

satu kali ini de pu bapa pu temang dari skola,\\
one time d.prox 3sg poss father poss friend from school\\
STT dorang pergi \\
theological.seminary 3pl go \\

‘this one time her father’s friends from school, theological seminary, they went ’ [081006-023-CvEx.0062]

The source location indicated with dari ‘from’ can also be nonspatial figurative as in the prepositional predicate clauses dari uang ‘up to the money’ in ( Example_10.13 ), or dari ko ‘up to you’ in ( Example_10.14 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing nonspatial figurative source locations
styleExampleTitle

yo, tong mo biking cepat, smua itu dari uang\\
yes 1pl want make be.fast all d.dist from money\\

‘yes, we want to do (it) quickly, all that (is) up to the money’ (Lit. ‘ from money’) [080927-006-CvNP.0034]

pinda ke IPA itu dari ko saja\\
move to natural.sciences d.dist from 2sg just\\

‘switching (from Social Sciences) to Natural Sciences, that (is) up to you alone’ (Lit. ‘ from you’) [081023-004-Cv.0023]

The examples in ( Example_10.9 ) to ( Example_10.14 ) also illustrate that dari ‘from’ introduces animate and inanimate, as well as nominal and pronominal referents. In the corpus one pronominal complement of dari ‘from’ is unattested, namely 2pl.

Derived from its spatial semantics, dari ‘from’ also very commonly introduces nonspatial temporal source locations, which are always encoded by peripheral adjuncts. The temporal starting point can be encoded by a noun that indicates time as in dari pagi ‘from the morning’ in ( Example_10.15 ), or by a temporal ad verb as in dari dulu ‘from the past’ in ( Example_10.16 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing temporal starting points
styleExampleTitle

tra bole tutup pintu, dari pagi buka pintu\\
neg permitted close door from morning open door\\
sampe malam\\
until night\\

‘you shouldn’t close the door, (you should keep it) open from morning until night’ [081110-008-CvNP.0108]

jadi itu suda kebiasaang dari dulu\\
so d.dist already habit from first\\

‘so that (tradition) has already become a custom from the past’ [081014-007-CvEx.0063]

Finally, elative dari ‘from’ is also used in comparative constructions marking degree or identity. In such constructions, dari ‘from’ functions as the mark of comparison which introduces the standard. In ( Example_10.17 ), for instance, dari ‘from’ serves as the mark in a comparative construction marking degree, namely superiority, while in ( Example_10.18 ) it serves as the mark in a comparative construction marking identity, namely dis similarity (for details on comparative constructions, see § Para_11.5 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing standards of comparison
styleExampleTitle

dia lebi besar dari smua ana ana \\
3sg more be.big from all rdp child \\

‘[in that class] he’s bigger than all the kids [in it]’ [081109-003-JR.0001] The original recording says dari smuat rather than dari smua ‘than all’. Most likely the speaker wanted to say dari smua temang ‘than all friends’ but cut himself off to replace temang ‘friend’ with ana ana ‘children’.

sifat ini laing dari ko\\
nature d.prox be.different from 2sg \\

‘this disposition is different from you’ [081110-008-CvNP.0089]
summary: Elative **dari** ‘from’ primarily marks direction away from or out of a source location, most often a spatial one, but it can also express figurative nonspatial sources and temporal starting points. It occurs in peripheral adjuncts, as oblique arguments with motion verbs, and in nonverbal predicates; it can introduce both nominal and pronominal referents, though one pronominal form is unattested in the corpus. In addition, **dari** functions in comparative constructions to mark the standard of comparison, including both superiority and dissimilarity.

section: Prepositions encoding location in space and time
text:
The preposition sampe ‘until’ introduces nonspatial temporal endpoints which are always encoded by peripheral adjuncts. Given these semantics, sampe ‘until’ typically introduces nouns that indicate time, as in sampe sore ‘until the afternoon’ in ( Example_10.19 ); that is, animate or pronominal referents of sampe ‘until’ are unattested.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing time-denoting nouns
styleExampleTitle

saya tidor sampe sore\\
1sg sleep until afternoon\\

‘I slept until the afternoon’ [081015-005-NP.0033]

Typically, peripheral prepositional phrases can be moved to other positions within the clause with no change in meaning. This does not, however, apply to the example in ( Example_10.19 ). When the prepositional phrase is moved to the front it denotes the temporal starting rather than the temporal endpoint of tidor ‘sleep’, as in ( Example_10.20 ). Hence, the meaning changes to ‘come afternoon’ (literally ‘reaches the afternoon’). One initial explanation for this change in meaning is that the utterance in ( Example_10.20 ) expresses a sequence of two events, namely the sampe ‘reaching’ of the afternoon and subsequently the tidor ‘sleeping’. In that case, sampe sore does not express the prepositional phrase ‘until afternoon’ but the verbal clause ‘reached the afternoon’ or ‘come afternoon’. This explanation, however, requires further investigation.

styleExampleTitle
Clause-initial position
styleExampleTitle

sampe sore saya tidor\\
reach afternoon 1sg sleep\\

‘ come afternoon I slept’ (Lit. ‘ reach the afternoon’) [Elicited BR120817.008]

Temporal sampe ‘until’ also introduces temporal adverbs that denote a temporal endpoint as in sampe skarang ‘until now’ in ( Example_10.21 ). Overall, however, these constructions are very rare in the corpus.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing temporal adverbs
styleExampleTitle

tapi sampe skarang blum brangkat\\
but until now not.yet leave\\

‘ but until now (the team) hasn’t yet left’ [081023-002-Cv.0001]

The preposition sampe ‘until’ has trial word class membership. Besides introducing prepositional phrases, sampe is also used as the bivalent verb ‘reach’, or as an anteriority-marking conjunction that introduces temporal clauses (see § Para_14.2.3.3 for its uses as a conjunction; see also § Para_5.14 ).
summary: The preposition **sampe** ‘until’ expresses nonspatial temporal endpoints and typically takes time-denoting nouns such as *sore* ‘afternoon’; animate or pronominal complements are not found. While peripheral prepositional phrases are usually movable, fronting **sampe**-phrases changes the meaning to a temporal starting point, suggesting a different analysis in which **sampe** functions as the verb ‘reach’; it can also introduce temporal adverbs like *skarang* ‘now’, though these uses are rare. The word **sampe** has trial word class membership, also appearing as a bivalent verb and as an anteriority-marking conjunction.

section: Prepositions encoding location in space and time
text:
Two of the prepositions of location may be omitted if the semantic relationship between the complement and the predicate can be deduced from the context. The prepositions are locative di ‘at, in’, as illustrated with the contrastive examples in ( Example_10.22 ) and ( Example_10.23 ), and allative ke ‘to’, as shown in ( Example_10.24 ) and ( Example_10.25 ).

When locative di ‘at, in’ introduces a spatial location and combines with a position verb such as tidor ‘sleep’, as in ( Example_10.22 ) and ( Example_10.23 ), the preposition can be elided. Both the preceding verb and the complement of di ‘at, in’ are already deictic and therefore allow the elision of di ‘at, in’: the position verb tidor ‘sleep’ implies the notion of static location, while the complement sana ‘over there’ signals the position of the location.

styleExampleTitle
Prepositional phrases with elided locative di ‘at, in’
styleExampleTitle

ko punya mama ada tidor di sana\\
2sg poss mother exist sleep at l.dist \\

‘your mother is sleeping over there’ [081006-025-CvEx.0007]

a, omong kosong, ko masuk tidor Ø sana suda\\
ah! way.of.talking be.empty 2sg enter sleep l.dist already\\

‘ah, nonsense, you just go inside (and) sleep over there’ [081023-001-Cv.0057]

Along similar lines allative ke ‘to’ can be omitted, when the preposition introduces a location and combines with a motion verb that also expresses direction such as masuk ‘enter’ in ( Example_10.24 ) and ( Example_10.25 ). Again, both the verb and the complement of ke ‘to’ are deictic, thereby allowing the elision of ke ‘to’: the verb masuk ‘enter’ implies the notion of motion and direction, while the complement hutang ‘forest’ denotes the location toward which the motion is directed.

styleExampleTitle
Prepositional phrases with elided allative ke ‘to’
styleExampleTitle

smua masarakat masuk ke hutang\\
all community enter to forest\\

‘the entire community went into the forest’ [081029-005-Cv.0012]

smua masuk Ø hutang\\
all enter forest\\

‘all went (into) the forest’ [081029-005-Cv.0111]

The elision typically affects prepositional phrases with common nouns denoting locations as in ( Example_10.25 ), or locatives as in ( Example_10.23 ). In addition, the elision can also affect prepositional phrases with location nouns as in ( Example_10.26 ) and ( Example_10.27 ): in ( Example_10.26 ) the omitted preposition is locative di ‘at, in’, whereas in ( Example_10.27 ) it is allative ke ‘to’.

styleExampleTitle
Prepositional phrases with elided preposition and location noun complement
styleExampleTitle

baru kitong taru Ø depang to?\\
and.then 1pl put front right?\\

‘and then we put (the cake down) (in) front, right?’ [081011-005-Cv.0031]

itu yang sa bilang, kalo dong pinda Ø sebla bole\\
d.dist rel 1sg say if 3pl move side may\\

‘that’s why I said, ``if they move (to) the (other) side (that’s) alright''' [081011-001-Cv.0144]

Elision of di ‘at, in’ and ke ‘to’ is not possible, though, in nonverbal prepositional predicate clauses as this would create nominal clauses with unacceptable semantics. This is illustrated with elided di ‘at, in’ in ( Example_10.28 ), which is based on the example in ( Example_10.4 ), and with elided ke ‘to’ in ( Example_10.29 ), which is based on the example in ( Example_10.8 ).

styleExampleTitle
Nonverbal prepositional predicate clauses with elided locative di ‘at, in’ and allative ke ‘to’
styleExampleTitle

* sa Ø IPS satu\\
1sg social.sciences one\\

[About course tracks in high school:] (‘I (am) Social Sciences I’) [based on 081023-004-Cv.0020]

* sa Ø ruma-sakit\\
1sg hospital\\

(‘I (am) the hospital’) [based on 081015-005-NP.0047]

Elision of elative dari ‘from’ and temporal sampe ‘until’ is also not possible, as illustrated in ( Example_10.30 ) and ( Example_10.31 ). In the example in ( Example_10.30 ), which is based on ( Example_10.10 ), elative dari ‘from’ is omitted, resulting in an ungrammatical utterance. In the example in ( Example_10.31 ), which is based on ( Example_10.19 ), temporal sampe ‘until’ is elided. The result is a change in meaning of the entire utterance: ‘I slept (the entire) afternoon’.

styleExampleTitle
Prepositional phrases with elided elative dari ‘from’ and temporal sampe ‘until’
styleExampleTitle

* sa harus kluar Ø kam pu kluarga\\
1sg have.to go.out 2pl poss family\\

(‘[I hadn’t thought that] I would have to depart your family’) [Elicited BR120817.009]

saya tidor Ø sore\\
1sg sleep afternoon\\

‘I slept (the entire) afternoon’ [Elicited BR120817.010]
summary: The passage explains that the locative preposition di ‘at, in’ and the allative ke ‘to’ can be omitted when their meanings are recoverable from context, especially when they occur with deictic verbs like tidor ‘sleep’ and masuk ‘enter’ plus locative or motion-related complements. This elision can also occur with some location nouns, but it is not allowed in nonverbal prepositional predicate clauses, and eliding elative dari ‘from’ or temporal sampe ‘until’ is generally impossible, with the latter yielding a meaning change rather than a grammatical omission.

section: Prepositions encoding accompaniment/instruments, goals, and benefaction
text: Papuan Malay employs four prepositions encoding accompaniment/instruments, goals, and benefaction: comitative dengang ‘with’ (§ Para_10.2.1 ), goal-oriented sama ‘to’ (§ Para_10.2.2 ), benefactive untuk ‘for’ (§ Para_10.2.3 ), and buat ‘for’ (§ Para_10.2.4 ).
summary: Papuan Malay uses four prepositions to express accompaniment, instruments, goals, and benefaction. These are dengang ‘with’ for comitative/instrumental meanings, sama ‘to’ for goals, and untuk ‘for’ and buat ‘for’ for benefactive meanings.

section: Prepositions encoding accompaniment/instruments, goals, and benefaction
text:
Prepositional phrases introduced with comitative dengang ‘with’, with its short form deng, typically express accompaniment with animate or inanimate associates. Also very often, dengang ‘with’ introduces instruments. In addition, dengang ‘with’ introduces objects of mental verbs and the notion of identity in comparison constructions.

The associates introduced with dengang ‘with’ are most commonly animate human as in deng mama-tua ‘with aunt’ in ( Example_10.32 ), deng de pu temang temang ‘with his friends’ in ( Example_10.33 ), or in deng kamu ‘with you’ in ( Example_10.34 ). These examples also show that the complements of dengang ‘with’ can be nouns or personal pronouns. Besides animate associates, dengang ‘with’ also introduces inanimate associates, as in deng motor ‘with (his) motorbike’ in ( Example_10.35 ), or in deng itu ‘with those (spices)’ in ( Example_10.36 ). The associates introduced with dengang ‘with’ are either encoded in peripheral adjuncts as in ( Example_10.32 ), or ( Example_10.34 ) to ( Example_10.36 ), or in nonverbal predicates as in ( Example_10.33 ). The example in ( Example_10.33 ) also illustrates that prepositional phrases functioning as nonverbal predicates can be modified by adverbs, such as prospective masi ‘still’; such modification is unattested for prepositional phrases having other functions.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing associates
styleExampleTitle

sebentar Hurki datang ko pulang deng mama-tua\\
in.a.moment Hurki come 2sg go.home with aunt\\

‘in a moment (when) Hurki comes, you’ll go home with me (‘ aunt’)’ [081011-006-Cv.0003]

Roni masi deng de pu temang temang\\
Roni still with 3sg poss rdp friend\\

‘Roni is still with his friends’ [081006-031-Cv.0011]

slama sa tinggal deng kamu sa kerja\\
as.long.as 1sg stay with 2pl 1sg work\\

‘as long as I stayed with you I worked’ [080919-006-CvNP.0014]

de jatu deng motor\\
3sg fall with motorbike\\

‘he fell with (his) motorbike’ [081006-020-Cv.0008]

itu nanti kitong tumbuk baru masak deng itu\\
d.dist very.soon 1pl pound and.then cook with d.dist \\

‘later we’ll pound those (spices and) and then cook with them’ [081010-001-Cv.0196]

Instruments introduced with comitative dengang ‘with’ are expressed in peripheral adjuncts as in deng pisow ‘with a knife’ in ( Example_10.37 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing instruments
styleExampleTitle

bapa de pukul sa deng pisow\\
father 3sg hit 1sg with knife\\

‘(my) husband stabbed me with a knife’ [081011-023-Cv.0167]

In addition, comitative dengang ‘with’ introduces oblique arguments for mental verbs such as mara ‘feel angry (about)’ in ( Example_10.38 ), takut ‘feel afraid (of)’ in ( Example_10.39 ), or perlu ‘need’ in ( Example_10.40 ). Bivalent verbs such as mara ‘feel angry (about)’ or takut ‘feel afraid (of)’ do not require but allow two syntactic arguments (see § Para_5.3.1 and § Para_11.1 ). That is, speakers quite commonly encode patients, such as orang in ( Example_10.38 ) or setang ‘evil spirit’ in ( Example_10.39 ), as oblique arguments rather than as direct objects.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing objects of mental verbs
styleExampleTitle

kalo saya mara dengang orang begitu sa takut\\
if 1sg feel.angry(.about) with person like.that 1sg feel.afraid(.of)\\

‘if I was angry with someone like that I’d feel afraid’ [081110-008-CvNP.0067]

adu, kang dong terlalu takut dengang setang\\
oh.no! you.know 3pl too feel.afraid(.of) with evil.spirit\\

‘oh no!, you know, they feel too afraid of evil spirits’ [081025-006-Cv.0198]

mama-ade sa perlu deng mama-ade\\
aunt 1sg need with aunt\\

‘aunt, I need you (‘ aunt’)’ (Lit. ‘need with aunt’) [081014-004-Cv.0004]

Comitative dengang ‘with’ is also used in comparative constructions. As the mark of comparison, dengang ‘with’ introduces the standard of comparison in identity-marking constructions. In ( Example_10.41 ), for example, dengang ‘with’ serves as the mark in a similarity construction, while in ( Example_10.42 ) it is the mark in a dis similarity construction (for more details on comparative constructions, see § Para_11.5 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing standards of comparison
styleExampleTitle

de sombong sama deng ko\\
3sg be.arrogant same with 2sg \\

‘she’ll be as arrogant as you (are)’ [081006-005-Cv.0002]

orang Papua beda dengang orang Indonesia\\
person Papua be.different with person Indonesia\\

‘Papuans are different from Indonesians’ [081029-002-Cv.0009]

The preposition dengang ‘with’ has dual word class membership; it is also used as an addition-marking conjunction (§ Para_14.2.1.1; see also § Para_5.14 ).
summary: The comitative preposition dengang, with the short form deng, typically marks accompaniment with animate or inanimate associates, and it can also introduce instruments, oblique objects of mental verbs, and standards of comparison in identity or difference constructions. Its complements may be nouns or personal pronouns, and these phrases can function as peripheral adjuncts or as nonverbal predicates; when used as nonverbal predicates, they can be modified by adverbs such as masi ‘still’.

section: Prepositions encoding accompaniment/instruments, goals, and benefaction
text:
The goal preposition sama ‘to’ is rather general in its meaning. Typically, it translates with ‘to’ but depending on its context it also translates with ‘of, from, with’. The complement always denotes an animate referent which can be encoded in a noun or in a personal pronoun.

As the exchange in ( Example_10.43 ) shows, sama ‘to’ usually introduces oblique goal or recipient arguments of transfer verbs, such as bawa ‘bring’ in ( Example_10.43a ) or kasi ‘give’ in ( Example_10.43b ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing goals or recipients
styleExampleTitle

Speaker-1: ko bawa ke sana ko bawa sama ade\\
2sg take to l.dist 2sg take to ySb\\
Speaker-1: ‘bring (the ball) over there, bring (it) to (your) younger cousin’\\
5pt

Speaker-2: e, kasi bola sama ade\\
hey! give ball to ySb\\
Speaker-2: ‘hey, give the ball to (your) younger cousin’ [081011-009-Cv.0015-0016]

Also very commonly, sama ‘to’ introduces oblique addressee arguments for communication verbs, such as bicara ‘speak’ in ( Example_10.44 ) or minta ‘request’ in ( Example_10.45 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing addressees
styleExampleTitle

sa minta maaf, e tadi sa bicara kasar sama ko\\
1sg ask pardon uh earlier 1sg speak be.coarse to 2sg \\

‘I apologize, uh, a short while ago I spoke to you harshly’ [081115-001a-Cv.0277]

de minta apa sama kitorang kitorang kasi\\
3sg ask what to 1pl 1pl give\\

‘(whenever) she (our daughter) asks us (for) something, we give (it to her)’ [081006-025-CvEx.0022]

Goal preposition sama ‘to’ denotes the goal of a transfer or communication without concurrently marking this goal as the beneficiary of the event talked about. In this it contrasts with benefactive untuk ‘for’ and buat ‘for’; compare the examples in ( Example_10.43b ) and ( Example_10.44 ) with kasi/ bicara untuk ‘give/speak to and for’ in ( Example_10.55 ) and ( Example_10.56 ) in § Para_10.2.3 (p. Example_10.56) and with kasi/ bicara buat ‘give/speak to and for’ in ( Example_10.65 ) and ( Example_10.66 ) in § Para_10.2.4 (p. Example_10.65).

In addition, sama ‘to’ introduces oblique arguments of mental verbs, such as ingat ‘remember’ in ( Example_10.46 ), mara ‘feel angry (about)’ in ( Example_10.47 ), or takut ‘feel afraid (of)’ in ( Example_10.48 ). Most of the objects of mental verbs introduced with sama ‘to’ can also occur with comitative dengang ‘with’ (§ Para_10.2.1 ): compare mara sama ‘feel angry about’ in ( Example_10.47 ) with mara dengang ‘feel angry with’ in ( Example_10.38 ), or takut sama ‘feel afraid of’ in ( Example_10.48 ) with takut dengang ‘feel afraid of’ in ( Example_10.39 ) footnote-1.

Overall, however, the range of verbs is smaller for sama ‘to’ than for comitative dengang ‘with’.

The semantic distinctions between sama ‘to’ and dengang ‘with’ are subtle. When speakers want to emphasize the agent of the mental verb they employ sama ‘to’. If they want to signal that the object of the mental verb is also involved in the mental process talked about, they use comitative dengang ‘with’. The contrastive examples in ( Example_10.47 ) and ( Example_10.48 ) illustrate this distinction. In ( Example_10.47a ) sama ‘to’ emphasizes the fact that the agent de ‘3 sg ’ mara ‘feels angry’ about the patient pak Bolikarfus ‘Mr. Bolikarfus’ whereas the patient himself is not involved in this mental process. By contrast, in ( Example_10.47b ) deng(ang) ‘with’ signals that in some ways the patient pak Bolikarfus ‘Mr. Bolikarfus’ has contributed to the agent’s anger. Likewise, in ( Example_10.48a ) sama ‘to’ focuses on the fact that the agent dia ‘3 sg ’ takut ‘feels afraid (of)’; again, the patient ana ana Tuhang ‘God’s children’ is not involved in this mental process. In ( Example_10.48b ), by contrast, deng(ang) ‘with’ signals that the patient ana ana Tuhang ‘God’s children’ has contributed in some ways to the agent’s fear.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing objects of mental verbs The examples in ( Example_10.47a ) and ( Example_10.48a ) are taken from the corpus while the examples in ( Example_10.47b ) and ( Example_10.48b ) are elicited.
styleExampleTitle

biar dia masi muda tapi Fitri ingat sama Roni\\
although 3sg still be.young but Fitri remember to Roni\\

‘even though she was still young, Fitri was thinking of Roni’ [081006-024-CvEx.0067]

de mara sama pak Bolikarfus\\
3sg feel.angry(.about) to father Bolikarfus\\
‘he was angry about Mr. Bolikarfus’ [081014-016-Cv.0042]
5pt

de mara deng pak Bolikarfus\\
3sg feel.angry(.about) with father Bolikarfus\\
‘he was angry with Mr. Bolikarfus’ [Elicited BR120817.001]

memang dia takut sama ana ana Tuhang\\
indeed 3sg feel.afraid(.of) to rdp child God\\
‘(that evil spirit) indeed he/she feels afraid of God’s children’ [081006-022-CvEx.0175]
5pt

memang dia takut deng ana ana Tuhang\\
indeed 3sg feel.afraid(.of) with rdp child God\\
‘(that evil spirit) indeed he/she feels afraid of God’s children’ [Elicited BR120817.001]

Furthermore, although not very frequently, sama ‘to’ introduces animate associates. As with comitative dengang ‘with’ (§ Para_10.2.1 ), associates are expressed in peripheral adjuncts as in sama dorang ‘with them’ in ( Example_10.49 ), or in nonverbal predicates as in sama saya ‘with me’ in ( Example_10.50 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing animate associates
styleExampleTitle

Papeas maing maing sama dorang\\
Papeas rdp play to 3pl \\

‘Papeas is going to play with them’ [080918-001-CvNP.0040]

hanya tiga saja sama saya\\
only three just to 1sg \\

‘just only three (of my children) are with me’ [081006-024-CvEx.0001]

The goal preposition sama ‘to’ has trial word class membership. That is, besides being used as a preposition, it is also used as the stative verb sama ‘be same’ and, although not very frequently, as an addition-marking conjunction (see § Para_5.14; see also § Para_14.2.1.3 for its uses as a conjunction). In terms of its etymology, U. Tadmor (p.c. 2013) notes that “ sama was borrowed from Sanskrit into Malay in ancient times with the meaning ‘same’. Much later it also came to mean ‘with’ in Bazaar Malay”.
summary:
The preposition sama ‘to’ is a general goal marker that typically translates as ‘to’ but can also mean ‘of, from, with’, and it always takes an animate complement. It commonly introduces recipients or addressees with transfer and communication verbs, and it can also mark oblique objects of mental verbs and occasional animate associates.

Semantically, sama differs from benefactive prepositions such as untuk and buat because it marks only the goal, not the beneficiary. It also contrasts with comitative dengang ‘with’: sama tends to highlight the experiencer or agent of a mental state without implying the object’s involvement, and it has a narrower verb range; additionally, sama is used as a stative verb meaning ‘be same’ and occasionally as a conjunction.

section: Prepositions encoding accompaniment/instruments, goals, and benefaction
text:
The benefactive preposition untuk usually translates with ‘for’; depending on its context, however, it also translates with ‘to, about’. The preposition introduces animate and inanimate, as well as nominal and pronominal referents. In most cases, the referents are beneficiaries or recipients (148 tokens). In this regard, untuk ‘for’ is similar to benefactive buat ‘for’ (§ Para_10.2.4 ). Contrasting with buat ‘for’, however, untuk ‘for’ has a wider distribution and more functions in that it (1) combines with demonstratives, (2) introduces inanimate referents, and (3) introduces circumstance.

Beneficiaries introduced with untuk ‘for’ are typically animate human, as in ( Example_10.51 ), ( Example_10.53 ) or ( Example_10.54 ). The beneficiary can, however, also be animate nonhuman, as in untuk anjing dorang ‘for the dogs’ in ( Example_10.52 ).

Usually, untuk ‘for’ follows bivalent verbs such as buat ‘make, do’ or biking ‘make’, and introduces beneficiaries encoded by peripheral adjuncts, as in ( Example_10.51 ) or ( Example_10.52 ), respectively. Only rarely is the beneficiary encoded by a nonverbal prepositional predicate (2 tokens) as in untuk tamu ‘for the guests’ in ( Example_10.53 ), or an adnominal prepositional phrase (2 tokens) as in untuk kafir ‘for unbelievers’ in ( Example_10.54 ). As for the low token frequencies of two each, one consultant suggested that these constructions are not native Papuan Malay but represent instances of code-switching with Indonesian. The low frequencies support this statement.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing animate beneficiaries
styleExampleTitle

Tuhang buat mujisat untuk kita\\
God make miracle for 1pl \\

‘God made a miracle for us’ [080917-008-NP.0163]

yang sa pu bini biking malam untuk anjing dorang\\
rel 1sg poss wife make night for dog 3pl \\

‘[I fed the dogs with papeda] which my wife had made in the evening for the dogs’ [080919-003-NP.0002]

ikang sedikit, itu untuk tamu\\
fish few d.dist for guest\\

‘(as for) the few fish, those are for the guests’ [081014-011-CvEx.0008]

di sana kang masi tempat untuk kafir\\
at l.dist you.know still place for unbeliever\\

‘(the area) over there, you know, is still a location for unbelievers’ [081011-022-Cv.0238]

With transfer verbs, untuk ‘for’ introduces benefactive recipients, and with communication verbs it introduces benefactive addressees. That is, the referent is not merely a recipient or addressee. Benefactive untuk ‘for’ indicates that the referent is also the beneficiary of the transfer or communication, hence ``benefactive recipient'' and ``benefactive addressee''. This is illustrated with kasi untuk ‘give to and for’ in ( Example_10.55 ), and bicara untuk ‘speak to and for’ in ( Example_10.56 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing benefactive recipients and addressees
styleExampleTitle

sa kasi hadia untuk kamu\\
1sg give gift for 2pl \\

‘I’ll give gifts to you for your benefit’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1332]

jadi sperti itu, harus bicara untuk dorang, ceritra\\
so similar.to d.dist have.to speak for 3pl tell\\
untuk dorang\\
for 3pl \\
