‘so it’s like that, (we) have to speak to them (our children) for their benefit, talk to them for their benefit’ [081014-007-CvEx.0136]

Besides introducing animate referents, untuk ‘for’ also introduces inanimate beneficiaries that are concrete, abstract, or temporal. In ( Example_10.57 ), the beneficiary is inanimate concrete: kamar mandi ‘the bathroom’. In ( Example_10.58 ), the beneficiary is inanimate abstract: distal demonstrative itu ‘ d.dist ’ summarizes the speaker’s previous statements about balanced birth rates across families related by marriage. In ( Example_10.59 ) and ( Example_10.60 ), the beneficiary is temporal: taung ini ‘this year’ in ( Example_10.59 ) and besok ‘tomorrow’ in ( Example_10.60 ). Overall, however, these uses of benefactive untuk ‘for’ are quite rare, with the corpus including only very few examples.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing inanimate beneficiaries
styleExampleTitle

tong mo pake untuk kamar mandi\\
1pl want use for room bathe\\

‘we want to use (the corrugated iron sheets) for the bathroom (roof)’ [080925-003-Cv.0005]

lahir ana suku A., a, saya lahir\\
give.birth child ethnic.group A. ah! 1sg give.birth\\
suku Y. tujuangnya hanya untuk itu\\
ethnic.group Y. purpose: 3possr only for d.dist \\

[About the exchange of bride-price children:] ‘(our daughter) will give birth to a child (for) the A. family, well, I give birth for the Y. family its purpose is only for that (namely, a balanced birth rate across families)’ [081006-024-CvEx.0079]

untuk taung ini kam kas los sa dulu\\
for year d.prox 2pl give loosen 1sg first\\

‘ for (the rest of) this year you release me (from my duties) for now’ [080922-002-Cv.0084]

tong dari sa pu temang pinjam trening untuk besok\\
1pl from 1sg poss friend borrow tracksuit for tomorrow\\

‘we (are back) from my friend (from whom we) borrowed a tracksuit for tomorrow’ [081011-020-Cv.0052]

In addition, untuk ‘for’ introduces peripheral adjuncts that express the notion of circumstance, as in untuk seng itu ‘about those corrugated iron sheets’ in ( Example_10.61 ), or untuk masala tahang lapar ‘about the problem of enduring to be hungry’ in ( Example_10.62 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing circumstance
styleExampleTitle

tanya Sarles, bapa, untuk seng itu\\
ask Sarles father for corrugated.iron d.dist \\

‘father, ask Sarles about/for those corrugated iron (sheets)’ [080925-003-Cv.0003]

sa bilang, untuk masala tahang lapar kitong\\
1sg say for problem hold.(out/back) be.hungry 1pl \\
bisa tahang lapar juga e?\\
be.able hold (out/back) be.hungry also eh\\

‘I say about the problem of enduring to be hungry, we can also endure being hungry, eh?’ [081025-009a-Cv.0118]

The preposition untuk ‘for’ has dual word class membership; it is also used as a conjunction that introduces purpose clauses (§ Para_14.2.4.3; see also § Para_5.14 ).
summary:
The benefactive preposition untuk usually means ‘for’, but depending on context it can also mean ‘to’ or ‘about’. It introduces nominal or pronominal beneficiaries and recipients, most often animate humans, but it can also mark animate nonhumans, inanimate beneficiaries, and circumstance; unlike benefactive buat ‘for’, it has a wider distribution and can combine with demonstratives.  

With transfer and communication verbs, untuk marks benefactive recipients and addressees, indicating that the referent benefits from the action as well as receives it. The text also notes that these inanimate and circumstantial uses are rare, and that untuk additionally functions as a conjunction introducing purpose clauses.

section: Prepositions encoding accompaniment/instruments, goals, and benefaction
text:
The core semantics of the preposition buat ‘for’ are benefactive; that is, it introduces beneficiaries and benefactive recipients. In this, it is similar to benefactive untuk ‘for’. Otherwise, as already mentioned in § Para_10.2.3, buat ‘for’ is more restricted in its distribution and functions: (1) it is not attested to combine with demonstratives, (2) it only rarely introduces inanimate referents, and (3) it is not attested to introduce other complements such as circumstance.

Most commonly, buat ‘for’ follows bivalent action verbs such as putar ‘stir’, and introduces peripheral adjuncts denoting human beneficiaries as in buat de bapa ‘for her father’ in ( Example_10.63 ). Considerably less frequently, buat ‘for’ introduces beneficiaries encoded by adnominal prepositional phrases, as in buat torang ‘for us’ in the exchange in ( Example_10.64 ).

styleExampleTitle
Introducing animate beneficiaries
styleExampleTitle

Ika biking papeda putar buat de bapa\\
Ika make sagu.porridge stir for 3sg father\\

‘Ika made sagu porridge, she stirred (it) for her father’ [081006-032-Cv.0071]

Speaker-1: sa juga dengang ini kaka siapa tu\\
1sg also with d.prox oSb who d.dist \\
Speaker-1: ‘I was also with, what’s-his-name, that older brother, who-is-it?’
5pt

Speaker-2: satpam buat torang\\
security.guard for 1pl \\
Speaker-2: ‘ our security guard’ (Lit. ‘the security guard for us)’ [081025-006-Cv.0109]

Benefactive buat ‘for’ also introduces benefactive recipients and addressees encoded by oblique arguments, as shown in ( Example_10.65 ) and ( Example_10.66 ), respectively. Hence, like untuk ‘for’ (§ Para_10.2.3 ), benefactive buat ‘for’ contrasts with goal-oriented sama ‘to’ (§ Para_10.2.2 ), which expresses recipients and addressees, as in ( Example_10.43 ) to ( Example_10.45 ), without, however, signaling the concurrent notion of beneficiary.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing benefactive recipients and addressees
styleExampleTitle

slama ini de tida kasi uang buat saya\\
as.long.as d.prox 3sg neg give money for 1sg \\

‘so far he hasn’t given (any) money to me for my benefit’ [081014-003-Cv.0034]

sa perna bicara buat satu ibu \\
1sg once speak for one woman \\

‘once I talked to a woman for her benefit ’ [081011-024-Cv.0073]

Benefactive buat ‘for’ also introduces inanimate beneficiaries, as in the adnominal prepositional phrase buat natal ‘for Christmas’ in ( Example_10.67 ). This use, however, is very rare with the corpus including only this one example.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing inanimate beneficiaries
styleExampleTitle

pi ambil kayu bakar, kayu bakar buat Natal\\
go fetch wood burn wood burn for Christmas\\

‘(we) went to get firewood, firewood for Christmas’ [081006-017-Cv.0014]

The preposition buat ‘for’ has dual word class membership; it is also used as the bivalent verb buat ‘make’ (see § Para_5.14 ).
summary:
The preposition buat ‘for’ has benefactive semantics, introducing beneficiaries and benefactive recipients, much like benefactive untuk ‘for’. However, its distribution is more restricted: it does not combine with demonstratives, rarely introduces inanimate referents, and is not used for circumstance complements.  

It most often follows bivalent action verbs and marks human beneficiaries, but it can also introduce beneficiaries or addressees in oblique phrases and, very rarely, inanimate beneficiaries such as buat Natal ‘for Christmas’. The text also notes that buat is homonymous with the bivalent verb buat ‘make’.

text: Papuan Malay employs three prepositions of comparison: similative sperti ‘similar to’ (§ Para_10.3.1 ) and kaya ‘like’ (§ Para_10.3.2 ), and equative sebagey ‘as’ (§ Para_10.3.3 ). All three introduce similes that express explicit resemblance or equatability between two bases of comparison.
summary: Papuan Malay uses three prepositions of comparison: similative *sperti* ‘similar to’ and *kaya* ‘like’, and equative *sebagey* ‘as’. These prepositions introduce similes that explicitly express resemblance or equatability between two bases of comparison.

text:
The preposition sperti ‘similar to’ introduces similes that highlight resemblance or likeness in some respect between the two bases of comparison. Hence, sperti ‘like’ is similar to kaya ‘like’; for the distinctions between both similative prepositions see the discussion in § Para_10.3.2.

Very commonly, sperti ‘similar to’ forms peripheral adjuncts, as in sperti klawar ‘similar to a cave bat’ in ( Example_10.68 ). Also quite frequently, sperti ‘similar to’ expresses resemblance in oblique arguments of some bivalent verbs, as in ( Example_10.69 ): sperti manusia ‘similar to a human’ is the oblique object of the change verb jadi ‘become’. In addition, sperti ‘similar to’ introduces the simile in nonverbal predicates with the complement being a common noun, a personal pronoun as in sperti ko ‘similar to you’ in ( Example_10.70 ), or a demonstrative as in sperti itu’ like that’ in ( Example_10.71 ). Finally, although rather infrequently, sperti ‘similar to’ expresses resemblance in adnominal prepositional phrases, as in baju sperti ini ‘clothes like these’ ( Example_10.72 ). The examples in ( Example_10.68 ) to ( Example_10.72 ) also illustrate that sperti ‘similar to’ introduces animate and inanimate, as well as nominal and pronominal referents. In the corpus only singular pronominal complements of sperti ‘similar to’ are attested.

de bisa terbang sperti klawar\\
3sg be.able fly similar.to cave.bat\\

‘he/she (the evil spirit) can fly similar to a cave bat’ [081006-022-CvEx.0137]

setang itu de bisa jadi sperti manusia\\
evil.spirit d.dist 3sg be.able become similar.to human.being\\

‘that evil spirit, he/she can become similar to a human’ [081006-022-CvEx.0010]

kalo kaka sperti ko kaka malu\\
if oSb similar.to 2sg oSb feel.embarrassed(.about)\\

‘if I (‘older sibling’) were similar to you, I (‘older sibling’) would feel ashamed’ [081115-001a-Cv.0040]

mama pu hidup sperti itu\\
mother poss life similar.to d.dist \\

‘my (‘mother’s’) life is like that’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0932/0938]

dorang tida pake baju sperti ini, pake daung daung\\
3pl neg use shirt similar.to d.prox use rdp leaf\\

‘they don’t wear clothes like these, (they) wear leaves’ [081006-023-CvEx.0007]

The preposition sperti ‘similar to’ has dual word class membership; it is also used as a conjunction that introduces similarity clauses (§ Para_14.2.6; see also § Para_5.14 ).
summary:
The preposition **sperti** ‘similar to’ introduces similes expressing resemblance between two items, and is functionally comparable to **kaya** ‘like’. It commonly appears in peripheral adjuncts and oblique arguments, can also mark similes in nonverbal predicates and, more rarely, in adnominal phrases; the examples show that it can refer to animate or inanimate, nominal or pronominal entities, with only singular pronominal complements attested in the corpus.  

In addition, **sperti** has dual word-class membership: besides being a preposition, it is also used as a conjunction introducing similarity clauses.

text:
The core semantics of the preposition kaya ‘like’ are similative: it indicates likeness between the two bases of comparison, similar to sperti ‘similar to’. In terms of its etymology, U. Tadmor (p.c. 2013) notes that the preposition kaya ‘like’ is distinct from the stative verb kaya ‘be rich’: stative “ kaya ‘be rich’ “was borrowed from Persian into Classical Malay” while similative kaya ‘like’ “was borrowed from Javanese into colloquial varieties of Indonesian many centuries later. There is no etymological connection between the two”.

Unlike sperti ‘like’, however, kaya ‘like’ is not attested to combine with demonstratives. Moreover, kaya ‘like’ is semantically distinct from sperti ‘similar to’, as discussed below.

Most commonly, kaya ‘like’ forms peripheral adjuncts, as in kaya burung ‘like a bird’ in ( Example_10.73 ). This example also illustrates that kaya ‘like’ co-occurs with some of the same verbs as sperti ‘similar to’, such as terbang ‘fly’ in ( Example_10.68 ) (§ Para_10.3.1 ). Less frequently, kaya ‘like’ introduces the simile in nonverbal predicates as in kaya buaya ‘like a crocodile’ in ( Example_10.74 ). These examples also illustrate that typically the referent is animate and nominal; for an inanimate referent see the example in ( Example_10.77 ), and for a pronominal referent see ( Example_10.76b ).

styleExampleTitle
Signaling overall likeness or resemblance
styleExampleTitle

bisa terbang kaya burung, bisa merayap kaya ular\\
be.able fly like bird be.able creep like snake\\

‘(the evil spirit) can fly like a bird, can creep like a snake’ [081006-022-CvEx.0031]

dong bilang soa-soa kang, kaya buaya\\
3pl say monitor.lizard you.know like crocodile\\

‘they call (it) a monitor lizard, you know, (it’s) like a crocodile’ [080922-009-CvNP.0053]

The semantic distinctions between kaya ‘like’ and sperti ‘similar to’ are subtle. While both signal likeness in terms of appearance or behavior, they differ in terms of their semantic effect. Similative kaya ‘like’ signals overall resemblance between the two bases of comparison. By contrast, the semantic effect of sperti ‘similar to’ is more limited: it signals likeness or resemblance in some, most often implied, respect. This distinction is illustrated in the contrastive examples in ( Example_10.75 ) and ( Example_10.76 ).

In ( Example_10.75a ), kaya ‘like’ signals overall physical resemblance: the speaker’s brother has the same facial features as their father. By contrast, in the elicited example in ( Example_10.75b ) sperti ‘similar to’ signals limited or partial resemblance: that is, father and son share specific facial features. In ( Example_10.70 ), repeated as ( Example_10.76a ), a teacher relates a conversation she had with a socially maladjusted student. Employing sperti ‘similar to’, the teacher signals that she refers to some specific aspects of the student’s behavior: kalo kaka sperti ko ‘if I (‘older sibling’) were similar to you (with respect to the behavior you’re displaying at school)’. If, by contrast, the teacher had used kaya ‘like’, as in the elicited example in ( Example_10.76b ), the semantic effect of the comparison would have been much wider, not only referring to the student’s behavior at school but signaling overall resemblance between the speaker and her student.

styleExampleTitle
Semantic distinctions between kaya ‘like’ and sperti ‘similar to’
styleExampleTitle

de pu muka kaya de pu bapa\\
3sg poss face like 3sg poss father\\
‘his (my brother’s) face is like his father’s (face)’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1445]
5pt

de pu muka sperti de pu bapa\\
3sg poss face similar.to 3sg poss father\\
‘his (my brother’s) face is similar to his father’s (face)’ [Elicited BR120817.007]

kalo kaka sperti ko kaka malu\\
if oSb similar.to 2sg oSb feel.embarrassed(.about)\\
‘if I (‘older sibling’) were similar to you, I (‘older sibling’) would feel ashamed’ [081115-001a-Cv.0040]
5pt

kalo kaka kaya ko kaka malu\\
if oSb like 2sg oSb feel.embarrassed(.about)\\
‘if I (‘older sibling’) were like you, I (‘older sibling’) would feel ashamed’ [Elicited BR120817.006]

Signaling overall resemblance, similative kaya ‘like’ is also used when the speaker wants to make a more expressive, metaphorical comparison as in ( Example_10.77 ). This example also illustrates that the referent can be inanimate.

styleExampleTitle
Introducing expressive similes
styleExampleTitle

smua jalang kaya kapal kayu\\
all walk like ship wood\\

‘[because they were so hungry] (they) all were strolling around like wooden boats’ [081025-009a-Cv.0188]

The preposition kaya ‘like’ has dual word class membership; it is also used as a conjunction that introduces similarity clauses (§ Para_14.2.6; see also § Para_5.14 ).
summary:
The preposition kaya ‘like’ is similative, marking overall likeness or resemblance between two items, and it is etymologically distinct from the stative verb kaya ‘be rich’. Unlike sperti ‘similar to’, kaya cannot combine with demonstratives and typically forms peripheral adjuncts or introduces similes, often with animate nominal referents but sometimes with inanimate or pronominal ones.  

Although kaya and sperti both express similarity, kaya indicates broader, overall resemblance, while sperti refers to similarity only in some more limited or implied respect. The text also notes that kaya has dual word-class membership, since it can function as a conjunction introducing similarity clauses.

text:
The equative preposition sebagey ‘as’ introduces similes that express equatability between the two bases of comparison in terms of specific roles or capacities. Hence, sebagey ‘as’ contrasts with the similarity prepositions sperti ‘similar to’ (§ Para_10.3.1 ) and kaya ‘like’ (§ Para_10.3.2 ) which express resemblance and likeness.

Most commonly, the complement is expressed in an adnominal prepositional phrase. In ( Example_10.78 ), for example, sebagey ‘as’ links the head nominal torang ‘ 1pl ’ to the role-encoding adnominal constituent kepala kampung ‘village heads’. Following mono- or bivalent action verbs, sebagey ‘as’ expresses equatability in peripheral adjuncts. In ( Example_10.79 ), for example, sebagey ‘as’ follows the communication verb bicara ‘speak’ and relates the role-encoding complement ibu camat ‘Ms. Subdistrict-Head’ to the clausal subject ko ‘ 2sg ’. The corpus also includes two examples in which sebagey ‘as’ introduces nonverbal predicates to express equatability, as for example in ( Example_10.80 ) between the predicate kepala acara ‘the head of the festivity’ and the clausal subject sa ‘ 1sg ’.

torang sebagey kepala kampung juga penanggung-jawap\\
1pl as head village also responsibility\\

‘we as village heads are also bearers of responsibility’ [081008-001-Cv.0035]

sebentar di Diklat ko bicara\\
a.moment at government.education.program 2sg speak\\
sebagey ibu camat\\
as woman subdistrict.head\\

‘a bit later at the government education and training (office) you’ll speak as Ms. Subdistrict-Head’ [081010-001-Cv.0099]

paling sa tra kerja, sa sebagey kepala acara\\
most 1sg neg work 1sg as head festivity\\

[About organizing a festivity:] ‘most likely I won’t (have to) work, I’ll be the head of the festivity’ (Lit. ‘ as the head ’) [080919-004-NP.0068]

As for the syntactic properties of its complements, the examples in ( Example_10.78 ) to ( Example_10.80 ) show that equative sebagey ‘as’ introduces common nouns, as similative sperti ‘similar to’ (§ Para_10.3.1 ) and kaya ‘like’ (§ Para_10.3.2 ) do. Unlike the findings for both similative prepositions, however, the corpus does not include prepositional phrases in which sebagey ‘as’ introduces personal pronouns. Neither are examples attested in which sebagey ‘as’ combines with demonstratives as sperti ‘similar to’ does.
summary:
The equative preposition sebagey ‘as’ is used to express equatability between two terms in terms of roles or capacities, and it contrasts with the similative prepositions sperti ‘similar to’ and kaya ‘like,’ which express resemblance. It typically appears in adnominal prepositional phrases or as a peripheral adjunct after verbs, and it can also introduce nonverbal predicates.  

Its complements are common nouns, but the corpus does not show sebagey ‘as’ combining with personal pronouns or demonstratives, unlike the similative prepositions.

text:
Prepositional phrases consist of a preposition and a noun phrase complement which is obligatory and may not be fronted. The preposition indicates the grammatical and semantic relationship of the complement to the predicate. Prepositional phrases in Papuan Malay are formed with eleven different prepositions:

enumerate

Prepositions encoding location in space or time: di ‘at, in’, ke ‘to’, dari ‘from’, and sampe ‘until’

Prepositions encoding accompaniment/instruments, goals, or benefaction: dengang ‘with’, sama ‘to’, untuk ‘for’, and buat ‘for’

Prepositions encoding comparisons: sperti ‘similar to’, kaya ‘like’, and sebagey ‘as’

enumerate

A substantial number of the prepositions have dual word class membership, two have trial class membership. That is, three prepositions are also used as verbs, namely buat ‘for’, sama ‘to’, and sampe ‘until’ (see § Para_5.3 ). Six prepositions are also used as conjunctions, namely dengang ‘with’, kaya ‘like’, sama ‘to’, sampe ‘until’, sperti ‘similar to’, and untuk ‘for’ (see § Para_5.12 and Para_14). (Variation in word class membership is discussed in § Para_5.14.)

Prepositional phrases take on different functions within the clause and combine with different types of syntactic constituents. The complements of the prepositions take different semantic roles within the clause, depending on the prepositions they are introduced with. These findings are summarized in Table_10.1 to Table_10.3; in these tables, the prepositions are listed according to the order in which they are discussed in this chapter, starting with di ‘at, in’. Empty cells signal unattested constituent combinations.

Table_10.1 lists the three syntactic functions that prepositional phrases can take within the clause according to the prepositions they are introduced with, that is, their functions as peripheral adjuncts, nonverbal predicates, and arguments. In addition, Table_10.1 lists those prepositions that introduce modifying, adnominal prepositional phrases and those that are also used as conjunctions.

With respect to their complements, the data in Table_10.2 shows that the prepositions combine with different constituents from different word classes, namely nouns, personal pronouns, demonstratives, locatives, and temporal adverbs.

Lastly, the complements of prepositions take different semantic roles within the clause, depending on the prepositions they are introduced with. These different semantic roles are summarized in Table_10.3 with the primary role underlined.

If the context allows the disambiguation of the semantic relationship of the complement to the predicate, two of the prepositions of location can be omitted: locative di ‘at, in’ and allative ke ‘to’.
summary:
Prepositional phrases in Papuan Malay consist of an obligatory noun phrase complement headed by a preposition, and the preposition marks the complement’s grammatical and semantic relation to the predicate. The language has eleven prepositions, grouped by meaning into location/time, accompaniment/instrument/goal/benefaction, and comparison, and several of these also belong to other word classes such as verbs or conjunctions.  

These phrases can function as peripheral adjuncts, nonverbal predicates, or arguments, and their complements may be nouns, pronouns, demonstratives, locatives, or temporal adverbs with different semantic roles depending on the preposition. In some contexts, the locative preposition di ‘at, in’ and the allative ke ‘to’ may be omitted if the meaning is clear.

text:
This chapter discusses different types of verbal predicate clauses in Papuan Malay, in which a verb occupies the syntactic and semantic core of the clause. In Papuan Malay verbal clauses, the predicate typically follows the subject and, in transitive clauses, precedes the direct object. In negated verbal clauses, the negator precedes the predicate.

Papuan Malay verbal clauses can be distinguished into intransitive and transitive clauses; this distinction is discussed in § Para_11.1. The subsequent sections describe special types of (in)transitive clauses: causative clauses in § Para_11.2, reciprocal clauses in § Para_11.3, existential clauses in § Para_11.4, and comparative clauses in § Para_11.5. The main points of this chapter are summarized in § Para_11.6. Negation is described in § Para_13.1.
summary:
This chapter describes verbal predicate clauses in Papuan Malay, where the verb is the syntactic and semantic center of the clause. In these clauses, the predicate normally follows the subject and, in transitive clauses, comes before the direct object; in negated clauses, the negator appears before the predicate.  

The chapter distinguishes intransitive and transitive verbal clauses and also covers special clause types such as causative, reciprocal, existential, and comparative clauses. Negation is treated elsewhere in the grammar.

text:
Papuan Malay verbal clauses can be intransitive, monotransitive, or ditransitive. Typically, intransitive clauses are formed with monovalent verbs which take one core argument; as discussed below, though, bi- and trivalent verbs also occur in intransitive or monotransitive clauses. Monotransitive clauses are usually formed with bivalent verbs which take two core arguments, the subject and a direct object. These two types of verbs and verbal clauses are the most common ones in Papuan Malay. In addition, Papuan Malay has ditransitive clauses formed with a small number of trivalent verbs which take three core arguments, a subject and two objects.

It is important to note, though, that in Papuan Malay the trivalent verbs allow but do not require three syntactic arguments. Likewise, bivalent verbs allow but do not require two arguments. That is, in clauses with tri- or bivalent verbs, core arguments are often elided when they are understood from the context. (See also Margetts.2007's Margetts.2007 cross-linguistic typology for the rather common elision of syntactic arguments.)

Given this syntactic mismatch between valency and transitivity, this section on transitivity is not organized in terms of intransitive, monotransitive, and ditransitive clauses. Instead, it is organized in terms of the valency of the verbs, and describes how the three verb classes are used in transitive and/or intransitive clauses. Verbal clauses with monovalent verbs are discussed in § Para_11.1.1, with bivalent verbs in § Para_11.1.2, and with trivalent verbs in § Para_11.1.3. (The properties of verbs are described in § Para_5.3. For details on optional linguistic expressions providing additional information about the setting of the events or states depicted by the verbs, see Para_10; see also § Para_5.2.5.)
summary: Papuan Malay verbal clauses may be intransitive, monotransitive, or ditransitive, corresponding most commonly to monovalent, bivalent, and a small number of trivalent verbs. However, bivalent and trivalent verbs do not require all of their possible core arguments to be expressed, since these arguments are often omitted when recoverable from context. Because valency and transitivity do not match straightforwardly, the section is organized by verb valency rather than by clause type.

text:
Papuan Malay has a large open class of monovalent verbs. Involving only one participant, they always occur in intransitive clauses (490 monovalent verbs are attested in the corpus; for a list of examples see Table_5.14 in § Para_5.3.1 ).

Semantically, the attested 490 verbs can be divided into dynamic ones (139 verbs) and stative ones (351 verbs), as is typical of languages lacking a class of adjectives. The former denote actions, while the latter designate states or more time-stable properties. Syntactically, however, there are no distinctions between dynamic and stative verbs.

Typically, monovalent verbs follow their clausal subjects, as shown with dynamic lari ‘run’ in ( Example_11.1 ), and with stative bagus ‘be good’ in ( Example_11.2 ).

styleExampleTitle
Monovalent verbs with canonical subject- verb word order
styleExampleTitle

o, babi lari\\
oh pig run\\

‘o, the pig ran’ [080919-004-NP.0021]

itu bagus skali\\
d.dist be.good very\\

‘that is very good’ [081025-003-Cv.0267]

If speakers want to emphasize the predicate with a monovalent stative verb, they can front it, such as stative bagus ‘be good’ in ( Example_11.3 ). In this case, the predicate is set-off by a boundary intonation, which is achieved by marking the stressed syllable of the verb with a slight increase in pitch (“ \' ”). Consultants disagree, however, whether monovalent dynamic verbs can be fronted. While two consultants stated that dynamic jatu ‘fall’ in the elicited example in ( Example_11.4 ) can be fronted, a third one rejected the example as ungrammatical. Furthermore, one of the consultants who accepted the verbal clause in ( Example_11.4 ) suggested that the fronting of monovalent dynamic verbs is a recent development and that older Papuan Malay speakers would not use such a construction.

styleExampleTitle
Preposed monovalent verbs
styleExampleTitle

bágus skali itu\\
be.good very d.dist \\

‘very good is that’ [081025-003-Cv.0270]

o, játu dia!\\
oh fall 3sg \\

‘oh, he fell!’ [Elicited BR131227.001]

The subject can also be omitted if it can be inferred from the context. In ( Example_11.5 ) the elided subject is sa ‘ 1sg ’, and in ( Example_11.6 ) it is dia/ de ‘ 3sg ’.

styleExampleTitle
Elision of the subject argument
styleExampleTitle

siang Ø jalang, trus malam Ø duduk menyanyi sampe jam dua\\
day walk next night sit sing until hour two\\

‘(during) the day (I) went (over there), then in the evening (I) sat about (and) sang (songs) until two o’clock (in the morning)’ [080923-003-CvNP.0002]

Speaker-2: adu, Ø nakal\\
oh.no! be.mischievous\\
[Speaker 1: ah, that Petrus!]\\
Speaker-2: oh no!, (he’s) mischievous’ [081115-001a-Cv.0033]
summary: Papuan Malay has a large class of monovalent verbs, all of which occur in intransitive clauses and take only one participant. These verbs are semantically divided into dynamic and stative types, but there is no syntactic distinction between them; by default they follow the subject, though stative verbs can be fronted for emphasis and speakers disagree about whether dynamic verbs can also be fronted. The subject may also be omitted when it is recoverable from context.

text:
Papuan Malay has a large open class of bivalent verbs (535 are attested in the corpus; for a set of examples see Table_5.14 in § Para_5.3.1 ). Bivalent verbs have two core arguments, a subject and an object. In terms of their semantic roles, “two-place predicates take an agent-like argument A, and a non-agent-like argument P”, adopting Margetts.2007 terminology. As mentioned, though, bivalent verbs in Papuan Malay allow but do not require two syntactic arguments. Examples of bivalent verbs are bunu ‘kill’ in ( Example_11.7 ) and potong ‘cut’ in ( Example_11.8 ).

styleExampleTitle
Bivalent verbs with two arguments and canonical subject-verb-object order
styleExampleTitle

kalo ko masi mo berjuang kitorang bunu ko\\
if 2sg still want struggle 1pl kill 2sg \\

‘if you still want to fight, we’ll kill you’ [081029-004-Cv.0072]

jadi kamu potong sapi\\
so 2pl cut cow\\

‘so you cut up the cow’ [080925-005-CvPh.0007]

The monotransitive clauses in ( Example_11.7 ) and ( Example_11.8 ) illustrate the canonical subject-verb-object order for bivalent verbs. If speakers want to emphasize the object, they can also front it. Unlike clauses with preposed monovalent verbs, though, there is no clear boundary intonation to set-off the preposed object arguments from the rest of the clause. In ( Example_11.9 ), the preposed object paylot ‘pilot’ is marked with a slight increase in pitch of its stressed penultimate syllable (“ \' ”) and it is separated from the rest of the clause with a comma intonation (“ ”). Besides, the ultimate syllable of bunu ‘kill’ receives final lengthening, signaled with the vowel tripling. In ( Example_11.10 ), the preposed object remains unmarked but the clause-final verb potong ‘cut’ is marked with a slight increase in pitch of its stressed penultimate syllable.

styleExampleTitle
Bivalent verbs with preposed object arguments
styleExampleTitle

páylot dorang bunuuu\\
pilot 3pl kill\\

‘the pilot they killed’ [081025-004-Cv.0040]

dong dua pu telefisi sidi dua dia pótong\\
3pl two poss television CD.player two 3sg cut\\

‘the television (and) both CDs of the two of them he destroyed’ [081011-009-Cv.0006]

When one or both of the core arguments are understood from the context, they can be omitted, as shown in ( Example_11.11 ) to ( Example_11.16 ).
At this point in the research, the number of clauses with overt and elided core arguments has not been quantified to examine which strategy is the preferred one. Elision of the object argument is illustrated for bunu ‘kill’ in ( Example_11.11 ), and potong ‘cut (up) in ( Example_11.12 ).

styleExampleTitle
Elision of the object argument and retention of the subject argument
styleExampleTitle

kalo prempuang melahirkang laki laki dong bunu Ø\\
if woman give.birth rdp husband 3pl kill \\

‘[indeed, these women can’t live with men,] when a woman gives birth to a boy, they kill (him)’ [081006-023-CvEx.0058]

tong potong Ø hari itu\\
1pl cut day d.dist \\

‘[we shouldered it, the pig, (and) carried (it) to the garden shelter,] we cut (it) up that day’ [080919-003-NP.0013-0014]

Elision of the subject argument is demonstrated for bunu ‘kill’ in ( Example_11.13 ), and potong ‘cut’ in ( Example_11.14 ).

styleExampleTitle
Elision of the subject argument and retention of the object argument
styleExampleTitle

Ø bunu dia, Ø bunu dia\\
kill 3sg kill 3sg \\

‘(they) kill him, (they) kill him’ [081006-022-CvEx.0088]

baru Ø potong pisang di tenga tenga to?\\
and.then cut banana at rdp middle right?\\

‘and then (we) cut the bananas in the middle, right?’ [080922-009-CvNP.0041]

Finally, speakers can also omit both core arguments at the same time, as shown for bunu ‘kill’ in ( Example_11.15 ), and potong ‘cut’ in ( Example_11.16 ).

styleExampleTitle
Elision of the subject and object arguments
styleExampleTitle

Ø bunu Ø tapi kasi hidup lagi\\
kill but give live again\\

[About sorcerers who can resurrect the dead:] ‘(they) kill (him) but (they) make (him) live again’ [081006-022-CvEx.0087]

Ø potong Ø kecil kecil\\
cut rdp be.small\\

‘(I) cut (the meat) very small’ [080919-003-NP.0016]
summary: Papuan Malay has a large class of bivalent verbs with two semantic core arguments, an agent-like A and a non-agent-like P, but these verbs do not require both arguments to be overtly expressed. The passage illustrates their canonical subject-verb-object order, optional object fronting, and the omission of either the subject, the object, or both when the referents are recoverable from context.

text:
Papuan Malay has a small number of trivalent verbs with three core arguments, that is, a subject, and two objects. In the corpus seven trivalent verbs are attested: ambil ‘fetch’, bawa ‘bring’, bli ‘buy’, ceritra ‘tell’, kasi ‘give’, kirim ‘send’, and minta ‘request’.

In terms of their semantic roles, three-place predicates “take an agent-like A, a participant that will label R on the basis of its most common role as recipient (but that may also be a beneficiary, goal, addressee, location, or source), and a T (typically some thing or information conveyed by A to R)”, applying Margetts.2007 terminology. As mentioned, though, trivalent verbs in Papuan Malay allow but do not require three syntactic arguments.

Trivalent verbs exhibit dative alternation in that they appear in ditransitive clauses with double-object constructions (§ Para_11.1.3.1 ), or in monotransitive clauses with oblique constructions (§ Para_11.1.3.2 ). Alternatively, the R and T arguments can be combined into one noun phrase with an adnominal possessor (§ Para_11.1.3.3 ). Another option is to omit the R and/or T arguments (§ Para_11.1.3.4 ). The distributional frequencies for these strategies are discussed in § Para_11.1.3.5.
summary:
Papuan Malay has a small set of trivalent verbs with three core semantic roles: an agent-like A, an R argument that is most often a recipient but can also have other roles, and a T argument, usually the thing or information transferred. Seven such verbs are attested in the corpus: *ambil* ‘fetch’, *bawa* ‘bring’, *bli* ‘buy’, *ceritra* ‘tell’, *kasi* ‘give’, *kirim* ‘send’, and *minta* ‘request’.

These verbs allow, but do not require, three syntactic arguments. They show dative alternation through double-object ditransitives or monotransitive oblique constructions, and the R and T arguments can also be combined in one noun phrase with an adnominal possessor or omitted altogether.

text:
In Papuan Malay ditransitive clauses with double-object constructions, the R and T arguments are unflagged and occur in the order R-T. In this construction type, as puts it, the semantically peripheral R is brought “center-stage” while the T has “status as the ‘second object’”. Cross-linguistically, the R typically precedes the T which, as suggest, “probably derives from the fact that the R is generally human (and often definite) and thus tends to be more topical than the T, which is typically inanimate (and often indefinite)”.

Papuan Malay double object constructions with R-T word order are presented in ( Example_11.17 ) to ( Example_11.23 ). Overall, however, double-object constructions are not very common in Papuan Malay. The corpus contains only 30 constructions among a total of 1,160 verbal clauses formed with trivalent verbs (2.6%). This total excludes serial verb constructions formed with kasi ‘give’ (see § Para_11.2.1.2 ).

The T can also precede the R in double-object constructions, as shown in ( Example_11.24 ) and ( Example_11.25 ). This T-R order “is relatively widespread in South-East Asia”, as point out. Building on Dik.1997 notion of “iconic sequencing”, suggest that “the order T-R is more iconic than the order R-T, because in the unfolding of the event the T is first involved in the action, which reaches the R only in a second step”.

In Papuan Malay, however, T-R constructions are even less common than R-T constructions; the corpus contains 17 constructions among the total of 1,160 verbal clauses formed with trivalent verbs (1.5%). All of them are formed with kasi ‘give’, as in ( Example_11.24 ) and ( Example_11.25 ). In 12 of them, the T is nasihat ‘advice’ as in ( Example_11.24 ), in two it is ijing or ijing ijing ‘permission’ as in ( Example_11.25 ), and in the remaining three the Ts are ana ‘child’, kemerdekaang ‘independence’ and swara ‘voice’.

summary: Papuan Malay double-object ditransitive clauses are uncommon overall, with unflagged R-T order being more frequent than T-R order. The R is usually a personal pronoun and typically precedes the T, while the rarer T-R order occurs only with *kasi* ‘give’ and is argued to be more iconic because the T is involved in the event before the R.

text:
One common alternative to double-object constructions is the “oblique strategy” in which “the verb takes only two direct arguments and the third participant is expressed as an oblique argument or an adjunct”. Very commonly, it is the R that is expressed with a prepositional phrase; hence “ R-type oblique”. Alternatively, the T is encoded in this manner; hence, “T-type oblique”. (; see also.) Alternatively, the oblique strategy is also called “‘dative alternation’, earlier ‘dative shift’ or ‘dative movement’”; an alternative term for “R-type obliques” is “indirective alignment”.

In Papuan Malay oblique constructions, it is always the R that is expressed as an oblique, with the R following the T, as shown in ( Example_11.26 ) to ( Example_11.32 ). Overall, however, R-type oblique constructions are not very common. The corpus contains only 41 R-type obliques among the total of 1,160 verbal clauses formed with trivalent verbs (3.5%). Moreover, in the corpus, R-type obliques are not attested for all seven verbs (the examples for bawa ‘bring’ in ( Example_11.27 ), bli ‘buy’ in ( Example_11.28 ), and kirim ‘send’ in ( Example_11.31 ) are elicited). Most R-type obliques are introduced with the benefactive prepositions buat ‘for’ or untuk ‘for’ (26/41 tokens – 63%), while the remaining 15 R-type obliques are formed with goal-oriented sama ‘to’. (The semantics of the three prepositions are discussed in § Para_10.2.)

summary:
The passage describes the oblique strategy as an alternative to double-object constructions in which a trivalent verb takes two direct arguments and the third participant is expressed as an oblique, often as an R-type oblique where the recipient is marked by a prepositional phrase. In Papuan Malay, only the R is expressed as an oblique, and such constructions are relatively rare in the corpus: 41 out of 1,160 trivalent verbal clauses, with most using the prepositions buat/untuk ‘for’ and the rest sama ‘to’.  

Among these R-type obliques, the recipient is usually expressed as a noun phrase rather than a personal pronoun.

text:
Another, cross-linguistic alternative to encode the R and T arguments is to express them in an adnominal possessive construction, in which “the agent and the theme are expressed as syntactic arguments of the verb, while the R-type participant, which will be the beneficiary with transfer verbs [ ], is expressed as a grammatical dependent of the theme, namely as its possessor”.

In Papuan Malay, speakers use adnominal possessive constructions when the T is definite. The corpus includes 14 such constructions among the 1,160 clauses formed with trivalent verbs (1.2%). Examples are given for ambil ‘fetch’ in ( Example_11.33 ), bli ‘buy’ in ( Example_11.34 ), and kasi ‘give’ in ( Example_11.35 ). In each case, the possessor denotes the benefiting R of the event expressed by the verb; the possessum denotes the T as the anticipated object of possession. In the corpus, the possessor is typically encoded by a personal pronoun (13/14 tokens – 93%), as in ( Example_11.34 ) and ( Example_11.35 ). Only in one construction, presented in ( Example_11.33 ), the possessor is expressed with a noun, namely the proper noun Sofia. (Adnominal possession is described in detail in Para_9.)

This pattern is rare in the corpus: it occurs in 14 of 1,160 clauses with trivalent verbs, and it is used when the theme is definite. The possessor usually refers to the R and is normally a personal pronoun, with only one example using a noun.

text:
Elision is a third alternative to double-object constructions and used when the T and/or R are understood from the context. In this case, one or both of them can be omitted. In the corpus, this strategy is used in 1,058 of 1,160 verbal clauses formed with trivalent verbs (91%).

Most often the R is elided and the T retained (601/1,058 tokens – 57%); these distributional frequencies are further discussed in § Para_11.1.3.5. Examples are given for bli ‘buy’ in ( Example_11.36 ), ceritra ‘tell’ in ( Example_11.37 ), and kirim ‘send’ in ( Example_11.38 ).

summary:
The passage describes elision as a strategy in trivalent-verb clauses where the theme (T) and/or recipient (R) is recoverable from context and can therefore be omitted. In the corpus, elision is very common: most often R is omitted while T is retained, less often T is omitted while R is retained, and in a substantial number of cases both T and R are omitted.

When R is retained but T is elided, R is more often expressed as an oblique than as a direct object, and in both patterns the retained R is usually a nominal rather than a pronoun. The text gives examples from verbs such as bli ‘buy’, ceritra ‘tell’, kirim ‘send’, bawa ‘bring’, kasi ‘give’, and minta ‘request’.

text:
The above description of how Papuan Malay trivalent verbs are used in verbal clauses shows three types of variation, namely in word order, in encoding the R and T arguments, and in eliding one or both of these arguments. The data also indicates distributional preferences for these three variation types. Summarizing this variation, this section provides an explanation for the distributional frequencies and preferences in terms of salience.

Cross-linguistically, ditransitive alignment variation is related to distinctions between the R and T arguments in terms of three “salience scales (animacy, definiteness, person)”, with presenting the following scale for “differential R marking”: See also Comrie.1989 animacy hierarchy, Dixon.1979 agency scale, and Silverstein.1976 hierarchy of features.

styleIIndented
1st/2nd 3rd proper noun human nonhuman
styleIIndented

When the R is more salient than the T, speakers favor a double-object construction. This preference applies especially to pronominal Rs, which are the most salient ones. Otherwise, as states, the oblique construction is the favored one:

styleIIndented
Special (“indirective” or “dative”) R-marking is the more likely, the lower the R is on the animacy, definiteness, and person scales.
styleIIndented

The same distributional preferences apply to Papuan Malay, as shown in Table_11.2. Before discussing the distribution of nominal and pronominal Rs, however, Table_11.1 gives an overview of the distributional frequencies for trivalent verbs in the different constructions types discussed in the preceding sections.

Table_11.1 shows that Papuan Malay disfavors clauses in which both the R and T arguments are overtly mentioned. Double-object constructions are rare (4.1%); the 47 clauses include 30 clauses with R-T order and 17 with T-R order. Likewise, R-type oblique constructions are rare (3.5%). Adnominal possessive constructions with an R possessor are even rarer (1.2%). Instead, trivalent verbs usually occur in clauses with elided R and/or T arguments (91%). Details on elision are presented in Table_11.3.

As for the distribution of nominal and pronominal Rs, Table_11.2 indicates clear preferences. Only five nominal Rs occur in double-object constructions (6%), and about one third in R-type oblique constructions (28/90 tokens – 31%). Besides, one nominal R is used in an adnominal possessive construction (1%). Instead, most nominal Rs occur in clauses with elided T arguments (56/90 tokens – 62%; Table_11.3 gives details on elision). By contrast, about half of the pronominal Rs occur in double-object constructions (42/87 tokens – 48%), while 13 Rs are used in R-type oblique constructions (15%). Another 13 Rs occur in adnominal possessive constructions (15%; compare with one token for nominal Rs). Yet another 19 Rs occur in clauses with elided T (22%; compare with 56 nominal Rs).

This tendency for pronominal Rs to occur in double-object constructions, while nominal Rs are more often used in R-type oblique constructions is in line with Haspelmath.2007b scale for differential R marking, presented above. As mentioned, this scale suggests that speakers favor a double-object construction when the R is more salient than the T, a preference that applies especially to pronominal Rs. Otherwise, speakers favor an oblique construction.

There is one exception, though. When speakers want to signal that a pronominal R is also the beneficiary of the transfer, they encode this R as an R-type oblique, which is introduced with benefactive buat ‘for’ or untuk ‘for’ (both prepositions and their semantics are discussed in § Para_10.2 ). This benefactive marking of the R is not possible in double-object constructions. Hence, speakers have to use an R-type oblique construction; this also applies to the 13 pronominal Rs in the corpus occurring in R-type oblique constructions. In nine of them (70%), the oblique is introduced with a benefactive preposition.

As already discussed, however, Papuan Malay disfavors constructions in which the R and T arguments are both overtly mentioned. Instead, trivalent verbs usually occur in clauses in which the R and/or T arguments are elided (1,058/1,160 tokens – 91%; see Table_11.1). Most often, the more salient R is omitted while the less salient T is retained (601/1,058 tokens – 57%), as shown in Table_11.3. Clauses in which the R and the T are both elided at the same time are also rather common (382/1,058 tokens – 36%). Only rarely, the T is omitted while the R is retained (75/1,058 tokens – 7%).

Retention of the R most often affects nominal Rs ( nom -R) (56/75 tokens – 75%); most of them are encoded as R-type obliques (39/56 tokens – 70%). Retention of pronominal Rs ( pro -R), which are more salient than nominal ones, is much less frequent (19/75 tokens – 25%). In light of the data given in Table_11.2, one would expect the 19 pronominal Rs to be encoded as direct objects rather than as R-type obliques. As shown in Table_11.3, however, ten of the 19 pronominal Rs are encoded as R-type obliques (53%). Again, this has to do with their marking as benefactive Rs: seven of the ten pronominal Rs are introduced with a benefactive preposition, similar to the 13 pronominal R-type obliques listed in Table_11.2.

An explanation for this preference to delete the R argument and to retain the T argument is given by in her study on asymmetries in double-object constructions (DOC) in English. The author explains the optional deletion of the R arguments “as sensitive to topic”, in that it applies “to those elements of [Information Structure ] that have already been activated and are accessible to speaker and hearer. More topical information is easily backgrounded, which explains why the recipient is more easily deleted” ( Polinsky.1998). Hence, presents the following implication: “If the patient of DOC can undergo optional deletion, the recipient of DOC can undergo optional deletion, too”.

This observation that the more accessible argument can be deleted also provides an explanation for the preference of Papuan Malay to elide the more salient R argument and to retain the less salient T argument.
summary: The passage shows that Papuan Malay trivalent verbs vary in word order, how the R and T arguments are encoded, and whether one or both arguments are omitted, with strong distributional preferences. These preferences are explained in terms of salience: pronominal, more salient Rs tend to appear in double-object constructions, while less salient nominal Rs more often occur in oblique constructions, and in clauses with elision the more salient R is commonly omitted while the T is retained.

text: The observed tendency to omit the R and/or T arguments has also been noted for western Austronesian languages in general. In these languages, as points out, “there are few (if any) morphosyntactic constraints on the omission of coreferential arguments in clause sequences. That is, the possibility to omit a coreferential argument is not restricted to subject arguments”. This also applies to other eastern Malay varieties, such as Ambon Malay, and Manado Malay. Along similar lines, notes for the Oceanic language Teop that “[all] three arguments of ditransitive constructions can be elided in both topical and non-topical positions”. These studies, however, do not discuss whether the languages under investigation have a preference for omitting the R or the T arguments in ditransitive constructions, and what the reasons for such a preference might be. An exception is Klamer.2013 study on ‘give’-constructions in heritage and baseline Ambon Malay. Noting that elision affects the R but not the T, the authors suggest that these distributional preferences are due to “a difference in the prominence of T and R” ( Klamer.2013).
summary: Western Austronesian languages generally show few morphosyntactic restrictions on omitting coreferential arguments in clause sequences, and this can apply to arguments beyond the subject, including in ditransitive constructions. However, most studies do not address whether speakers preferentially omit R or T; an exception is Klamer (2013) on Ambon Malay, which finds that elision affects R but not T and attributes this to differences in their prominence.

text:
Papuan Malay employs three types of causative constructions: syntactic, lexical, and periphrastic causatives.

Generally speaking, causative clauses are constructions which involve two events: “(1) the causing event in which the causer does something, and (2) the caused event in which the causee carries out an action or undergoes a change of condition or state as a result of the causer’s action”. Hence, causative constructions are the result of a valency-increasing operation: in addition to the arguments of the cause event, or “non- causative predicate”, there is also the “causer”. This valency-increasing operation is possible with intransitive and transitive events.

Cross-linguistically, four major strategies of encoding the notion of causation can be distinguished: lexical, morphological, syntactic, and periphrastic causatives. These constructions differ with respect to the degree of “structural integration” between the causing event, or the “predicate of cause”, and the caused event, or the “predicate of effect”. Lexical causatives show a maximal degree of structural integration in that the cause and effect are encoded in a single lexical item. Periphrastic causative constructions, by contrast, show the least degree of structural integration in that the cause and effect are encoded in two separate clauses. According to, however, lexical causatives do not “qualify as causatives sensu stricto” as they do not involve a morphological or syntactic change; neither do periphrastic constructions qualify as ``causatives sensu stricto'' given their biclausal structure.

Morphological and syntactic causatives differ from lexical and periphrastic causatives in that they integrate the cause with the caused event into a single predication. Hence, a causativized intransitive event yields a transitive causative construction, while a caus\-a\-tiv\-ized transitive caused event yields a ditransitive construction. The integration of the causer is achieved by demoting the agent of the caused event, the causee. Cross-linguistically, notes the following grammatical relation hierarchy for this process: “subject direct object indirect object oblique object”; that is, “the causee occupies the highest (leftmost) position on this hierarchy that is not already filled”.

As mentioned, Papuan Malay uses three of the four types of causative constructions: lexical, syntactic, and periphrastic causatives; morphological causatives are unattested. The main topic of this section is syntactic causatives (§ Para_11.2.1 ), since only they qualify as ``causatives sensu stricto''. Lexical and periphrastic causatives are mentioned only briefly in § Para_11.2.2 and § Para_11.2.3, respectively. The main points of this section are summarized in § Para_11.2.4.
summary: Papuan Malay uses three causative types: lexical, syntactic, and periphrastic, while morphological causatives are unattested. The passage explains that causatives involve a causing event and a caused event, with the causer added as an extra argument, and that syntactic and morphological causatives are structurally integrated into one predication, unlike lexical and periphrastic causatives. The section focuses mainly on syntactic causatives because they are the only type that qualify as “causatives sensu stricto.”

text:
In syntactic causatives, or “ compound” causatives, the notion of causation is encoded in a monoclausal construction which consists of two constituents, namely a causative verb, which expresses the notion of cause, and a second constituent that denotes the effect.

In Papuan Malay syntactic causatives, a serial verb construction V 1V 2 encodes the causation: the causative verb V 1 expresses the cause event and the V 2 the caused event. Two free verb forms are used as causative verbs: trivalent kasi ‘give’ and bivalent biking ‘make’. In kasi-causatives the V 2 can be monovalent or bivalent while in biking-causatives the V 2 is always monovalent.

Semantically, causatives with kasi ‘give’ focus on the outcome of the causation or manipulation. Causatives with biking ‘make’, by contrast, focus on the manipulation of circumstances that ultimately leads to the caused event or effect. This is shown with the contrastive examples in ( Example_11.47 ) and ( Example_11.48 ) both of which are formed with monovalent stative bersi ‘be clean’. In ( Example_11.47 ), kasi bersi ‘cause to be clean’ stresses the outcome of the washing process, namely that the clothes are clean. In the elicited example in ( Example_11.48 ), by contrast, biking bersi ‘make clean’ focuses on the manipulation itself, which leads to the effect that the clothes are clean.

styleExampleTitle
kasi ‘give’ versus biking ‘make’ causatives
styleExampleTitle

‘(if you have to do laundry at night time) wash (your clothes), clean (them, and hang them up) to dry’ [081011-019-Cv.0009]

malam cuci pakeang biking bersi jemur\\

‘(if you have to do laundry at night time) wash (your clothes), clean (them, and hang them up) to dry’ [Elicited BR131103.001]

The following sections discuss the syntax and semantics of Papuan Malay syntactic causatives in more detail. The two verbs that qualify as causative verbs are presented in § Para_11.2.1.1, followed by a description of syntactic causatives with the causative verb kasi ‘give’ in § Para_11.2.1.2, and with biking ‘make’ in § Para_11.2.1.3.
summary: Papuan Malay syntactic, or compound, causatives are monoclausal serial verb constructions in which a causative verb expresses the cause event and a following verb expresses the caused event. The two causative verbs are free forms kasi ‘give’ and biking ‘make’: kasi-causatives allow monovalent or bivalent V2s and emphasize the outcome of causation, while biking-causatives require a monovalent V2 and emphasize the manipulation that leads to the effect.

text:
The Papuan Malay verbs which express the notion of cause in syntactic causatives, kasi ‘give’ and biking ‘make’, are used synchronically as full transitive verbs, as shown in ( Example_11.49 ) to ( Example_11.51 ). Trivalent kasi ‘give’ exhibits dative alternation, as illustrated with the double-object constructions in ( Example_11.49 ) and the R-type oblique construction in ( Example_11.50 ) (see § Para_11.1.3 for more details on dative alternation). The transitive uses of biking ‘make’ are illustrated in ( Example_11.51 ).

a, kam kasi sa air ka\\
ah 2pl give 1sg water or\\

‘ah, you give me water, please’ [080919-008-CvNP.0005]

de kasi sratus ribu sama Madga\\
3sg give one.hundred thousand to Madga\\

‘he gave one hundred thousand (rupiah) to Madga’ [081014-003-Cv.0008]

Ika biking papeda\\
Ika make sagu.porridge\\

‘Ika made sagu porridge’ [081006-032-Cv.0071]
summary: Papuan Malay *kasi* ‘give’ and *biking* ‘make’, which can express causation in syntactic causatives, are synchronically used as full transitive verbs. *Kasi* is trivalent and shows dative alternation, appearing in both double-object and oblique constructions, while *biking* is illustrated in a straightforward transitive use.

text:
As a causative, trivalent kasi ‘give’, with its short form kas, is used with two types of verbal bases: monovalent ones (§ Para_11.2.1.2.1 ), or bivalent ones (§ Para_11.2.1.2.2 ). Semantically, causative kasi ‘give’ highlights the outcome of a causation.

Monovalent bases

Cross-linguistically, in causatives with monovalent bases, the agent of the caused event is demoted from its intransitive subject function (S) to the transitive object or patient (P) function, while the incoming causer takes the transitive subject or agent (A) function. This strategy, which corresponds to Comrie.1989 mentioned causative hierarchy, is also used in Papuan Malay causatives with monovalent bases. This is illustrated with the monoclausal causative constructions in ( Example_11.52 ) to ( Example_11.59 ): causatives with monovalent non-agentive bases are presented in ( Example_11.52 ) to ( Example_11.55 ) and causatives with monovalent agentive bases in ( Example_11.56 ) to ( Example_11.59 ). (Compare also with the biclausal causative constructions in § Para_11.2.3.)

In causatives with monovalent non-agentive bases, the effect expression can be a stative verb such as panjang ‘be long’ in ( Example_11.52 ), or a non-agentive dynamic verb such as gugur ‘fall (prematurely)’ in ( Example_11.54 ). The resulting V 1V 2 expressions function as transitive predicates.

Cross-linguistically, causative constructions receive different readings, depending on the causee’s level of agentivity. This also applies to Papuan Malay. When the causee has no control, the causative receives a “manipulative or directive” reading, while it receives an “assistive or cooperative” reading, when the causee has some level of agentivity ( Kulikov.2001).

In causatives with monovalent non-agentive bases, as in ( Example_11.52 ) to ( Example_11.55 ), the causer controls the event while the causee has no control. Hence, these causatives always receive a directive reading. Likewise, causatives with monovalent agentive bases receive a directive reading when the causee is inanimate, or animate but helpless. This is the case in ( Example_11.57 ) and ( Example_11.58 ). When, by contrast, the causee has some level of control, as in ( Example_11.56 ), the causation is less direct; hence, the causative receives an assistive reading. Sometimes, however, the reading of a causative is ambiguous, as in ( Example_11.59 ). If the causee Dodo is unconscious out of fear and thereby helpless, the causative receives the directive reading ‘remove’. But if Dodo is conscious and can move, the causative receives the assistive reading ‘enable to come out’.

Bivalent bases

In causatives with bivalent bases, the cross-linguistically expected operation is for the patient (P) of the caused event to retain its P function and for the agent (A) of the caused event to be demoted to the indirect object function.

Papuan Malay, however, uses a different strategy, in that all the arguments involved shift their functions. That is, the A of the caused event, or causee, is demoted to the P function. In turn, the P of the caused event is moved out of the core into an oblique slot; as an oblique, P is encoded in a prepositional phrase introduced with comitative dengang ‘with’, with its short form deng (see also § Para_10.2.1 ). This is shown with the examples in ( Example_11.60 ) and ( Example_11.61 ).

In ( Example_11.60 ), for instance, the original A, or causee, anjing ‘dog’, is demoted to the P function and juxtaposed to the V 1V 2 construction. Semantically, the causee becomes the theme argument of the causative expression kas makang ‘give to eat’. With the P slot being taken, the original P papeda ‘sagu porridge’ is moved out of the core into an oblique slot.

styleExampleTitle
Causatives with bivalent bases: Demoting the A and P functions
styleExampleTitle

saya kas makang anjing deng papeda\\
1sg give eat dog with sagu.porridge\\

‘I fed the dogs with papeda’ [080919-003-NP.0002]

dia kasi minum kitong dengang kopi air\\
3sg give drink 1pl with coffee water\\

‘he’ll give us coffee and water to drink’ [080919-004-NP.0069]

In the attested causatives with bivalent bases, the causees are able to control their own actions. Therefore, kasi ‘give’ receives an assistive or cooperative reading, as in ( Example_11.60 ) and ( Example_11.61 ). Causative with bivalent bases and inanimate, or animate but helpless referents are unattested.
summary:
Papuan Malay causative kasi ‘give’ is used with monovalent and bivalent verbal bases, and it emphasizes the result of a causation. With monovalent bases, the intransitive subject becomes the patient while the causer becomes the agent; these causatives can have directive readings when the causee lacks control, or assistive readings when the causee has some control.  

With bivalent bases, Papuan Malay shifts all roles: the original agent is demoted to patient, and the original patient is moved out of the core into an oblique phrase introduced by deng/dengang ‘with’. In the attested examples, these causatives have assistive or cooperative readings because the causees can control their actions.

text:
As a causative, bivalent biking ‘make’ is used with monovalent bases. Semantically, this causative type stresses the causer’s manipulation of circumstances, which leads to the caused event or effect. That is, biking-causatives are causer-controlled, with the causee having no control. Therefore, causatives with biking ‘make’ are formed with monovalent non-agentive bases, or with monovalent agentive bases with inanimate or with animate but helpless causees. This is shown in ( Example_11.62 ) to ( Example_11.67 ). Overall, though, biking-causatives are rare in the corpus.

The causative in ( Example_11.62 ), for example, is formed with non-agentive stative pusing ‘be dizzy, be confused’. The use of biking ‘make’ stresses the manipulating behavior of the causer ana ana ‘children’ which leads to the effect pusing ‘be worried’; the causee mama ‘mother’ has no control. The elicited examples in ( Example_11.63 ) and ( Example_11.64 ) contrast with the corresponding kasi-causatives in ( Example_11.54 ) and ( Example_11.55 ). They show that biking-causatives are also formed with monovalent non-agentive dynamic bases, such as gugur ‘abort’ or tenggelam ‘sink’, respectively. Again, the manipulation itself is stressed. The base can also be agentive dynamic if the causee is animate but helpless. This is illustrated with the elicited example in ( Example_11.65 ), which contrasts with the corresponding kasi- causative in ( Example_11.57 ). The base is agentive dynamic hidup ‘live’ but the animate causee is helpless and therefore has no control.

Causatives with agentive bases are unacceptable. This is due to the fact that biking-causatives focus on the causer’s manipulation of circumstances itself while the causee has no control. This is illustrated with the unacceptable biking-causatives in ( Example_11.66 ) and ( Example_11.67 ), which are formed with monovalent dynamic duduk ‘sit’ and bivalent makang ‘eat’, respectively. The two elicited examples contrast with the corresponding kasi-causatives in ( Example_11.56 ) and ( Example_11.60 ).
