[Addressing a guest:] ‘wow!, I thought ( you) were still in Arbais’ [081011-011-Cv.0044]
summary: In nonverbal clauses, the subject may be a noun phrase or noun, a personal pronoun, or a demonstrative, and in some cases it may be omitted when the context makes it recoverable. The passage illustrates these options across nominal, quantifier, prepositional, and numeral clauses, showing that elided subjects are understood from earlier discourse or from the addressee context.

text:
In nonverbal clauses with nominal predicates, a noun or a noun phrase conveys the main semantic content.

In Papuan Malay, nominal clauses have three functions: (1) to describe the subject, (2) to identify the subject, and (3) to express possession of an indefinite possessum. Nominal predicates always receive a static reading.

Nominal predicates conveying a description of the subject are also referred to as “ascriptive predications”, adopting Hengeveld.1992 terminology: they describe a particular entity that is denoted by the subject of the clause such that `` s is a member of n / np ''. That is, an ascriptive clause asserts that this entity belongs to the class of entities specified in the nonreferential nominal predicate. By contrast, nominal predicates expressing identification are “equative predicates”. They are referential and equate the particular entity denoted by the subject of the clause to the entity specified in the predicate such that `` s is n / np ''. (See;.) In nominal clauses conveying the notion of possession the subject embodies the semantic role of possessor while the predicate functions as an indefinite possessum such that `` possessor has a possessum ''.

Papuan Malay ascriptive, equative, and possessive nominal predicates are different in terms of their semantics, but not in terms of their structure. That is, Papuan Malay does not distinguish the three nominal predicate types as far as their syntactic or intonational features are concerned; all three are formed by juxtaposition of two noun phrases with the subject preceding the predicate. This is illustrated with the ascriptive clauses in ( Example_12.9 ) and ( Example_12.10 ), the equative clauses in ( Example_12.11 ) and ( Example_12.12 ), and the possessive clauses in ( Example_12.13 ) to ( Example_12.16 ).

In the ascriptive clause in ( Example_12.9 ), the subject saya ‘ 1sg ’ is asserted to belong to the class of manusia ‘human being’. In the ascriptive clause in ( Example_12.10 ), the subject ko ‘ 2sg ’ is part of the class of prempuang Demta ‘Demta girls’. The equative clause in ( Example_12.11 ) identifies the predicate ade ‘younger sibling’ with the subject dia ‘ 3sg ’. Along similar lines, the equative clause in ( Example_12.12 ) identifies the predicate klawar ‘cave bat’ with the subject itu ‘ d.dist ’. The example in ( Example_12.11 ) also shows that nonverbal predicates can be modified with adverbs, such as masi ‘still’.

styleExampleTitle
Ascriptive clauses
styleExampleTitle

misalnya saya manusia biasa\\
for.example 1sg human.being be.usual\\

[About humans and evil spirits:] ‘for example, I am a normal human being’ [081006-022-CvEx.0025]

ko prempuang Demta, ko pulang ke Demta!\\
2sg woman Demta 2sg go.home to Demta\\

‘you are a Demta girl, go home to Demta!’ [081006-025-CvEx.0014]

styleExampleTitle
Equative clauses
styleExampleTitle

dia masi ade\\
3sg still ySb\\

‘she’s still (my) younger sister’ [080927-009-CvNP.0038]

o, itu klawar\\
oh! d.dist cave.bat\\

‘oh, that was a bat’ [081023-001-Cv.0041]

The nominal clauses in ( Example_12.13 ) to ( Example_12.16 ) express possession of an indefinite possessum. In ( Example_12.13 ), the subject saya ‘1 sg ’ has the semantic role of possessor, while the predicate empat ana ‘four children’ functions as the possessum. In ( Example_12.14 ), the possessor de ‘3 sg ’ is juxtaposed to the possessum ana kecil ‘small child’. The possessive clauses in ( Example_12.13 ) and ( Example_12.14 ) encode inalienable possession relations. The clauses in ( Example_12.15 ) and ( Example_12.16 ), by contrast, denote alienable possession relations, namely between a human referent and animate nonhuman ikang ‘fish’ in ( Example_12.15 ) and inanimate glang puti ‘silver/tin bracelets’ in ( Example_12.16 ). (Alternatively, possession of an indefinite possessum can be encoded by an existential clause; for details see § Para_11.4.2. Possession of a definite possessum is encoded by an adnominal possessive construction; for details see Para_9 and also § Para_11.4.1.)

styleExampleTitle
Possessive clauses: Possession of an indefinite possessum
styleExampleTitle

saya empat ana\\
1sg four child\\

‘I have four children’ [081006-024-CvEx.0001]

baru de ana kecil lagi\\
and.then 3sg child be.small again\\

‘moreover, she has a small child again’ [081010-001-Cv.0070] In a different context, de ana kecil can also receive the equative reading ‘she (is) a small child’.

de satu, sa satu\\
3sg one 1sg one\\

[Joke about two fishermen:] ‘he has one (fish), I have one (fish)’ [081109-011-JR.0008]

orang Biak kang glang puti\\
person Biak you.know bracelet be.white\\

[About bride-price customs:] ‘you know, the Biak people have silver/tin bracelets’ [081006-029-CvEx.0007]

These examples also show that the predicate of a nominal clause can be a noun such as ade ‘younger sibling’ in ( Example_12.11 ), or klawar ‘cave bat’ in ( Example_12.12 ), or a noun phrase, such as manusia biasa ‘normal human being’ in ( Example_12.9 ) or empat ana ‘four children’ in ( Example_12.13 ).

If speakers want to emphasize the predicate, they can front it as for instance orang pintar ‘smart person’ in ( Example_12.17 ). The predicate is set-off by a boundary intonation in that the stressed penultimate syllable of the verbal modifier pintar ‘be clever’ is marked with a slight increase in pitch (“ \' ”). In the second clause in ( Example_12.17 ) the speaker repeats his statement, this time however returning to the canonical subject-predicate word order.

styleExampleTitle
Fronted nominal predicates
styleExampleTitle

trus orang píntar dia, dia orang pintar\\
next person be.clever 3sg 3sg person be.clever\\

‘and then a smart person he is, he’s a smart person’ [081029-005-Cv.0169]
summary:
Papuan Malay nominal clauses use a noun or noun phrase as the main predicate and have three functions: ascriptive, equative, and possessive. Although these types differ semantically, they share the same structure: two juxtaposed noun phrases with the subject preceding the predicate, and nominal predicates always have a static reading.

Ascriptive clauses describe the subject as a member of a class, equative clauses identify the subject with the predicate, and possessive clauses express possession of an indefinite possessum. The passage also notes that predicates may be nouns or noun phrases, and that speakers can front the predicate for emphasis.

text:
In numeral and quantifier clauses, a numeral or quantifier conveys the main semantic content; again, these predicates receive a static reading. As in nominal clauses, the subject precedes the predicate. Structurally, numeral and quantifier predicates are identical to noun phrases with a postposed numeral or quantifier (see § Para_8.3 ). Semantically, numeral and quantifier clauses have determining function in that they express specific properties of the subject, namely those of number and quantity, such that `` s is num / qt '' as illustrated in ( Example_12.18 ) to ( Example_12.21 ).

In ( Example_12.18 ), a husband relates that in a neighboring village a woman gave birth to a snake. His wife contradicts this statement, asserting that it was not one snake but that the ular ‘snake’ were dua ‘two’. The analysis of the dua ‘two’ as a numeral predicate and not as an adnominal modifier is confirmed by the following fact. In the context of these utterances it is possible to insert existential ada ‘exist’ between the subject ular ‘snake’ and the predicate dua ‘two’ which gives the emphatic progressive reading ular ada dua ‘the snakes were being two’ or ‘the snakes were indeed two’ (see also § Para_5.4.1 ). If ular dua was a noun phrase with the reading of ‘two snakes’, existential ada ‘exist’ would have to precede or follow the noun phrase such that ada ular dua ‘there were two snakes’ or ular dua ada ‘the two snakes exist’. In ( Example_12.19 ), predicatively used satu ‘one’ and dua blas ‘twelve’ convey information about the numeric quantities of their respective subjects bulang ‘moon’ and de ‘3 sg ’. The first clause di langit ini bulang satu cannot be interpreted as a prepositional predicate clause (see § Para_12.4 ) in which bulang satu functions as a noun phrase which takes the subject slot. Such a reading would imply that there are several moons with the speaker talking about one of them: bulang satu ‘a certain moon’ (see § Para_5.9.4 for a more detailed discussion of satu ‘one’).

styleExampleTitle
Numeral predicates
styleExampleTitle

Husband: dia melahirkang ular\\
3sg give.birth snake\\
Husband: ‘she gave birth to a snake’
5pt

Wife: ular dua\\
snake two\\
Wife: ‘ two snakes’ (Lit. ‘the snakes (were) two’) [081006-022-CvEx.0002-0003]

di langit ini bulang satu tapi di kalender de dua blas\\
at sky d.prox month one but at calendar 3sg two teens\\

‘in this sky there is one moon, but in the calendar there are twelve’ (Lit. ‘the moon (is) one it (is) twelve’) [081109-007-JR.0002]

In ( Example_12.20 ) and ( Example_12.21 ), predicatively-used universal quantifier smua ‘all’ and mid-range quantifier banyak ‘many’ express the nonnumeric quantities of their respective subjects orang Sulawesi ‘Sulawesi people’ and pisang masak itu ‘that ripe banana’.

styleExampleTitle
Quantifier predicates
styleExampleTitle

katanya orang Sulawesi smua\\
it.is.being.said person Sulawesi all\\

‘it’s being said (that) they are all Sulawesi people’ (Lit. ‘Sulawesi people (are) all’) [081029-005-Cv.0106]

baru dong bawa pisang masak, pisang masak itu banyak\\
and.then 3pl bring banana cook banana cook d.dist many\\

‘and then they brought ripe bananas, those ripe bananas were many’ [081006-023-CvEx.0071]
summary: Numeral and quantifier clauses have a static reading, with the subject preceding a numeral or quantifier that carries the main semantic content. They are structurally like noun phrases with a postposed numeral or quantifier, but semantically they function to specify a subject’s number or quantity, as in examples where “two,” “one,” “twelve,” “all,” or “many” are used predicatively.

text: Nonverbal clauses with prepositional predicates convey information about the relation between a figure and a ground, such that `` figure is in relation to ground ''. The figure is encoded by the clausal subject and the ground by the complement of the prepositional phrase. This phrase is juxtaposed to the subject and functions as the clausal predicate. Semantically, two types of prepositional predicate clauses can be distinguished: locational clauses (§ Para_12.4.1 ), and non locational clauses (§ Para_12.4.2 ). The precise semantic relation between figure and ground is defined by the preposition that heads the prepositional phrase. (For a detailed discussion of prepositions and prepositional phrases see Para_10.)
summary: Nonverbal clauses with prepositional predicates express a relation in which the figure, encoded as the clausal subject, stands in relation to the ground, encoded as the complement of the prepositional phrase. The prepositional phrase is placed beside the subject and serves as the clausal predicate, and its head preposition determines the exact semantic relation. Two semantic types are distinguished: locational and non-locational clauses.

text:
Locational predicate clauses typically express information about the locational relation, spatial or figurative, between a figure and the ground, as shown in ( Example_12.22 ) to ( Example_12.26 ). In addition, locational predicates can have presentative function, as shown in ( Example_12.28 ). In Papuan Malay, the specific kind of relation is conveyed by prepositions encoding location, namely locative di ‘at, in’, allative ke ‘to’, or elative dari ‘from’, (see also § Para_10.1 ). The ground can be encoded by a common (proper) noun or a noun phrase. Unlike prepositional phrases in verbal clauses, locative di ‘at, in’ and allative ke ‘to’ cannot be omitted from prepositional clauses with nominal complements as this would result in nominal clauses with unacceptable semantics (for more details on the omission of prepositions encoding location, see § Para_10.1.5 ); the exceptions are preposed prepositional clauses with locative complements, as in ( Example_12.27 ) to ( Example_12.29 ).

Spatial locational predicates denote static or dynamic relations between a figure and the ground, depending on the semantics of the preposition. In ( Example_12.22 ), locative di ‘at, in’ expresses the spatial location of the figure dia ‘ 3sg ’ at the ground kampung ‘village’. In ( Example_12.23 ) allative ke ‘to’ signals the motion of the figure dep mama ‘her mother’ toward the goal Pante-Barat. While this kind of prepositional predicate is not possible in English, it does occur in other languages such as colloquial German. Hence, ( Example_12.23 ) easily translates into ihre Mutter ist nach Pante-Barat. In ( Example_12.24 ), elative dari ‘from’ conveys the motion of the figure sa ‘1 sg ’ away from the source Sawar. More frequently, however, motion away from a source is encoded by a verbal phrase such as kluar dari ruma ‘left home’ in ( Footnote_Example_12.1 ) below:
-5pt

sa kluar dari ruma sa punya orang-tua\\
1sg go.out from house 1sg poss parent\\
‘I left home, my parents’ (Lit. ‘ went out from the house’) [081115-001b-Cv.0045]

styleExampleTitle
Static and dynamic spatial locational relations between figure and ground
styleExampleTitle

memang dia di kampung\\
indeed 3sg at village\\

‘indeed, he was in the village’ [080918-001-CvNP.0014]

dep mama ke ini Pante-Barat\\
3sg: poss mother to d.prox Pante-Barat\\

‘her mother (went) to, what’s-its-name, Pante-Barat’ [080919-006-CvNP.025]

sa dari Sawar\\
1sg from Sawar\\

‘I (just returned) from Sawar’ [080927-004-CvNP.0003]

Locational predicates also express figurative locational relations between a figure and the ground. In ( Example_12.25 ), locative di ‘at, in’ conveys a figurative locational relation between the figure saya ‘1 sg ’ and the ground IPS satu ‘Social Sciences I’. Along similar lines, elative dari ‘from’ conveys a figurative relation in ( Example_12.26 ). This example is part of a conversation about a building project that was put on hold due to the lack of funding. The figure smua itu ‘all that’ refers to the delayed project while the ground uang ‘money’ denotes the nonspatial source from which this delay originates. Figurative predicates with allative ke ‘to’ are unattested.

styleExampleTitle
Figurative locational relation between figure and ground
styleExampleTitle

sa di IPS satu\\
1sg at social.sciences one\\

[About course tracks in high school:] ‘I am in Social Sciences I’ [081023-004-Cv.0020]

smua itu dari uang\\
all d.dist from money\\

‘all that (depends) on the money’ (Lit. ‘ from the money’) [080927-006-CvNP.0034]

If speakers want to emphasize the predicate, they can front it. The corpus, however, includes only three utterances with fronted prepositional predicates, which are presented in ( Example_12.27 ) to ( Example_12.29 ). In each case the locative preposition di ‘at, in’ is omitted and the complement is a locative, such as proximal sini ‘ l.prox ’ in ( Example_12.27 ), or medial situ ‘ l.med ’ in ( Example_12.28 ) and ( Example_12.29 ). One anonymous reviewers suggests an alternative reading of the situ-clause. The clause situ alang-alang ‘there ( emph ) (is only) cogongrass’ parallels the preceding clause sebla tida ada ruma ‘on that side aren’t (any houses)’. Hence, the predicate is not situ ‘ l.med ’ but ada ‘exist’, with the latter having been elided: situ Ø alang-alang ‘there ( emph ) (is only) cogongrass’. Fronted prepositional predicates with distal sana ‘ l.dist ’ are also possible, but unattested in the corpus. (For more details on the omission of prepositions encoding location, see § Para_10.1.5.)

styleExampleTitle
Fronting of prepositional predicates
styleExampleTitle

Ø sini bua bua banyak\\
l.prox rdp fruit many\\

‘ here ( emph ) are many different kinds of fruit (trees)’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0418] Alternatively, the utterance in ( Example_12.27 ) could be interpreted as a numeral predicate clause with a locational adjunct, with bua bua ‘ rdp -fruit’ as the subject, banyak ‘many’ as the predicate, and sini ‘ l.prox ’ as a preposed locational adjunct, giving the literal reading ‘here the various fruit (trees) are many’.

sebla tida ada ruma Ø situ alang-alang\\
side neg exist house l.med cogongrass\\

‘on that side aren’t (any) houses, there ( emph ) (is only) cogongrass’ [081025-008-Cv.0149]

Ø situ Natanael Ø situ Martin Ø situ Aleks\\
l.med Natanael l.med Martin l.med Aleks\\

[Choosing among potential candidates for the upcoming local elections:] ‘[Burwas (village can have) two candidates,] there ( emph ) is Natanael, there ( emph ) is Martin, there ( emph ) is Aleks’ [080919-001-Cv.0117]
summary:
Locational predicate clauses in Papuan Malay express spatial or figurative relations between a figure and a ground, and they may also serve a presentative function. These clauses use locative **di** ‘at, in’, allative **ke** ‘to’, or elative **dari** ‘from’, with the ground expressed by a noun or noun phrase, and unlike related verbal-clause prepositional phrases, **di** and **ke** cannot normally be omitted with nominal complements.

The prepositions can mark either static or dynamic spatial relations, depending on their meaning, and **di** and **dari** also occur in figurative locational predicates, while figurative uses of **ke** are not attested. Predicate fronting is possible for emphasis, but the corpus shows only a few such cases, all with omitted **di** and locative complements like **sini** or **situ**.

text:
Prepositional clauses with non locational predicates convey information about the non\-lo\-ca\-tional, static relation between a figure and the ground. Semantically, Papuan Malay distinguishes three types of non locational predicates, namely “ associative” or “ comitative predicates”, “simulative predicates”, and “benefactive predicates”, adopting Dryer.2007 terminology. Overall, however, non locational prepositional clauses do not appear to be very common; the corpus contains only few examples.

Papuan Malay comitative predicates are formed with prepositions encoding accompaniment/instruments or goals, namely comitative dengang ‘with’, with its short form deng, and goal preposition sama ‘to’ (see also § Para_10.2.1 and § Para_10.2.2 ). In ( Example_12.30 ), deng(ang) ‘with’ denotes the accompaniment of the figure Roni by the ground de pu temang temang ‘his friends’. In ( Example_12.31 ), sama ‘to’ signals the association of the implied figure ana ‘child’ with the ground saya ‘1 sg ’.

styleExampleTitle
Comitative predicates
styleExampleTitle

Roni masi deng de pu temang temang\\
Roni still with 3sg poss rdp friend\\

‘Roni is still with his friends’ [081006-031-Cv.0011]

hanya tiga saja sama saya\\
only three just to 1sg \\

‘just only three (of my children) are with me’ [081006-024-CvEx.0001]

Simulative predicates are formed with prepositions encoding comparisons, that is, similative sperti ‘similar to’ and kaya ‘like’ and equative sebagey ‘as’ (see also § Para_10.3 ). In ( Example_12.32 ) sperti ‘similar to’ establishes a simulative relation between the figure de ‘3 sg ’ and the ground Sofia. Along similar lines, kaya ‘like’ denotes a simulative relation between the figure de ‘ sg ’ and the ground de pu bapa ‘his father’ / Siduas in ( Example_12.33 ). In ( Example_12.34 ), sebagey ‘as’ expresses equatability between the figure sa ‘ 1sg ’ and the ground kepala acara ‘the head of the festivity’. (See § Para_10.3.1 and § Para_10.3.2 for a detailed discussion of the prepositions sperti ‘similar to’ and kaya ‘like’ and their semantics.)

styleExampleTitle
Simulative predicates
styleExampleTitle

de sperti Sofia\\
3sg similar.to Sofia\\

‘she’s similar to Sofia’ [081115-001a-Cv.0283]

de pu muka kaya de pu bapa e kaya Siduas\\
3sg poss face like 3sg poss father eh like Siduas\\

‘his face is like his father, eh, like Siduas’ (face)’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1446]

paling sa tra kerja, sa sebagey kepala acara\\
most 1sg neg work 1sg as head festivity\\

[About organizing a festivity:] ‘most likely I won’t (have to) work, I’ll be the head of the festivity’ (Lit. ‘ as the head ’) [080919-004-NP.0068]

Benefactive predicates are formed with the benefactive preposition untuk ‘for’ (see also § Para_10.2.3 ). In ( Example_12.35 ), for instance, untuk ‘for’ conveys a benefactive relation between the figure itu ‘ d.dist ’ and the ground masarakat ‘community’. In the corpus, however, benefactive predicates are rare.

styleExampleTitle
Benefactive predicates
styleExampleTitle

uang besarnya itu untuk masarakat tapi pejabat\\
money be.big: 3possr d.dist for community but official\\
yang makang banyak\\
rel eat many\\

‘most of that money, that’s for the community but (it’s) the officials who take lots (of it)’ [081029-004-Cv.0002]
summary: Papuan Malay has three main kinds of non-locational prepositional clauses: comitative, simulative, and benefactive predicates, though these constructions are rare in the corpus. Comitative predicates use prepositions such as deng(ang) and sama to express accompaniment or association, simulative predicates use sperti, kaya, and sebagey to express similarity or equality, and benefactive predicates use untuk to mark a beneficiary.

text: Papuan Malay employs three syntactically distinct types of nonverbal predicate clauses, namely nominal, numeral, quantifier, and prepositional predicate clauses. These clauses are formed by juxtaposition of the two main constituents; no copula intervenes. The three clause types also have distinct semantic functions. Nominal predicates have ascriptive or equative function and also encode possession. Numeral and quantifier predicates have determining function. Prepositional predicates encode locational or non locational relations between a figure and the ground.
summary: Papuan Malay has three syntactically distinct types of nonverbal predicate clauses formed by simple juxtaposition of their main constituents, with no copula. These include nominal predicates, which are used for ascriptive, equative, and possessive meanings, numeral and quantifier predicates, which have a determining function, and prepositional predicates, which express locational or non-locational relations between a figure and a ground.

text: This chapter describes negative, interrogative, and directive clauses in Papuan Malay. Negative clauses formed with the negators tida/ tra ‘ neg ’ and bukang ‘ neg ’ are discussed in § Para_13.1. Interrogative clauses, including polar and alternative questions, are described in § Para_13.2. Directive clauses, including imperatives, adhortatives, permissions, obligations, and prohibitives, are the topic of § Para_13.3.
summary: This chapter outlines three clause types in Papuan Malay: negative, interrogative, and directive clauses. It notes that negative clauses use the negators *tida/tra* and *bukang*, interrogative clauses include polar and alternative questions, and directive clauses cover imperatives, adhortatives, permissions, obligations, and prohibitives.

text: In Papuan Malay, negative clauses are formed with the negation adverbs tida/ tra ‘ neg ’ or bukang ‘ neg ’. Negator tida/ tra ‘ neg ’ is used for the negation of verbal, existential, and nonverbal prepositional clauses (§ Para_13.1.1 ). Negator bukang ‘ neg ’ is used to negate nonverbal clauses, other than prepositional ones, and to mark contrastive negation (§ Para_13.1.2 ). (Negative directives or prohibitives are discussed in § Para_13.3.3.)
summary: In Papuan Malay, negative clauses are formed with the negation adverbs **tida/tra** and **bukang**. **Tida/tra** is used to negate verbal, existential, and nonverbal prepositional clauses, while **bukang** negates other kinds of nonverbal clauses and is also used for contrastive negation.

text: The negators tida ‘ neg ’ and tra ‘ neg ’ negate different types of clauses; they always precede the predicate which they negate. Negation of verbal clauses is discussed in § Para_13.1.1.1, of existential clauses in § Para_13.1.1.2, and of nonverbal prepositional clauses in § Para_13.1.1.3. Negator tida ‘ neg ’ also provides negative responses to polar questions, as discussed in § Para_13.1.1.4. With the exception of negative responses to polar questions, both negators are used interchangeably.
summary: The negators **tida** ‘neg’ and **tra** ‘neg’ both precede the predicate they negate and are used to negate different clause types, including verbal, existential, and nonverbal prepositional clauses. Aside from their use in negative responses to polar questions, where **tida** is specifically used, the two negators are interchangeable.

text:
As a negator of verbal clauses, tida/ tra ‘ neg ’ negates stative verbs such as baik ‘be good’ in ( Example_13.1 ), dynamic verbs such as datang ‘come’ in ( Example_13.2 ), bivalent verbs such as pukul ‘hit’ in ( Example_13.3 ), or trivalent verbs such as bli ‘buy’ in ( Example_13.4 ). The example in ( Example_13.5 ) illustrates negation of a causative construction.

The contrastive examples in ( Example_13.1 ) and ( Example_13.2 ) also show that tida ‘ neg ’ and tra ‘ neg ’ are used interchangeably with no differences in function or meaning. In the corpus, however, speakers more often use tida ‘ neg ’ than tra ‘ neg ’ (1,491 vs. 794 tokens) ( bukang ‘ neg ’ is attested with 208 tokens; see § Para_13.1.2 ).

styleExampleTitle
Negation of verbal clauses with tida/ tra ‘ neg ’
styleExampleTitle

nanti dia pikir saya tida baik nanti de\\
very.soon 3sg think 1sg neg be.good very.soon 3sg \\
pikir kitong tra baik\\
think 1pl neg be.good\\

‘very soon he’ll think that I’m not good very soon he’ll think that we are not good’ [080919-004-NP.0052-0053]

de tra datang de tida datang\\
3sg neg come 3sg neg come\\

‘she did not come she did not come’ [081010-001-Cv.0204-0205]

sa tida pukul dorang\\
1sg neg hit 3pl \\

‘I don’t hit them’ [080917-010-CvEx.0048]

kalo bapa tra bli sa HP, biar suda tida apa apa\\
if father neg buy 1sg cell.phone let already neg rdp what\\

‘if you (‘father’) won’t buy me a cell phone, just let it be, no problem’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0461]

baru kamu tra kas kluar uang bayar\\
and.then 2pl neg give go.out money pay\\

[Encouraging teenagers to take free English classes:] ‘and then you won’t have to pay fees’ (Lit. ‘ not give (to) come out’) [081115-001a-Cv.0160]
summary: The negators *tida* and *tra* are used to negate verbal clauses across a range of verb types, including stative, dynamic, bivalent, trivalent, and causative constructions. They appear to be interchangeable in function and meaning, though the corpus shows *tida* is used more often than *tra*; *bukang* is also attested but less frequently.

text:
Existential clauses are also negated with tida/ tra ‘ neg ’, as illustrated in ( Example_13.6 ) to ( Example_13.10 ). Examples for negated one-argument clauses are given in ( Example_13.6 ) to ( Example_13.8 ), and for two-argument clauses in ( Example_13.9 ) to ( Example_13.10 ). (Existential clauses are discussed in detail in § Para_11.4.)

The respective one-argument clauses in ( Example_13.6 ) and ( Example_13.7 ) illustrate negated existence and negated availability of indefinite/nonidentifiable theme expressions. The example in ( Example_13.8 ) demonstrates negation of a definite/identifiable theme expression. One-argument clauses denoting negative possession of a definite/identifiable possessum are unattested in the corpus; instead, the preferred type of existential clause to express negative possession is a two-argument clause, as shown in ( Example_13.9 ) and ( Example_13.10 ).

styleExampleTitle
Negation of one-argument existential clauses with tida/ tra ‘ neg ’
styleExampleTitle

tra ada kamar mandi\\
neg exist room bathe\\

‘(there) were no bathrooms’ [081025-009a-Cv.0059]

tida ada air minum\\
neg exist water drink\\

‘(there) was no drinking water’ [081025-009a-Cv.0060]

ketrampilang juga tra ada\\
skill also neg exist\\

[About training activities for women:] ‘ neither do (they) have (any) skills’ (Lit. ‘(their) skills also don’t exist’) [081010-001-Cv.0145]

Negation of two-argument existential clauses is shown in ( Example_13.9 ) and ( Example_13.10 ). The negated clauses attested in the corpus always express absence of possession, such as the negative possession of ana ‘child(ren)’ in ( Example_13.9 ), or air ‘water’ in ( Example_13.10 ).

styleExampleTitle
Negation of two-argument existential clauses denoting possession
styleExampleTitle

sodara prempuang itu tida ada ana\\
sibling woman d.dist neg exist child\\

‘that sister doesn’t have children’ [081006-024-CvEx.0005]

dong tra ada air\\
3pl neg exist water\\

‘they didn’t have water’ [080919-008-CvNP.0013]
summary: Existential clauses are negated with *tida/tra* ‘neg’, and the text distinguishes between one-argument and two-argument clauses. One-argument clauses can express negated existence, negated availability, and negation of both indefinite and definite theme expressions, but one-argument clauses for negative possession of a definite possessum are not attested in the corpus. Instead, negative possession is typically expressed by two-argument existential clauses, which in the attested examples always denote absence of possession, such as not having children or water.

text:
Prepositional predicates are also negated with tida/ tra ‘ neg ’, as shown in ( Example_13.11 ) and ( Example_13.12 ). (Negation of other types of nonverbal clauses is discussed in § Para_13.1.2; for more details on nonverbal clauses see Para_12.)

styleExampleTitle
Negation of nonverbal prepositional clauses with tida/ tra ‘ neg ’
styleExampleTitle

saya tida sperti prempuang laing to?\\
1sg neg similar.to woman be.different right?\\

‘I’m not similar to other women, right?’ [081011-023-Cv.0173]

tong tra ke kampung\\
1pl neg to village\\

‘we do not (go) to the village’ [080917-003a-CvEx.0048]
summary: Prepositional predicates are negated with **tida/tra** meaning ‘neg’. The passage illustrates this with examples such as “I’m not similar to other women” and “we do not go to the village,” and notes that other types of nonverbal clauses are discussed elsewhere.

text:
In addition, tida/ tra ‘ neg ’ provides negative responses to polar questions, when negating verbal constructions, as shown in ( Example_13.13 ) and ( Example_13.14 ). Negator tida ‘ neg ’ can stand alone as in ( Example_13.13 ), or it can occur in the negative existential phrase tida ada ‘no’ (literally ‘(it) doesn’t exist’). Negator tra ‘ neg ’, by contrast, cannot stand alone; it always occurs in the negative existential phrase tra ada ‘no’, as in ( Example_13.14 ). (See also § Para_13.2.2.1.)

styleExampleTitle
Negator tida/ tra ‘ neg ’ in responses to polar questions
styleExampleTitle

Speaker-2: tida, dia balap\\
neg 3sg race\\

[About an accident:] [Speaker-1: ‘what did he do? (was he) drunk?’]\\
Speaker-2: ‘ no, he was racing (his motorbike)’ [081014-013-NP.0003-0004]

Speaker-2: tra ada, muara baru \\
neg exist river.mouth be.new \\

[Discussing the depth of a river mouth:] [Speaker-1: ‘isn’t (it) deep?’]\\
Speaker-2: ‘ no, (this is) the new river mouth [(it’s) the old river mouth that is (deep)]’ [080927-003-Cv.0010-0011]
summary: The passage explains that both **tida** and **tra** can be used to give negative answers to polar questions when negating verbal constructions. However, **tida** may stand alone or appear in the negative existential phrase **tida ada** ‘no,’ while **tra** cannot stand alone and must always occur in the phrase **tra ada** ‘no.’

text:
Negator bukang ‘ neg ’ has three functions. One function is to negate nonverbal clauses, a second one is to mark contrastive negation, and a third function is to provide negative responses to polar questions.

Nonverbal clauses are typically negated with bukang ‘ neg ’, which always precedes the nonverbal predicate. Prepositional predicates are the exception; they are negated with tida/ tra ‘ neg ’ (see § Para_13.1.1.3 ). (In the corpus, bukang ‘ neg ’ is attested with 208 tokens, as compared to 1,491 tida ‘ neg ’ and 794 tra ‘ neg ’ tokens.)

In ( Example_13.15 ) and ( Example_13.16 ), bukang ‘ neg ’ negates nominal predicates, and in ( Example_13.17 ) a quantifier predicate. (Nonverbal clauses are discussed in detail in Para_12.)

styleExampleTitle
Negation of nonverbal clauses with bukang ‘ neg ’
styleExampleTitle

de bukang gembala sidang di situ\\
3sg neg pastor (church.)gathering at l.med \\

‘he’s not a congregational pastor there’ [080925-003-Cv.0032]

sa bukang orang yang seraka\\
1sg neg person rel be.greedy\\

‘I’m not a person who is greedy’ [080917-010-CvEx.0214]

pisang bukang sedikit\\
banana neg few\\

‘there (were) quite a few bananas’ (Lit. ‘the bananas (were) not few’) [080925-003-Cv.0158]

A second function of bukang ‘ neg ’ is to express contrastive negation of an entire proposition. Contrastive negation implies an alternative in the sense of ``the situation is not that X (but Y)''. Very often the alternative is expressed overtly, but this is not obligatory. Depending on its scope, bukang ‘ neg ’ occurs between the subject and the predicate or clause-initially. Its contrastive uses in prepredicate position are shown with the examples in ( Example_13.18 ) and ( Example_13.19 ). Unlike tida/ tra ‘ neg ’, contrastive bukang ‘ neg ’ also occurs clause-initially, as shown in ( Example_13.20 ) and ( Example_13.21 ).

styleExampleTitle
Contrastive negation with bukang ‘ neg ’
styleExampleTitle

mama ni bukang hidup deng orang-tua di kampung,\\
mother d.prox neg live with parent at village\\
mama ni hidup deng orang di luar\\
mother d.prox live with person at outside\\

‘(the situation was) not (that) I (‘mother’) here lived with (my) parents in the village, (but) I (‘mother’) here lived with strangers away from home’ [081115-001b-Cv.0043]

pernikaang ini bukang dari manusia, dari Tuhang to?\\
marriage d.prox neg from human.being from God right?\\

‘(the situation is) not (that) marriage is from man, (but it is) from God, right?’ [081110-006-CvEx.0239]

bukang dong maing, dong taguling di pecek\\
neg 3pl play 3pl be.rolled.over at mud\\

‘(the situation was) not (that) they played (football, but) they got rolled over in the mud’ [081109-001-Cv.0025]

bukang dong taru ijing tapi dong taru hadir\\
neg 3pl put permission but 3pl put attend\\

[About students who falsified the attendance book:] ‘(the situation is) not (that) they wrote down (their absences as) permitted (absences), but they wrote (them) down as (having) attended’ [081023-004-Cv.0018]

This function of bukang ‘ neg ’ to signal contrastive negation has also been noted for Ambon Malay, Manado Malay, Ternate Malay, and Standard Malay and Standard Indonesian (; ).

Speakers also use bukang ‘ neg ’ in single word clauses to contradict an interlocutor’s statements. They may submit an alternative to the negated proposition as in ( Example_13.22 ), or they may reply with bare bukang ‘ neg ’.

styleExampleTitle
Contradiction of an interlocutor’s statements with bukang ‘ neg ’
styleExampleTitle

Speaker-2: bukang, de punya pacar\\
neg 3sg poss date\\

[Speaker-1: ‘(it was) her husband!’]\\
Speaker-2: ‘ no, (it was) her lover’ [081006-022-CvEx.0043-0045]

Finally, speakers employ bukang ‘ neg ’ to give contrastive negative responses to polar questions, as in the elicited example in ( Example_13.23 ). This example contrasts with the one in ( Example_13.13 ) in which the speaker uses tida ‘ neg ’ to respond to the same question as in ( Example_13.23 ). While tida ‘ neg ’ in ( Example_13.13 ) merely negates a verbal construction, bukang ‘ neg ’ in ( Example_13.23 ) marks contrastive negation, similar to its uses in ( Example_13.18 ) to ( Example_13.21 ). Again, speakers can add the correct response as in ( Example_13.23 ) or reply with bare bukang ‘ neg ’. (For more details on polar questions see § Para_13.2.2.)

styleExampleTitle
Contrastive uses of bukang ‘ neg ’ in responses to polar questions
styleExampleTitle

Speaker-2: bukang, dia balap\\
neg 3sg race\\

[About an accident:] [Speaker-1: ‘what did he do? (was he) drunk?’]\\
Speaker-2: ‘ no, (it happened because) he was racing (his motorbike)’ [Elicited MY131126.001]
summary: Bukang ‘neg’ has three main functions: it negates nonverbal clauses, marks contrastive negation, and serves as a negative response to polar questions. It typically precedes nominal or quantifier predicates in nonverbal clauses, though prepositional predicates are negated instead by tida/tra. In contrastive uses, bukang can occur before the predicate or clause-initially, and speakers can use it alone or with an explicit alternative to contradict a prior statement or answer a polar question.

text: In Papuan Malay, three types of interrogative clauses can be distinguished: (1) content, or information questions which elicit new information (§ Para_13.2.1 ), (2) polar questions which elicit yes-no answers (§ Para_13.2.2 ), and (3) alternative questions which require the interlocutor to choose the supposedly right answer from a list of possible answers (§ Para_13.2.3 ).
summary: Papuan Malay has three types of interrogative clauses: content questions, which ask for new information; polar questions, which expect yes-no answers; and alternative questions, which ask the interlocutor to choose the correct answer from a set of possibilities. These three clause types are distinguished by the kind of response they elicit.

text: In Papuan Malay, content questions eliciting new information are formed with the interrogatives, as discussed in § Para_5.8. The discussion of their positions and functions within the clause entails a description of content questions. Therefore, content questions are not further discussed here.
summary: In Papuan Malay, content questions that ask for new information are formed with interrogatives. Since the positions and functions of these interrogatives within the clause are already discussed elsewhere, content questions are not further described here.

text: Papuan Malay polar questions, that is questions that elicit yes-no answers, can be unmarked and neutral, or marked and biased, as shown in § Para_13.2.2.1 and § Para_13.2.2.2, respectively. Both sections also describe how polar questions are answered.
summary: Papuan Malay polar questions, which seek yes-no answers, may be either unmarked and neutral or marked and biased. The passage also notes that both of the cited sections explain how such polar questions are answered.

text:
Generally speaking, unmarked polar questions are “neutral with respect to the answer the speaker expects”. That is, neutral questions do not indicate whether speakers would like their interlocutors to answer with ``yes'' or with ``no''. More specifically, polar questions can express positive polarity or negative polarity. A negative polar question differs “from the positive question in communicating [ ] that the speaker already has his own opinion, but that he is interested in getting the hearer’s reaction”.

These observations also apply to Papuan Malay, as demonstrated in the examples in ( Example_13.24 ) to ( Example_13.30 ).

Syntactically, the examples show that neutral polar questions have the same structure as the corresponding declarative clauses. The only distinction between the two clause types is that polar questions are marked with a rising intonation, as shown in ( Example_13.24a ).

The examples also show that polar questions can express positive polarity as in ( Example_13.24 ), ( Example_13.25 ), ( Example_13.27 ), and ( Example_13.29 ), or negative polarity as in ( Example_13.26 ), ( Example_13.28 ), and ( Example_13.30 ).

Furthermore, the examples in ( Example_13.24 ) to ( Example_13.30 ) show how neutral polar questions are answered. Polar questions with positive answers are presented in ( Example_13.24 ) to ( Example_13.26 ), and those with negative answers in ( Example_13.27 ) to ( Example_13.29 ). An alternative strategy to answer polar questions is illustrated in ( Example_13.30 ).

Positive answers to polar questions are typically formed with affirmative yo ‘yes’ or the interjection mm-mm ‘mhm’. This applies to positive questions as in ( Example_13.24 ) and ( Example_13.25 ), as well as to negative ones as in ( Example_13.26 ). In answering, speakers may also echo part of the question and/or provide additional information, as in ( Example_13.24b ) and ( Example_13.26b ).

Negative answers to neutral positive or negative polar questions are formed in three ways, as discussed in § Para_13.1.1.4 and § Para_13.1.2. Negative replies to polar questions are formed with tida ‘ neg ’ as shown in ( Example_13.13 ), repeated as ( Example_13.27 ), or with the negative existential phrase tida/ tra ada ‘(it) doesn’t exist’, as in ( Example_13.14 ), repeated as ( Example_13.28 ), when negating verbal constructions. Negative answers to polar questions are formed with bukang ‘ neg ’, as in ( Example_13.23 ), repeated as ( Example_13.29 ), when negating nonverbal constructions.

At times, speakers employ an alternative strategy to respond to polar questions as shown in ( Example_13.30 ). Speakers may reply to a polar question without giving an explicit answer in the affirmative or negative. Instead they provide additional information and leave it to their interlocutor to interpret this answer as a positive or a negative reply. This is shown with the implied negative answer in ( Example_13.30b ). When interlocutors do not know the answer, they typically reply with tida/ tra taw ‘(I) don’t know’.

summary: Unmarked polar questions in Papuan Malay are neutral about whether the expected answer is yes or no, and they have the same syntax as declarative clauses, differing only in rising intonation. The language allows both positive and negative polar questions, and answers may be given with affirmative forms like yo ‘yes’ or mm-mm ‘mhm’, with negative forms such as tida, tida/tra ada, or bukang depending on the construction, or by giving an indirect response that leaves the polarity to be inferred.

text:
Marked polar questions are defined as questions which convey a bias toward the expected answer, hence “biased” questions ( in ). Biased questions allow speakers “to express [ their] belief that a particular answer is likely to be correct and to request assurance that this belief is true”. More specifically, positively biased questions signal that the speaker is in favor of a positive answer, while negatively biased questions indicate that the speaker expects a negative answer.

Papuan Malay biased questions are presented in ( Example_13.31 ) to ( Example_13.35 ). While the corpus contains both positively and negatively biased questions, positively biased ones, as in ( Example_13.31 ) to ( Example_13.33 ), occur much more often than negatively biased ones, as in ( Example_13.34 ) or ( Example_13.35 ).

Biased questions are usually formed with the tags to ‘right?’ or e ‘eh?’. Prosodically, these questions are marked with a rising pitch on the tag (see § Para_5.13.1 for more details concerning the semantics of both tags). The examples in ( Example_13.31a ) and ( Example_13.32a ) show positive bias, while ( Example_13.34a ) and ( Example_13.35a ) show negative bias, using the negator tida/ tra ‘ neg ’. Less often, a positive bias is marked with affirmative yo ‘yes’ as in ( Example_13.33a ). Answers to biased polar questions follow the same patterns as answers to unbiased ones, as discussed in § Para_13.2.2.1.

summary: Marked polar questions are biased questions that signal the speaker’s expectation that a particular answer is likely, with positive bias favoring a positive answer and negative bias favoring a negative one. In Papuan Malay, both types occur, but positive bias is much more frequent, and these questions are usually formed with the tags *to* ‘right?’ or *e* ‘eh?’ accompanied by rising pitch on the tag; less often, positive bias is marked with affirmative *yo* ‘yes*. Answers to these questions follow the same patterns as answers to unbiased polar questions.

text:
In Papuan Malay, alternative questions are formed with the alternative-marking conjunction ka ‘or’ (see also § Para_14.2.2.2 ). They require the interlocutor to choose the supposedly right answer from a list of possible answers, as shown in ( Example_13.36 ) to ( Example_13.41 ).

The alternatives can be overtly listed as in ( Example_13.36 ) or ( Example_13.37 ), in which case they are linked with postposed ka ‘or’. The question can also contain just one proposition and its negation, as in ( Example_13.38 ) or ( Example_13.39 ), in which case the proposition is marked with ka ‘or’ followed by negator tida ‘ neg ’. Rather often, though, the negator is omitted, as in ( Example_13.40 ) and ( Example_13.41 ).

bapa pake kartu apa ka? AS ka? Simpati ka?\\
father use card what or AS or Simpati or\\

‘you (‘father’) use what (kind of SIM) card? AS or Simpati?’ [081014-016-Cv.0012]

sa tu biasa bilang sama ana ana di skola,\\
1sg d.dist be.usual say with rdp child at school\\
sala ka? benar ka?\\
be.wrong or be.true or\\

‘I ( emph ) usually ask the kids in school, ``(is this) right or wrong?''' [081014-015-Cv.0029]

kira kira bisa kenal bapa ka tida?\\
rdp think be.able know father or neg \\

‘do you think you can recognize me (‘father’) or not?’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1301]

mama Rahab ada datang ke ruma ka tida?\\
mother Rahab exist come to house or neg \\

‘did mother Rahab come ( emph ) to the house or not?’ [081110-003-Cv.0001]

de su datang ka?\\
3sg already come or\\

‘did he already come or (not)?’ [080925-003-Cv.0138]

ko ada karet ka?\\
2sg exist rubber or\\

‘do you have rubber bands or (not)?’ [081110-004-Cv.0008]
summary: In Papuan Malay, alternative questions are formed with the conjunction ka ‘or’ and require the addressee to choose the correct answer from a set of alternatives. The alternatives may be stated explicitly and linked by postposed ka, or the question may present a proposition and its negation, with ka followed by tida ‘not’; in many cases, however, the negator is omitted.

text: In Papuan Malay, three different types of directive clauses can be distinguished: imperatives and hortatives (§ Para_13.3.1 ), permissions and obligations (§ Para_13.3.2 ), and prohibitives (§ Para_13.3.3 ). They are used with any kind of predicate. Syntactically, directive clauses have the same structure as declarative clauses.
summary: Papuan Malay has three types of directive clauses: imperatives and hortatives, permissions and obligations, and prohibitives. These clauses can be used with any kind of predicate, and syntactically they have the same structure as declarative clauses.

text:
Papuan Malay employs imperatives and hortatives to issues commands. Imperatives always involve the second person, given that the addressee is the one who is expected to carry out the requested action, as shown in ( Example_13.42 ) to ( Example_13.46 ). In hortatives, by contrast, any person other than the addressee is expected to carry out the requested action. Hence, hortatives involve first and third persons, as shown in ( Example_13.47 ) to ( Example_13.51 ). In addition, Papuan Malay also employs a number of strategies to strengthen or soften commands, as demonstrated in ( Example_13.52 ) to ( Example_13.61 ).

Imperative constructions have a second person subject, as shown in ( Example_13.42 ) and ( Example_13.43 ). The clauses in ( Example_13.42a ) and ( Example_13.43a ) are formed with second singular ko ‘ 2sg ’ subjects. Depending on the context they can receive a declarative or an imperative reading. It is also possible to omit the addressee, as demonstrated in ( Example_13.42b ) and ( Example_13.43b ). Single word imperatives, as in ( Example_13.42b ), are rare, however. (The uses of suda ‘already’ in directive clauses, as in ( Example_13.43b ), are discussed together with the examples in ( Example_13.54 ) and ( Example_13.55 ).)

styleExampleTitle
Imperatives: Syntactic structure Documentation: bangung ‘wake up’ 081006-022-CvEx.0081, 080918-001-CvNP.0038; pulang ‘go home’ 081006-025-CvEx.0013, 081006-007-Cv.0001.

-13pt

More examples of imperatives clauses are presented in ( Example_13.44 ) to ( Example_13.46 ), with second person singular addressees in ( Example_13.44 ) and ( Example_13.46 ), and second person plural addressees in ( Example_13.45 ). These examples also illustrate that imperatives are formed with trivalent verbs as in ( Example_13.44 ), bivalent verbs as in ( Example_13.45 ), or monovalent verbs such as stative diam ‘be quiet’ in ( Example_13.46 ); see also monovalent dynamic pulang ‘go home’ in ( Example_13.43 ).

[A mother addressing her young sons:] ‘[hey, you two go bathe in the sea already!,] then you two wash (your) trousers there!’ [080917-006-CvHt.0007]

‘ you don’t talk again!, you be quiet!’ [081029-004-Cv.0072]

Hortatives are typically expressed with clause-initial biar ‘let’. It exhorts the addressee to let or allow the desired future state of affairs come true, as illustrated in ( Example_13.47 ) to ( Example_13.50 ).

kalo nanti tong maing biar sa cadangang!\\

‘later when we play (volleyball), let me be a reserve!’ [081109-001-Cv.0154]

‘ let us live there!’ [081110-008-CvNP.0091]

yo, biar de juga liat sa!\\

‘yes, let her also see me!’ [081015-005-NP.0013]

let 3pl rdp mock father neg rdp what right?\\

‘ let them mock me (‘father’)!, it doesn’t matter, right?’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0180]

First person plural hortatives can also be formed without biar ‘let’, as shown in ( Example_13.51 ). In this case, the context shows whether the utterance is a hortative such as the first kitong dua pulang ‘(let) the two of us go home!’ token, or a declarative such as the second occurrence of kitong dua pulang ‘the two of us went home’.

First person plural hortatives without clause-initial biar ‘let’
styleExampleTitle

dia bilang, Ø kitong dua pulang! trus kitong dua pulang\\
3sg say 1pl two go.home next 1pl two go.home\\

‘he said, ‘ (let) the two of us go home!’ then the two of us went home’ [081015-005-NP.0035]

Papuan Malay also uses a number of strategies to strengthen or soften commands. Strengthening is illustrated in ( Example_13.52 ) to ( Example_13.55 ) and softening in ( Example_13.56 ) to ( Example_13.61 ).

Speakers can add ayo ‘come on’ or suda ‘already’ to commands or requests to make them more urgent and to strengthen them. Urgency-marking ayo ‘come on’ can occur clause-initially, as in the imperative in ( Example_13.52 ) and in the hortative in ( Example_13.53 ), or clause-finally, also in ( Example_13.52 ); ayo ‘come on!’ is unattested in hortatives with third persons. Urgency-marking suda ‘already’, by contrast, always takes a postpredicate position as in the imperative in ( Example_13.54 ) and the hortative in ( Example_13.55 ).

styleExampleTitle
Strengthening commands with ayo ‘come on’ or suda ‘already’
styleExampleTitle

‘ come on!, go to Ise, come on!’ [080917-008-NP.0065]

ey, kam dua pi mandi di laut suda!\\
hey! 2pl two go bathe at sea already\\

‘hey, you two go bathe in the sea already!’ [080917-006-CvHt.0007]

ana kecil biar dong makang suda!\\
child be.small let 3pl eat just\\

‘(as for) the small children, let them eat already!’ [081002-001-CvNP.0051]

Requests or commands can be softened by adding clause-initial coba ‘try’ as in ( Example_13.56 ), mari ‘hither, (come) here’ as in ( Example_13.57 ), or tolong ‘please’ (literally ‘help’) as in ( Example_13.58 ). This applies most often to imperatives, as in ( Example_13.56 ) and ( Example_13.58 ), and less often to hortatives, as in ( Example_13.57 ).

styleExampleTitle
Softening commands with clause-initial coba ‘try’, mari ‘hither, (come) here’, or tolong ‘help’
styleExampleTitle

sa bilang, coba ko tanya dorang!\\

‘I said, `` try asking them!''' [081025-008-Cv.0076]

a, mari kitong turung olaraga!\\

‘ah, come, (let) us go down (to the beach) to do sports!’ [080917-001-CvNP.0003]

tolong ceritra tu plang plang!\\
help tell d.dist rdp be.slow\\
summary: Papuan Malay uses imperatives to issue commands to second-person addressees, while hortatives are used when the expected actor is a first- or third-person participant. Imperatives may have overt or omitted second-person subjects and can be formed with tri-, bi-, or monovalent verbs; hortatives are often marked with clause-initial biar ‘let,’ though first-person plural hortatives may also occur without it. Commands can be strengthened with ayo ‘come on’ or suda ‘already,’ and softened with coba ‘try,’ mari ‘come here,’ or tolong ‘please.’

text:
[Addressing another adult:] ‘ please, talk ( emph ) slowly!’ [081015-005-NP.0015]

Requests or commands can also be mitigated by adding in postpredicate position the temporal ad verb dulu ‘first, in the past’ as in ( Example_13.59 ), the focus ad verb saja ‘just’ as in ( Example_13.60 ), or the clause-final tag e ‘eh?’ as in ( Example_13.61 ). (For more details on adverbs see § Para_5.4 and on tags see § Para_5.13.1.)

styleExampleTitle
Softening commands with clause-final dulu ‘first, in the past’, saja ‘just’, or e ‘eh’
styleExampleTitle

sabar dulu!, sabar dulu!\\
be.patient first be.patient first\\

‘be patient for now!, be patient for now!’ [080921-004b-CvNP.0051]

sa blang, jalang saja!\\
1pl say walk just\\

‘I said, ``just walk!''' [080917-008-NP.0117]

ko kasi sama kaka mantri e?!\\
2sg give to oSb male.nurse eh\\

‘give (the keys) to the male nurse, eh?!’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0167]
summary: Requests and commands can be softened by adding certain elements after the predicate: the temporal adverb *dulu* ‘first, in the past,’ the focus adverb *saja* ‘just,’ or the clause-final tag *e* ‘eh?’. The examples show these forms being used to make imperatives less direct, such as “be patient for now,” “just walk,” and “give the keys to the male nurse, eh?”

text:
Papuan Malay permissions are expressed with the auxiliary verb bole ‘may’, as illustrated in ( Example_13.62 ) to ( Example_13.65 ), while obligations are formed with the auxiliary verb harus ‘have to’, as shown in ( Example_13.66 ) and ( Example_13.67 ).

Permission-marking bole ‘may’ most often occurs in single-word clauses, following a clause which depicts the permitted event or state, as in ( Example_13.62 ) or ( Example_13.63 ). Less often, bole ‘may’ occurs between the subject and the predicate, as in ( Example_13.64 ). Only rarely, bole ‘may’ occurs clause-initially, where it has scope over the entire clause, as ( Example_13.65 ).

styleExampleTitle
Permissions with bole ‘may’
styleExampleTitle

kamu mo pacar, bole\\
2pl want date may\\

[Addressing teenagers:] ‘(if) you want to date (someone) you may / are allowed to (do so)’ [081011-023-Cv.0269]

ko mancing dari jembatang, bole\\
2sg fish from bridge may\\

[Addressing her son:] ‘(if) you’re fishing from the bridge, (you) may (do so) / are allowed to (fish)’ [081025-003-Cv.0058]

setiap kegiatang apa saja dorang bole kerja\\

‘whatever activity, they may / are allowed to carry (it) out’ [080923-007-Cv.0013]

kalo tinggal di Arbais, bole ko tokok sama sama\\

dengang kaka\\
with oSb\\

‘[my husband said, ‘(here in my village) don’t extract and crush the sago, you just knead and filter it,] when you’re staying in Arbais, (it is) allowed (that) you (extract and) crush (the sago) together with (your) older sibling’ [081014-007-CvEx.0058]

Obligation-marking harus ‘have to’ typically takes a prepredicate position, as in ( Example_13.66 ). Alternatively, harus ‘have to’ can occur clause-initially, where it has scope over the entire clause and reinforces the obligation, as in ( Example_13.67 ).

bli pecis, sa harus ambil senter\\

harus kitong baik deng orang\\
have.to 1pl be.good with person\\

‘we have to ( emph ) be / (it’s) obligatory (that) we are good to (other) people’ [081110-008-CvNP.0166]
summary: Papuan Malay expresses permission with the auxiliary *bole* ‘may’ and obligation with *harus* ‘have to’. *Bole* most often follows the clause describing the permitted event, but it can also appear between the subject and predicate or, more rarely, clause-initially with scope over the whole clause. *Harus* usually occurs before the predicate, and when clause-initial it emphasizes the obligation.

text:
Papuan Malay prohibitives are typically formed with the negative imperative jangang ‘ neg.imp, don’t’. Its main function is to signal the addressee that the action of the verb is forbidden, as illustrated in ( Example_13.68 ) to ( Example_13.71 ). Quite often, however, a prohibitive is softened, as shown in ( Example_13.73 ) to ( Example_13.77 ).

The main function of negative imperative jangang ‘ neg.imp ’, with its short form jang, is to signal a straight-out prohibitive. It occurs between the subject and the predicate, as in ( Example_13.68 ) and ( Example_13.69 ), or clause-initially where it has scope over the entire clause and reinforces the prohibitive, as in ( Example_13.70 ) and ( Example_13.71 ). Besides, speakers also employ jangang ‘ neg.imp ’ as stand-alone clauses which provide a response to a preceding prohibitive, in the sense of ``(I would) never (do such a thing)'', as in ( Example_13.72 ).

styleExampleTitle

Wili ko jangang gara gara tanta dia itu!\\

‘ don’t you go!’ [081025-006-Cv.0192]

Prohibitives can be softened by employing tida/ tra bole ‘shouldn’t’ (literally ‘may not’). Most often, tida/ tra bole ‘may not’ occurs between the subject and the predicate, as in ( Example_13.73 ) and ( Example_13.74 ). Alternatively, although rarely, it occurs clause-initially, where it has scope over the entire clause, as in ( Example_13.75 ). In addition, speakers use tida/ tra bole ‘may not’ as stand-alone clauses, which refer back to the speakers’ own or their interlocutors’ preceding statements about a state of affairs, as in ( Example_13.76 ) and ( Example_13.77 ), respectively.

text:
This chapter describes how Papuan Malay combines constituents such as clauses or phrases by overt marking with conjunctions. The Papuan Malay conjunctions can be divided into two major groups, those combining same-type constituents, such as clauses with clauses, and those linking different-type constituents, such as verbs with clauses. In combining constituents, the conjunctions belong to neither of the conjuncts they combine in semantic terms. They do, however, form intonation units with the constituents they mark. Most conjunctions occur at the left periphery of the clause. Typically, an intonational break separates the conjunction from a preceding constituent. A second strategy to combine constituents is juxtaposition which is mentioned only briefly.

Papuan Malay has 21 conjunctions which link same-type constituents and two which combine different-type constituents. Most of the conjunctions conjoining same-type constituents link clauses with clauses. Traditionally, clause-linking conjunctions are divided into coordinating and subordinating ones: “coordinating conjunctions are those that assign equal rank to the conjoined elements” whereas “subordinating conjunctions are those that assign unequal rank to the conjoined elements, marking one of them as subordinate to the other”. Modifying this terminology by employing the more general term “dependency” rather than “subordination”, defines the distinction between coordination and dependency as follows:

quote
In a coordination structure of the type A(-link-)B, A and B are structurally symmetrical in some sense, whereas in a dependency structure of the type X(-link-)Y, X and Y are not symmetrical, but either X or Y is the head and the other element is a dependent.
quote

According to, this distinction between coordination and dependency in terms of symmetry “is often thought of as a difference in the syntactic/structural relations of the elements”. As points out, however, “it is sometimes not evident whether a construction exhibits a coordination relation or a dependency relation”; this applies, for instance, to “languages that lack agreement and case-marking”.

The lack of a clear opposition between coordination and dependency in terms of structural relations also applies to clause combining in Papuan Malay: clauses marked with a conjunction are not distinct from unmarked clauses in terms of their morphosyntax and word order. This is shown in ( Example_14.1 ) to ( Example_14.3 ) with purpose-marking supaya ‘so that’. Omitting the conjunction from the two purpose clauses in ( Example_14.1 ) leaves two grammatically complete and correct clauses: saya harus kas makang dia ‘I have to give him/her food’ and dia kenal saya lebi ‘he/she can know me better’.

styleExampleTitle
Purpose marking supaya ‘so that’ linking two clauses
styleExampleTitle

saya harus kas makang dia, supaya dia kenal saya lebi dekat, supaya de bisa taw saya punya nama\\
1sg have.to give eat 3sg so.that 3sg know 1sg more near so.that 3sg be.able know 1sg poss name\\
‘I have to give him/her food so that he/she can know me better, so that he/she can know my name’ [080919-004-NP.0079]

When a conjunction is missing an argument, the result is still a grammatically complete and correct clause. In the purpose clause in ( Example_14.2 ), for instance, the subject obat ‘medicine’ is elided. This elision, however, does not signify a grammaticalized gap that signals the dependent status of the purpose clause marked with supaya ‘so that’. Instead, the elision is due to the fact that speakers often omit arguments and other constituents if these can be inferred. In ( Example_14.2 ) the elided subject obat ‘medicine’ is understood from the context.

styleExampleTitle
Purpose clause with elided subject argument
styleExampleTitle

ibu itu de mo kasi obat, tapi ko harus priksa dara, supaya Ø harus cocok\\
woman d.dist 3sg want give medicine but 2sg have.to check blood so.that have.to be.suitable\\
‘that lady, she wants to give (you) medicine, but you have to (get your) blood checked so that (the medicine) fits’ [080917-007-CvHt.0003]

In Papuan Malay, elision of core arguments is not limited to clauses marked with conjunctions. It is a generalized phenomenon, as demonstrated with the reported direct speech in ( Example_14.3 ) (see also § Para_11.1 ). The original utterance is given in ( Example_14.3a ), while in ( Example_14.3b ) the elided constituents are given in brackets, such as purposive supaya ‘so that’ Alternatively, the conjunction sampe ‘until, with the result that’ could fill this slot. or the subject of the purpose clause, kaki ‘foot, leg’.

styleExampleTitle
Elision as a generalized phenomenon
styleExampleTitle

malam Kapolsek bilang, kalo dapat tembak kaki pata\\
night head.of.district.police say if get shoot foot break\\
5pt

malam Kapolsek bilang, kalo [kam] dapat [dia,] tembak [de pu] kaki [ supaya] [kaki] pata\\
night head.of.district.police say if [ 2pl] get [ 3sg] shoot [ 3sg poss] foot [so.that] [foot] break\\
[Reply to the question about who the police were looking for:] ‘[(they’re looking for Martin,] (last) night the head of the district police said, ``if (you) get (him), shoot (his) leg ( so that it) breaks''' [081011-009-Cv.0048/0050]\\

This data shows that, in terms of structural relations, the opposition between coordination and dependency does not apply to purpose-marking supaya ‘so that’. Neither does the distinction apply to the other clause-combining conjunctions.

Given that cross-linguistically this lack of a clear-cut opposition between coordination and dependency in terms of structural relations is not uncommon, suggests defining ``both coordination and dependency in semantic terms''. He also notes, however, that even the distinction on semantic grounds “is often difficult to apply” ( Haspelmath.2007c; see also; ).
summary: Papuan Malay uses overt conjunctions to combine constituents, with most conjunctions linking clauses and occurring at the left edge of the clause; juxtaposition is also possible but only briefly mentioned. The passage argues that, unlike a traditional coordination/dependency contrast based on structural asymmetry, clause linking in Papuan Malay does not show a clear morphosyntactic difference between conjoined and unmarked clauses, as illustrated by purpose-marking *supaya* ‘so that’ and by widespread argument elision. It concludes that coordination and dependency are better defined in semantic terms, though even this distinction can be difficult to apply.

text:
This difficulty also applies to clause combining in Papuan Malay. Therefore, in discussing clause combining in Papuan Malay at this point in the current research, no attempt is being made to distinguish between coordination and dependency on semantic grounds. Instead, this chapter describes the following aspects: (1) the meaning which the different Papuan Malay conjunctions convey, (2) the position which a given conjunction takes within its clause, and (3) the position which the clause marked with a conjunction takes vis-à-vis the clause it is conjoined with. For lack of a better term, the clause that is not marked with a conjunction is labeled as the ``unmarked clause'' throughout the remainder of this chapter. This label is used as a working term only for practical purposes.

In addition to the 21 conjunctions combining same-type constituents, Papuan Malay also has two conjunctions which link different-type constituents, namely complementizer bahwa ‘so that’ and relativizer yang ‘ rel ’. Both are subordinating conjunctions, in that they “serve to integrate a clause into some larger construction”, adopting Schachter.2007 definition. Complementizer bahwa ‘that’ marks a clause as an argument of the verb as illustrated in ( Example_14.4 ), while relativizer yang ‘ rel ’ integrates a relative clause within a noun phrase as demonstrated in ( Example_14.5 ).

styleExampleTitle
Conjunctions combining different-type constituents
styleExampleTitle

sa cuma taw bahwa de ada di sini\\
1sg just know that 3sg exist at l.prox\\
‘I just know that he was here’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0180]

baru Iskia dia pegang sa punya lutut yang tida baik\\
and.then Iskia 3sg hold 1sg poss knee rel neg be.good\\
‘and then Iskia held my knee that is not well’ [080916-001-CvNP.0003]

Conjunctions linking same-type constituents are described in § Para_14.2 and those linking different-type constituents are discussed in § Para_14.3. Unless mentioned otherwise, the clausal conjunctions combine clauses with same-subject coreference as well as those with a switch in reference. Juxtaposition is briefly mentioned in § Para_14.4. The main points of this chapter are summarized in § Para_14.5.
summary:
The passage says that, for Papuan Malay clause combining, the chapter does not try to distinguish coordination from dependency on semantic grounds. Instead, it focuses on the meanings of conjunctions, their position within the clause, and the position of the clause they mark, using “unmarked clause” as a practical term for the clause without a conjunction.

It also notes that Papuan Malay has two subordinating conjunctions linking different types of constituents: the complementizer bahwa ‘that’, which marks a clause as a verb argument, and the relativizer yang ‘rel’, which introduces a relative clause inside a noun phrase. The chapter then separates discussion of conjunctions linking same-type versus different-type constituents, and briefly mentions juxtaposition.

text: This section discusses conjunctions which combine same-type constituents. In terms of the semantic relations which they signal, the conjunctions fall into six groups, that is conjunctions marking addition (§ Para_14.2.1 ), alternative (§ Para_14.2.2 ), time and/or conditions (§ Para_14.2.3 ), consequence (§ Para_14.2.4 ), contrast (§ Para_14.2.5 ), and similarity (§ Para_14.2.6 ).
summary: The passage explains that conjunctions combine constituents of the same type. It classifies them into six semantic groups: addition, alternative, time and/or condition, consequence, contrast, and similarity.

text:
Addition-marking conjunctions combine constituents denoting events, states, or entities which are “closely linked and valid simultaneously”, employing Rudolph.1996 definition.

Papuan Malay employs three addition-marking conjunctions. Most often addition is encoded with the comitative preposition dengang ‘with’ (670 tokens); as a conjunction, it typically conjoins noun phrases, as discussed in § Para_14.2.1.1. Much less often, Papuan Malay employs conjunctive dang ‘and’ (24 tokens); it typically joins two clauses, as described in § Para_14.2.1.2. Even less often, addition is encoded with the goal-oriented preposition sama ‘to’; as a conjunction it links noun phrases with human referents (8 tokens), as shown in § Para_14.2.1.3. (For details on variation in word class membership see § Para_5.14.)
summary: Papuan Malay has three addition-marking conjunctions that link constituents denoting events, states, or entities that are closely connected and valid at the same time. The most frequent is the comitative preposition **dengang** ‘with’, which typically conjoins noun phrases, followed by **dang** ‘and’, which usually joins clauses, and the least frequent is the goal-oriented preposition **sama** ‘to’, which links noun phrases with human referents.

text:
The comitative preposition dengang ‘with’, with its short form deng, typically conjoins noun phrases (654 tokens). The conjoined referents can be animate as in ( Example_14.6 ), or inanimate as in ( Example_14.7 ). The fact that Papuan Malay employs the same marker for “ noun phrase conjunction and comitative phrases” suggests that, in terms of Stassen.2013b typology, Papuan Malay is a `` with -language''. Occasionally, deng(ang) ‘with’ also links verb phrases (16 tokens) as in ( Example_14.8 ). The linking of clauses with comitative dengang ‘with’ is unattested in the corpus. (Besides, comitative dengang ‘with’ is also used to encode inclusory conjunction constructions, as discussed in § Para_6.1.4; for a detailed discussion of preposition dengang ‘with’, see § Para_10.2.1.)

bapa dengang bapa-tua pi biking kebung \\
father with older.uncle go make garden \\
‘father and uncle went to work (together) in the garden ’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0629]

apa biologi dengang apa astronomi dengang bahasa Inggris\\
what biology with what astronomy with language England\\
[About a school competition] ‘[later they’ll participate in the Olympiad contest in,] what-is-it, biology and, what-is-it, astronomy and English’ [081115-001a-Cv.0111-0113]

nene jam dua malam datang deng menangis\\
grandmother hour two night come with cry\\
‘at two o’clock in the morning grandmother came crying’ (Lit. ‘come with cry’) [081014-008-CvNP.0001]
summary: The comitative preposition *dengang* ‘with’ (short form *deng*) is mainly used to conjoin noun phrases, whether the referents are animate or inanimate, which suggests that Papuan Malay is a “with-language” in Stassen’s typology. It can occasionally link verb phrases, but clause linking with comitative *dengang* is not found in the corpus.

text:
The conjunction dang ‘and’ typically links two clauses (168 tokens), as in ( Example_14.9 ). Less often, it links noun phrases (24 tokens) as in ( Example_14.10 ) and ( Example_14.11 ), or verb phrases (10 tokens) as in ( Example_14.12 ). Usually, the noun phrases have human referents as in ( Example_14.10 ); coordination of inanimate referents, as in ( Example_14.11 ), is rare.

de pegang de punya prahu, dang de dayung, dang de bilang, \\
3sg hold 3sg poss boat and 3sg paddle and 3sg say\\
‘he took his boat and he paddled and he said, ’ [080917-008-NP.0018]

sa kas taw mama dang mama-ade, nanti kam \\
1sg give know mother and aunt very.soon 2pl \\
‘I let mother and aunt know, ``later you ''' [080919-007-CvNP.0001]

de suda taw ruma dang kampung\\
3sg already know house and village\\
‘he already knew the house and the village’ [080923-006-CvNP.0002]

pagi helikopter turung dang kembali ke Anggruk\\
