‘in the morning the helicopter came down and returned to Anggruk’ [081011-022-Cv.0228]
summary: The conjunction **dang** ‘and’ most commonly links two clauses, but it can also join noun phrases or, less often, verb phrases. When it coordinates noun phrases, the nouns usually refer to humans; coordination of inanimate noun phrases is rare.

text:
The goal-oriented preposition sama ‘to’ occasionally links noun phrases with human referents (8 tokens), as in ( Example_14.13 ). The coordination of clauses or verb phrases with sama ‘to’ is unattested in the corpus. Goal-oriented sama ‘to’ has trial word class membership. That is, besides being used as a preposition and an addition-marking conjunction, it is also used as the stative verb sama ‘be same’ (see § Para_5.14; see also § Para_10.2.2 for a detailed discussion of preposition sama ‘to’ and how it is distinct from comitative dengang ‘with’). As mentioned in § Para_10.2.2, the goal preposition sama ‘to’ is rather general in its meaning. Typically it translates with ‘to’ but depending on its context it also translates with ‘of, from, with’. For more information regarding the etymology of sama ‘to’, see Footnote Footnote_10.225 in § Para_10.2.2 (p. Footnote_10.225).

Aris sama Siduas i deng de i pu maytua, sama dep i, de i punya maytua\\
Aris to Siduas with 3sg poss wife to 3sg:poss 3sg poss wife\\
‘[all (of you will) be taken (on board,)] Aris and Siduas i and his wife i, and his i, his i wife’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0493/0497] The subscript letters indicate which personal pronouns have which referents.
summary: The goal-oriented preposition **sama** ‘to’ occasionally links noun phrases with human referents, but it is not attested in the corpus joining clauses or verb phrases. It has **triple word-class membership**: it functions as a preposition, an addition-marking conjunction, and the stative verb **sama** ‘be same’; its meaning is generally ‘to’, though in context it may also be translated as ‘of, from, with’.

text: In Papuan Malay, two conjunctions mark alternative, namely disjunctive ato ‘or’ (§ Para_14.2.2.1 ) and disjunctive ka ‘or’ (§ Para_14.2.2.2 ).
summary: Papuan Malay has two conjunctions used to mark alternative/disjunction: ato ‘or’ and ka ‘or’. These are described in separate sections of the grammar.

text:
Generally speaking, the notion of disjunction is defined as “a logical relationship between propositions” in the sense that “[i]f the logical disjunction of two propositions is true, then one or both of the component propositions can be true”.

In Papuan Malay, disjunction is marked with ato ‘or’ which always occurs at the left periphery of the constituents it combines. Most often, disjunctive ato ‘or’ joins clauses, as in ( Example_14.14 ). Also quite often, ato ‘or’ links noun phrases as in ( Example_14.15 ). Only rarely ato ‘or’ links prepositional phrases as in ( Example_14.16 ), or verb phrases as in ( Example_14.17 ).

kalo saya susa, ato saya biking acara, nanti dia bantu saya \\
if 1sg be.difficult or 1sg make ceremony very.soon 3sg help 1sg\\
‘if I have difficulties or I make a festivity, then he’ll help me’ [080919-004-NP.0065]

kalo tong pu uang satu juta, ato satu juta lima ratus, tong bisa bakar natal\\
if 1pl poss money one million or one million five hundred 1pl be.able burn Christmas\\
‘if we had one million or one million five hundred (thousand rupiah), we could have a Christmas party’ (Lit. ‘burn (the) Christmas (fire)’) [081006-017-Cv.0016]

jadi kalo dia, suku dari situ, dari Masep suda bunu orang di, a, Karfasia, ato di Waim, na \\
so if 3sg ethnic.group from l.med from Masep already kill person at umh Karfasia or at Waim well \\
‘so if it, the ethnic group from there, from Masep has already killed someone at, umh, Karfasia or at Waim, well ’ [081006-027-CvEx.0002]

dong bilang, a, tunggu minum dulu, ato makang dulu\\
3pl say ah! wait drink first or eat first\\
‘they said, ``ah, wait, please drink or eat''' (Lit. ‘drink first or eat first’) [080925-003-Cv.0111]\\
summary: In Papuan Malay, disjunction is expressed with ato ‘or,’ which is a left-peripheral particle placed before the constituents it links. It most commonly connects clauses and noun phrases, while links between prepositional phrases or verb phrases are rare.

text:
Disjunctive ka ‘or’ signals series or sequences of alternatives. Occurring at the right periphery of a constituent, it indicates that a list of alternatives is not exhaustive. That is, a few possible options are overtly mentioned, while others are implied. To make the notion of ``non-exhaustive list of alternatives'' explicit, the conjunction marks an interrogative as the final enumerated constituent. Typically, disjunctive ka ‘or’ links noun phrases, as in ( Example_14.18 ) and ( Example_14.19 ). In ( Example_14.18 ), the notion of a ``non-exhaustive list'' is implied, while in ( Example_14.19 ) it is overtly marked with apa ka ‘or something else’ (literally ‘what or’). Less often, ka ‘or’ combines prepositional phrases as in ( Example_14.20 ), or clauses as in ( Example_14.21 ); the linking of verbs with ka ‘or’ is unattested in the corpus. Another function of ka ‘or’, not discussed here, is to mark interrogative clauses (see § Para_13.2.3 ).

nanti banjir ka, hujang ka, guntur ka\\
very.soon flooding or rain or thunder or\\
‘[it’s not allowed to kill the snake otherwise] later (there’ll be) flooding, or rain, or thunder ( or something else)’ [081006-022-CvEx.0004]

sa deng kaka Petrus pikir, mungking klapa ka, apa ka yang ada di depang\\
1sg with oSb Petrus think maybe coconut or what or rel exist at front\\
[About a motorbike trip:] ‘I and older brother Petrus thought, ``maybe it is a coconut or something else that is in front (of us)''' [081023-004-Cv.0002]

ko lapor di umum ka, di keuangang ka\\
2sg report at general or at finance.affairs or\\
[About a government office:] ‘you (should) report to the general (office), or the finance (office) ( or some other office)’ [081005-001-Cv.0011]

waktu ko ada potong babi ka, potong ikang ka, ato dapat ikang ka kuskus ka, waktu lewat kasi saja\\
time 2sg exist cut pig or cut fish or or get fish or cuscus or time pass.by give just\\
‘[when (your) friends and relatives,] when you are carving a pig or carving fish ( or carving something else), or (when you) get a fish or cuscus (or something else), when (they) walk by, just share (it with them)’ [080919-004-NP.0060]
summary: Disjunctive **ka** ‘or’ marks a sequence of alternatives and, when placed at the right edge of a constituent, signals that the list is **non-exhaustive**, with additional options implied beyond those overtly mentioned. It typically links noun phrases, but can also combine prepositional phrases or clauses; verb linking with **ka** is not attested in the corpus. In some cases the non-exhaustive interpretation is made explicit by forms like **apa ka** ‘or something else,’ and **ka** also has another function as a marker of interrogative clauses.

text:
Papuan Malay conjunctions marking temporal relations indicate relative time; that is, the temporal reference point is determined by the context. Providing a reference point for the events or states depicted in the unmarked clause, time-marking conjunctions signal sequence relations, anteriority, or posteriority. Con\-dition-mark\-ing conjunctions introduce clauses which expresses conditions, while the unmarked clauses describe events or states which could come about once the conditions have been met.

In many languages, there is no distinction between conditional ``if'' and temporal ``when'' clauses, as point out. This also applies to Papuan Malay. Therefore, both types of linkings are discussed here.

This section describes five conjunctions: sequential trus ‘next’ (§ Para_14.2.3.1 ) and baru ‘and then’ (§ Para_14.2.3.2 ), anteriority-marking sampe ‘until’ (§ Para_14.2.3.3 ) and seblum ‘before’ (§ Para_14.2.3.4 ), and posteriority-marking/ conditional kalo ‘when, if’ (§ Para_14.2.3.5 ). Papuan Malay does not have a conjunction that marks temporal simultaneity between two clauses. Instead speakers use the common noun waktu ‘time’ when they want to signal that the events described in each clause happened at the same time, as in ( Footnote_Example_14.4 ) below:
-5pt

waktu saya tinggal di kampung sa kerja sperti laki laki\\
time 1sg stay at village 1sg work similar.to rdp husband\\
‘ when I lived in the village, I worked like a man’ (Lit. ‘ (at that) time’) [081014-007-Pr.0048]
summary:
Papuan Malay conjunctions marking temporal relations express relative time, with the reference point supplied by context; they can indicate sequence, anteriority, or posteriority, while condition-marking conjunctions introduce clauses whose conditions enable the unmarked clause. The language does not distinguish clearly between conditional “if” and temporal “when,” so both are discussed together.  

The text identifies five conjunctions: sequential *trus* ‘next’ and *baru* ‘and then,’ anteriority-marking *sampe* ‘until’ and *seblum* ‘before,’ and posteriority-marking/conditional *kalo* ‘when, if.’ Papuan Malay lacks a conjunction for temporal simultaneity; instead, speakers use the noun *waktu* ‘time’ to indicate that two events occurred at the same time.

text:
The sequential conjunction trus ‘next’ marks temporal relations between clauses or phra\-ses in an iconic way by organizing events in their logical and temporal order. When combining clauses, trus ‘next’ always occurs in clause-initial position. The conjunction has dual word class membership; it is also used as the monovalent verb trus ‘be continuous’ (see § Para_5.14 ).

In terms of subject reference, an initial investigation of the attested trus ‘next’ tokens in the corpus suggests the following. The conjunction more often links clauses with a switch in reference (269 tokens), as in ( Example_14.22 ), than those with same-subject coreference (101 tokens). This quantitative data modifies Donohue.2003 observations that trus ‘next’ “is a commonly used connective when there is same-subject coreference condition between clauses”. Less often, trus ‘next’ combines noun phrases, as in ( Example_14.23 ), or prepositional phrases, as in ( Example_14.24 ).

waktu Sofia lewat mandi to? di kamar mandi, trus Nusa juga lewat, Sofia ikat handuk, de mo lewat masuk ke kamar, trus Nusa de bicara dia\\
when Sofia pass.by bathe right? at room bathe next Nusa also pass.by Sofia tie.up towel 3sg want pass.by enter to room next Nusa 3sg speak 3sg\\
‘when Sofia passed by to bathe, right?, in the bathroom, then Nusa also passed by, Sofia had tied (her) towel (around her waist), she wanted to pass by (and) enter the (bath)room, then Nusa spoke to her’ [081115-001a-Cv.0263]

de pu potong selesay ambil ubi, trus daung petatas daung singkong, trus apa lagi sayur bayam\\
3sg poss cut finish get purple.yam next leaf sweet.potato leaf cassava next what again vegetable amaranth\\
[A recipe:] ‘(once) the cutting up (of the pig meat) is done, take purple yam, then sweet potato leaves, cassava leaves, then, what else, amaranth vegetables’ [081014-017-CvPr.0033]

jalang banyak to?, di atas, tenga, trus di laut, trus di pante sana\\
walk many right? at top middle next at sea then at coast l.dist\\
‘[I was confused (about) the road, you know,] (there) were many roads, right?, in the upper part (of the village), in the middle, and then at the sea, and then at the beach over there’ [081025-008-Cv.0018]
summary:
The sequential conjunction **trus** ‘next’ marks temporal relations between clauses or phrases in an iconic order, and when linking clauses it always appears in clause-initial position. It is also a separate verb meaning ‘be continuous.’  

Corpus data show that **trus** more often links clauses with a **switch in reference** than clauses with same-subject coreference, which revises earlier claims that it is commonly used when the subject is the same. Less often, it connects noun phrases or prepositional phrases.

text:
The sequential conjunction baru ‘and then’ most commonly also marks temporal succession by ordering events in their logical and temporal sequence, as shown in ( Example_14.25 ). In addition, although less often, the conjunction introduces contrast clauses, as illustrated in ( Example_14.26 ). The conjunction has trial word class membership; that is, besides being used as a conjunction, it is also used as the stative verb baru ‘be new’ and as the temporal ad verb baru 'recently' (see § Para_5.14; see also § Para_5.4.5 for its adverbial uses).

Typically, baru ‘and then’ occurs in clause-initial position where it marks an immediate subsequent event or action, similar to sequential trus ‘next’ (§ Para_14.2.3.1 ). Concurrently, however, the conjunction signals another piece of information, as shown in ( Example_14.25 ) (note that this example presents contiguous text). Depending on the context, the conjunction marks noteworthy parts and/or signals a new aspect or perspective regarding the event or discourse unfolding. In this case baru translates with ‘but then’, as in ( Example_14.25b ) or ‘and then’ as in ( Example_14.25c ). Alternatively, the conjunction signals that the event depicted in its clause does not occur until after the event of the preceding clause. In this case, it translates with ‘only then’, as in ( Example_14.25a ). In marking contrastive sequentiality, baru ‘and then’ differs from trus ‘next’ which indicates neutral sequentiality (see § Para_14.2.3.1 ).

As for subject reference, an initial inspection of the baru ‘and then’ tokens in the corpus suggests that the conjunction more often links clauses with a switch in reference (524 tokens), as in ( Example_14.25b ), than clauses with same-subject coreference (455 tokens), as in ( Example_14.25a and Example_14.25c ). In this respect, baru ‘and then’ behaves like trus ‘next’ (see § Para_14.2.3.1 ).

styleExampleTitle
Combining clauses with baru ‘and then’ in clause initial position: Sequential reading
styleExampleTitle

tong jaga dia i sampe jam satu, baru tong tidor,\\
1pl guard 3sg until hour one and.then 1pl sleep\\
[About a sick relative:] ‘we watched her until one o’clock, only then did we sleep’.
10pt

baru Pawlus de j sandar di de i pu badang begini,\\
and.then Pawlus 3sg lean at 3sg poss body like.this\\
‘ but then Pawlus was leaning against her body like this’
10pt

baru de j kas pata leher ke bawa di atas de i pu bahu\\
and.then 3sg give break neck to bottom at top 3sg poss shoulder \\
‘ and then he bent his neck down onto her shoulder’ (Lit. ‘give to break neck’) [080916-001-CvNP.0005-0006]

Occasionally, the conjunction occurs at the right periphery of a contrast clause. Summarizing what has been said before, it marks the propositional content of its clause as true despite the contents of the preceding unmarked clause. In this case, the conjunction receives the counter-expectational reading ‘after all’, as in ( Example_14.26 ). As this contrast-marking function of the conjunction is marginal, it is not further discussed in § Para_14.2.5.

styleExampleTitle
Combining clauses with baru ‘and then’ in clause final position: Counter-expectational reading
styleExampleTitle

sa tra akang kasi kaing, sa juga dinging stenga mati, ada anging baru\\
1sg neg will give cloth 1sg also be.cold half dead exist wind and.then\\
‘I wasn’t going to give (her my) cloth, I was also half dead (from being) cold, it was windy after all’ [081025-006-Cv.0048]
summary:
The conjunction **baru** ‘and then’ most commonly marks **temporal succession**, typically in clause-initial position, where it can indicate an immediate next event or a delayed event with readings such as ‘only then,’ ‘but then,’ or ‘and then.’ Less often, it introduces **contrast clauses**, including a marginal clause-final use with a counter-expectational meaning like ‘after all.’

In addition, **baru** is a **trial-class word**: besides functioning as a conjunction, it also serves as the stative verb **baru** ‘be new’ and the temporal adverb **baru** ‘recently.’ Corpus data suggest it more often links clauses with a **switch in reference** than with same-subject coreference, similar to **trus** ‘next,’ though **baru** differs from **trus** in expressing contrastive or noteworthy sequentiality rather than neutral sequence.

text:
The conjunction sampe ‘until’ introduces a temporal clause which follows the unmarked clause. The conjunction has trial word class membership; that is, besides being used as a conjunction, it is also used as the bivalent verb sampe ‘reach’ and as the temporal preposition sampe ‘until’ (see § Para_5.14; see also § Para_10.1.4 for its prepositional uses).

Usually, sampe ‘until’ marks anteriority. That is, it signals that the event or state of the unmarked clause occurs prior to that of the temporal clause, as shown in ( Example_14.27 ). Concurrently, sampe ‘until’ marks temporal extent in that it indicates that the event or state of the unmarked clause continues until the event or state of the temporal clause comes about. Depending on the context, temporal sampe ‘until’ can also receive a resultative reading in the sense of ``with the result that'', as in ( Example_14.28 ). Given that the resultative reading of sampe ‘until’ is the derived, marginal one, this result-marking function of sampe ‘until’ is not further discussed in § Para_14.2.4.

de harus taru di mata-hari, sampe de jadi papeda\\
3sg have.to put at sun until 3sg become sagu.porridge\\
[Before an ancestor had fire to heat water:] ‘[when he wanted to make sagu porridge,] he had to leave (the sago) out in the sun until it turned into sagu porridge’ [080922-010a-CvNF.007-0008]

Fredi pu tangang dia palungku kaca, jadi dia rabik, sampe brapa jahitang\\
Fredi poss hand 3sg punch glass so 3sg tear until several stitch\\
[About an accident:] ‘Fredi’s hand hit glass, so it was torn with the result that (he got) several stitches’ [081006-032-Cv.0066]
summary: The conjunction **sampe** ‘until’ introduces a temporal clause that follows the unmarked clause, and it has multiple word-class uses, also functioning as the verb ‘reach’ and as the temporal preposition ‘until.’ In its usual temporal use, it marks **anteriority** and **temporal extent**, indicating that the event in the unmarked clause occurs before and continues until the event in the temporal clause. In some contexts it can also have a **resultative** meaning ‘with the result that,’ though this use is described as derived and marginal.

text:
Anteriority-marking seblum ‘before’ also introduces a temporal clause. The conjunction seblum ‘before’ is historically derived from the aspectual ad verb blum ‘not yet’: se-blum ‘one-not.yet’ (see § Para_5.4.1 ). It indicates – similar to sampe ‘until’ – that the event or state of the unmarked clause occurs prior to that of the temporal clause. Unlike sampe ‘until’, however, seblum ‘before’ does not signal extent. The temporal clause with seblum ‘before’ can precede or follow the unmarked clause, as shown in ( Example_14.29 ) and ( Example_14.30 ), respectively. In the corpus, however, the temporal clause more often precedes the unmarked clause (21 tokens) rather than follows it (8 tokens).

de bilang, seblum kitong pergi ke kota, kitong cuci muka dulu\\
3sg say before 1pl go to city 1pl wash front first\\
‘he said, `` before we go to the city, we wash (our) faces first''' [080917-008-NP.0126]

saya suda punya rencana juga, seblum sa kluar\\
1sg already have plan also before 1sg go.out\\
‘[when I hunt without taking dogs, I leave in the night,] I also already have a plan before I leave’ [080919-004-NP.0002]
summary: *Seblum* ‘before’ introduces a temporal clause and is historically derived from *blum* ‘not yet’ with the prefix *se-*. It indicates that the event or state in the unmarked clause occurs before that of the temporal clause, similar to *sampe* ‘until’ but without implying extent. The *seblum* clause may come before or after the main clause, though it more often precedes it in the corpus.

text:
The conjunction kalo ‘when, if’ signals temporal relations, namely posteriority, and/or conditional relations between two clauses. The clause it introduces always precedes the unmarked clause.

Whether kalo ‘when, if’ receives a temporal reading as in ( Example_14.31 ) and ( Example_14.32 ), or a conditional reading, as in ( Example_14.33 ) and ( Example_14.34 ), is context-dependent. Quite often, though, both interpretations are possible, as shown in ( Example_14.35 ). As mentioned, this lack of a “distinction between ‘if’ clauses and ‘when’ clauses” is also found in other languages; examples are “Indonesian and certain languages of Papua New Guinea”.

When marking posteriority, kalo translates with ‘when’; it signals that the event or state of the unmarked main clause occurs subsequent to that of the temporal clause, as in ( Example_14.31 ). When the conjunction co-occurs with the retrospective ad verb suda ‘already’, or with its short form su, it projects these events or states to the future; in this case kalo translates with ‘once’. That is, in combination with suda ‘already’, the conjunction signals that the event or state of the unmarked clause will eventuate, once that of the temporal clause has come about, as in ( Example_14.32 ).

styleExampleTitle
Combining clauses with kalo ‘when/after’: Temporal reading
styleExampleTitle

kalo dong tendang de pu kaki tu, dia pegang bola\\
when 3pl kick 3sg poss foot d.dist 3sg hold ball\\
[About a football match:] ‘ when they kicked those legs of his, he grabbed the ball’ [081006-014-Cv.0004]

jadi kalo dong su tinggal di kota begini, dong snang tinggal, tida maw pulang ke kampung\\
so if 3pl already stay at city like.this 3pl feel.happy(.about) stay neg want go.home to village\\
‘so once they’ve lived in the city like this, they’re happy to stay (here), (they) don’t want to return home to the village’ [080927-009-CvNP.0059]

In a different context, the conjunction receives a conditional reading and signals, what calls, ``indicative conditional'' relations or ``counterfactual conditional'' relations. In such a context kalo translates with ‘if’. An indicative conditional relation indicates that it is possible for the condition presented in its clause to be met. In this case the event or state of the unmarked clause will also come about, as shown in ( Example_14.33 ). When conditional kalo ‘if’ co-occurs with retrospective suda ‘already’, the clause receives a counterfactual conditional reading. That is, it signals that the condition was not met in the past. If the condition had been met, however, then the event or state of the unmarked clause would also have come about. This is illustrated in ( Example_14.34 ).

styleExampleTitle
Combining clauses with kalo ‘if’: Conditional reading
styleExampleTitle

kalo ko alpa, kitong tra jalang\\
if 2sg be.absent 1pl neg walk\\
[Talking to her son about an upcoming trip:] ‘ if you play hooky, we won’t go’ [080917-003a-CvEx.0038]

kalo sa su pake em kaca-mata tu, mungking sa su gila\\
if 1sg already use uh glasses d.dist maybe 1sg already be.crazy\\
‘ if I’d been wearing, uh, those (sun)glasses, I might already be crazy’ [080919-005-Cv.0007]

Rather commonly, kalo ‘when, if’ allows both a temporal and a conditional reading, as in ( Example_14.35 ).

styleExampleTitle
Combining clauses with kalo ‘when, if’: Temporal and/or conditional reading
styleExampleTitle

kalo bapa datang, pluk bapa\\
when/if father come embrace father\\
‘ when/if you (‘father’) come (here), (I’ll) embrace you (‘father’)’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0360]
summary: The conjunction **kalo** ‘when, if’ links two clauses and can express either a temporal relation of posteriority or a conditional relation, with the clause it introduces always preceding the unmarked clause. Its interpretation depends on context: it may mean ‘when’ for temporal sequences, ‘if’ for indicative or counterfactual conditionals, and in many cases both readings are possible. When combined with **suda/su** ‘already’, it can project the event into the future in temporal uses (‘once’) or mark a past unrealized condition in counterfactual conditionals.

text: A consequence-marking conjunction indicates that the event or state of its clause is the outcome of an event or state depicted in the unmarked clause. Papuan Malay has five such conjunctions: resultative/ causal jadi ‘so, since’ (§ Para_14.2.4.1 ), purposive supaya ‘so that’ (§ Para_14.2.4.2 ), purposive untuk ‘for’ (§ Para_14.2.4.3 ), causal karna ‘because’ (§ Para_14.2.4.4 ), and causal gara-gara ‘because’ (§ Para_14.2.4.5 ). In addition, although rarely, temporal sampe ‘until’ has result-marking function in the sense of ``with the result that''; given that this function is marginal, it is discussed in § Para_14.2.3.3 and not here.
summary: Consequence-marking conjunctions express that the event or state in one clause results from the event or state in an unmarked clause. Papuan Malay has five such conjunctions: resultative/causal *jadi* ‘so, since’, purposive *supaya* ‘so that’ and *untuk* ‘for’, and causal *karna* and *gara-gara* ‘because’. The temporal conjunction *sampe* ‘until’ can rarely also mark result with the meaning ‘with the result that’, but this use is marginal.

text:
The resultative/ causal conjunction jadi ‘so, since’ most often marks a resultative relation between two clauses, as shown in ( Example_14.36 ). In addition, although less often, the conjunction signals a causal relation, as illustrated in ( Example_14.37 ). The conjunction has dual word class membership; it is also used as the bivalent verb jadi ‘become’ (see § Para_5.14 ).

Typically, jadi ‘so, since’ occurs in initial position of a result clause that follows the unmarked clause. Here, the conjunction signals that the event or state of its clause results from that of the unmarked clause, as in ( Example_14.36 ); hence, jadi translates with ‘so’.

styleExampleTitle
Combining clauses with jadi ‘so, since’: Clause-initial position
styleExampleTitle

tong tra snang dengang dia, jadi kitong malas datang dia pu ruma\\
1pl neg feel.happy(.about) with 3sg so 1pl be.listless come 3sg poss house\\
‘we don’t feel happy about her, so we don’t want (to) come to her house’ [080927-006-CvNP.0032]

Alternatively, but less often, the conjunction occurs in clause-final position of a cause clause where it marks a causal relation with the preceding unmarked clause, as in ( Example_14.37 ). In this position, the conjunction signals that something depicted in its clause is the cause for the event or state of the unmarked clause, and that the result depicted in the unmarked clause is anticipated. Hence, jadi translates with ‘since’. In that the result is expected, causal jadi ‘since’ differs from neutral causality-marking karna ‘because’ (see § Para_14.2.4.4 ).

styleExampleTitle
Combining clauses with jadi ‘so, since’: Clause-final position
styleExampleTitle

Musa ini, e, de loyo loyo ini, de bangung tidor jadi\\
Musa d.prox uh 3sg rdp be.weak this 3sg wake.up sleep so\\
[About a small boy:] ‘Musa here, uh, right now he’s kind of weak since he woke up from sleeping’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1435/1437]
summary: The conjunction jadi can mark either a resultative relation, most commonly, or a causal relation, less often. In clause-initial position it introduces a result clause meaning “so,” while in clause-final position it marks a cause clause meaning “since,” with the result in the unmarked clause being expected; this use differs from neutral causal karna ‘because’. It also has a second word-class use as the verb jadi ‘become’.

text:
Purposive supaya ‘so that’ introduces a purpose clause which follows the unmarked clause. The conjunction signals that the event or state of its clause is the intended outcome of the deliberate activity depicted in the unmarked clause. Most often, supaya ‘so that’ introduces a purpose clause with an overt subject (96/129 tokens – 74%), as in ( Example_14.38 ). Less often, the conjunction introduces a purpose clause with elided subject (33/129 tokens – 26%), as in ( Example_14.39 ).

mace ko sendiri yang ikut, supaya ko atur makangang di sana!\\
wife 2sg alone rel follow so.that 2sg arrange food at l.dist\\
‘you wife yourself (should) go with (them) so that you organize the catering over there!’ (Lit. ‘(it’s) you wife yourself who ’) [081025-009a-Cv.0032]

e, angkat muka, supaya Ø liat orang!\\
hey! lift front so.that see person\\
‘hey, lift (your) face so that (you) see (the other) people!’ [081110-008-CvNP.0101]
summary: Purposive **supaya** ‘so that’ introduces a purpose clause that follows an unmarked clause and expresses the intended outcome of the deliberate action in the first clause. It most often appears with an overt subject in the purpose clause (74% of tokens), but it can also occur with an elided subject (26%).

text:
As a conjunction, the benefactive preposition untuk ‘for’ signals a purpose relation between two clauses (for a description of preposition untuk ‘for’, see § Para_10.2.3 ). Purposive untuk ‘for’, like supaya ‘so that’ (see § Para_14.2.4.2 ), introduces a purpose clause which expresses the intended outcome of the purposeful activity depicted in the preceding unmarked clause, as shown in ( Example_14.40 ) and ( Example_14.41 ). Usually, untuk ‘for’ introduces a purpose clause with an elided subject (115/163 tokens – 71%), as shown with the second untuk ‘for’ token in ( Example_14.40 ). Much less often the conjunction introduces a purpose clause with an overt subject (48/163tokens – 29%), as shown with the first untuk ‘for’ token in ( Example_14.40 ), or as in ( Example_14.41 ).

tadi ana bilang, bapa dorang siap saja, untuk kita ke sana a, sa juga siap, untuk Ø bawa kamu ke sini\\
earlier child say father 3pl get.ready just for 1pl to l.dist ah! 1sg also get.ready for bring 2pl to l.prox\\
‘a short while ago you (‘child’) said, `` father and the others are ready for us (to move) to ( Sarmi over) there'', ah, (in that case) I’m also ready to bring you (to Sarmi) here’ (Lit. ‘ for (me to) bring you’) [080922-001a-CvPh.1241]

tida bole, ini, kamu datang, untuk kamu skola\\
neg may d.prox 2pl come for 2pl go.to.school\\
‘[you shouldn’t hate each other, (you) shouldn’t infuriate each other,] (you) shouldn’t (do all this), what’s-its-name, you came (here) to go to school’ (Lit. ‘ for you (to) go to school’) [081115-001a-Cv.0272]

The attested data indicates that untuk ‘for’ differs from supaya ‘so that’ in that untuk ‘for’ most often introduces purpose clauses with elided subjects. By contrast, supaya ‘so that’ most often introduces purpose clauses with overt subjects.
summary: The benefactive preposition/conjunction untuk ‘for’ can mark a purpose relation between clauses by introducing a purpose clause that states the intended outcome of the preceding action. In the attested data, it most often appears with an elided subject in the purpose clause, though it can also occur with an overt subject. This differs from supaya ‘so that’, which more often introduces purpose clauses with overt subjects.

text:
Causal karna ‘because’ signals a neutral causal relation between two clauses by introducing a cause clause which gives the reason for the event or state depicted in the unmarked clause. Usually the cause clause follows the unmarked clause, as in ( Example_14.42 ). In combination with adversative tapi ‘but’ (see § Para_14.2.5.1 ), however, it can precede the unmarked clause, as in ( Example_14.43 ). In this case the unmarked clause is often introduced with resultative jadi ‘so’. Signaling neutral causality, karna ‘because’ is distinct from causal jadi ‘since’ which marks expected results (see § Para_14.2.4.1 ), and from causal gara-gara ‘because’ which marks emotive causal relations (see § Para_14.2.4.5 ).

saya bisa pulang, karna sa su dapat babi\\
1sg be.able go.home because 1sg already get pig\\
[Hunting a wild pig:] ‘I can return home because I already got the pig’ [080919-004-NP.0024]

dong memang piara de di situ, tapi karna mama dong pu bapa-ade, tapi karna tete meninggal, jadi dong pu kluarga ini yang piara\\
3pl indeed raise 3sg at l.med but because mother 3pl poss uncle but because grandfather die so 3pl poss family d.prox rel raise\\
‘they took indeed care of him there, but because the uncle of mama and her companions [umh, who’s actually the youngest offspring,] but because grandfather died, so (it’s) their family here who took care of him’ [080919-006-CvNP.0006-0008]
summary: Causal **karna** ‘because’ marks a neutral causal relation by introducing a clause that gives the reason for the event or state in the unmarked clause, and it usually follows that clause. When combined with adversative **tapi** ‘but’, it can precede the unmarked clause, which is then often introduced by resultative **jadi** ‘so’. It differs from causal **jadi** ‘since’, which signals expected results, and **gara-gara** ‘because’, which expresses emotive causality.

text:
The causal conjunction gara-gara ‘because’ indicates an emotive causal relation between two clauses by introducing a cause clause which gives the reason for the circumstances depicted in the unmarked clause. Thereby, gara-gara ‘because’ is distinct from karna ‘because’ which marks neutral causal relations. The conjunction has dual word class membership; it is also used as the bivalent verb gara ‘irritate’ (see § Para_5.14 ).

Most often, the cause clause marked with gara-gara ‘because’ follows the unmarked clause, as in ( Example_14.44 ). Alternatively, the cause clause can precede the unmarked clause. In this case, adversative tapi ‘but’ (see § Para_14.2.5.1 ) precedes gara-gara ‘because’, as in ( Example_14.45 ), in the same way as tapi ‘but’ precedes karna ‘because’ (see § Para_14.2.4.4 ).

sap prut sakit, gara-gara sa makang nasi\\
1sg:poss stomach be.sick because 1sg eat cooked.rice\\
‘my stomach was sick because I ate rice’ [081025-009a-Cv.0046]

tapi gara-gara Nofela bi, gara-gara Nofela bicara deng bapa, bapa pu hati tergrak \\
but because Nofela tru-speak because Nofela speak with father father poss liver be.moved \\
[Phone conversation between a father and his daughter:] ‘[(if) I had just spoken to Siduas, maybe I wouldn’t have felt moved to come (and pick you up), right?,] but because you (‘Nofela’) spoke[ tru], because you (‘Nofela’) spoke with me, my (‘father’s) heart was moved [so I’ll definitely come (and pick you up)]’ [080922-001a-CvPh.1082-1083]
summary:
The causal conjunction *gara-gara* ‘because’ introduces an emotive causal relation, giving the reason for the situation in the unmarked clause, and it contrasts with *karna* ‘because’, which marks neutral causation. It also has dual word-class membership, since it can function as the bivalent verb *gara* ‘irritate’.

Typically, the *gara-gara* clause follows the main clause, but it can also precede it; when it does, *tapi* ‘but’ appears before *gara-gara*, just as with *karna*.

text: Contrast-marking conjunctions are cross-linguistically defined as conjunctions that signal that the events or states described in two clauses “are valid simultaneously”, but that the information given in one clause “marks a contrast to the information” given in the other clause. This section describes four Papuan Malay contrast-marking conjunctions: adversative tapi ‘but’ and habis ‘after all’ (§ Para_14.2.5.2 and § Para_14.2.5.1 ), oppositive padahal ‘but actually’ (§ Para_14.2.5.3 ), and concessive biar ‘although’ (§ Para_14.2.5.4 ). In addition, temporal baru ‘and then’ has contrast-marking function in that it signals counter-expectation in the sense of ``after all''; as this function is marginal it is discussed in § Para_14.2.3.2 and not here.
summary: Contrast-marking conjunctions link two clauses whose situations are both valid at the same time, while indicating that one clause contrasts with the other. In Papuan Malay, the main contrast-marking conjunctions are adversative *tapi* ‘but’ and *habis* ‘after all’, oppositive *padahal* ‘but actually’, and concessive *biar* ‘although’. The temporal conjunction *baru* ‘and then’ can also express a contrastive, counter-expectation meaning like ‘after all’, but this use is marginal.

text:
Adversative tapi ‘but’ occurs in interclausal position. It marks an adversative contrast relation between the clause it introduces and the preceding unmarked clause, as shown in ( Example_14.46 ) and ( Example_14.47 ).

de bisa maing gitar, tapi de malu\\
3sg be.able play guitar but 3sg feel.embarrassed(.about)\\
‘she can play the guitar but she feels shy (about it)’ [081014-015-Cv.0008]

jadi sa punya bapa kasi saya untuk Iskia, tapi Iskia kawing sala, Iskia kawing sa punya kaka\\
so 1sg poss father give 1sg for Iskia but Iskia marry be.wrong Iskia marry 1sg poss oSb\\
‘so my father gave me to Iskia, but Iskia married improperly, Iskia married my older sister’ [081006-028-CvEx.0005]
summary: Adversative *tapi* ‘but’ occurs between clauses and introduces an adversative contrast with the preceding unmarked clause. The examples show it linking a statement of ability or narrative development to a contrasting clause that expresses embarrassment or an unexpected, opposed outcome.

text:
Adversative habis ‘after all’ also marks an adversative relation between two clauses. The conjunction has dual word class membership; it is also used as the monovalent verb habis ‘be used up’ (see § Para_5.14 ).

Introducing a contrast clause that follows the unmarked clause, habis ‘after all’ summarizes what has been said before and signals that the propositional content of its clause is true in spite of the content of the preceding unmarked clause, as shown in ( Example_14.48 ) and ( Example_14.49 ). At the same time, the conjunction signals that the interlocutor is expected to know that this content is true. Thereby habis ‘after all’ is distinct from adversative tapi ‘but’ (see § Para_14.2.5.2 ). Adversative habis ‘after all’ is also distinct from counter-expectational baru ‘after all’ which merely summarizes what has been said before (see § Para_14.2.3.2 ). The exchange in ( Example_14.49 ) illustrates that there does not need to be an overt unmarked clause which precedes the contrast clause: speakers also use habis ‘after all’ to reply to an interlocutor’s statements.

bilang bapa, kirim tong uang, habis sa susa to?\\
say father send 1pl money after.all 1sg difficult right?\\
‘say (to) father, ``send us money, after all, I have difficulties, right?''' [080922-001a-CvPh.0866]

Speaker-1: ko baru masuk klas satu ini?\\
2sg recently enter class one d.prox \\
Speaker-1: ‘recently you got into first grade (of middle school)?’
10pt

Speaker-2: yo, habis sa gagal\\
yes after.all 1sg fail\\
Speaker-2: ‘yes, after all, I failed (the last exams)’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0965-0966]
summary:
Adversative **habis** ‘after all’ marks a contrastive relation between two clauses and, unlike the verb **habis** ‘be used up,’ it functions as a conjunction. It introduces a clause that presents its content as true despite the previous unmarked clause, while also implying that the interlocutor is expected to know this, making it distinct from adversative **tapi** ‘but’ and counter-expectational **baru** ‘after all.’  

The text also notes that **habis** can be used without an overt preceding clause, serving as a reply to another speaker’s statement.

text:
The conjunction padahal ‘but actually’ introduces a contrast clause, which follows the unmarked clause. Concurrent to marking contrast, the conjunction signals that the propositional content of its clause is surprising and unexpected given the content of the unmarked clause. Thereby, padahal ‘but actually’ is more oppositive than tapi ‘but’ (see § Para_14.2.5.1 ). This is illustrated in ( Example_14.50 ) and ( Example_14.51 ).

ana ini, sa pikir de suda lewat, padahal de tidor di atas kayu kayu\\
child d.prox 1sg think 3sg already pass.by but.actually 3sg sleep at top rdp wood\\
‘this child, I thought he’d already passed by, but actually he was sleeping on top of the wood’ [081013-004.Cv.0004]

bulang oktober sa pu alpa cuma dua saja, bayangkang, padahal sa alpa banyak\\
month October 1sg poss be.absent just two just image but.actually 1sg be.absent many\\
[About the speaker’s school attendance:] ‘imagine!, in October I had just only two (official) absences, but actually I was absent many times’ (Lit. ‘my absences were many’) [081023-004-Cv.0014]
summary: The conjunction **padahal** ‘but actually’ introduces a contrast clause that follows the unmarked clause. It not only marks contrast but also indicates that the clause content is surprising or unexpected in light of the preceding clause, making it more oppositive than **tapi** ‘but’.

text:
Concessive biar ‘although’ marks concessive relations between two clauses. The conjunction has dual word class membership; it is also used as the bivalent verb biar ‘let’ (see § Para_5.14 ).

Introducing a concession clause, biar ‘although’ signals that despite the event or state depicted in its clause, the event or state depicted in the unmarked clause occurred. Usually, the concession clause precedes the unmarked clause, whereby the concession is emphasized, as in ( Example_14.52 ). Alternatively, although less often, it can follow the unmarked clause, in which case the content of the latter clause is emphasized, as in ( Example_14.53 ).

yo, biar makangang tinggi, de ambil\\
yes although food be.high 3sg fetch\\
[About a greedy child:] ‘yes, although the food is (placed) high (up on a shelf), he takes (it)’ [081025-006-Cv.0254]

jangang tinggal di ruma, tida bole, biar dulu orang-tua dong bilang begini\\
neg.imp stay at house neg may although first parent 3pl say like.this\\
‘[so you kids have to go to school,] don’t stay home, (that’s) not allowed, although the parents said so in the past’ [081110-008-CvNP.0036]
summary: Biar ‘although’ marks concessive relations between two clauses and also has another use as the verb biar ‘let’. It indicates that despite the situation in the concessive clause, the event in the unmarked clause still occurs. The concession clause usually comes first to emphasize the concession, but it can also follow the main clause when the latter is emphasized.

text:
As conjunctions, the similative prepositions sperti ‘similar to’ and kaya ‘like’ mark similarity between two clauses. Introducing similarity clauses, both signal that the event or state depicted in the unmarked clause is similar to that described in the similarity clause. The similarity clause always follows the unmarked clause.

Derived from their prepositional semantics, sperti ‘similar to’ signals likeness in some, often implied, respect, while kaya ‘like’ marks overall resemblance, as shown in ( Example_14.54 ) and ( Example_14.55 ), respectively. (See § Para_10.3.1 and § Para_10.3.2 for a detailed discussion of the prepositions sperti ‘similar to’ and kaya ‘like’ and their semantics.)

mama dia lupa kamu, sperti kacang lupa kulit\\
mother 3sg forget 2pl similar.to bean forget skin\\
‘mother forgot you (in a way that is) similar to a bean forgetting its skin’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0932]

tong taputar kaya kitong ni ana ana perjalangang yang taputar\\
1pl be.turned.around like 1pl d.prox rdp child journey rel be.turned.around\\
‘[we were looking for a bathroom, good grief! there were no bathrooms,] we wandered around like we here were children on a trip wandering around’ [081025-009a-Cv.0059]
summary: As conjunctions, *sperti* ‘similar to’ and *kaya* ‘like’ introduce similarity clauses in which the event or state in the unmarked clause is compared with that in the similarity clause. The similarity clause always follows the unmarked clause. *Sperti* marks likeness in some often implied respect, while *kaya* marks overall resemblance.

text: This section describes two conjunctions which combine different-type constit\-uents. Complementizer bahwa ‘that’ links a clause to a bivalent verb (§ Para_14.3.1 ), while relativizer yang ‘ rel ’ integrates a relative clause within a noun phrase (§ Para_14.3.2 ).
summary: The section describes two conjunctions that combine different kinds of constituents. Complementizer **bahwa** ‘that’ links a clause to a bivalent verb, while relativizer **yang** ‘rel’ integrates a relative clause within a noun phrase.

text:
The complementizer bahwa ‘that’ marks a clause as the complement of a verb. Cross-linguistically, it is typically bivalent “verbs of utterance and cognition” that take complements. This also applies to Papuan Malay. The corpus contains 68 complement clauses with bahwa ‘that’. In 37 cases (54%), the complement-taking verb is taw ‘know’, followed by bilang ‘say’ (5 tokens), ceritra ‘tell’(4 tokens), and liat ‘see’ (3 tokens).

Two structural patterns are attested for complementation with bahwa ‘that’. Usually, the verb is followed by the clausal complement with bahwa ‘that’ (61 tokens), as in ( Example_14.56 ) and ( Example_14.57 ). Alternatively, although much less often, the verb is followed by an object which is followed by the clausal complement (8 tokens), as in ( Example_14.58 ). Typically, speakers report speech in the form of direct speech rather than in direct speech as in ( Example_14.58 ) (see also § Para_6.2.1.1 ).

summary: The complementizer bahwa ‘that’ marks a clause as the complement of a verb, and in Papuan Malay this most often occurs with verbs of cognition and utterance. In the corpus, 68 such complement clauses are found, most commonly with taw ‘know’, and the usual structure is verb + bahwa-clause, though a smaller number show verb + object + bahwa-clause.

text:
Relativizer yang ‘ rel ’ introduces relative clauses which function as modifiers within noun phrases (see also § Para_8.2.8 ). Typically, the relative clause follows its head nominal, as in ( Example_14.59 ) and ( Example_14.61a ). However, yang ‘ rel ’ can also introduce a headless relative clause. Cross-linguistically, headless relative clauses can be used “when the head noun is non-specific” or when “the specific reference to the head is clear”. This also applies to Papuan Malay. In ( Example_14.60 ), for instance, the head nominal is non-specific, while in ( Example_14.61b ) the reference to the head is clear (“Ø” signifies the implied head nominal).

The remainder of this section describes the grammatical positions which can be relativized in Papuan Malay. The data in the corpus shows that, in terms of Keenan.1977 ``Accessibility Hierarchy'', Papuan Malay allows relativization on all five positions, namely:

center
subject direct object indirect object oblique possessor
center

Cross-linguistically, as points out, relativization of these positions involves two different “case recoverability strategies” which allow to identify “the role of the referent of the head noun within the relative clause”, namely the “gap strategy” or “ pronoun retention”. Both strategies are also found in Papuan Malay. Relativization of subject, direct and oblique object arguments is achieved with the gap strategy, while relativization of obliques and possessors involves pronoun retention.

When core arguments are relativized, a gap is left. This gap, signified with ``Ø'', occurs where the relativized noun phrase would be situated if it were expressed overtly. Relativization of the subject argument is illustrated in ( Example_14.62 ), and of the direct object argument of a bivalent verb, namely biking ‘make’, in ( Example_14.63 ). The examples in ( Example_14.64 ) and ( Example_14.65 ) illustrate the relativization of the direct object positions in double-object constructions; in both examples the trivalent verb is kasi ‘give’. In ( Example_14.64 ), the R argument papeda ‘sagu porridge’ is relativized. In ( Example_14.65 ), the T argument Efana ini ‘this Efana’ is relativized. (Verbal clauses with bivalent and trivalent verbs are discussed in detail in § Para_11.1.2 and § Para_11.1.3, respectively.)

tong bagi buat kitorang yang Ø potong itu, buat sodara sodara yang Ø tinggal di kampung\\

[About hunting a wild pig:] we divided (the meat) for us who cut (it) up that day, (and) then for the relatives and friends who live in the village’ [080919-003-NP.0014]

‘I fed the dogs with the sagu porridge which my wife had prepared for the dogs in the evening’ [080919-003-NP.0002]

Fitri yang de bapa kasi Ø ijing mo ikut ke kampung\\

‘(it was) Fitri whom her husband gave permission to go with (us) to the village’ (Lit. ‘her (daughter’s) father ’) [080925-003-Cv.0211]

Efana ini yang dia i kas dia j Ø\\
Efana d.prox rel 3sg give 3sg \\
[About an ancestor’s first wife:] ‘(it was) this Efana that he i (‘Aris’) gave (to) him j (‘Oten’)’ [080922-010a-CvNF.0062] The subscript letters indicate which personal pronouns have which referents.

Obliques and possessors are relativized via pronoun retention. That is, a retained personal pronoun explicitly marks the relativized position within the relative clause. This is illustrated with the relativization of an oblique argument in ( Example_14.66 ), and of a possessor in ( Example_14.67 ). (For a discussion of interrogative mana ‘where, which’ and its adnominal uses, see § Para_5.8.3; for details on adnominal possessive constructions, see Para_9.)

kalo ana mana yang sa duduk ceritra deng dia, itu ana itu, de hormat torang\\
if child where rel 1sg sit tell with 3sg d.dist child d.dist 3sg respect 1pl\\
‘as for which kid with whom I sit and talk, that is that kid, she respects us’ [081115-001a-Cv.0282]

itu kaka satu itu yang dia punya ade prempuang itu tinggal deng Natanael tu\\
d.dist oSb one d.dist rel 3sg poss ySb woman d.dist stay with Natanael d.dist\\
‘that is that one older brother whose younger sister is staying with Natanael’ [080922-001a-CvPh.0888]
summary:
The passage explains that Papuan Malay uses the relativizer yang to introduce relative clauses that modify noun phrases, and it can also introduce headless relative clauses when the head noun is non-specific or its reference is clear. It further states that Papuan Malay allows relativization of all five positions on the Accessibility Hierarchy: subject, direct object, indirect object, oblique, and possessor.

For core arguments, relativization uses a gap strategy, with an empty position marked by Ø in the relative clause. For obliques and possessors, Papuan Malay uses pronoun retention, where a retained personal pronoun marks the relativized position explicitly.

text:
Juxtaposition is another strategy in Papuan Malay to link constituents, namely same-type constituents, such as noun phrases, prepositional phrases, verbs, or clauses.

Juxtaposition of noun phrases, as in ( Example_14.68 ) to ( Example_14.73 ), occurs considerably less often in the corpus than conjoining with a conjunction. Most often, three, four or five noun phrases are juxtaposed to enumerate entities, while juxtaposition of just two noun phrases occurs less often. These findings reflect the results of Stassen.2000 typological study of noun phrase conjunction which shows that juxtaposition is “a minor strategy” which is often used “in list-like enumerations”. According to, “the general trend all over the world is that zero-coordination tends to be marginalized into specific functions or is replaced altogether by overt marking strategies”. suggests that this development is due to the global increase in bilingualism and in literacy. With respect to bilingualism, observes that “an astonishing number of coordinating conjunctions have been recently borrowed into languages that previously had none”. As for the role of literacy, notes that, whereas in oral language intonation suffices to signal the syntactic structure of juxtaposed constituents, written language requires the overt and “systematic specification of the precise nature of link” to disambiguate syntactic relations.

Papuan Malay combines different prosodic features to indicate the structure of the juxtaposed noun phrases: final vowel lengthening (orthographically represented by a sequence of three vowels), slight increase in pitch of the stressed syllable (“ \' ”), intonation breaks (“ ”), non-final intonation pattern with level pitch (“ -- ”), and end-of-list intonation with fall pitch (“ ”). The enumeration structure in ( Example_14.68 ) is indicated with an increase in pitch, and the last item is marked off by the demonstrative itu ‘ d.dist ’. In ( Example_14.69 ), the enumeration is signaled with an increase in pitch as well as intonation breaks; the last item has an end-of-list intonation. In ( Example_14.70 ), the structure is marked with a slight increase in pitch and final vowel lengthening of the first and third coordinands while the fourth item has an end-of-list intonation. The second and third coordinands form a compact intonation unit, separated from the first and fourth coordinands by intonation breaks. After another intonation break following the fourth coordinand, the fifth coordinand is added as an afterthought.

Juxtaposed noun phrases are less common than conjoined noun phrases and are mainly used for list-like enumerations, with prosodic cues such as pitch increase, vowel lengthening, intonation breaks, and end-of-list intonation helping mark the structure.

text:
Papuan Malay conjunctions typically conjoin same-type constituents. Most of them combine clauses with clauses. Only two link different-type constituents, such as verbs with clauses. Typically, the conjunctions occur at the left periphery of the constituent they mark.

The 21 conjunctions linking same-type constituents are divided into six groups according to the semantic relations they signal:

enumerate
Addition: dengang ‘with’, dang ‘and’, sama ‘to’.
Alternative: ato ‘or’ and ka ‘or’.
Time and/or condition: trus ‘next’, baru ‘and then’, sampe ‘until’, seblum ‘before’, and kalo ‘when, if’.
Consequence: jadi ‘so, since’, supaya ‘so that’, untuk ‘for’, karna ‘because’, and gara-gara ‘because’; time-marking sampe also has result-mark\-ing function in the sense of ``with the result that''.
Contrast: tapi ‘but’, habis ‘after all’, padahal ‘but actually’, and biar ‘although’; time-marking baru also marks contrast in the sense of ``after all''.
Similarity: sperti ‘similar to’ and kaya ‘like’.
enumerate

A substantial number of the conjunctions have dual word class membership, two have trial class membership. More specifically, seven conjunctions are also used as verbs, namely baru ‘and then, after all’, biar ‘although’, habis ‘after all’, jadi ‘so, since’, sama ‘to’, sampe ‘until’, and trus ‘next’ (see § Para_5.3 ). Six conjunctions are also used as prepositions, namely dengang ‘with’, kaya ‘like’, sama ‘to’, sampe ‘until’, sperti ‘similar to’, and untuk ‘for’ (see § Para_5.11 and Para_10). One conjunction is also used as an ad verb, namely baru ‘and.then’. Besides, alternative-marking ka ‘or’ is also used to mark interrogative clauses (see § Para_13.2.3 ). Variation in word class membership is discussed in § Para_5.14.

The main features of the conjunctions are summarized in two tables. Table_14.1 lists the conjunctions and the different types of constituents they link. For those linking more than one constituent type, the primary type is underlined. Empty cells signal unattested constituent combinations.

Table_14.2 gives an overview of the positions which the conjunctions take within the clause, and the position the clause marked with a conjunction takes vis-à-vis the unmarked clause. Almost all conjunctions occur in clause-initial position, while only two occur in clause-final position. Typically, the clause marked with a conjunction follows the unmarked clause; only a few conjunctions mark clauses which precede the unmarked clause. Two of the conjunctions have two functions each, which belong to different semantic groupings, namely baru ‘and then, after all’ and sampe ‘until, with the result that’. Both conjunctions are listed in each of the respective groupings.

The conjunctions combining different-type constituents discussed in this chapter are the complementizer bahwa ‘that’ and the relativizer yang ‘ rel ’. Complementizer bahwa ‘that’ links a clause to a bivalent verb, while relativizer yang ‘ rel ’ integrates a relative clause within a noun phrase.
summary: Papuan Malay conjunctions usually link constituents of the same type, most often clauses, and they typically occur at the left edge of the constituent they mark; only two conjunctions link different types of constituents. The same-type conjunctions are grouped by meaning into addition, alternative, time/condition, consequence, contrast, and similarity, and many of them also belong to other word classes such as verbs, prepositions, or adverbs. The two different-type conjunctions are the complementizer bahwa ‘that,’ which links a clause to a bivalent verb, and the relativizer yang, which introduces relative clauses inside noun phrases.
